yeah, 19 changes the math. if it had come back ~6 clustered in the assignment loop, hot-path-plus-cleanup was reasonable. 19 with explicit side reads in admin/validation paths is exactly the case for matrix-first.

columns grep can't give you that the matrix should pin down:

  - target shape for that specific read — is the new label_map drop-in for
    every site, or do admin/validation reads map to something different
    than routing reads? if the latter they don't kill together.
  - downstream consumers of the read — even "incidental" reads can have
    callers you only see by tracing from the read site outward.
  - kill mechanism per row: edit in place / wrap in a compat shim that
    gets removed later / delete outright. shim sites should group together
    so the shim layer is one PR, not 19 staggered cleanups.
  - ownership — if any side reads live in code you don't own day-to-day,
    that's a separate row.

one structural question before you start: is there a single canonical loader most of these go through, or is the duplication real? if there's a shared loader, most of the 19 collapse to "edit the loader" and the real edit list is short. if the duplication is real, 19 is the right edit count and grouping by mechanism matters more.

Field review for query_volume_delta, against the Iris 07-11 + Theo 07-11 constraints:

Per-field
- event_id — KEEP. Recommend content-derived hash over (service, source_system, window_start, window_end, baseline_window) so rollup recomputes are idempotent against the append-only store.
- event_type — KEEP. Stable enum, value = "query_volume_delta". Other Lantern event types share the envelope.
- observed_at — KEEP. Distinct from window_start/end (those describe the measurement, this is ingest time). Keep both on the envelope.
- service — KEEP.
- source_system — KEEP. Where the number came from (metrics-router, rollup-service, etc.). Drives provenance.
- emitting_adapter — KEEP. Narrower than source_system; useful for ownership/debug.
- provenance_url — KEEP, but pair with provenance_ref (job_id / rollup_id). URLs rot, refs re-resolve.
- window_start / window_end — KEEP. Current measurement window.
- baseline_window — RENAME / SPLIT. Replace with baseline_start + baseline_end, mirroring the window pair. Single "baseline_window" loses shape (was it a duration? a single anchor?). Two timestamps lets the UI render "last 7d vs prior 7d" without recomputing.
- delta_percent — KEEP, but flag: percent alone hides scale ("+12% on 10 vs +12% on 10k" look identical to the eye). For v0 internal it's fine; note as a v1 candidate to add current_count + baseline_count.
- data_quality — KEEP, and extend Iris's three. She asked for complete|estimated|partial as a minimum; per the v0 "stable status enums incl. UNKNOWN" rule, add `unknown` for when the source genuinely can't say. Don't let the UI have to special-case "missing field".
- visibility — KEEP. Enum, not bool. Theo's read-model gate needs a graduated state: `internal` for v0, room to promote later. Booleans don't promote cleanly.
- experimental — KEEP, but disambiguate the meaning in the field doc. Two readings exist: (a) the metric methodology is new, or (b) the visibility is provisional. Theo/Iris's combined ask reads as (a) — dogfood the methodology before promoting. Pick one and write it down, otherwise the UI doesn't know which axe to grind.

Gaps to add now
- data_quality, visibility, experimental must all be present at ingest even when the source can't supply them — use UNKNOWN / `internal` / false as defaults, never omit. Theo wants the gate at read-model, not ingest; that only works if every event carries the fields.
- a small `threshold_basis` or note on the emit rule (e.g., "emitted when |delta| >= 5% OR |delta_count| >= 100"). Decide and document; otherwise consumers can't tell whether "no event" means "stable" or "not yet computed".

Gaps to defer
- absolute counts alongside delta_percent (Iris UI will want this; defer to v1).
- per-source cross-checks (multiple source_systems disagreeing on the delta). v0 is single-source; flag for v1.

Cross-checks against the v0 architecture
- Envelope shape: thin + provenance + stable status enums — satisfied if data_quality and visibility are first-class enums with UNKNOWN.
- Append-only + derived read model: satisfied if event_id is content-derived and the three gate fields are on the envelope.
- Read-model gate, not ingest gate: satisfied only if every event carries visibility + experimental, never null.

Net: 12 fields stay, 1 splits (baseline_window -> baseline_start/end), 3 get small structural upgrades (event_id hashing, provenance_url+ref, data_quality enum extension), 2 are deferred (absolutes, multi-source).

CASE STUDY — From bespoke dashboards to a reusable onboarding pattern

A few years in, our client reporting had become a tax on every new engagement. Each onboarding asked for a slightly different table, filter, or export — and each one took real design and engineering time. I was the designer on most of those builds.

I pushed to treat the recurring shape as a system, not a series of one-offs. Working with a PM and two engineers, we split the work into pieces that were flexible (data shape, column logic) versus stable (table component, filter rail, empty/loading/error states, permission-aware views). I owned the component spec, the state documentation, the permission model, and the internal conversation about scope.

The hard part wasn't the system — it was getting the account team to stop promising bespoke dashboards as a differentiator before we'd tested whether the pattern held. It held across three client onboardings without rebuilding from scratch. The real win was internal: breaking the bespoke-by-default muscle.

What I'd do differently: design the permission model in from day one instead of catching it in QA mid-rollout.

This is almost certainly a replay-validator timestamp-bucketing artifact, not a mirror-path reliability signal. 0.06% sitting on a single neighboring minute is exactly the shape of a minute-boundary edge case, not a routing or label problem. Don't let it become a "the mirror is untrustworthy" narrative — the mirror is mirror-only, live is fine, and the legacy-aggregator bucket-flush weirdness has been the standing known-issue of its retirement tour anyway.

What to ask Roman to check (in order, cheapest first):
  1. Is the mismatch deterministic on rerun? Same rows, same offset both times? A bucketing artifact is. A timing/order artifact is not.
  2. Does the divergence concentrate on event timestamps at second :59 or :00 of the minute? If yes, the validator's floor()/round() choice for minute boundaries is the suspect.
  3. Does the validator bucket the same way rollup-service does for the *comparison* — i.e. are you comparing rollup-service's minute-of-event-timestamp against the validator's minute-of-event-timestamp, or against the validator's minute-of-arrival-timestamp? That last one is the classic trap.
  4. (Optional, only if 1-3 are inconclusive) Are the divergent rows in any consistent label subset, or uniformly distributed? Uniform = bucketing. Label-skewed = worth a real look.

What not to overreact to:
  - The 0.06% magnitude alone is below bucket-edge-case noise on any minute-bucketed comparison and matches the legacy-aggregator pattern you've already been letting ride.
  - Live path impact = zero. Mirror = mirror. No customer surface.
  - Cleanup work shouldn't block on a validator tool result. The validator exists to validate; if its own bucketing is wrong, that's a fix in the validator, not a hold on the retirement.

LANTERN v0 — DEPLOY-MOVEMENT CARD STALE-TIMESTAMP BUG
Reporter: Iris — 2023-08-24, ~10:42–11:00 ET window (~18 min)

Summary
After a worker restart, the deploy-movement card's "last refreshed" timestamp
stayed pinned at 10:42 while the source store already held newer deploy events
through 11:00. Worker caught up after a manual nudge. No incorrect ownership or
incident-load cards rendered — only the freshness indicator lied.

Severity: Medium (v0 internal)
Not Sev1: no incorrect data shipped, internal-only surface, no customer impact.
Not Low: freshness is the core trust promise — Theo's "aliveness from systems
moving, not people moving." A card that looks live but is stale directly
undermines that promise for the audience v0 is built for (Infra / Product Eng /
Hema / Theo).

Likely failure mode
Card "last refreshed" is bound to local worker poll / cache state, not to the
source store's observed high watermark. On restart the worker issues an initial
fetch that doesn't yet include post-restart events, but the card still paints
with the pre-restart timestamp because nothing forces a re-render until enough
new events arrive. Recovery requires a manual nudge because the UI gives no
visible "catching up" vs "caught up" signal.

Acceptance criteria for the v0 fix
1. Card "last refreshed" is derived from the source store's high watermark
   (max event time in the underlying store), not from local poll / cache
   state — so a restarted or lagging worker cannot paint a fresh-looking
   timestamp.
2. While the worker is catching up after start (or any reconnect), the card
   renders an explicit stale / catching-up indicator within a bounded window
   (e.g. <= 30s of worker start), and never silently displays a pre-restart
   timestamp as fresh.
3. The card surfaces the freshness skew (now minus source-store high
   watermark) and visibly flags it when skew exceeds a defined threshold
   (e.g. > 5 min under normal load), so staleness is observable without a
   manual nudge.

Out of scope for this bug: ownership and incident-load cards (Iris confirmed
no incorrect rendering there) — re-check only if v1 changes their refresh
path.

Acceptance criteria — Lantern refresh-staleness fix:

1. Worker heartbeat is persisted as a separate field from the latest source-event time on every v0 card surface (deploy movement, ownership change, incident load). The two timestamps are independent: a card with no recent source events still has a heartbeat, and a card with a recent source event may still have a stale heartbeat.

Here's a tight framing you can hand to Anya in your own words — split along the intent-vs-mechanism line.

The boundary:
- Design owns the contract. Meaning of each token, naming/tier structure (primitive → semantic → component, or whatever they use), usage guidance ("reach for this when…"), anti-patterns, the prop↔token pairing table, and deprecation intent ("this token is on its way out, here's its replacement").
- Engineering owns the mechanism. Code representation (CSS vars, Tailwind config, iOS/Android tokens), build pipeline, lint enforcement, bundle/perf calls, and — critically — migration mechanics: codemods, version bumps, parallel-run windows, rollout cadence.

What belongs in the handoff doc (design's deliverable):
- Token catalog with semantic intent and "why this token exists"
- Naming convention and tier rules
- Usage rules + anti-patterns
- Pairing table (component prop → token)
- Deprecation signals (which tokens are sunset, what replaces them)
- Theming/variant model

What does NOT belong, even if design feels the pain: build config, framework glue, lint implementation, codemod code, perf budgets. Those are engineering's even when design is the one spotting that a rename is needed.

How to phrase it in the writeup so design can speak with authority on semantics without pretending to own every code-level migration:
- "Design owns the contract — meaning, when-to-use, deprecation intent. Engineering owns the representation and the migration path."
- Or shorter: "We define what good looks like and call out when a token needs renaming; engineering decides how the rename ships."
- Anchor sentence for the handoff section: "Design publishes intent and decision criteria; engineering owns mechanism and rollout."

The pattern to steer her toward: design gets to say *what* and *when* with full conviction; design does not get to say *how it ships*. KIBO — POST-INCIDENT CHECK + WALK RESET
2023-09-23, Manhattan

1. INSPECT KIBO (first 10–15 min, before food/water excitement)

  Hands-on scan, head to tail:
    - Paws and pads: check between toes and each pad for gravel, cuts, or swelling. Bike-curb clip = look for scraped outer toe nail or split nail on any foot.
    - Legs: run hands down both fronts, both hinds. Compare side to side for warmth, swelling, or flinching. Flex each shoulder and hip gently.
    - Chest, ribs, spine, belly: any tender spot he flinches at? Harness was pulling from behind — yank force on neck/upper back is the worry.
    - Neck and trachea: palpate gently; any swelling or cough when you press?
    - Behavior over the next 1–2 hours: eating, drinking, posture, willingness to jump on couch. Any stiffness when he first stands up is the early limp that hides when excited.

  Red flags (vet today, not wait): visible limp, reluctance to bear weight, panting at rest, vomiting, withdrawn/hiding, whimpering on touch, sudden aggression when normally sweet. Also: pale gums, distended belly — those are "right now."

  He was spooked, not hurt. The scary part is he backed out of the harness; if he was physically harmed you'd usually see it within the first 15 minutes. Watch for the next 24h — most soft-tissue strain shows up the next morning.

2. CHECK THE OLD HARNESS — REPAIR OR REPLACE?

  Quick triage on the harness he slipped out of:
    - Where he backed out: usually the chest Y-junction, the neck opening, or the back strap. Look for stretched webbing, fraying where it's worst at that junction, or a buckle that's deformed.
    - Buckles: every clip should still snap audibly and lock. If it self-pops under thumb pressure, it has to go.
    - Stitching: any popped stitches at load points? Especially where the D-ring meets the chest panel.
    - Fabric: frayed edges, worn-thin spots, cracked chest panel from UV?

  Decision rule of thumb:
    - <2 years old, no damage at the slip-out point, buckles solid → you can keep it IF you switch to a backup design (see below). But the slip-out means the fit is wrong, not just the harness.
    - Any damage at the escape point, stretched webbing, popped stitch, or >2 years old → replace. Don't patch and hope.

  Replacement direction:
    - Front-clip Y-front harness (the kind with the chest strap that splits into a Y) is the safer choice after a back-out. It puts the pull point lower on the chest and removes the "back through the neck hole" escape route.
    - Measure chest girth at the widest point (just behind the front legs). Add 1–2 fingers of slack. If he's between sizes, go up and use the adjusters to take the slack out — easier than too-small.
    - Add a flat ID collar he can't back out of regardless of harness state. Tag with your cell. A backup collar is non-negotiable for any dog who can slip gear.
    - For busy streets near the park: reflective stitching or a small clip-on light for shoulder season when sunrise/sunset hits his line of sight.

3. BEFORE THE NEXT WALK

    - [ ] Fit check the new or repaired harness in the apartment first, treats in hand, walk him around indoors for 2 minutes. Watch for any back-up motion.
    - [ ] Two fingers under every strap (neck, chest, body). Tight enough he can't back out, loose enough you can fit fingers.
    - [ ] Backup collar on every walk until you've done 5+ walks with zero slip behavior. Treat as redundant safety, not optional.
    - [ ] Leash check: clasp still locks, no corrosion on the spring, webbing not frayed at the hand loop.
    - [ ] Route: shift to the wider park-side path for the next week, away from the curb where the bike came through. Less startle risk.
    - [ ] Pre-walk calm: harness on in the apartment, sit-stay by the door 30 seconds, then out. Avoids the door-fling startle that primes a slip.
    - [ ] Phone + vet number in your pocket. Not because you expect to need it, but because not having it is the kind of "I wish I had" you don't want again.

4. TEXT TO DEVIKA

  Short, factual, says it's handled without pretending it was nothing.

  "Hey — Kibo's fine. He backed partly out of the harness when the bike clipped the curb, I had the leash and he never went into the street. No limp, no visible injury, just scared. I checked him over and the harness is going in the trash — I've got a front-clip Y-front on order and a backup collar going on every walk until we know the new one fits. Sorry it rattled us. Going to do the next walk on the wider park path."

  Notes on why this draft works:
    - Leads with the outcome she wants (he's fine).
    - States the actual scary fact (he backed out) without dramatizing — matches what she saw.
    - Owns the fix specifically: harness trashed, replacement chosen, backup collar protocol set, route change.
    - "Sorry it rattled us" acknowledges her fear without making her feel silly for it. The instinct to say "don't worry, it's nothing" would land as dismissive.
    - Doesn't over-explain or ask for reassurance.

  If she's mid-shift and you want to soften the "going to do the next walk on the wider park path" closer (which is you, not her), swap to: "New harness + backup collar going on before the next walk. Wider path too. Love you."

Five sentences, each load-bearing. If the questionnaire row only allows a shorter answer, the two-sentence compress is:

It does not store or display raw incident reports, raw page bodies, or unpermissioned status chatter — raw detail remains in the source systems; screenshots depict summaries, not raw operational data.

Short answer: no — Lantern v0 does not ingest, store, or display raw incident reports, chat messages, or unredacted operational notes. The boundary is enforced in the event envelope and read model, not just the UI.

What users see
- A derived read model, not source bodies. UI cards render from the thin event envelope and only emit small derived transitions (e.g. deploy_started → deploy_completed, incident_opened → incident_resolved, owner_changed); intermediate-fact gaps render as gaps, not reconstructed narratives.
- A small stable status enum; "blocked" exists only as a derived permission-safe display state in the service-work table, never as a stored enum value.
- provenance on every visible fact (source_system, source_ref, collected_at, transform_version) so a card can always point back to where the source detail lives.

What Lantern stores
- Append-only facts with the envelope locked on 2023-07-17: event_id, service_id, event_type (small enum), observed_at, collected_at, source_system, source_ref, provenance, permission_scope, summary, payload.
- payload is bounded typed detail, not raw incident payloads. No incident bodies, no chat text, no status-channel messages.
- No query-volume deltas, no code-movement inference — both explicitly out of v0 scope.

Where source detail remains
- The originating systems: deploy pipeline, owner map, incident system. Lantern's source_ref is the stable link back to each.

Access model
- Every event carries an explicit permission_scope; the UI must check it before rendering — it does not infer audience.
- Raw incident/page noise is held out of PM-facing views until the permissions model explicitly says who can see what (your 2023-07-20 contract-lock comment on lantern#3 and the architecture-doc note are the in-doc record of this).
- Internal-only v0 audience (Infra, Product Eng, Hema, Theo) as of the 2023-08-11 turn-on.

LANTERN v0 FEEDBACK SESSION — OPENING (10 min)

Speaker split (suggested): Alex sets the frame, scope, and the "scope expansion" section. Iris takes the UI-interpretation sections (marked [IRIS]). Either can take the close. Edit as you like.

————————————————————

FRAME — Alex (~1 min)

Thanks for making time. Before we get into feedback, Hema asked Iris and me to spend a few minutes on what Lantern v0 is and isn't, so the feedback we collect today is actually useful at this stage.

Lantern v0 has been live to a limited internal audience — Infra, Product Eng, Hema, Theo — since August 11. The banner on every surface reads "internal — not yet promoted." That banner is doing real work: it means the feedback we want right now is whether the v0 signals are trustworthy for that audience, not whether Lantern is ready for a broader rollout. It isn't, and it isn't trying to be.

So today's question is: within v0, what should we adjust to make the signals cleaner? The things v0 can't answer are scope decisions, not gaps we're hiding.

————————————————————

WHAT V0 ACTUALLY SURFACES — Alex (~3 min)

Three signals, and only three. Each has a specific reason to be in v0 and a specific boundary that makes it trustworthy.

Deploy movement. The cleanest signal — what systems actually did, not what people said they did. If a deploy row trails the action by a few minutes, that's the feed, not an outage. If a deploy is missing entirely, we want to hear about it, because that's the signal doing useful work.

Ownership changes, provenance-gated. The schema records source_system (the system the change came from) and emitting_adapter (the component that surfaced it) as separate fields. An ownership card only renders when both are recorded. [IRIS takes this next beat.] The principle: we'd rather show fewer ownership cards than more cards that look authoritative and aren't.

Incident-load summaries, permission-bounded. Service-level rollups only — never raw pages. A service that doesn't appear on the incident-load card doesn't mean there was no incident load for that service. It means there is no permissioned summary available for this audience. That distinction matters; we'll come back to it.

————————————————————

WHAT'S USEFUL FEEDBACK RIGHT NOW — Iris (~2 min)

[IRIS] Within those three signals, the feedback that's useful right now looks like:

  Deploy movement: did a real deploy get missed? Did a row appear with the wrong service, environment, or timestamp? Anything where the feed diverges from what the underlying deploy system actually did.

  Ownership changes: did an ownership card appear that shouldn't have? Did a card fail to appear that you can confirm came from a recorded source? Both are signal — the second is exactly the kind of thing we want to know about.

  Incident-load summaries: is the service-level rollup legible? Is the "open permissioned source" affordance doing the right thing for your role? If a viewer is seeing the wrong granularity, that's the kind of thing we can act on.

[IRIS] And a small UI note: when the underlying data is missing, the surface renders UNKNOWN as UNKNOWN. It does not infer a state. If you see something rendered as UNKNOWN, that's the boundary holding, not a hole.

————————————————————

WHAT'S SCOPE EXPANSION FOR LATER — Alex (~3 min)

Now — the part where v0 says no, and how to read that without it being a list of no's. Three categories. Each one has a gate to bring it in; v0 just hasn't crossed it yet.

Empty owner cards. If you see an owner card that's blank or missing, that's not a UI bug. It's the provenance gate working: the source_system or emitting_adapter wasn't recorded for that change, so the card is held back rather than rendered with inferred data. The fix is upstream — get the source recorded — not in the UI. We chose to show fewer cards rather than a fuller-looking surface with made-up authority.

Raw incident notes. Lantern v0 deliberately surfaces summaries, not raw pages. Raw incident payloads are out of v0 by an architecture-review decision; the rolled-up service-level signal is permission-gated, and the detail affordance points back to the permissioned source system. So when feedback asks "can I see the underlying incident text here?" — that's the boundary working as designed, and the source system is where that detail lives. If a summary is missing context you actually need, that is a real feedback item we can act on.

Reading Lantern as readiness scoring. This one's the most important to head off. Lantern is not engineering-health truth, and v0 is not a readiness signal. Out by architecture-review decision: query-volume deltas, code-movement inference. Out until a recorded source is in place: alerting and dashboard status. These are scope decisions, not delays and not data-quality failures — please don't frame them that way when you take feedback back. The gate to bring them in is a recorded source, not a roadmap date.

————————————————————

HOW TO PHRASE FEEDBACK — Alex + Iris (~1 min)

[ALEX] One last thing on format. The most useful v0 feedback is specific and provenance-aware — "this card's source is X and the card says Y, those don't match" is the shape we can act on. "Can Lantern also show Z" is scope expansion, and we want to capture those separately so they route to the right conversation instead of landing on v0.

[IRIS] And if something looks wrong — empty where you expected data, missing where you expected a card — please flag it. Most of those will be the boundary working correctly, but we want to know which ones aren't, and the only way to find out is to hear about them.

[ALEX] With that, Iris and I will take questions on scope, then we'll go around for the actual feedback. Thanks.

————————————————————

Live-path vs. replay/mirror (read second — the most important distinction):
- Live-path label changes can create enforcement work. If metrics-router or shard-keeper is asked to carry a new label or change label semantics, that's a service-level change and it has to clear label-change preflight.

Matrix (3 rows × 5 columns — added "cost intuition / preflight signal" from Cyrus's notes):

Row 1 — Label limits
- Failure signal: a label family crosses the agreed active-series or cardinality threshold while live traffic is carrying it; downstream query cost or storage growth shows up without an obvious single owner.
- Source of truth: live-path label/cardinality metrics from metrics-router and shard-keeper (per-service), not the mirror-validation lane.
- Rollback criteria: YES for live-path changes. If a label-family limit fires on the live path and the source of truth confirms it, the change is a rollback candidate.
- Cost intuition / preflight signal (Cyrus, advisory): high-cardinality label families (e.g. user/request-scoped identifiers, free-text, unbounded enums) cluster the storage/query cost. Preflight signal = "expected cardinality growth × retention window × query fanout" as a directional indicator — used as a preflight flag, not a pricing claim.
- Owner: enforcement trade-off inside metrics-router / shard-keeper — Alex. Cost framing — Cyrus (advisory). Service-level decision on where the limit lives — Alex.

Row 2 — Alert-source semantics
- Failure signal: an alert fires from a source that no longer reflects the intended live-path state (e.g. mirror-validation lane output is being treated as live, or a deprecated rollup-service read is being honored).
- Source of truth: alert routing config + live-path label/source identity in metrics-router. Replay-window output is NOT the source of truth here.
- Rollback criteria: YES for live-path changes. If alert-source semantics drift on the live path, roll back to the prior routing config.
- Cost intuition / preflight signal (Cyrus, advisory): mirroring or replaying an alert source multiplies its storage/query footprint without adding live-path signal. Preflight signal = "is this alert source mirrored or replayed, and if so is the mirror clearly labeled non-live?" — directional flag only.
- Owner: alert routing + source identity in metrics-router — Alex. Cost framing on mirrored/replayed alert sources — Cyrus (advisory).

Row 3 — Label-change preflight
- Failure signal: a config or parser change adds or renames labels without checking cardinality behavior, owner, or rollback/non-rollback semantics before push.
- Source of truth: the PR + the preflight checklist (sample counts, source label, owner, rollback/non-rollback semantics, mirror-vs-live path).
- Rollback criteria: NO on its own. A preflight gap is investigation evidence and a Q4 controls input. It becomes a rollback criterion only when paired with a live-path change that itself fails Row 1 or Row 2. Replay or mirror movement surfaced via preflight is not, by itself, a rollback trigger.
- Cost intuition / preflight signal (Cyrus, advisory): for each new or renamed label, the preflight asks the directional question — "which label family does this fall into, and what's the expected fanout shape?" That's a preflight signal, not a cost claim. The answer informs the service-level decision; it doesn't replace it.
- Owner: preflight checklist shape and enforcement inside metrics-router / shard-keeper — Alex. Label-family cost framing for the preflight question — Cyrus (advisory).

Reading the matrix:
- Rows where "Rollback criteria: YES" require live-path evidence. Mirror or replay movement is explicitly out of scope as a trigger.
- Rows where "Rollback criteria: NO" produce investigation evidence and feed Q4 controls work; they don't trigger action on their own.

Non-goals (held over from 10/13): no customer dashboard, no legacy retirement, no general telemetry rewrite. First cut stays narrow: label limits + alert-source semantics + label-change preflight. Live-path rollback semantics stay separate from replay/mirror validation.

Cardinality Guardrails — first control slice, PR / review checklist (first pass, 2023-10-25; scope locked 2023-10-24). Applies to any change to metrics-router or shard-keeper that touches labels, alert wiring, or downstream rollup consumption. Each line is reviewer-actionable: mark Pass or Fail. Any Fail blocks merge unless remediated inline. Risk-based, not blanket — high-cardinality labels are not forbidden by default.

SECTION 1 — LABEL-CARDINALITY PREFLIGHT (metrics-router + shard-keeper)

1.1  New label keys:
     Pass only if (a) every new label key is named in the PR description, AND (b) a steady-state distinct-count projection is included with the assumption stated.
     Fail if a new key ships with no projection, or with "TBD" / unbounded and no justification.

1.2  Risky label families (per-run IDs, request IDs, session IDs, user/org IDs, experiment IDs, timestamps, raw URLs, free-form tags):
     Pass only if the diff has been scanned and one of: (a) none present, (b) any present are bounded explicitly in code or config with the bound cited, (c) any present are flagged in the PR description with a one-line risk note and a follow-up owner.
     Fail if a risky family appears with no bound and no risk note.

1.3  Cardinality delta vs. current baseline:
     Pass only if the projection is compared to the current router / shard-keeper baseline (cite a number or runbook link) and the delta is called out even when small.
     Fail if the projection is given without a baseline.

1.4  Ongoing monitoring owner:
     Pass only if a service + team is named to watch the new key once shipped (the PR author is fine).
     Fail if the key would ship as an orphan — out of scope for this slice's protections.

SECTION 2 — ALERT-SOURCE CLASSIFICATION

2.1  Source class declared per touched signal:
     Pass only if each alert or rollback-touching signal in the diff carries one of: live, replay, mirror, validation. Treat untagged as Fail.
     Fail if the source class is missing, ambiguous, or only inferable from the panel name.

2.2  Replay and mirror are NOT wired to live rollback triggers:
     Pass only if any replay / mirror signal in the diff is confirmed disconnected from rollback automation and paging paths.
     Fail if a replay or mirror panel sits on a rollback path, or shares a routing key with a live signal without an explicit split.

2.3  Validation movement is not a rollback criterion:
     Pass only if the PR and any updated runbook text do not treat backfill, replay, or validation-window movement as a reason to roll back metrics-router or shard-keeper.
     Fail if a rollback criterion depends on validation or backfill movement.

2.4  Q3 replay / mirror confusion is not reintroduced:
     Pass only if the change does not collapse distinct sources into a single signal an oncall could mistake for a live regression.
     Fail if a single dashboard or alert now mixes live + non-live sources without a visible split.

SECTION 3 — ROLLUP-SERVICE PARITY (label names crossing service boundaries)

3.1  Label-name cross identified:
     Pass only if the PR explicitly lists every label name rollup-service will see change (rename, removal, type change, units change). If none, state "no cross" and pass.
     Fail if a label change is in the diff but the cross is not surfaced.

3.2  Parity confirmed with rollup-service owner before merge:
     Pass only if a comment or linked thread shows the rollup-service owner (Nadia) has confirmed downstream consumers can absorb the change in lockstep. Reference the Apr 17 label mismatch as the reason this gate exists.
     Fail if the cross is identified but parity is unconfirmed, or confirmation is post-merge only.

3.3  Migration / dual-write plan present for any rename:
     Pass only if any rename carries a dual-write window or migration plan with the cleanup owner and a target date.
     Fail if a rename ships with a hard cut and no plan — Apr 18 outage pattern.

SECTION 4 — LIVE-VS-VALIDATION ROLLBACK BOUNDARY
(applies at canary / rollback time — included so reviewers spot violations before they ship)

4.1  Cardinality canary firing during a declared load test:
     Pass only if, at canary time, the new high-cardinality label is confirmed present ONLY on load-test traffic before any rollback decision. Reference the Aug 16 canary (unbounded experiment_id from the load test, not a router regression).
     Fail if rollback proceeds without isolating the label to load-test traffic.

4.2  Rollback criteria cited in the PR or runbook:
     Pass only if rollback criteria cite live metrics-router signals only — write drops, downstream lag, router error rate, deploy regression. Replay, mirror, and validation are explicitly excluded.
     Fail if any non-live source is part of the rollback trigger.

SECTION 5 — NON-GOALS (this slice does NOT do these — flag and out of scope)

  - Not a dashboard. No new Cardinality Guardrails dashboard in this slice.
  - Not legacy-aggregator retirement. Hema's direction is unchanged; do not couple.
  - Not a telemetry pipeline rewrite.
  - Not blanket-prohibiting high-cardinality labels. Risk-based, not forbidden-by-default.
  - Not cost-model enforcement. Cyrus's cost-model role remains advisory; do not block merges on cost projections.
  - Not an ownership-map change. Running this checklist does not promote anyone to default Cardinality Guardrails owner. Same principle as the Sep 22 backup-≠-owner-map line.
  - Not authorizing shard-keeper solo preflight. Metrics-router checklist can run with Alice on non-prod / canary, and ingest-edge staging under the deploy-pipeline rules; shard-keeper preflight stays paired with Alice or backed by the Cyrus team.

REVIEWER SIGN-OFF

  - Pass to merge when every Section 1–3 item is Pass, every Section 4 item is Pass at canary time, and no Section 5 line has been silently expanded by the change.
  - Fail and request changes when any Section 1–3 item is Fail, or any Section 5 non-goal has been crossed.

The dull tightness on a lengthened stride or when you "think about pushing off" is the stretch-shortening cycle under load — the exact mechanism that strains a calf. Walking, stairs, and single-leg raises are low-load, so baseline tolerance is back, but the reactive stuff is still symptomatic. Translation: anything bouldering asks you to do (toe-off into the next move, lower or step down off the wall, hop between problems, even stand up from a sit-start) re-loads the exact pattern that still lights up.

Honest take: that's a "meet your friend for coffee" day, not an "easy session" day. The problem with bouldering isn't the climbing moves, it's the dozen small reactive loadings between them. One "easy" session is enough to re-set the clock to where you were last weekend.

That said, here's the plan for both branches so you can decide in the moment.

PRE-SESSION GATE (only if you're genuinely on the fence)

Before you commit, run this 5-minute check:
  - 5 min easy walk
  - 2x15 double-leg calf raises
  - 2x10 single-leg calf raises, slow
  - 10 small hops in place (just an inch off the ground), each side

If any of those reproduces the dull tightness, sharp pain, or makes the calf "wake up" in a way that wasn't there on the walk — skip. If everything stays quiet, you're clear for an extremely narrow session.

IF YOU CLIMB: THE NARROW PLAN

Warmup (15-20 min):
  - 5-7 min easy walk or slow stationary bike to get blood flowing
  - 2x15 double-leg calf raises
  - 2x10 single-leg calf raises per side
  - 10 min easy traversing on jugs, no problems yet, no standing starts

Allowed only:
  - Vertical or slab problems on big holds
  - Static movement only — every move should feel slow and deliberate
  - Downclimb deliberately, every time; never hop off or drop
  - Limit to 3-4 problems total, ~45 minutes cap
  - If a problem requires a move that feels "pushy" or "lungy," walk off

Avoid entirely:
  - Dynos, jump moves, anything you'd call a lunge to a far hold
  - Heel hooks — deep dorsiflexion under load is exactly your symptom mechanism
  - Toe hooks
  - Drop-offs / jumping down from any height
  - Mantles that require a calf push to stand up
  - Re-positioning around the gym between boulders
  - Any move where you notice yourself "thinking about pushing off"

STOP SYMPTOMS (back off or end the session immediately)

  - Dull tightness returns or gets louder than baseline during warmup or the first problem
  - Any sharp, pinching, or grabbing sensation
  - Calf awareness that doesn't fade as you climb
  - Cramping, warmth, or new swelling
  - The moment you start guarding or limping

Red flags (stop, ice, and consider getting it checked):
  - New pop or snap
  - Sharp pain that doesn't resolve within a minute
  - Visible swelling, bruising, or warmth
  - Pain at rest or at night
  - Numbness or tingling in the foot

SAFER ALTERNATIVE (the better call today)

Pick one — all keep you social without loading the calf reactively:

  - Meet your friend for coffee, tea, or lunch instead. A plain "calf's still a little grumpy, rain check for Tuesday" lands fine.
  - 30-45 min flat walk together at an easy pace, normal stride (not lengthened).
  - Flat easy spin on a stationary bike — 30 min, light resistance, seated. Real workout, doesn't load the stretch-shortening cycle.
  - Upper-body / hips / thoracic mobility session, or a yoga class that skips deep lunges and calf-loading poses (no chaturanga, no warrior, no down-dog holds).
  - Light hangs on a pull-up bar with feet on a chair — zero calf load.

Save bouldering for Tuesday or whenever the calf has been fully quiet for 48 hours. By then the "think about pushing off" signal should be gone, and you'll climb with full confidence instead of with a foot on the brake the whole session.

RECOMMENDATION

Skip today, meet your friend for coffee or a flat walk, give it two more quiet days, then climb Tuesday clean. The session you're skipping is the one that lets you actually climb hard again soon.

TONIGHT (5 min)

  Recheck the paw in good light: pad surface, between toes, webbing, around each nail.
  Look for: cuts, cracks, embedded grit or ice-melt pellet, red or raw skin, swelling, bleeding.
  Compare to the other front paw and the back paws — easiest way to spot "different."

  Quick gait check across the room: any head-bob, shortened stride, shifting weight off it?
  If skin looks intact: thin layer of paw balm or vaseline on the pads. Skip if anything's open.

TOMORROW MORNING (before the walk)

Kibo eating, drinking, and acting like himself this morning is genuinely reassuring — but you're right to keep this in its own category. Linear foreign bodies (ribbon, string, tinsel, thread, dental floss) are specifically dangerous because a piece can anchor at one end — most often under the tongue, sometimes at the pylorus or a flexure of the gut — and the intestine's normal peristalsis can then saw along it, which is how perforation happens. The frustrating part is that early on, dogs are usually completely normal. So: no panic, but no false reassurance either. Here's the plan.

24–48 HOUR WATCH PLAN

Keep the day boring and predictable — normal meals, normal water, normal short walks, normal bedtime. Don't fast him or change his diet; normal intake actually helps a small piece move through.

Once per watch window (morning, afternoon, evening, before bed, plus once overnight if you're up), do a quick 30-second check:

  - appetite — ate normally, picked at food, or skipped
  - energy — flat, normal, or subtly off
  - stool — formed, soft, diarrhea, none; any blood, mucus, or black/tarry color
  - belly — soft, tucked, tight, or "prayer position" (rear up, chest down = pain)
  - mouth — drooling, repeated swallowing, or pawing at the face can mean ribbon caught under the tongue
  - any vomiting at all

Track it in your head or on a note. The point isn't to stare at him; it's that if something changes you can tell the vet "fine at breakfast, skipped dinner, vomited twice overnight" instead of "I think he was okay."

One thing worth doing now while he's calm: gently lift his lip and look under his tongue and along the sides of his mouth. If a piece is anchored there you'll sometimes see the end. Only do this if he'll tolerate it without a struggle — not seeing anything isn't reassuring, it just means you didn't see anything.

WHAT NOT TO DO

Do NOT induce vomiting. With linear objects, vomiting can drag an anchored end through tissue and turn a watch-and-wait situation into a surgical one. This is one of the few times the usual "make him throw it up" instinct is wrong.

Do NOT pull on a piece if you ever see ribbon hanging from his mouth or his rectum. Same reason — if the other end is anchored internally, pulling can saw through gut.

Do NOT give laxatives, mineral oil, bread-to-wrap-it, or any home "helper" without a vet on the phone. Normal food is fine; improvising is not.

Do NOT skip meals as a precaution — an emptier gut means more aggressive peristalsis on whatever's in there.

Do NOT watch him like a hawk or restructure the whole house. Extra stress and unpredictability don't help, and you want him to act normally so you can actually spot "not normal" against the baseline.

CALL THE VET OR URGENT CARE IF ANY OF THESE SHOW UP

  - Any vomiting at all — especially repeated, or anything that looks like blood or coffee grounds
  - Dry heaving or retching without producing anything
  - Skipping more than one meal, or being picky when he normally isn't
  - Diarrhea, especially with blood; black/tarry stool; no stool at all for 24+ hours; straining
  - Belly looks swollen, hard, or painful to touch; "prayer position"; growling or snapping when you touch his sides or back
  - Pawing at the mouth, drooling, or repeated swallowing (could mean ribbon caught under the tongue — fixable if found, dangerous if missed)
  - Increasing lethargy — not "lazy," but "not himself and getting less himself"
  - Anything else where your read is "this is different from this morning"

IF YOU CALL, SAY:

"Suspected ingestion of 1–2 inches of curling ribbon, [when it happened]. He's currently asymptomatic — eating, drinking, normal energy, no vomiting. I haven't induced vomiting or given anything. Do you want to watch and wait, or do you want to see him now?"

Many asymptomatic dogs with a small linear ingestion are managed with watch-and-wait. Some vets will want a baseline X-ray or ultrasound as a record; ribbon often doesn't show on plain X-ray, so if symptoms appear later they may need contrast or ultrasound. Either way, calling now and saying "asymptomatic but watching" puts it on their record, which is useful if you end up going in overnight.

ONE THING YOU SAID, NOTED

You pulled most of it away — so the piece he may have swallowed is probably the broken-off end. Doesn't change the plan, just means you don't have to second-guess that it might have been a longer piece he chewed off himself.

Bottom line: he's acting like himself and that's the right baseline. The next 24–48 hours are a watch window, not a crisis. If anything on the call-the-vet list shows up, don't wait it out. If he stays flat-normal through the whole window, you're almost certainly clear — and a quick "my dog might have eaten ribbon on [date], he stayed asymptomatic" note to your regular vet on Monday is cheap and useful.

STAGING-ONLY JITTER EXPERIMENT — ACCEPTANCE THRESHOLDS
Scope: ingest-edge staging, 100 simulated clients, injected 503, retry switched from fixed 1 s to full-jitter [0, 2 s]. This defines pass/fail for the rerun. It is NOT a production rollout, broader staging fan-out, or collector-wide tuning decision.

1. PEAK CONCURRENT RETRIES (smoothing — primary signal)
   - Peak concurrent in-flight retry ops at the exporter, measured in 1 s windows, ≤ 0.6× baseline peak (~60 vs ~100). Defines "smoothing actually happened".
   - No surviving sawtooth: in the retry-arrival histogram, the 0.9–1.1 Hz band must hold ≤ 15% of retries (baseline is ~near-100% in that band). Smoothing without killing the 1 Hz spike = fail.
   - Either condition fails = rerun does not demonstrate smoothing.

2. STAGING p99 (latency budget)
   - Per-request p99 over the run ≤ baseline p99 + 1 s. This is the theoretical upper bound given the 0–2 s jitter (worst 1% of clients wait ~2 s vs the old fixed 1 s); tighter than +1 s is unreasonable, looser hides a real regression.
   - Hard ceiling: no single client observes > 2 s of added retry-wait before acceptance. Config max must be honored in practice.

3. COMPLETION-TIME TRADEOFF (must not hide throughput loss)
   - Total wall-clock to drain all retries after the 503 clears ≤ baseline. Jitter should help or at worst tie here; a regression is a fail.
   - p99 client finish time (from 503 injection to that client's last point acked) ≤ baseline p99 + 1 s. Acceptable smoothing tax on the worst-luck tail.
   - Throughput floor: aggregate accepted points/sec averaged across the run ≥ 0.9× baseline. > 10% throughput loss = the smoothing isn't worth it.

4. ZERO TOLERANCE (any one trips the experiment)
   - Dropped writes = 0. Same bar as the existing retry-only canary (sha:0a91b7c lineage); matches prior discipline.
   - Duplicate-accepted points = 0. Jitter raises the chance the retry lands before the prior attempt's response is fully processed; dedup/idempotency must hold. Count via the dedup window or per-point accept log; > 0 = hard fail.
   - Backpressure counter (queue-rejected / refused spans) stays visible throughout the run. Disappearance is signal-hiding, not a clean win.

STOP / ROLLBACK
   - Any hard fail above → stop the run, revert the jitter knob via the normal deploy-pipeline rollback (the same path used for the prior staging retry-only canary).
   - Nothing in this threshold set authorizes prod rollout, broader staging fan-out, or collector-wide tuning. Promotion decisions are a separate conversation after the rerun data is in.

The current test confirms the diagnosis: 94/100 clients stacked at t=1s is exactly what synchronized fixed-delay retries look like, and zero drops / zero duplicate-accepts mean the retry path itself is fine — the issue is purely the synchronization pattern. Full jitter [0, 2s] keeps the same mean (1s) and same cap (2s) and is the standard de-sync move; on the rerun the sawtooth should disappear, peak concurrent retries should drop substantially, and p99 should improve while drops and duplicates hold.

Same three signals as before — dropped writes stay 0, backpressure counter stays visible, retry log volume doesn't hide real pressure. Two specific watch-items given the shape of this change:

- Retries firing near 0s re-hit upstream immediately after it 503'd. Harmless in this synthetic setup, but worth flagging if the failure source ever moves to a real upstream (where you don't want to slam a recovering service at t+ε).
- Dedup is a non-issue here — max delay 2s sits well inside both the 15-min current window and the 5-min window from the 2024-01-12 experiment, so duplicate-accepts should hold trivially.

PRE-ARRIVAL CHECK (at home, ~45 min before kickoff)

  Tell Diego + one teammate before kickoff: "Calf's on a cap, 20 min max today, I'll rotate off every five." That's the whole announcement.
  Structure the 20 min as 4 x 5-min shifts with mandatory off-windows:
    Shift 1 (0-5 min): play. Cap your top-end at ~80%. No full sprints, no contested 50/50s at speed, no jumping headers.
    Off (5-6 min): walk a half-lap, water, shake out the calf.
    Shift 2 (6-11 min): same cap. Listen to the calf.
    Off (11-12 min): same.
    Shift 3 (12-17 min): same. If there has been ANY tightness, grab, or "something's different" feeling in shifts 1-2 -> skip shift 3, you're done at 17 min.
    Off (17-18 min): longer 2-3 min walk + water.
    Shift 4 (18-20 min): only play this if shifts 1-3 were completely clean. If you're hesitating, sit out.

  Position ask: if it's easy to do, take central mid or stay-side rather than a full-back overlapping role. Less sprint dependency.

STOP SIGNALS - stop IMMEDIATELY (not at the next sub break):
  - Any grab, pull, pinch, or "twinge" in the calf during a play.
  - Sharp or localized pain anywhere along the calf.
  - Tightness that doesn't fully resolve within 1 walking-recovery minute.
  - You're limping without deciding to.
  - The calf just feels "different" or "off" in a way you can't name. Trust it.

OFF-LIMITS FOR THE FULL SESSION (even if it feels great):
  - Full sprints / 100% effort.
  - Hard cutting or sharp direction changes at speed.
  - Jumping for headers, contested 50/50s at speed, goal-line dives.

POST-SESSION (within 1 hour, then next morning)
  - 5 min flat walk cool-down before you leave the field.

Both questions are well-chosen — they're the two questions that actually surface whether the team has shipped a system together or just talked about one. Staying in your lane.

**Q1 — boundary after handoff**

Pressure-test: A working answer names the boundary by *artifact*, not by org chart. Design holds semantics, naming intent, usage guidance, and the examples. Engineering holds build mechanics, platform constraints, and migration timing. The line gets redrawn at PR review and at deprecation, not at "who's in charge." A weak answer is "it depends" with no example, or one side quietly claiming the other's territory (design over code, engineering over naming). Also watch for process gates instead of working boundaries — that's a sign the boundary exists on paper only.

The signal this reveals: whether they've actually shipped a component, hit a real disagreement about it, and renegotiated the line in the wild. If their answer sounds too clean, they haven't done it yet.

**Q2 — exception ownership**

Pressure-test: A working answer names *who writes the deviation down* (almost always the team shipping the exception, not design) and *who is on the hook for retiring it*. Design usually owns cleanup at the system level — making sure the exception either folds back in or gets consciously retired — but engineering owns the follow-through on the consuming surface. A shared exceptions log with a triage cadence is the cleanest version. A weak answer is "we'll figure it out later" with no owner, or "design catches it in review" (that's a service-layer answer, not a partner one). The worst version is exceptions that became permanent forks because no one tracked them.

The signal: whether they've lived through deadline pressure *and* the cleanup after. If they only have a story about shipping the exception, they haven't earned the answer yet. If they have a story about how a past exception got retired, that's the real tell.

**Small wording tweaks**

- Q1: swap "divided between" for "where the boundaries sit between." Same ask, drops the zero-sum undertone so it can't read as territorial even before they answer.
- Q2: "removing it later" → "retiring it." Tighter, same meaning. If you want one more nudge, "who documents it and where" makes the implicit ask for a *written* system visible without adding a question.

That's it. No rewrite, no extra questions, no outreach.

The diagnosis is right. Three structural issues, each with concrete evidence from the last few weeks:

1. The 15-minute client-retry assumption is doing the work that licenses the 5-minute dedup carve-out. That's not a logical sequence. The dedup window has to cover the worst-case *legitimate* retry from any compliant client, which is independent of how long most clients retry. Yuki's 2024-01-12 sample had a maximum retry gap of 11m12s and p99.8 of 7m40s; those are normal retries, not edge cases. A receiving service that drops dedup state at 5 minutes silently turns a normal late retry into either a duplicate write or a silent drop. The two statements have to be untangled before this lands.

2. "Any 2xx is durable" is what made the received-batches panel look like a double-write last week — ingress ack is not stored point. A cross-service invariant that collapses those puts platform on the hook for downstream writes that platform doesn't own. The 2xx has to cover receipt only, with a separate signal from the receiving service that the write actually persisted. Same shape as the 2023-10-30 `route_pattern` leak: a label crossed a layer boundary and nobody could tell which side broke because the layers weren't named.

3. "Platform owns exceptions" is the structural consequence. If client retry, ingress ack, dedup, and durability all live in one sentence, every breach is platform's fault because no other layer has a committed behavior to point at. That's the legible-ownership gap Hema named for Q1.

What a clean version partitions:

  - Client retry budget — client's call, but it's a public bound the rest of the system has to tolerate.
  - Ingress 2xx — platform's commitment covers receipt, not durability.
  - Dedup window — receiving service's call, with a floor set by the worst legitimate retry from a compliant client (today: 15 min, evidence-backed).
  - Durability — a separate signal from the receiving service that the write reached permanent storage.

Each layer gets one owner, one observable signal, and one failure mode the invariant doesn't permit. The current draft fails all three per layer.

Three problems with the draft, in order of severity.

1. The 5-minute dedup carve-out reopens a closed decision and creates a silent correctness hole. The 2024-01-17 review of ingest-edge's dedup window closed the 15→5 minute shortening with the 30-day retry-gap distribution showing p99.9=10m48s and max=13m37s — real traffic retries past 5 minutes routinely. A retry landing after the dedup window expires would be accepted as a fresh batch, which is exactly the duplicate-batches class of incident the 2024-01-09 customer case was about, and the one dedup was protecting against. The 5-min experiment was run with no retries injected past 5 min, so it didn't observe the failure mode it was introducing — the gap between the test workload and the 30-day distribution is the signal. The carve-out shouldn't exist; if memory pressure is the driver, the answer is structured eviction by key class or per-tenant caps, not a shorter retention horizon.

2. "The platform team owns exceptions" walks back the Hema+Theo scope agreement. Your lane is invariant definition, failure-mode review, and ownership/escalation legibility — not catch-all exception ownership. Exceptions need to land with the service whose invariant is being excepted from (metrics-router, ingest-edge, shard-keeper, Guardrails, Lantern), written down with the cost of the exception, with platform as the route only for cases that genuinely cross service boundaries. Otherwise exceptions accumulate as undocumented debt owned by no one, and "platform owns exceptions" becomes exactly the catch-all you're not supposed to be.

3. "Downstream services may treat any 2xx response as durable" is underspecified. Durability depends on the sender's commit semantics — a 2xx returned before fsync or before the write crosses the sender's persistence boundary isn't durable, and downstream shouldn't have to know per-sender what the sender did. Either qualify it (2xx only after the sender has committed to its own persistence boundary) or restrict it to services that publish a durability contract.

CONTRADICTIONS AND OWNERSHIP GAPS — CYRUS DRAFT (2024-01-22 09:48 EST)

The draft as recalled rests on three assumptions:
  A. Every client retries for at least 15 minutes.
  B. Receiving services may keep dedup state for only 5 minutes when backpressure is bounded.
  C. Any 2xx is durable.

These are not jointly coherent. The joint fails open, and the failure mode makes the platform the catch-all exception owner — which is exactly the risk you flagged.

1. RETRY HORIZON vs DEDUP RETENTION (A vs B)
   - If clients retry 15 minutes and dedup is held 5 minutes, attempts arriving between minutes 5 and 15 bypass dedup entirely.
   - Yuki's 30-day sample (2024-01-17): p99.9 retry gap = 10m48s, max = 13m37s. Real retries routinely land past minute 5.
   - The 2024-01-09 case worked only because the retry arrived inside the dedup window. A retry at minute 11 would have produced a duplicate. The draft is one bad day away from that case being a real incident, not a clean dedup.

2. 2xx ≠ DURABLE (C vs observed behavior)
   - The 2024-01-09 case: first attempt got upstream write acknowledgement, client saw 504, retry was dedup'd to zero new points, retry still returned 2xx (dedup'd acceptance).
   - "Any 2xx is durable" classifies that dedup'd retry as durable while it accepted zero points. It also conflates ingress ack with persistence.

3. ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BOUNDARY NOT DEFINED
   - Three boundaries are blurred into one word: ingress 2xx (we accepted responsibility), upstream write ack (we persisted or queued), downstream durability (survives downstream failure). The received-batches panel counts ingress attempts, not stored points — that distinction is invisible in the draft.

4. DEDUP IDENTITY NOT PINNED
   - Stable retry identity is implied by 2024-01-09 (batch b-771 dedup'd correctly) but is not stated as a contract. If identity is built from per-attempt fields (timestamp + counter), retries won't collide and dedup retention becomes irrelevant regardless of window.

5. OWNERSHIP GAPS (impl + ops)
   - Retry horizon: who publishes, who consumes? The draft leaves it as a universal client assumption — no owner.
   - Dedup retention: which service holds it, who rolls it back, who pages when it shrinks? "Receiving services" names none.
   - 2xx-as-durable: who is responsible when it isn't? Silence makes the platform own every retry edge case.
   - Runbook / on-call: not addressed. The 2023-11-10 candidate debrief flagged this exact failure mode — "on-call can sort it out during the incident" — as the ownership weakness. The draft repeats it.


PROPOSED TIGHTER INVARIANT STRUCTURE

Five pillars. Each carries: contract text, impl owner, ops owner, failure mode, detection signal.

PILLAR 1 — SUPPORTED RETRY HORIZON
  Contract: ingest-edge publishes a supported retry horizon H. Attempts retried within H are covered by dedup. Attempts retried past H fail explicitly, not as silent duplicates.
  Initial value: H = 15 minutes — matches the locked production behavior, not a new guarantee.
  Evidence: Yuki 2024-01-17, 30-day p99.9 gap 10m48s, max 13m37s. 15 minutes is tight against the observed max (~1m23s headroom).
  Implication: replace "every client retries 15 min" with "ingest-edge supports a 15-min retry horizon; longer retries are out of contract and surface as failures, not duplicates".
  Impl owner: ingest-edge.
  Ops owner: ingest-edge on-call; runbook entry for horizon breach.
  Failure mode: retry past H → duplicate. Detection: stored-point fan-out check at sampled timestamps. Page ingest-edge on-call.

PILLAR 2 — STABLE RETRY IDENTITY
  Contract: a retry MUST carry the same dedup identity as its original. Identity = batch ID + content-addressable hash of the payload. Not per-attempt fields.
  Evidence: 2024-01-09 case — b-771 dedup'd because identity survived the retry. If identity had been per-attempt, dedup wouldn't have fired and the retry would have double-stored.
  Implication: metrics-router constructs the identity; ingest-edge matches on it. Identity construction is test-covered (not just happy path).
  Impl owner: metrics-router (construction), ingest-edge (match).
  Ops owner: metrics-router on-call (primary), ingest-edge on-call (secondary).
  Failure mode: identity drift → duplicates despite intact retention. Detection: per-batch dedup-miss rate. Page metrics-router on-call.

PILLAR 3 — DEDUP RETENTION WITH SAFETY MARGIN
  Contract: dedup retention R ≥ H + safety margin. The margin is documented, not implicit.
  Production state today: R = 15 min, H = 15 min, margin ≈ 0. Yuki's max gap of 13m37s sits inside this margin by ~1m23s. One wider retry and we dedup-miss.
  The draft's R = 5 min is directly contradicted by both the 15-min client behavior and Yuki's 10m48s p99.9 gap. Reject the 5-minute proposal — there is no evidence base for it.
  Recommended posture: R = 30 min with H = 15 min (margin = 15 min), OR keep R = H = 15 min and alert on dedup-miss rate as the explicit signal that margin is too thin. Pick one explicitly; do not leave it implicit.
  Impl owner: ingest-edge.
  Ops owner: ingest-edge on-call; runbook entry for retention shrinkage, memory pressure, index rebuild.
  Failure mode: R < H → dedup-miss → duplicates. Detection: dedup-miss rate SLO alert, retention gauge. Page ingest-edge on-call.

PILLAR 4 — DEFINED ACKNOWLEDGEMENT BOUNDARY
  Contract: three named boundaries, each with a distinct signal:
    (a) Ingress 2xx = "ingest-edge accepted the batch and owns dedup". NOT a storage claim.
    (b) Upstream write ack = "the batch has been written or queued for downstream".
    (c) Downstream durability = "stored and queryable". Surfaced via a separate signal — query API and/or status endpoint — not inferred from 2xx.
  Implication: drop "any 2xx is durable". The received-batches panel must be labeled "ingest attempts, not stored points" — the wording from the 2024-01-09 customer reply, codified into the product.
  Impl owner: ingest-edge (boundary definition + panel labeling).
  Ops owner: ingest-edge on-call.
  Failure mode: customer infers durability from 2xx → duplicates-that-aren't. Detection: support ticket pattern + periodic panel-label clarity audit.

PILLAR 5 — MAPPED SERVICE OWNERSHIP (impl + ops)
  Contract: every pillar names an implementation owner and an operations owner. The ops owner has a runbook entry and an escalation path that is NOT "on-call sorts it out during the incident".
  Mapping:
    Pillar 1 (horizon):       impl = ingest-edge,            ops = ingest-edge on-call
    Pillar 2 (identity):      impl = metrics-router + ingest-edge, ops = metrics-router on-call (primary), ingest-edge on-call (secondary)
    Pillar 3 (retention):     impl = ingest-edge,            ops = ingest-edge on-call
    Pillar 4 (ack boundary):  impl = ingest-edge,            ops = ingest-edge on-call
    Cross-pillar parity (the 2023-10-30 route_pattern lesson): impl = Guardrails, ops = per-service on-call via preflight
  Failure mode: any pillar without a named ops owner defaults to "platform owns the exception" — the catch-all risk you flagged. Refuse unsigned pillars.


WHAT THIS CHANGES IN THE DRAFT
  - "every client retries 15 min" → ingest-edge supports a 15-min horizon; out-of-horizon retries fail explicitly.
  - "receiving services may keep dedup state for 5 min" → removed. 5 minutes is contradicted by the 15-min client behavior and by Yuki's data.
  - "any 2xx is durable" → three named boundaries; 2xx = accepted, durability = separate signal.
  - implicit retry identity → contract-pinned identity construction with test coverage.
  - no ownership → named impl + ops owner per pillar, runbook entries, escalation path.
  - dedup retention gets an explicit safety margin and a dedup-miss rate alert.


OPEN QUESTIONS FOR CYRUS / HEMA
  1. Widen the horizon (R = 30, H = 15) to buy margin, or keep R = H = 15 and alert on dedup-miss? Recommend widening if Yuki's 30-day sample generalizes; either way, the choice must be explicit.
  2. Where does downstream durability surface — query API, status endpoint, or both? Needs an owner before Pillar 4 closes.
  3. Does Guardrails own the cross-pillar parity check (the 2023-10-30 route_pattern lesson), or does each service self-attest? Q4 Guardrails already lock the preflight shape; this slots in.
  4. Wes's 2024-01-15 jitter rerun (full jitter 0–2s instead of fixed 1s) — does it shift the gap distribution enough to change H? p99 470ms at fixed 1s is benign; jitter likely tightens the distribution but should be re-measured before the horizon gets locked in writing.

Each service owns its own acknowledgement boundary: a successful response attests only that the named boundary within that service has been reached durably, and nothing beyond it. Work that has not yet reached the boundary — or that occurs past it on the way to a downstream service — remains retryable; clients must consult each service's documented retry horizon before scheduling a retry rather than assume a uniform cross-service durability state. Because the boundary, and what counts as durable at it, is defined per service, a 2xx from one service is not interchangeable with a 2xx from another, and the supported retry horizon must be discoverable from each service's contract.

Smoky chickpeas & blistered tomatoes over warm pita, lemon-garlic yogurt on top. One skillet, ~25 min, eating around minute 25.

Sauce first (2 min, one bowl — also your serving bowl):
- 3/4 cup Greek yogurt
- 1 small clove garlic, grated or mashed to a paste
- zest of half the lemon + 1 tbsp juice
- drizzle of olive oil, pinch of salt
- Stir, set aside.

Order of operations:

1. (0:00) Skillet, 2 tbsp olive oil, medium heat. Add 2 cloves garlic (thinly sliced), 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp smoked paprika. Stir 30 sec — fragrant, not brown.

2. (0:01) Add both cans of chickpeas (drained, patted dry on a towel) and ~1.5 cups halved cherry tomatoes. Big pinch salt. Cook 10-12 min, stirring every couple min, until tomatoes collapse and the chickpeas pick up a little crust. Splash of water if anything sticks.

3. (0:13) Add spinach in 2-3 handfuls, tossing until just wilted (~2 min). Kill the heat.

4. (0:15) Tear both pitas into rough chunks, tuck into the skillet, toss so they soak up the pan sauce and warm through (~1 min).

5. Divide between two plates (or eat from the pan). Big spoonfuls of yogurt sauce on top, the other lemon half cut into wedges for squeezing.

Why this order: the sauce is a 2-min cold prep while the skillet heats, so it's ready long before the chickpeas; chickpeas are the longest cook so they go in first; spinach wilts in the residual heat at the end; pita goes in last so it's hot the moment you sit down.

Dish count: one bowl, one skillet, two plates, one cutting board, one knife. Nothing piles up.

STAY WARM (next 2.5 hr)

The play portion only goes 20 → ~22 min (+10%), which is the conservative side of a normal progression. The extra 10 minutes is warm-up extension (5 → 8) and a new 5-minute cool-down — both protective, not provocative. The structure is sound.

Calf stop signs — end the session vs. just notice

End the session for any of these:
- A grab, snap, or sharp pull mid-stride or on push-off (not the same as muscular ache)
- Localized pain on a specific move (cut, push-off, lengthened stride) that doesn't clear in 2-3 steps
- Tightness that doesn't fade within ~60 seconds of walking it off
- Any change in how you move — a hitch, a limp, a "different" feel even without sharp pain
- Tingling, numbness, or sudden weakness (different category — nerve/vascular; stop immediately)
- Calf pain at rest, swelling, or warmth appearing during play

Notice but not necessarily end:
- General muscular fatigue or low-grade burn across the whole calf
- Mild heaviness that eases as you slow down
- Warm-up tightness in the first few minutes that resolves once blood flow picks up
- Mild next-day muscular soreness that matches the rest of the body

SUBJECT: Re: HTTP 415 on remote_write after SDK 4.7.1 upgrade — content-encoding mismatch

This is not an ingest-side regression. Your endpoint is healthy and we have not changed the wire contract on this route. The 415 is content-encoding negotiation:

  - This remote_write endpoint advertises Content-Encoding: gzip and Content-Encoding: snappy. It does not advertise zstd.
  - SDK 4.7.1 changed the default Content-Encoding on outbound batches to zstd. The endpoint rejects the batch pre-ingest with 415 because zstd is not in the advertised set. No points are written; the batch stays in the client's retry buffer, which is why you see the burst instead of a quiet failure.

Fix on your side:

  1. In the SDK/Collector remote_write exporter config, set compression_encoding (or equivalent) to gzip or snappy. Either is fine — pick the one your downstream tooling already handles. If the SDK exposes a per-target override, scope it to this endpoint.
  2. Restart the affected process so the new compression setting takes effect. The buffered backlog will start draining once the encoding switch is live; leave retry/backoff at defaults.
  3. Do not bump batch size or relax backoff to "fix" the backlog — that just hides the negotiation mismatch.

How to confirm the backlog drains (please verify from your side, don't take our word for it):

  - Client-side: watch the exporter's pending-batch / queue gauge (e.g. exporter_queue_size, pending_batches, or your SDK's buffered-batch counter). It should drop from its outage spike back to a steady low within one retry interval and reach ~0 within a few minutes — not creep, not plateau above zero.
  - Wire-side: tail the exporter logs for this endpoint. 4xx rate should return to baseline (effectively zero) and 2xx should resume. No new 415s should appear after the restart.
  - Server-side: once the client flushes, the per-tenant accepted-samples rate for this endpoint should match the pre-upgrade baseline shape, with no gap larger than one batch interval. If you want a direct read, your account team can pull the per-tenant accepted-samples counter for the window covering the 415 storm and compare against the prior window.

If after the switch you still see 415s, or the queue gauge does not drain within ~10 minutes, send back:

  - One full request (redacted) showing the actual Content-Encoding header on the wire,
  - The exporter queue/pending-batch gauge over the post-restart window,
  - The SDK/Collector version string and the exact compression_encoding value set.

That tells us whether it's still a negotiation mismatch or something else on the path.

We have not made any changes on our side and there is no platform incident here. The fix is the encoding switch on the client.

Diagnosis (different bug than avg-of-quantiles, same family — fake p99):

Why the current query is invalid given those bucket layouts:

  `sum by (le, route)` collapses across build_channel, but the two populations don't share boundaries:

    Stable:  100, 250, 500, 1000
    Canary:  100, 250, 750, 1000

  At the sum, `le=500` carries only stable's rate (canary has no le=500), `le=750` carries only canary's rate (stable has no le=750), and the [500,1000] mass comes from different latency ranges in each population. The combined `le` series isn't a CDF — gaps, non-monotonic in the worst case. histogram_quantile will still interpolate and return a number, but it isn't the stable p99 (410), isn't the canary p99 (740), and isn't any aggregate p99 — it's a third value falling out of malformed input.

Minimal fix — preserve build_channel:

    histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, route, build_channel) (rate(router_request_duration_ms_bucket[5m])))

  histogram_quantile is well-defined within each channel because each population has its own monotonic bucket structure. The 410 and 740 then show up as two distinct series.

Deeper fix — reconcile bucket layouts across stable and canary:

  The mismatch is itself a canary-hygiene problem. As long as stable and canary emit histograms with different boundaries, any aggregation that collapses across them is suspect — panels, recording rules, SLO math, alerts. Two options:

    1. Pin canary to the stable bucket layout for the duration of the rollout. Cheap, least surprising.
    2. Re-emit both with a shared layout (SDK / middleware change). Cleaner long-term.

  Until that's resolved, every existing recording rule / alert that drops build_channel over `router_request_duration_ms_bucket` should be reviewed — likely more than one is silently producing a fake p99 right now.

Grounding line for her: the strongest answer names a real moment, names what she owned, and names what she let engineering own. Anything that sounds like she shipped the code is the cue to step back.

Three areas, one backbone. The panel is testing whether the ownership split you landed in the first round holds up under three different pressures: scale (convergence), constraint (feasibility pushback), and time (exception already shipped). The answers should sound like the same person making the same calls in different conditions. If they do, that's the signal.

**1. Local variants → shared component**

What's being tested: whether you scope the work honestly, or pretend the variants are more alike than they are.

Start with the audit. Inventory the variants and split them into three buckets — shared behavior (the mental model users have in common), surface differences (styling, density, context, which the shared API can absorb), and true exceptions (where the variant actually does something different). The exceptions are the work. If you ignore them, the migration stalls at the first team that needs to keep their quirk. So you'd name them, document why each one exists, and decide with engineering which can be parameterized into the shared API and which have to stay outside it.

Sequence by blast radius, not by surface area. The variant closest to the shared spec and lowest-risk to swap goes first. The one with the most state divergence goes last, or gets its own migration track with its own owner. Don't promise parity you haven't audited — if a variant has different loading behavior or different state transitions, say so.

Ownership signal: design owns the spec — semantics, states, usage examples. Engineering owns the API surface, deprecation path, and migration timing.

**2. Engineering feasibility changes the preferred sequence**

What's being tested: when the plan breaks, do you protect the outcome or protect the plan?

The constraint usually shows up as "we can't ship this in that order" or "this state transition isn't safe to expose yet." When that happens, separate what's load-bearing from what's sequencing. The behaviors and states don't move — the order does. Reconfirm with engineering what the new feasible path is, then walk back through the spec and ask which behaviors depend on the old sequence. Some will. Those need a substitute path or a documented gap, not a silent drop.

The handoff artifact is where this gets visible. When you revise the sequence, update the spec with the new ordering and note which decisions changed and why. The non-goals and unsettled API questions from your original handoff don't change — those are still yours to revisit.

Ownership signal: design re-baselines the spec when feasibility shifts the path. Engineering re-baselines the build plan. The two land at the same time, not sequentially.

Trap: don't let "feasibility" quietly shrink the scope. If a behavior gets dropped because it didn't fit the new sequence, that's a scope cut, not a sequencing change. Name it.

**3. Temporary exception has shipped**

What's being tested: whether you have a retirement plan, or just shipped a permanent fork.

Evidence over opinion. The retirement check needs three signals — usage data (how many surfaces adopted it, is it spreading), friction data (is the workaround causing real pain or just theoretical pain), and scope drift (is it staying narrow or expanding into adjacent use cases). Three outcomes from there:

- Usage bounded, friction low, scope stayed narrow → retire when the standard component catches up.
- Usage spreading, friction real → promote to standard. The shared spec gets revised, the API gets generalized, the exception log entry closes.
- Scope drifted, the workaround became a parallel system → bigger conversation, probably a redesign of the standard component.

Owner: the team that shipped the exception owns the follow-through on the consuming surface — that's engineering. Design owns the system-level cleanup and the spec revision. Both names go in the log entry with a review date. The exception lives in a shared log, not a doc someone has to dig for, and there's a triage cadence so entries don't go stale.

Trap: don't let the exception become permanent by silence. The most common failure mode is no one checks back. The review date is the safety net, and it only works if it's named at ship time, not added later.

**Thread across all three**

Scope the work honestly, hold the ownership boundary, make the follow-up visible. The behaviors and states are design's; the build mechanics and API are engineering's; the exception log and retirement criteria are shared, with names attached. If the panel hears the same vocabulary and the same handoff shape in each answer, you've landed it.

One thing not to fold in: the API-versus-documentation question from December. It's a separate thread and will dilute the ownership story if it creeps in here.
