SUBJECT: Re: ingest-edge out-of-order rejects — diagnosis and mitigation

Diagnosis: Rejects are isolated to one target being scraped by two collectors on offset 15-second schedules with identical external labels. Ingest-edge treats samples with the same label set as one logical series, so the two writers are competing for it and their offset arrival times are being rejected as out-of-order. Other targets ingest normally and shared ingest-edge error rate, latency, and queue depth are flat — this is writer duplication, not a platform regression.

Immediate mitigation: Disable one of the two collectors (or its scrape config for that target) so a single active writer holds the series. Keep the other on standby until labels are differentiated. The reject pattern will continue as long as both writers are active.

Supported HA setup: For two writers to coexist on the same target, each must emit a stable, bounded distinguishing label — typically `cluster` (small fixed set) and `replica` (fixed N). Both must be present on both writers, derived from a small enum, and consistent across restarts. This keeps active series bounded and lets ingest-edge treat the writers as separate logical series.

What NOT to use as labels: pod UIDs (unbounded across restarts and deploys), request IDs, container IDs, or any per-request / per-pod identifier. These are cardinality explosions — ingest-edge enforces a per-tenant active-series cap, and once a label set blows past it the tenant will start seeing new-series rejects on otherwise healthy traffic.

Recovery checks after the second writer is stopped and labels are corrected:
  1. Reject count for the target returns to baseline within a few minutes.
  2. `up` and sample rate for the target stay stable from the surviving writer, with no gaps at the 15-second boundary that the second writer would have filled.
  3. Active-series count for the tenant does not increase.
  4. Shared ingest-edge metrics (error rate, latency, queue depth) remain flat.
  5. If HA is re-enabled: confirm each writer's `cluster` / `replica` labels are present, bounded, and stable across a restart cycle before sending both writers real traffic.

SUBJECT: Re: ingest-edge "out-of-order sample" rejects — diagnosis and fix

Diagnosis: The error "out-of-order sample" with two collectors scraping the same target on identical labels but offset 15s schedules is the standard HA duplicate-write pattern. Each collector remote-writes the same `{tenant, metric, labels, timestamp}` tuple, and whenever a write for an older timestamp arrives after a newer timestamp has already been written for that series, the receiver rejects it as out-of-order. The other targets and shared ingest-edge signals (error rate, latency, queue depth) are all flat, which rules out ingest-edge health, clock issues on either collector, and per-tenant ingest limits.

Why only this one target: the two collectors are racing on every target, but most targets have short, consistent scrape durations and consistent remote-write latency, so writes land in order most of the time. The affected target's scrape or remote-write timing is variable enough that the second collector's write for timestamp T regularly lands after the first collector's write for timestamp T+15s, which is the only window that produces a visible reject. Reducing jitter on that target would reduce the rate but not eliminate the rejects — the structural cause is the missing replica labels.

Immediate mitigation: drop to one active writer for that target until the HA labels are in place. Pick one of:
- Set `remote_write.enabled: false` on one of the two collectors, or
- Move the affected `scrape_configs` job to only one collector.

Once only one collector is writing the series, out-of-order rejects stop on the next scrape.

Proper HA fix: each collector needs stable, bounded external labels that distinguish it so ingest-edge's HA dedup can place each collector's writes in its own slot. The supported pair is:
- `cluster: <stable-cluster-name>` (same value on both collectors)
- `replica: A` on collector A, `replica: B` on collector B (each unique, bounded string)

With both collectors carrying unique `replica` labels and HA dedup enabled for the tenant on the receiver side, the two writers are treated as distinct replicas, dedup happens at query time, and out-of-order rejects stop without reducing to one writer. Out-of-order warnings in the logs typically also disappear; if any remain, they are real ordering issues inside a single replica.

Important: do not use pod UID, container name, hostname, request ID, or any other per-pod or per-request value as the `replica` label. Those are unbounded and will blow up active-series counts against the tenant cap. `cluster` and `replica` are both small fixed strings.

To verify recovery:
1. After dropping to one writer, reject count for that target returns to baseline within one scrape interval (15s) and the customer's other targets continue ingesting normally.
2. After applying `cluster` + unique `replica` external labels and re-enabling both writers, both replicas' samples appear in queries (dedup keeps one per timestamp), reject count drops to zero, and no other target regresses.
3. Active-series count for the tenant does not grow after the label change — confirms the new labels are bounded and not adding cardinality.

Note: the rejection mechanism here is at the receiver's write path, not at the scrape path, so it does not indicate loss of scrape coverage; the unaffected collector is still scraping successfully, its samples are simply being refused on write because they collide with the other collector's already-written samples for the same series.

Here's a cautious read based on what you described:

Keep-or-discard, item by item

1. Ice cream (soft)
   Keep. Ice cream is already at the edge of "frozen" at normal freezer temps; "soft" at 28°F means it lost structure but stayed below the 40°F danger zone the whole time. Refreeze it and use it first once things are normal — texture will be icy/grainy, but it's safe. Discard only if it develops an off smell or separates badly after refreezing.

2. Berries (partly thawed, still icy)
   Keep and refreeze. USDA guidance: food that still has ice crystals, or is at 40°F or below, can be refrozen safely. They will be mushier on next thaw, so plan to use them cooked — smoothies, sauce, muffins, jam — rather than raw.

3. Packaged chicken (hard, ice crystals, no leaked juices)
   Keep without hesitation. It never thawed. No ice crystals lost, no purge in the package = it sat below freezing the whole time.

Overall call: at 28°F you never crossed into the 40°F danger zone, so safety is fine. The only real cost is quality loss on the ice cream and the berries.

When to recheck the temperature
In about 1–2 hours after closing the door. A healthy freezer should pull the reading down several degrees per hour back toward 0°F. Check again at 4 hours and at ~6 hours — by then a normal machine should be sitting at or very near 0°F.

What would point to an appliance/door problem instead of just "door not fully shut"

- Temp is flat or rising at the 1–2 hour check instead of dropping.
- After 6 hours it's still well above 0°F (say, mid-teens °F or higher with the door confirmed closed).
- You see fresh frost or condensation on the door gasket, or the door doesn't click/latch firmly and springs open on its own.
- The compressor is silent, or it runs continuously for hours without the temp falling.
- A bag of water placed against the back wall doesn't freeze solid within a few hours.

If any of those show up, the suspect is the door gasket, the latch/hinge, or the compressor/thermostat — and you should stop relying on the freezer for new groceries until it's serviced. If the temp marches cleanly back to 0°F over a few hours, it's just a door that didn't fully close, and you don't need to do anything beyond normal.

Diagnosis: hold-across-wait deadlock (lock-ordering inversion).

Cycle:
  coordinator:  holds manifestMu, blocked in wg.Wait()
  workers 1-8:  blocked in manifestMu.Lock() at the top of markComplete
                -> never reach wg.Done()
                -> wg.Wait() never returns
                -> manifestMu never released

Why 812 made it through: workers finished their first batch and recorded completion before the coordinator reacquired manifestMu to enqueue the rest. After that acquisition, the lock never released again, so no worker could re-enter markComplete. The stall threshold is determined by whichever batch boundary sits just before the coordinator's second acquisition of manifestMu — 812 is that boundary here, not a manifest-count quirk.

Why this is cleanly bounded: workers stopped at a clean pre-markComplete line. They hold no locks and have not mutated `completed`. No external state past 812 needs rollback. Kill the replay; the lock releases as the process exits, and a corrected restart picks up from scratch.

Minimal fix (coordinator):

    manifestMu.Lock()
    enqueueRemaining(manifests)
    manifestMu.Unlock()   // moved before wg.Wait()
    wg.Wait()

The worker path is already correct: wg.Done() sits after manifestMu.Unlock(), which is the right order (signal-after-release). Only the coordinator side is wrong.

Optional follow-ups, not required for the fix:
  - `completed[id]` is only read after wg.Wait() returns. A sync.Map or a per-slot atomic counter removes the mutex from the hot path entirely and removes this class of bug.
  - If the queue itself only needs producer-side protection during the enqueue pass, a buffered work channel + close-to-drain is structurally harder to deadlock than mutex+waitgroup.
  - Add a timeout on wg.Wait() in the rehearsal harness so the next stall fails loud at 812/2000 instead of hanging the run until a human notices.

Good — that's a clean lock-order fix (release `manifestMu` before `wg.Wait()`) and the test profile (8 workers / 2k manifests / 60s) is exactly the right shape to catch a future regression without flaking. Twenty runs with checksum agreement is a strong signal; no prod impact is the only acceptable outcome here.

Why per-pod p99s can't be combined

Each pod's `quantile="0.99"` is the 99th percentile of that pod's own request distribution. The six pods see different request mixes and volumes, so their p99s are quantiles of disjoint subsets — not samples from one shared distribution.

A p99 is an order statistic, not an average, which means:

  - Averaging the six values doesn't reproduce the p99 of the combined traffic — the math simply doesn't work that way.
  - Request-count weighting doesn't fix it either. The weight is applied to scalar summaries, not the underlying distribution, so it can't recover tail behavior that the summary has already discarded. Two pods can report the same p99 while having very different tails (e.g., one slow request per thousand vs. one per hundred), and a weighted average hides that.

That's the gap you're seeing between the averaged number and the combined distribution in traces.

The right approach

Export cumulative histogram buckets (`*_bucket{le="..."}`) from each pod instead of a pre-computed summary quantile. Bucket counts are additive across pods, so you sum them by `le`, then apply `histogram_quantile` to the combined counts:

  histogram_quantile(
    0.99,
    sum by (le) (rate(<your_request_duration_seconds_bucket>[5m]))
  )

The result is the p99 of the actual service-wide distribution, computed from the underlying data rather than reconstructed from per-pod point estimates.

Quick practical take, three answers to your three questions, plus a note on finishing tonight.

Would superglue get in the way of a proper repair?

Yes, real risk. Cyanoacrylate (super glue / Krazy Glue) cures rigid — it's basically a hard plastic. The toe box flexes on every edging and toe-hook, so a rigid glue line in that seam cracks within a session or two and the separation reopens, usually worse, because the brittle glue fragments hold the rubber slightly apart. The second problem is contamination: if any CA wicks into the rubber-rubber seam or onto the rand, a resoler can't get a clean solvent-based weld later, because CA doesn't dissolve in the same solvents and leaves a film that blocks adhesion. So Ren's suggestion is friendly, but it's the kind of fix that makes a future proper repair either more expensive or impossible in that exact spot.

Is a flexible shoe adhesive reasonable for a separation this small?

Yes, reasonable as a stop-gap. Shoe Goo, Gear Aid Aquaseal SR, or any climbing-specific rubber contact cement (the solvent kind resolers actually use, e.g. Renia/Colle de Cologne) is made to stay flexible after cure. For 8 mm along an edge with the rand still intact and no fabric showing, a flexible adhesive should hold for weeks to months of normal use if the surface is prepped right: wipe with isopropyl alcohol, let it flash off, apply a thin coat, press or lightly clamp the seam closed, full 24 h cure before you put weight on it. It is not a permanent fix — the bond is weaker than a fresh vulcanized or solvent-welded joint, and the underlying failure mode (delamination) usually keeps progressing — but it buys real time and does not compromise a future repair.

Signs to stop using the shoe and take it to a climbing-shoe resoler:

- the separation grows past where you glued it, or reopens within a session or two of flexible adhesive
- the rand itself starts peeling away from the upper — rand-to-upper delamination is structural, not cosmetic
- fabric, mesh, or any upper material becomes visible through the gap
- you can see cuts, tears, or deformation in the rand rubber itself
- multiple delamination spots appear on the same shoe — usually means the overall bond is aging out (heat, sweat, UV, age), not just one weak spot
- the toe box loses its shape — the rand is what gives it structure, and once it goes the shoe climbs differently and the rest tends to follow
- the sole starts pulling away from the rand at the perimeter
- stitching at the toe starts coming undone
- the separation sits in a high-stress area (toe edge, inside forefoot) and keeps creeping despite repair

For tonight specifically: rand intact, no slip, 8 mm is small. You can finish the session if you're mindful — avoid hard toe-hooks, aggressive edging on tiny chips, and any move where the toe catches and twists hard. If the seam suddenly grabs wrong, the gap visibly widens mid-session, or you feel the rubber "pop" under load, just stop and call it a night; that's your cue the bond is actively failing, not just cosmetically separating.

Idempotency invariant (precise):

The smallest dedupe unit must equal the smallest unit of durable commit. Within a batch, segments commit independently — the batch is grouping metadata, not an atomic unit. So idempotency is scoped per segment. Two retries of the same segment produce exactly one durable write; two retries of different segments within the same batch each produce their own writes. This is the invariant that makes worker reassignment safe; collapsing it to the batch level does not, because an unacked segment would inherit dedup state from its (partially-committed) siblings and either get dropped or duplicate a sibling's commit depending on which retry lands first.

Smallest safe dedupe key:

  (tenant_id, segment_id)

segment_id is a globally unique idempotency key (UUID v4 or v7, client- or service-minted). batch_id is NOT in the key. tenant_id scopes storage; segment_id is the idempotency identity. Globally-unique-per-segment is what satisfies the cross-service "globally unique idempotency key" requirement at this boundary.

Commit ordering (rollup-service internal, in order):

  1. Segment write to durable segment store. Idempotency boundary keyed on segment_id. Retry that arrives after this commits sees the dedup record and returns 200 OK with no re-write.
  2. Per-batch completion is DERIVED from segment commits (e.g., commit log + counter, or per-batch marker updated only when all expected segments are present). It is not a separately-writeable state, so a worker dying here loses nothing the next worker can't reconstruct.
  3. Aggregate computation runs only after step 2 is observed.
  4. Aggregate write to durable object storage. This IS the rollup-service 200 OK boundary named in the cross-service invariant. Idempotency key on this write is (tenant_id, batch_id) — the one place batch_id earns its keep, because the aggregate is exactly batch-scoped.
  5. 200 OK returned to caller only after step 4 commits.

Every retryable boundary has its own dedup record; no boundary is wider than its dedupe key.

Focused failure tests:

Test A — worker reassignment, no crash:
Submit segment S to worker A. Worker A durably commits S, then fails to deliver the 2xx (network blip, client socket closed before response lands). Coordinator reassigns S to worker B. Worker B reads the dedup record for S's idempotency key and returns 200 OK as a replay.
Assertions: exactly one segment record for S; exactly one contribution to its batch aggregate; retry completes in one round-trip to worker B; no second segment write was attempted (check write log, not just final state).

Test B — crash-after-write-before-ack:
Submit segment S. Worker A commits S durably, then is killed (SIGKILL) before responding. Coordinator reassigns S to worker B. Worker B observes the prior commit and returns 200 OK.
Assertions: exactly one segment record; exactly one aggregate contribution; dedup table has exactly one entry for S's key with the original timestamp; no partial/half-state visible from worker A's death.

Test C — implied by A and B; worth naming because A/B do not cover it:
All 12 segments of batch B are durably committed; worker A begins aggregate computation and is killed before step 4 commits. Retry reassigns batch B's aggregation to worker B. Worker B observes per-batch completion, recomputes the aggregate deterministically from committed segments, writes it. Concurrent retry racing worker B sees the prior aggregate record (keyed on (tenant_id, batch_id)) and returns 200 OK.
Assertions: exactly one aggregate record; all 12 input segments accounted for in the aggregate; aggregate is bit-identical across recomputation (deterministic build).

Push this back to Cyrus if his draft keeps batch_id on the segment-level key, or if his ordering puts the 200 OK before the aggregate write, or if dedup retention is shorter than the documented caller retry horizon (15 min floor + margin, per the cross-service invariant). Those three are where this kind of design goes wrong in practice.

Three problems in the current shape; all three failure cases trace to them.

1. Key granularity is wrong. key = (tenantID, batchID) but the unit of work is one segment. Two ways this breaks:
   - Case 1 (first segment commits, eleven remain): once segment 1 marks the batch seen, segments 2-12 are silently skipped on the same loop. The whole batch is "done" after one write.
   - On a retry before any segment commits, nothing has marked the key, so all twelve segments re-execute writeSegment — including a duplicate of segment 1 if it had been durably written but not yet marked.

2. write / markSeen / ack is not atomic. Cases 2 and 3 hit the same window: the durable write succeeds, markSeen and ack do not. The reassigned worker calls seen(key), gets false, and writes the segment a second time. Duplicate at the storage layer regardless of whether seen() is worker-local memory or a shared map.

3. No content-addressable identity (Pillar 2 from the retry-invariant pass). Even with segment-level keys, two retries carrying the same segment_id but different bytes would be treated as the same segment. Identity must include the content hash; the current shape has neither segment_id nor hash.

Corrected shape — move dedup authority into the durable store, not into a worker-side map:

```
key := (tenantID, segment_id, content_hash)

# putIfAbsent is enforced by the store itself, atomically.
# this is the only authoritative dedup point.
ok := store.putIfAbsent(segment, key)
if !ok {
    return resolveDuplicate(...)   # already committed by a prior attempt, or content mismatch
}

markSeen(key)   # advisory fast-path only; not authoritative
ack(segment)
```

And the batch driver becomes:

```
for segment in batch.segments:
    process(segment)   # each segment is its own dedup unit
```

Case-by-case, against the corrected shape:

- Case 1: each segment runs independently. Segment 1 commits via putIfAbsent on its own key. Segments 2-12 each putIfAbsent on their own segment_id. No cross-segment dedup, no silent skips.
- Case 2: worker crashes after the store accepted putIfAbsent but before ack. Reassigned worker calls putIfAbsent again — store returns false, segment already present, no duplicate. The new worker issues ack; upstream sees one accepted segment.
- Case 3: same as case 2. Idempotency is owned by the store, so worker identity is irrelevant.

Open questions worth nailing before merging:

- Where does content_hash come from? Hash the segment bytes at submission and carry segment_id + hash through the queue; do not recompute on the worker side, or you reintroduce identity drift.
- markSeen becomes optional. If you keep it, treat it as a fast-path only — never let a hit skip the store call. A hit on the advisory map must still confirm with putIfAbsent.
- For B17 specifically: after this change, re-run a fault-injection pass that kills the worker between the putIfAbsent return and the ack. The acceptance criterion is one stored segment per segment_id at the end, not "no retry produced an error."
Closed clean — root cause was the helper (seconds→ms then written into time_unix_nano), fixed at source, no metric gap after retransmit. Thanks for the update.

One refinement worth recording against the discussion: the shipped key is `(tenant_id, batch_id, segment_id)`, not the `(tenant_id, segment_id)` we landed on. With UUID segment_ids the extra `batch_id` is strictly redundant — no invariant weakening, just makes log forensics self-documenting and gives a clean namespace handle if segment_id minting ever needs to become per-batch. Not worth reopening; flagging so the recorded shape matches what actually shipped, and so the next person looking at this code doesn't think `batch_id` in the key is load-bearing for correctness.

AERATOR CLEAN + REASSEMBLY

Since flow is normal with the aerator off and both supply valves are fully open, the blockage is confirmed in the aerator. Mineral grit in both hot and cold screens means the building's supply is carrying sediment that caught in the mesh — common after valve work or in older buildings, and not a supply-side fault.

WHAT NOT TO USE

  - No pins, needles, wire, toothpicks, or knife tips to punch through the screen holes. They distort or tear the mesh and change the flow pattern, or cause the aerator to leak after reassembly.
  - No bleach or oven cleaner. White vinegar is enough; chlorine attacks the rubber washer inside the aerator and chrome plating over time.
  - CLR is okay as a second resort for stubborn buildup, but rinse thoroughly — do not let it sit on the rubber gasket.
  - No abrasive pads or scrubbing powder on the chrome housing. They scratch the finish.
  - No wrench force on reassembly. Hand-tight plus a small nudge is plenty; overtightening cracks the housing or crushes the washer and creates a leak you will chase later.

CLEANING

  1. With the aerator in pieces, lay them out in order on a paper towel so you remember the stack. Most aerators are 3–5 pieces: outer housing, sometimes a flow restrictor, rubber washer, and the screen disc. A quick phone photo before disassembly is worth it.
  2. Soak the screen disc and any other fouled parts in a small cup of white vinegar for 20–30 minutes. That dissolves the mineral flakes.
  3. Use an old soft toothbrush to gently scrub the screen from both sides. Work the bristles across the mesh, not into it.
  4. Rinse all parts under running water. Shake out the screen.
  5. Wipe the faucet spout threads with a damp cloth to clear any leftover grit before reassembly — grit left on the threads is what causes post-reassembly leaks.

REASSEMBLY

  1. Stack the parts in the original order. Make sure the rubber washer sits flat and the screen seats squarely.
  2. Thread the housing on by hand until snug. If the aerator has a slotted brass body that takes a tool, wrap it with a rubber band, a strip of masking tape, or a thick rag before using pliers — never bare metal on chrome.
  3. Hand-tighten, then add at most a quarter-turn with the wrapped tool. Stop as soon as it feels firm.
  4. Turn the faucet on slowly and watch the spout end. The stream should be a smooth, non-spraying cone. Any sideways spray means a washer or screen is misaligned — disassemble and reseat, do not tighten harder.

STOP AND CALL THE BUILDING INSTEAD IF YOU SEE

  - Any wetness or drip at the supply valves, supply lines, or where they meet the faucet tailpiece. That is a packing-nut or supply-side issue, not the aerator — same class of leak the building super fixed on the cold shutoff in July 2023.
  - The faucet body itself (not the spout end) sweats, drips, or sprays when you run water. That points past the aerator to the cartridge or valve seat.
  - Pressure stays weak even with the aerator fully removed, or water comes out in stuttering bursts. That suggests a partially closed building-side riser valve or an upstream pressure issue.
  - The shutoff valves do not turn smoothly, only one direction, or will not reseat fully closed if you try to isolate the faucet. Do not force a stiff valve — call the super.
  - Orange or black sediment (not the white/clear mineral flakes you already saw), or water stays discolored after running 30–60 seconds. That can mean rust in the building's riser.
  - You damage the aerator housing threads (strip, crack, or round them off) and cannot get a seal. Stop and call rather than wrap it in tape as a permanent fix.

QUICK HOUSEKEEPING

  - You do not need to touch either shutoff for this job, so don't. Leaving them alone avoids stirring up the packing-nut drip from last summer.
  - Run the cold tap for 30–60 seconds before reinstalling the aerator to flush any loose sediment out of the spout so it does not immediately re-clog the screen.
  - Since both hot and cold showed grit, repeat the same flush on the hot side once the cold side is back together.

Nice — textbook outcome: clear screen, even stream, dry cabinet after a ten‑minute run. If hard‑water buildup returns in a few months, a quick vinegar soak of just the aerator (no disassembly) usually keeps flow steady before it gets noticeable again.

The lease math is fine (start + 30 min as an absolute instant). What breaks is the round-trip through storage: the expiration is being persisted in a form that loses or misapplies the timezone, so on restart it is interpreted against a UTC offset that has shifted across the DST jump.

Most likely pattern, given the symptom "expired immediately after restart on the spring-forward day":

  - Expiration (or creation, with TTL applied on reload) is serialized as a wall-clock string, a naive timestamp, or a duration alongside a naive local creation time.
  - On reload, it is parsed against time.Local. Across the spring-forward gap, the same wall-clock string maps to a different absolute instant — offset by exactly one hour, which is more than enough to make a 30-minute lease look already-expired the moment restart finishes.

Concretely, for a lease acquired at 01:55 local on the spring-forward Sunday in America/New_York:

  - True expiration (monotonic): 02:25 local pre-jump = 07:25 UTC.
  - Persisted as naive "2024-03-10 02:25:00".
  - Restart at 03:10 EDT = 07:10 UTC. The parser resolves "02:25 on 2024-03-10" against the post-jump zone → 06:25 UTC, which is 45 minutes before now. Lease looks expired.

That matches the framing you gave: the in-process computation produces the correct instant, but the on-disk form is not the same kind of value as the in-memory one.

Smallest unambiguous storage fix:

  Persist the expiration as an absolute UTC instant with full round-trip fidelity. Recommended form: Unix nanoseconds, int64. Round-trips perfectly, no parsing ambiguity, no string-format pitfalls. Acceptable alternative: RFC3339Nano with an explicit Z (UTC) or numeric offset, parsed back as UTC explicitly — only if human-readable storage matters for debugging.

What not to do:

  - Do not persist as a wall-clock string without offset.
  - Do not persist a time.Time through any serializer (JSON, gob, protobuf-without-wellknown-types) that drops Location. Go's time.Time equality compares Location too; a naive time is a different value.
  - Do not store the TTL as a duration alongside a naive local creation time and re-add on reload — that recreates the bug.
  - Do not store "minutes since local midnight" — that is fundamentally local-time and unfixable.

The change is one line at the persist site and one line at the parse site (force UTC). No lease-math refactor needed. If the lease has multiple persisted timestamps (creation, expiration, last-renewed), apply the same rule to all of them.

Tests Yuki should add — keep them tight, two are required:

1. Spring-forward boundary (anchored):

  - Pin time.Local to America/New_York for the test. Do not rely on the host TZ — CI is usually UTC and the bug will silently disappear there.
  - Acquire the lease at 01:55:00 local on 2024-03-10 (5 min before the jump, 25 min before the would-be expiration).
  - Persist through the real persistence path, not just in-memory, then load it back.
  - Advance the simulated clock to 03:10:00 EDT (post-jump).
  - Assert: lease is not expired. The real elapsed duration since acquisition is 75 minutes (the 60-min DST gap plus 15), and the persisted expiration must land at 07:25 UTC regardless of what the local clock now reads.
  - Optional but cheap: include a sub-assertion that the storage format itself round-trips losslessly across the gap — serialize a known instant at 02:30 (a non-existent local time on this date), reload, and check the absolute UTC value matches.

2. Ordinary date (regression baseline):

  - Same flow on a non-DST day, e.g. a Wednesday in mid-February.
  - Acquire at 14:00 local, persist + reload, assert the parsed-back expiration equals start + 30 min to the nanosecond.
  - Purpose: confirms the fix does not regress the non-DST path and gives Yuki a clean diff to read next to the DST test.

Two extra tests worth adding if they are essentially free:

  - Fall-back ambiguity on 2024-11-03: acquire at 01:30 local, persist + reload, assert the absolute instant is stable. Same bug class; if the fix is correct, this passes for free.
  - Format-only round-trip at a non-existent wall time (02:30 on the spring-forward day), no clock advance, just serialize → deserialize → equality on the UTC instant. Pins the storage layer itself, independent of any time advancement.

That is the whole patch surface: storage format change, parse-as-UTC, two tests covering the boundary and the baseline. If Yuki's existing tests already exercise the persistence path on UTC machines and never set time.Local, that is why this slipped through — the DST test is the missing piece, not a refinement of the existing coverage.

Bug confirmed — this is a zoneless-string TZ round-trip:

- `expires.In(localZone).Format(layout)` writes "2024-03-10 03:20:00" — a wall-clock string with no zone marker.
- `time.Parse(layout, stored)` on a zoneless layout returns UTC by default.
- So the EDT (`-04:00`) wall-clock 03:20 becomes `2024-03-10T03:20:00Z` on read — exactly 4h earlier than the intended `2024-03-10T07:20:00Z`.

Net effect: every replay interprets the lease as expiring 4h before it was acquired. The lease isn't actually short; the persisted representation just round-trips into the wrong zone. For a staging recovery test that happens to "work" (forces fresh lease acquisition); for any normal path it would silently shift the deadline by the local offset.

Minimal fix, pick one:
- **Write UTC**: `stored := expires.UTC().Format(layout)` — read side unchanged. Any existing local-zone row will parse off by the offset until reconciled.
- **Read with location**: `time.ParseInLocation(layout, stored, localZone)` — smallest diff, but assumes every writer used the same local zone (fragile across hosts).
- **Carry the zone**: include `-0700 MST` in the layout on both sides. No migration risk, slightly larger rows.

Recommended: UTC on write + a one-shot reconcile of any existing rows. Lowest long-term ambiguity.

Comment posted on `lantern-importer-failure-modes` (id `docc_1789242345370`). It calls out the snapshot-at-start failure mode Iris surfaced and requires fail-closed semantics: reauthorize before each source-page fetch and again before publication, invalidate partial material on any denial with an audit record, and force any retry to start from a fresh authorization context rather than reusing the original snapshot.

The current draft lets the failure sequence you described publish a partially-imported room with revoked access, using stale authorization. That's the wrong default — fix the importer, not the next sweep.

Required behavior, addressing each failure-mode concern:

- Reauthorize before every source-page fetch. The snapshot taken at job start must not gate subsequent fetches; each fetch checks current source permission state.
- Reauthorize immediately before publication. Import completion is not authorization to publish; a final check against current state is required to make the room visible.
- On any denial — initial, per-page, or pre-publication — fail closed and invalidate partial imported material. Do not rely on a downstream sweep to hide what was already made visible.
- A retry after worker failure must establish a fresh authorization context. The original snapshot is discarded with the failed attempt; the retry re-resolves source permissions from scratch.

Concretely for the 10-page case: if access is revoked after page 4 and the worker fails before page 5, the retry must observe revocation at its first reauthorization check (whether at the per-page fetch or earlier) and abort with the partial material discarded. The current draft would publish pages 1–4 before the sweep catches up — that's the bug.

Closed. UTC RFC3339Nano with explicit Z + absolute-instant comparison is the structurally right fix, and spring-forward, ordinary-date, restart-replay, and 100-run staging all green with no production impact is the right evidence set. Nothing left on my side.

What the rule actually evaluates

`avg by (service)` averages queue_age_seconds across every pod in the service, with no `rollout` label. Given:

  canary (4 pods) × 24 s mid  +  stable (36 pods) × 1.5 s mid   =  (96 + 54) / 40  ≈  3.75 s

That sits well below the 15 s threshold regardless of which end of each range you pick (range 3.1–4.4 s; stated 3.4 s is consistent).   avg by (service, rollout) (queue_age_seconds) > 15

With the same scenario:

  stable cohort avg ≈ 1.5 s — well below 15, stays clear

---

**Customer-facing language (concise, no quota-promise):**

Your minute-level p99 looks fine because the limit and your traffic are being averaged over the wrong window. The 120,000 samples/sec ceiling is enforced on a 1-second window with no burst credits, and every five minutes your flush concentrates ~1.68M samples into an 8-second window — that hits roughly 210,000 samples/sec for those 8 seconds, so ingest-edge returns 429s during each flush even though your 5-minute chart shows you well under quota. The 429s are correct enforcement of the per-second limit; the mismatch is between how your batches are shaped and how the limit is measured.

We're not able to raise the 120,000 limit as part of this — the quota is per-second, not per-minute, and a higher cap would just move the same burst into a larger bucket. The fix is on the client side: spread the same ~1.68M samples over a longer window so the per-second peak stays under 120,000. The mitigations below are sized to that math.

---

**Prioritized mitigation sequence (starts with smoothing/jitter, no quota increase):**

1. **Stretch the flush window (client-side, fastest win).** Spread the same ~1.68M-sample flush over 45–60 seconds instead of 8. That drops the per-second peak from ~210k to roughly 28–37k above baseline, so the 1-second window stays under 120k with margin. No pipeline change, no quota change. This is the first thing to try because it removes the 429s without any service-side work.

2. **Add ±20–30% random jitter to the flush interval and offset per-shard.** Keep the 5-minute cadence (or close to it) but randomize the start of each flush across a ~30s window and stagger shards so they don't fire in lockstep. Costs nothing, and it stops the synchronized spike from looking like a single 210k/s wall. Worth doing even after #1 because it hardens against accidental re-synchronization later.

3. **Split each flush into 3–5 sub-batches with a few hundred ms between them.** Same total volume, no scheduler rework, but each sub-batch lands in its own 1-second window so no single second exceeds 120k. Useful when the upstream system genuinely needs to push all 1.68M in a short burst — combine with #1 to keep the average down too.

4. **Tune the remote-write / exporter to use full jitter on retries (0–2s, not fixed 1s).** Independent of the flush question, but relevant because a fixed retry on a 429 produces a synchronized retry spike that re-trips the limit right after the original flush. Full jitter avoids that second peak. (Same pattern Wes validated in staging in January.)

5. **Re-check the minute-level chart after #1–#3.** The p99 should sit comfortably under 120k and the 429s should clear. If the customer is still seeing rejects after the flush is stretched, the cause is something other than the burst (timestamp skew, payload-size limit, auth header, etc.) and needs a separate triage — not a quota change.

What this sequence does **not** include, deliberately: any commitment to raise the 120,000/s limit. The 1-second window is a hard ceiling by design, and smoothing is the right answer because it also makes their traffic friendlier to their own dashboards and to any other tenant that shares the edge.

---

Lifecycle ordering. The bug is that construction runs before validation, the swap runs after validation, and there is no close. The fix is two phases with strict ownership: validate a fully-local new watcher first, install it, then retire the old one, in that order.

Phase A — build + validate, fully isolated from the live watcher:

  1. Construct the new watcher into a local variable. Do not write it to the shared field.
  2. Subscribe to every config path it needs (each fsnotify.Add allocates one inotify descriptor per path).
  3. Run every validation step: parse, schema, dry-run apply, etc.
  4. If anything in 1–3 fails, close the local watcher and return the error. The live watcher is untouched.
  5. If everything succeeds, flip a `validated` flag so the deferred close on the failure path is skipped.

Phase B — install + retire:

  6. Atomically swap the active-watcher pointer to the validated watcher. Single write under a mutex or atomic.Pointer.Store. The consumer goroutine reads this pointer each loop iteration, so a fresh load after the swap picks up the new watcher.
  7. Close the previously-active watcher. fsnotify.Close is safe to call while a consumer is selecting on Events/Errors — the channels close and any in-flight receive returns the zero value with ok=false.

The four invariants you actually need:

  - Validation never touches the live watcher. (New watcher stays in a local until step 6.)
  - A failed reload leaves the active watcher intact and releases the scratch one. (Defer in step 4 closes on every error path before the swap.)
  - The retired watcher is closed exactly once, after the swap is visible. (Step 7 runs only after step 6 returns the old pointer.)
  - No gap in event delivery across the swap. (Consumer re-reads the pointer; old watcher.Close closes its channel cleanly; new watcher is already installed as the next iteration's source.)

Sketch in Go — gofmt strict, no log.Fatal:

    var pending *fsnotify.Watcher
    var adopted bool
    defer func() {
        if !adopted && pending != nil {
            pending.Close()
        }
    }()

    pending, err = fsnotify.NewWatcher()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    for _, p := range cfg.Paths {
        if err = pending.Add(p); err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("watch %s: %w", p, err)
        }
    }
    if err = validate(cfg); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    adopted = true

    old := swapWatcher(pending)   // lock, r.watcher = pending, unlock, return old
    pending = nil                 // ownership transferred; defer is a no-op
    if old != nil {
        old.Close()
    }
    return nil

Consumer loop — single goroutine, re-reads the pointer per iteration, exits on stopCh:

    for {
        w := r.watcher.Load()      // *fsnotify.Watcher, atomic
        if w == nil {
            return
        }
        select {
        case ev, ok := <-w.Events:
            if !ok {
                continue           // old watcher closed; loop back, pick up the new one
            }
            r.handleEvent(ev)
        case err, ok := <-w.Errors:
            if !ok {
                continue
            }
            log.Printf("config watcher: %v", err)
        case <-r.stopCh:

Tests — table-driven, in-process, no real timing dependencies. Drive everything through the public Reload entry point.

1. Repeated successful reloads do not leak FDs.

  - Read baseline open-FD count from /proc/self/fd (count the directory entries).
  - Call Reload with a valid config N times. N=200 is comfortable; the bug appeared at 60.
  - Assert final FD count minus baseline ≤ 1 + a small constant for unrelated scaffolding. Anything tracking 1-per-reload is the leak.
  - Assert the active watcher pointer changed on every call (capture per iteration, all distinct, last matches the final swapWatcher result).
  - Diagnostic variant: in a loop, Reload → assert FD stable → Reload → assert FD stable. Catches the leak earlier than a single end-of-loop check.

2. Failed validation leaves the active watcher intact and releases the scratch one.

  - Install a known-good watcher; capture its pointer P0.
  - Table-drive the failure cases your validator can produce: Add against a missing path, syntax error, schema violation. Each row the same three assertions:
      a. Reload returns a non-nil error.
      b. The active watcher pointer is still P0.
      c. FD count is back to baseline — the deferred close must have run.
  - Follow-up: a subsequent Reload with a valid config still succeeds and swaps to a new pointer. Confirms the failure path didn't wedge the router.

3. Watching continues uninterrupted across the swap.

  The point isn't "no events dropped during the literal pointer-write instant" — that window is microseconds and there's no deterministic test for it. The operational meaning of "uninterrupted" is "after a swap, a fresh event on the same file is delivered", plus "the consumer correctly tracks the new watcher when the old watcher's channel closes".

  - Install the watcher on a temp config file.
  - Start a writer goroutine that touches the file (write + fsync + close) on a short interval, e.g., 5ms, for the duration of the test. Record every IN_CLOSE_WRITE it observes.
  - Concurrently, run M=50 reloads at a slower cadence (every ~20ms) using valid configs with slightly different content so each reload is a real swap.
  - Assert: writer.observed ≥ writer.attempts − tolerance, with tolerance small (a handful) and accounting only for events that legitimately raced the very first watcher before the test started.
  - Tighter per-reload pin: immediately after each Reload returns, do one synchronous write + short sleep, and assert the consumer's event channel delivers that write within the sleep. Pins "the new watcher is live immediately after Reload returns" — the property you actually care about.
  - If you want strict coverage of the pointer-tracking contract, write a stub consumer that holds a local copy of the watcher, then have the test swap the field out from under it and assert the next loop iteration reads the new pointer and that a closed-channel receive (ok=false) causes it to re-load rather than exit. Captures the contract without depending on fsnotify's internals.

One thing worth flagging for Nadia's patch that isn't in your three asks: the consumer loop's `if !ok { continue }` is what makes the swap safe. If the existing loop treats ok=false as a fatal/exit, a reload will kill the watcher goroutine on every successful swap. Worth checking before she lands the patch.

The difference between "rate is zero" and "series is absent":

`rate(metric[5m]) == 0` only evaluates for series that are currently in Prometheus's scrape results. Once an exporter dies, the series goes stale within a few scrape intervals and is dropped from query output. The expression then has no vector to compare against zero, so it never enters pending — it just disappears silently. That's why the missing-exporter case never alerts.

`absent_over_time(metric[15m]) == 1` is the explicit "no samples in this window" check. It returns 1 when no samples exist in the range, and returns nothing when samples exist (regardless of value or rate). It does not depend on the series being live in the current scrape.

These are two different signals — "alive but not incrementing" vs "completely absent." The customer's original ask (fires if the job stops reporting for 15 min) maps to the absent case. If they also care about a flat-but-alive counter, keep a separate `rate(...) == 0` rule; if they only care about the exporter being gone, use this:

  expr: absent_over_time(batch_completed_total{job="nightly"}[15m]) == 1
  for:  0m

`absent_over_time(...[15m])` already enforces the 15-minute window, so an additional `for:` would only add latency. The `== 1` is conventional for clarity; the alert rule treats any returned value as "active."

Test expectations:

Positive — alert SHOULD fire:
  1. No samples for 15+ minutes: `batch_completed_total{job="nightly"}` is never scraped, or its last sample ages past 15m. Expected: alert enters pending within one scrape, transitions to firing at the 15-minute mark, stays firing until samples resume.

Negative — alert should NOT fire:
  2. A recent sample: a single sample at t-1m, with or without prior history. Expected: `absent_over_time` returns an empty vector (samples exist in the window), alert stays clear. This case also catches stale-marker handling — Prometheus marks the series stale but `absent_over_time` only checks for presence in the window, not staleness.
  3. Continuously scraped counter that stays flat: `batch_completed_total{job="nightly"} = 1000` scraped at the normal interval with no increment for 15+ minutes. Expected: alert stays clear. Samples are present in the window; only the rate is zero. This is the territory of the original `rate() == 0` rule — if the customer also wants to alert on a stalled-but-alive exporter, keep both rules side by side.

Engineering answer, compact — drop-in shape for the proposal or a reply:

- One canonical source. Exactly one machine-readable file is authoritative. The JSON repo is the natural fit because it's already diff-able, reviewable in PRs, and toolable, but the principle is what matters: pick the one place edits land, and everything else is a view of it.

- Drift check, automated. A CI job (or pre-commit hook) diffs generated output against what's checked in and fails on mismatch, so drift surfaces at PR time, not at handoff.

The authoring surface — Figma or the repo — is your call as a team. The answer above holds either way as long as the canonical file is machine-readable and the rest is generated from it. Subject: Why your ingest request was rejected and how to resume

The 10 MiB limit applies to the decoded body, not the bytes you transmitted. The gateway measures the logical request size after decompression; your ~1.86 MiB on the wire expanded to ~14.2 MiB after decoding, which is what triggered the 413. gzip saves bandwidth in transit, but it does not give you a larger logical request — for compressible payloads the decoded size is what grows, not shrinks, so a smaller compressed body can still exceed the cap.

To get back to a green ingest path without changing the cap:

  1. Size batches by decoded content, not wire bytes. Target ~8 MiB per request so you have meaningful headroom under the 10 MiB cap.
  2. Your data compresses roughly 8:1, which means ~8 MiB decoded lands at roughly 1 MiB on the wire for this workload. Don't size batches in compressed bytes alone.
  3. The payload that was rejected is still buffered on your side and will be rejected again if you retry it as-is. Drain it in smaller chunks sized to the headroom above, and confirm 2xx responses before resuming normal cadence.
  4. The 10 MiB cap is a memory-protection limit on the ingest path and isn't raised on a per-customer basis. Staying under it is the only path forward here.

Reply on this thread once ingest is back to 2xx and we can close the ticket.

Concise pre-repair checklist (Sat, 2:00 PM slot)

1) Backup verification (do this BEFORE you leave)
   - iPhone: Settings → [your name] → iCloud → iCloud Backup → confirm a backup completed today. Also confirm a recent encrypted Finder/iTunes backup exists if you keep one. Open Photos, Messages, Notes, Wallet and confirm the latest items are present.
   - Android: Settings → Google → Backup → confirm "Back up to Google Drive" ran today, and that Photos sync is current. If your OEM has its own backup (Samsung Cloud, etc.), confirm it too.
   - Confirm you can sign in to your Apple ID / Google account from a second device AND have your 2FA codes reachable there. A backup you can't unlock is no backup.
   - Optional belt-and-suspenders: encrypted computer backup or a cloud export of the photo library if it's not already mirrored.

2) Account and payment protections
   - Do NOT sign out of Apple ID / Google account. Activation Lock / Factory Reset Protection is what stops a stolen phone from being reactivated — keep it on.
   - Disable Apple Pay / Google Pay (Wallet app or Settings). Removes cards from the NFC surface even though they remain in your account.
   - Sign out of banking apps you can quickly sign back into, and any work apps tied to SSO that hold sensitive tokens. Sign out of password manager if you want.
   - Rotate the screen-lock passcode AFTER pickup if you want a hard cut on what the technician saw; write the temp one down so you can hand the phone over unlocked.

3) Maintenance / repair mode (only if your phone has it)
   - iPhone: no first-party repair lock mode. Skip this step. Activation Lock stays on (see above).
   - Samsung: Settings → Device care → Maintenance mode → turn on. Reboots into a clean profile, hides personal data.
   - Other Android (Xiaomi/OnePlus/OPPO/Vivo/Honor): Settings → search "repair mode" or "service mode." If present, enable it.
   - If no repair mode exists, sign out of the apps you'd least want a stranger to scroll through (email, banking, socials) — but only ones you can sign back into quickly.

4) Document before handoff
   - Photos of all four sides + the cracked corner + the working screen, with a piece of paper showing today's date in frame.
   - IMEI: dial *#06# and save the number. Also note serial from Settings → General → About.
   - Write down the shop name, technician name, ticket/receipt number, promised return time.
   - Note what the technician says verbally: OEM vs aftermarket screen, warranty terms, data-handling policy, whether the battery will be touched.
   - Write down the temp passcode you gave them.

5) Power-down triggers — skip the repair if ANY of these appear between now and 2:00 PM
   - Battery swelling: screen lifts off the frame, a new gap at the seam, case no longer seats flush, the phone rocks on a flat surface.
   - Heat rising from any spot while idle or charging, especially around the cracked corner.
   - Sweet chemical, burnt plastic, or solvent smell.
   - Visible battery cell or silver pouch through a torn frame gap.
   - Loose glass shards or sharp fragments near edges, buttons, or charging port.
   - Frame visibly bent or twisted, even slightly.
   - Spontaneous restart, dimming, lines, or color shift appearing now even though it was clean earlier — flex connectors under cracked glass can fail mid-repair and take the panel with them.

   If any of those show up: power down, skip the 2:00 PM slot, and ask for a quote that includes battery + frame check before any screen work.

6) At handoff (60-second sanity step)
   - Watch them disconnect the battery BEFORE prying the screen. Good shops do this; if they don't, mention it.
   - Confirm which screen they're installing (OEM, refurbished OEM, aftermarket) — affects True Tone / color calibration on iPhones, brightness/color on AMOLED Androids.
   - Ask for the old screen back if you want to verify the swap.

Your current signs (working display/touch/cameras/charging/buttons, no swelling, no heat, no odor, no exposed battery, frame straight, no loose glass near the port) all read as safe to leave powered on for the walk to the shop. Verdict: REJECT the current shape. The 34% allocation win is real but irrelevant if the pool takes the pod OOM in steady state.

Memory-risk evidence (the part that matters):
  - 420 MiB → 910 MiB retained heap over 90 min at constant traffic = 490 MiB growth = 48% of the 1 GiB pod limit consumed in one soak. The 1 GiB limit is the hard line, not a target.
  - Retained heap does NOT fall back after traffic goes idle. That is the leak signature, not warm-up, not GC lag. A bounded warm-up plateau; an unbounded pool keeps climbing.
  - Per-buffer is 8 MiB. (910 - 420) / 8 ≈ 61 extra buffers retained at t=90m vs t=0. The pool is monotonically accumulating returned buffers with no release path. Extrapolate the slope: a 4–6h prod shift hits OOM well inside one maintenance window.
  - The 2024-02-05 runbook rule applies verbatim: monotonic memory rise with steady error/drop/dup counts is unsafe to advance. Zero drops and zero dups do not make a continuing resource slope safe.

Smallest safe bound for retained buffers:
  - Pool must be fixed-capacity, NOT unbounded. Cap = ceil(2 × p99 concurrent in-flight requests per pod). Tie the bound to workload shape, not a magic number.
  - Absolute defensive ceiling: 32 buffers (= 256 MiB pool floor max). With 420 MiB baseline that puts retained heap at 676 MiB at full pool = 66% of the pod limit, leaves 33% headroom for non-pool allocations. This ceiling holds even if the concurrency math is wrong.
  - Idle drain: any buffer unused for >60s must be returned to the runtime. The cap without the drain still leaks at low traffic — both are required. The current shape has neither.
  - Reject the unbounded variant outright. Do not propose a "monitored unbounded" middle ground; the evidence already shows it leaks.

Three tests required before any cohort advance. All run against the bounded + drain variant, not the current shape.

  A. Steady-load soak — 90 min minimum, 4 h preferred.
     Traffic: p50 of observed prod rate, held constant. Capture preflight per the 2024-02-22 checklist (cache-key dims + boundedness, baseline mem/queue-age p50-p95-p99/error rate/dropped/dup-accepted, build SHA + start time via deploy pipeline).
     Stop conditions (from the 2024-02-05 runbook): 15-min monotonic heap rise, OR queue-age rise with it, even if error/drop/dup stay flat → halt at current cohort and roll back via deploy pipeline.
     Pass: heap plateaus within first 30 min, p99 queue age within baseline, no monotonic rise after plateau, allocation profile shows the buffer type bounded at the cap.

  B. Burst-and-idle — the leak-shape test the original benchmark missed.
     5 min at 2× peak burst, then 15 min idle. Repeat 3 cycles.
     Pass: after each idle window, retained heap returns within 5% of pre-burst baseline AND pool size returns to pre-burst count. Current shape fails this immediately because it has no release path. Bounded-with-drain must pass all 3 cycles.

  C. Concurrency scaling.
     Sweep concurrent in-flight from 1 to 2× expected pod max, hold each level 20 min.
     Pass: pool size tracks concurrency and is bounded by 2× in-flight at each level; no growth past the absolute 32-buffer ceiling; allocation profile stays bounded across all levels; no goroutine-attributable growth.

General context: nothing in memory flags a personal allergy history or a sedative-medication preference — so I'll give you the conservative first-night/morning plan, lean toward the non-sedating OTC options for a workday, and include the warning-sign list you'd want.

Tonight (conservative, no-diagnosis plan)

- Rinse the pollen off: shower and wash your hair when you get home, change out of the clothes you walked in, and toss them in the hamper (not the bed). A saline nasal rinse (neti pot or squeeze bottle with distilled/cooled-boiled water) once tonight and once tomorrow morning helps clear the irritant load — often more effective than people expect.
- Eyes: cool compress (clean washcloth, cool water, eyes closed, 5–10 min). If the itching is driving you nuts, preservative-free artificial tears (the kind in individual vials) flush pollen out and are the least likely to sting or cause rebound.
- Environment for sleep: keep windows closed tonight, run the bedroom fan or AC if you have it, and don't hang today's park clothes where you'll breathe on them.
- Hydration and head-of-bed: extra water, and an extra pillow so your head is slightly elevated — that often helps the post-nasal drainage.
- Skip things that tend to make it worse tonight: rubbing your eyes (makes the itching rebound), and anything smoky or strongly fragranced in the apartment.

Over-the-counter options that won't unnecessarily sedate you during work

Pick one. For most adults with a routine seasonal flare, any of these on its own is enough; layering them is usually what causes grogginess.

- Non-sedating oral antihistamine — work-friendly:
  - Cetirizine (Zyrtec) 10 mg once daily. Effective for both the sneezing/itching and the eye symptoms. In most adults it is non-drowsy at the labeled dose, though a small subset do feel mild sedation — fine to try tonight at home first to know how you respond before a meeting day.
  - Loratadine (Claritin) 10 mg once daily or fexofenadine (Allegra) 180 mg once daily — both are essentially non-sedating. Fexofenadine in particular is the least likely to make you sleepy but can be a touch less potent for stubborn eye itching.
  - Tip: take it at the same time daily, and don't combine with Benadryl (diphenhydramine) "to help it work" — that's the move that knocks people out the next morning.
- For stubborn nasal symptoms, add a nasal steroid spray — most work-friendly long-term option:
  - Fluticasone (Flonase) or mometasone (Nasacort), two sprays per nostril once daily. These are not sedating. They don't kick in immediately, so start tonight and use daily through pollen season; peak effect is usually a week or so in. They also help the eye symptoms more than people expect by calming the nasal-ocular reflex.
- For spot eye relief beyond artificial tears: an over-the-counter antihistamine eye drop like ketotifen (Zaditor/Alaway) once or twice daily is non-sedating and works fast for the itching.

What to avoid tonight if you have anything important tomorrow: diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and doxylamine (Unisom SleepTabs). They are effective antihistamines but reliably sedating and you can still feel them in the morning.

Tomorrow morning

- Second saline rinse + a shower before you leave if possible (cleans the pollen you picked up overnight).
- Take your non-sedating antihistamine with water before anything caffeinated.
- Two sprays of the nasal steroid if you're using one.
- If you'll be outside on a commute: sunglasses are not just comfort — they cut the pollen load on the conjunctiva.
- Keep the saline bottle or individual vials in your bag for a lunchtime flush if it ramps up mid-day.

Warning signs that this is more than a routine allergy flare and worth prompt medical attention

Any one of these, tonight or tomorrow, means stop self-managing and contact a clinician or urgent care:

- Respiratory: wheezing, chest tightness, shortness of breath, cough that won't stop, or any sensation of throat/tongue swelling or trouble swallowing — those can be an allergic reaction or an asthma flare, not a routine hay-fever day. Also a fever ≥ 100.4°F (38°C), especially with colored or thick nasal discharge or facial pain/pressure that doesn't clear — that's a sinus infection red flag rather than allergy.
- Eye: any change in vision (blur, halos, loss of any part of your visual field), eye pain (not just itch), significant light sensitivity, new bright redness of the white of the eye, or a feeling of something stuck under the lid that won't clear with tears/flushes — those point to something other than allergic conjunctivitis (e.g., keratitis, iritis, infection, foreign body).
- Systemic: hives or a spreading rash, swelling of lips/face/tongue, vomiting or abdominal pain soon after eating (suggests food allergy cross-reacting, common with tree pollen), hoarseness, lightheadedness, or any sense of "this feels different from a normal allergy day" — those warrant same-day evaluation. A fever with body aches is not allergy and would push toward a clinic visit for a viral or infectious cause.
- Symptoms that don't start to improve within about 7–10 days of consistent OTC treatment, or that are severe enough to disrupt sleep or work — that's a reasonable trigger to see a clinician rather than tough it out.

If you're ever unsure which side of the line you're on, the safest move is to call your primary care's nurse line tonight; they'll tell you quickly whether it can wait until morning or whether you should be seen.

1. SAFE MOUTH DECONTAMINATION (do now, gentle)
   - Use a soft syringe (no needle) or a small cup of lukewarm water. Let water pool at the side of the mouth; do NOT squirt toward the back of the throat (aspiration risk).
   - Let him drool it out; do not tilt his head back.
   - Wipe the lips, gums, and tongue with a soft wet cloth to remove plant residue and any loose crystals.
   - If he wants a small lick of plain milk or plain yogurt, that is fine to offer — calcium can bind residual oxalate crystals and soothe mouth irritation. Do NOT force it. Wait 15–20 minutes after the rinse before offering anything.
   - After that pause, leave fresh water available; let him drink on his own.

2. WHO TO CALL NOW
   - For one small bite with only brief licking and a single drool, this is a mild exposure — not an emergency clinic trip on its own.
   - Best single call for tailored toxicology advice: ASPCA Animal Poison Control 888-426-4435 or Pet Poison Helpline 855-764-7661. Both are 24/7 and staffed by veterinary toxicologists. A fee applies per case.
   - Your regular vet is also a fine call when they open; they can confirm the same general plan.
   - Skip the ER vet unless section 5 triggers.

3. INFO TO HAVE READY BEFORE CALLING
   - Plant: pothos (Epipremnum aureum / Devil's Ivy), houseplant.
   - Exposure: one small crescent-shaped bite; no larger piece seen swallowed; remainder of plant moved out of reach.
   - Time: ~9:22 AM today (Sat Mar 30).
   - Symptoms so far: brief repeated licking, one drool event.
   - Symptoms NOT seen: no facial swelling, no vomiting, no weakness, no collapse, breathing normal, walking normally, alert.
   - Kibo's approximate weight, age, current medications, and any chronic conditions.

4. WHAT NOT TO DO
   - Do NOT induce vomiting.
   - Do NOT force food, water, milk, or any liquid into his mouth.
   - Do NOT give hydrogen peroxide, activated charcoal, salt, oils, Pepto, Benadryl, or any other medication without vet guidance.
   - Do NOT scrub the mouth roughly or apply alcohol/peroxide to the gums.
   - Do NOT wait and watch if symptoms escalate (see below) — call immediately.

5. SYMPTOMS MEAN EMERGENCY VET NOW (go straight to nearest ER clinic)
   - Any swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or throat.
   - Difficulty breathing, noisy breathing, panting at rest, pale/blue/gray gums.
   - Repeated vomiting, retching, or vomiting blood.
   - Persistent or escalating drooling beyond the single event.
   - Pawing at the face, rubbing face on the floor, refusing to be touched near the mouth.
   - Difficulty swallowing, gagging, or seeming to choke.
   - Refusal of water for several hours, signs of dehydration.
   - Lethargy, weakness, stumbling, or collapse.
   - Hiding, restlessness, or guarding the mouth/face that gets worse over 2–4 hours.

If any of those appear, skip the phone consult and go directly to the emergency veterinary clinic. A mild pothos nibble in a dog typically resolves with mouth rinsing and a few hours of monitoring; the watch window is the next 2–4 hours for swelling or breathing changes, and the next 24 hours for GI signs.

Here's a careful reconciliation checklist. The short version: the payment is real, the bank debit and Direct Pay confirmation are your proof, and entering it manually on Form 1040 line 26 is the correct path — sending another payment would create an overpayment you'd have to chase back.

ORIENTATION — what this payment almost certainly is
- A Direct Pay transaction dated Jan 15, 2024 for "estimated tax" / "1040-ES" is, by default, the Q4 2023 estimated tax payment (Jan 15, 2024 was the Q4 2023 deadline). It belongs on the 2023 return, not 2024.
- Direct Pay is federal only. A separate state estimated payment, if any, is irrelevant here.
- The $2,000 is a credit against 2023 total tax, not a payment of 2023 tax due — that distinction is why it lives on line 26, not on the balance-due line.

1. GATHER THE EVIDENCE BEFORE YOU TOUCH THE RETURN
- IRS Direct Pay confirmation: capture the confirmation number, payment date (Jan 15, 2024), amount ($2,000), tax type ("estimated tax / 1040-ES"), tax year selected (verify: 2023), and the last 4 of the bank account used.
- Bank statement or transaction detail showing the matching debit on or around Jan 15, 2024 for $2,000.
- The 2023 software return file (pre-entry copy if your software supports snapshots, so you can show the before/after delta).
- If a preparer is doing the return, your short note for them (template at the bottom).

2. ENTER IT ONCE, IN THE RIGHT PLACE
- Form 1040, line 26: "2023 estimated tax payments and amount applied from 2022 return." Manual entry of $2,000.
- In the software: skip the import; open the estimated tax payments / federal payments screen and add it manually. Do not also re-enter it on line 25 (that's withholding from W-2s and 1099-R/1099-MISC) and do not enter it on the balance-due line.
- Watch for a tax-year mismatch field — Direct Pay lets you choose 2023 vs. 2024 at checkout. Confirm the entry is tagged to 2023.
- If the software splits estimated payments by quarter, put all $2,000 in Q4 (the Jan 15, 2024 slot). Do not invent amounts for Q1–Q3.

3. RECOMPUTE AND VERIFY THE DELTA
- Recompute the return after entry.
- The new balance-due or refund should differ from the pre-entry result by exactly $2,000 in your favor:
  - If pre-entry was "balance due $X," post-entry should be "balance due $(X − 2,000)" or "refund $2,000 − X."
  - If pre-entry was already a refund $Y, post-entry should be "refund $(Y + 2,000)."
- If the delta is anything other than exactly $2,000, something double-counted or was mis-tagged — stop and review before filing.
- Check the underpayment-penalty / Form 2210 calculation. If the software now shows a penalty that wasn't there before, the line 26 entry didn't flow through to the 2210 module. Safe harbor: total tax owed after withholding is under $1,000, OR estimated payments + withholding are at least 90% of 2023 total tax, OR estimated payments + withholding are at least 100% of 2022 total tax (110% if 2022 AGI > $150k). Most filers hit one of these — but only if the $2,000 is in the right cell.

4. DOCUMENTATION TO KEEP WITH THE RETURN FILE
A one-page reconciliation note with:
  - Payment date: Jan 15, 2024
  - Amount: $2,000.00
  - IRS Direct Pay confirmation number
  - Tax year / type: 2023 estimated tax (1040-ES)
  - Bank debit reference (date, amount, last 4 of account)
  - Return entry: Form 1040, line 26, $2,000
  - Recomputed result: balance due / refund before vs. after (showing the $2,000 delta)
Attach copies of: Direct Pay confirmation, bank statement line, and the software summary page showing line 26 = $2,000. Keep these with your tax records for at least 3 years (and longer if you also have the corrected 1099-B from earlier this month, since that has its own retention).

5. IF THE IRS ACCOUNT TRANSCRIPT LATER DOESN'T SHOW IT
This does happen — payments can lag, post to a different cycle, or be misapplied. Order of operations:
- Wait 4–6 weeks after the payment date before worrying. A Jan 15 payment is normally visible on the January or February transcripts well before a March/April filing.
- After filing, an IRS account transcript (pulled at irs.gov → "Get Transcript") should reflect the payment applied to 2023. If it doesn't:
  a. Pull the transcript again ~30 days after filing — postings often take a cycle or two to appear.
  b. If still missing after 6 weeks post-filing, call IRS Individual / Payer Services with the Direct Pay confirmation number. They can trace by trace number from the confirmation.
  c. If the payment was misapplied (e.g., posted to 2024 instead of 2023), the IRS can move it internally — usually no Form 1040-X needed, but ask them to confirm in writing or note it on the call reference number.
  d. If the IRS eventually issues a bill for unpaid 2023 tax because they never saw the payment, your evidence package (Direct Pay confirmation + bank debit + line 26 of filed return + reconciliation note) is the dispute. Do not pay twice. Reference the confirmation / trace number on any correspondence.
- The Direct Pay confirmation number is the authoritative proof. Bank debit is corroborating. The filed return's line 26 ties the two together.

6. NOTE TO THE PREPARER (if applicable — drop-in template)
  "IRS Direct Pay payment of $2,000 on Jan 15, 2024 for 2023 estimated tax was missed by the software import (confirmation #XXXX, last 4 of account ####). Bank debit confirmed; do not initiate a duplicate payment. Please add manually to Form 1040 line 26. Reconciliation note and copies of the confirmation and bank line attached."

7. WHAT NOT TO DO
- Do not send a second $2,000 payment "just to be safe." The bank already debited; IRS already has the money. A second payment creates an overpayment that costs you time to recover.
- Do not add the $2,000 to withholding on line 25 — it's not withholding.
- Do not let the software default to "no estimated payments made" and silently proceed.
- Do not file before line 26 is correct, even if the rest of the return is ready — the underpayment penalty and balance due both depend on it.

Likely cause: IRS Direct Pay is a free-form ACH push from a bank account, not tied to your SSN in the importer's feed the way W-2 withholding is, so most tax software misses it on import. The IRS itself has the payment — your confirmation plus the matching $2,000 bank debit are the source of truth; no need to re-pay.

What to do:
  1. Give the confirmation to the preparer and have them enter the $2,000 manually on the 2023 Form 1040 estimated-tax line rather than relying on the import.
  2. (Optional belt-and-suspenders) Pull your IRS Tax Account transcript at irs.gov → "Get Transcript" — it will list the payment posted to tax year 2023. Useful if the preparer wants a second-source confirmation.

Lemon-couscous bowl with warm chickpeas, blistered tomatoes & wilted spinach, lemon-garlic yogurt on top. 25 min active, holds covered for ~20 min if she slips. One pot (couscous) + one skillet (chickpeas) + one bowl (sauce).

Quantities (for 2)
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained, patted dry on a towel
- ~3 oz baby spinach (2 big handfuls)
- 1 cup cherry tomatoes, halved (or left whole if small)
- 3/4 cup dry instant couscous
- 3/4 cup water or low-sodium broth
- 3/4 cup plain whole-milk yogurt (Greek)
- 1 small lemon: zest the whole thing, juice half into sauce, other half for finishing
- 3 garlic cloves: 1 grated into sauce, 2 minced for the pan
- 2 tbsp olive oil, split (1 for couscous pot, 1 for skillet)
- Spices: 1 tsp cumin, 3/4 tsp smoked paprika, pinch red pepper flakes, salt, black pepper
- Optional: chopped parsley or scallion greens to finish

Sequencing (target her arrival 9:30 → start 9:05)

9:05  Sauce (bowl): yogurt + grated garlic + most of the lemon zest + small squeeze of lemon juice + pinch salt + 1 tsp olive oil. Stir, cover, into the fridge.
9:05  Pot on high: water/broth + 1 tsp olive oil + pinch salt. Cover to bring to a boil.
9:06  Boil → stir in couscous, kill the heat, lid on tight. Don't touch for 10 min.
9:07  Skillet on medium: 1 tbsp olive oil, minced garlic, cumin, smoked paprika, red pepper flakes. 30 sec — just fragrant, not brown.
9:08  Chickpeas + tomatoes in. Season with salt and pepper. Medium-high, stir every minute or so. 6-7 min — you want the tomatoes to blister and split and the chickpeas to get a little color on them.
9:15  Add spinach in two handfuls, toss until just wilted, 1-2 min. Kill heat. Lid on.
9:17  Couscous: lid off, fluff with a fork. If it's clumped, splash 1 tbsp hot water and fork again.

Plate
Couscous on the bottom, chickpea-tomato-spinach mixture over it, big spoonful of yogurt sauce on top, finish with the reserved lemon zest, a squeeze of the other lemon half, a drizzle of olive oil, salt and pepper. Eat straight from the bowls — no second dish to wash.

Wait/hold if her departure slips
- Skillet (covered, off-heat): holds up to ~20 min. Tomatoes soften further but flavor holds. To reheat, low-medium 2-3 min covered — don't crank it, you don't want to overcook the spinach.
- Couscous (covered): holds 20+ min fine. Before serving, fork-fluff and splash 1 tbsp hot water if it's gone tight.
- Sauce (covered, fridge): pull out 5 min before plating so it isn't fridge-cold. Don't add the lemon zest to the sauce earlier than you have to — it dulls and bleeds color. (You already zested most of it in at the start, so just hold the reserved pinch for plating.)

Don'ts
- Don't add salt to the chickpeas until they're already in the pan — salt early pulls moisture and they steam instead of blister.
- Don't wilt the spinach with the tomatoes. It goes gray and watery. Add it last, off the heat is fine.
- Don't add the lemon to the chickpea pan. It dulls the smoky notes. Lemon only goes on sauce and as a finish squeeze.
