Quick read: the request is a soft pre-screen, not an application. The agent has confirmed the slot is independent of submission, which is the only thing that makes this question even worth thinking about — it means you're not trading your Saturday for compliance. But "soft" doesn't mean "free." Photo IDs and pay stubs are PII, and pre-viewing is exactly when you have the least leverage to control how that PII is stored, forwarded, or used later.

What I'd recommend providing now: nothing by way of actual documents. If you want to signal seriousness (and you don't have to), send a short plain-text email — names, occupations, employer, rough income bracket (e.g., "combined gross ~$X"), dog (breed/weight), intended move-in, and a line that says you'll bring full application materials if you decide to apply after seeing the unit. That covers everything a legitimate pre-screen is trying to filter on, with no documents changing hands. If the agent won't accept that and pushes for actual IDs/stubs before the viewing, that's a signal about how the rest of the process will go.

What to wait on — until after the viewing, and only if you decide to apply:
  - Photo IDs: hold. NY has no pre-viewing entitlement to these.
  - Pay stubs: hold. Pay stubs leak employer, exact income, pay cadence, and often the last 4 of an account or SSN — useful phishing fuel.
  - Current address: trivial on its own, but only relevant in an application package.
  - SSN / bank account / credit check authorization: not *** and would be a hard no pre-viewing regardless. If it comes up later, it's application-stage only, ideally through the building management's own process.
  - Any application fee: NY limits who can charge and how much; a viewing should never involve money changing hands.

Process safeguards before you hand anything over, application-stage:
  - Confirm exactly who you're sending to. Listing-agent email is fine for a viewing appointment; full application packets should go to the building's management/leasing office through their portal (Dotloop, DocuSign, building-specific system) — not as email attachments to an individual.
  - Verify the agent's identity against the NY DOS Division of Licensing Services public lookup if you haven't already. A referred broker is one thing; an unfamiliar agent who approached you is another.
  - Redact before you send: most application packets accept pay stubs with SSN and full account numbers blacked out. If they insist on unredacted, ask why and in writing.
  - Never pay an application fee to an individual agent's personal account; fees go to the managing entity.

Fit against your standing criteria, since you'll want to verify these on Saturday:
  - Rent $4,275 is under your $4,800 ceiling — fine on paper.
  - Pet-friendly per the listing — confirm what "friendly" means (breed/weight restrictions, pet rent, deposit).
  - Commute to Devika's Manhattan hospital: 402 45th St is in Sunset Park/Borough Park depending on the cross street; that's typically 40-55 min door-to-door on the D/N/R. Verify the specific cross street and the realistic morning time, not just the subway map time.
  - The 8x10 "second bedroom" is the single biggest thing to measure in person — that's a nursery-or-office room, not a real bedroom. If it's a flex space being marketed as a bedroom, the legal bedroom count and rent classification matter (and affect what a broker can lawfully charge).
  - You already planned to check street noise, actual measurements, laundry access, and lease fees in person — keep that list and add: pet addendum terms, broker fee structure (who pays, how much), and whether the unit is rent-stabilized or a free-market rental (the agent must disclose this in NY).

Bottom line: go to the viewing with zero documents sent. If the apartment is right and you decide to apply, that's when you produce an application packet — through the building's official channel, with redactions, after you've verified the agent and the management entity. Pre-viewing document handoff gives you nothing you can't get with a short email and costs you PII you can't un-share.

No terminal/exec here either — pure chat plus memory. I have enough from the prompt + memory context. Let me write the diagnosis.

Diagnosis

This is not an artifact-substitution problem. The artifact is authentic and intact. It is an attestation-subject mismatch — the artifact's identity in the registry does not match what the SLSA/in-toto attestation claims it built.

Why it's a mismatch, not substitution:

The expected subject is the digest of the manifest list (a fat manifest that points at per-platform child images). The attested subject is the digest of the linux/amd64 child image. Those two digests refer to different OCI objects:

- sha256:9f41d8c0... — the index/manifest-list object the deploy pipeline pinned for promotion (what the policy compares against).
- sha256:21b77a6e... — the per-platform image manifest the build actually produced and that the SLSA provenance was generated over.

The artifact on the wire is the correct linux/amd64 image. The provenance is correctly describing what was built. What's wrong is the deployment policy is asserting that the manifest list digest and the image digest are the same thing — they aren't, by construction in OCI registries.

This is a subject-format error in either the attestation generator or the verifier, not a tampering signal. If the artifact had been substituted, the attested subject would be a digest that exists in the registry but doesn't match the bytes you have — typically the attestation would still resolve but the hash of the pulled artifact would diverge from the attestation's subject. Here, both digests are real registry objects; they just refer to different layers of the same multi-arch image. So no provenance re-signing, no manifest regeneration, no --insecure-policy override is the right move.

Classification: attestation-subject mismatch (subject-format), not artifact-substitution.

Safe release correction (no bypass)

Pick one — both fix the verifier, neither touches the artifact or the attestation:

1. Verifier-side fix (smallest, preferred for staging): the policy should accept either the manifest list digest OR the resolved child-platform image digest. In Sigstore/cosign terms, the predicate's subject digests are a list, and multi-arch images legitimately attest per-platform images. Change the rule from "manifest digest == subject[0]" to "subject contains {expected_manifest_list_digest OR resolved_child_digest_for_target_platform}". This keeps the attestation valid, keeps the artifact valid, and unblocks staging.

2. Provenance-side fix (only if you want the attestation to mirror the manifest-list subject for downstream policy uniformity): re-run the provenance generator with --subject-image-ref pointed at the manifest list (not the child image), so subject[0] = sha256:9f41d8c0.... Then re-sign and re-upload the attestation. Don't republish the artifact.

What NOT to do:
- Do not pass --insecure-policy, --skip-attestation, or any verification bypass — that would actually create the substitution-failure mode this gate is meant to catch.
- Do not regenerate the linux/amd64 image hoping the digest changes to match — it won't, and if it does you've actually substituted bytes, which is the real failure mode.
- Do not rewrite the attestation to claim sha256:9f41d8c0... as its subject while the build really produced sha256:21b77a6e... — that's the only path here that would be lying about provenance.

Recommendation for this specific 3.8.2 staging release: apply option 1 to the verifier rule, re-run the gate against the existing staging artifact and existing attestation, then proceed with staging. If Nadia wants verifier-side changes to be reviewable, file it as a small verifier patch with a focused regression test (manifest-list subject case + per-platform-image subject case + true mismatch case) rather than a broader signing redesign. Pair with Wes per the shard-keeper pair-only rule before any prod promotion.

Validation is on the exemplar's own label set, not on the metric sample.

ingest-edge validates exemplar label values separately from sample (metric) label values. The 128-byte cap applies to each value on the exemplar itself. The exemplar carried by the affected sample has a `trace_id` label value of 142 bytes, so ingest-edge rejects the write (HTTP 400, "exemplar label value exceeds 128 bytes") before the request is accepted. The sample's metric labels and timestamps are validated under separate rules and were fine — the series is dropped because the exemplar attached to it fails its own check, not because of anything on the metric side.

Direct answers for Support:

1. Shortening an ordinary sample label will NOT help. Sample labels and exemplar labels are validated independently; the 400 is on the exemplar's `trace_id`, not on any metric label. Reducing a metric label leaves the exemplar untouched, so the request would still 400.

2. Resending the same payload will NOT succeed. Remote-write has no partial-success (unlike OTLP) — a 400 is a deterministic server-side reject of the whole payload. As long as the exemplar's `trace_id` is 142 bytes, every retry produces the same error.

What the customer must change before retrying:

- The exemplar's `trace_id` label value must be <= 128 bytes. This is fixed on the client side before remote-write submission; no server-side change is needed.
- 142 chars is well above the standard 32-hex-char W3C / OTel trace_id. They are almost certainly submitting a non-standard ID — vendor extension, embedded parent context, base64 of a longer payload, or `traceparent` concatenated with extra data. They should normalize in the remote-write client:
  - Prefer the canonical 32-hex-char trace_id (extract it from `traceparent` if that's the source).
  - Or hash to a fixed-length form (e.g., SHA-256 hex = 64 chars).
  - Truncation alone is lossy and collides; avoid it unless they're sure uniqueness is preserved.
- The full raw trace ID belongs in logs / traces / span attributes — not on the exemplar label. That matches the existing rule (raw identifiers stay in log fields; the metric/exemplar uses a bounded form).

After the client emits a normalized `trace_id` on the exemplar, the retry should accept. Nothing else in the payload needs to change.

DECISION: Reject the eviction proposal. Keep the 429-at-admission boundary.

WHY

The metrics-router queue sits at the durable-accept boundary. Once a request is queued, the caller can reasonably treat it as accepted under the same convention ingest-edge uses (202 Accepted = durably queued) and rely on the supported retry horizon (15 min, per the cross-service invariant). Evicting the oldest queued request silently drops durably-accepted work, breaks the idempotency invariant (smallest dedupe unit = smallest unit of durable commit), and gives the evicted caller no signal — so they retry, the retry gets admitted, and the "freshness" win is illusory because the evicted payload returns anyway. The 429 path is honest: we never claimed durability, so we can reject without breaking the contract.

The buffer-pool precedent from 2024-03-26 (64-buffer cap + drop-oversized) is the right pattern and aligns with what Wes is proposing: bound at the admission boundary (drop oversized pre-admit, reject on full post-admit). Never displace post-admit work.

If freshness is the real motivation, the right knobs are:
  - Per-tenant admission priority so a noisy tenant cannot starve fresh traffic
  - Age-based admission reject — reject if the queue's oldest item is already past a freshness budget, rather than silently evicting
  - Tighter cap on per-batch size, not on queue depth

FOCUSED TESTS REQUIRED BEFORE THIS CAN PROCEED

1. RETRY SIGNALING

  - 429 carries Retry-After (or equivalent retry-hint field) and the response body advertises the supported retry horizon. A client honoring the hint retries successfully within the horizon.
  - A retry after 429 that arrives within the horizon produces exactly one durable admit. rejected_total advances once on the reject, admitted_total advances once on the successful retry — never twice, never zero.
  - A retry that arrives past the horizon is rejected with an explicit error code, not silently absorbed and not silently accepted as a duplicate.
  - Partial-success / fanout accounting: a 429-then-retry pair is observable in logs as one rejected and one admitted, never as a duplicate accept.

2. ORDERING

  - Within a single tenant, batches admitted in arrival order are processed in arrival order across a queue-full transition (no head-of-line reordering across the fill/drain boundary).
  - A burst that triggers sustained 429s does not reorder the admitted batches that follow — the first batch admitted after the queue drains is the next arrival, not a backfilled one.
  - Per-tenant orderings are independent: one tenant's reject burst does not perturb another tenant's order.
  - Timestamps on admitted batches remain monotonic across the full fill/drain cycle.

3. ACCOUNTING

  - rejected_total advances by exactly 1 per 429 — no double-count under concurrent rejections, no leak under sustained burst, no under-count if the caller disconnects before reading the response.
  - admitted_total advances only on success; a rejected request later retried and admitted counts once (on success), not zero and not twice.
  - dropped_total stays at zero. This is the contract assertion: we do not silently drop post-admission work. Pin this as a hard invariant in the test.
  - Per-tenant rejected/admitted counters reconcile against the structured request log for a sustained-full window — no drift, no missing rows.
  - Capacity-math pin test: force sustained queue-full, assert rejected_total = N, admitted_total = cap, dropped_total = 0, queue_depth = cap exactly throughout.

4. RECOVERY AFTER QUEUE FALLS BELOW CAP

  - Once queue depth drops below the cap, the service resumes admitting immediately — no lingering throttle state, no false 429s on the first batch after recovery.
  - p99 latency returns to baseline within the documented recovery SLO (suggest 60s); queue age returns to baseline within 15 minutes per the runbook stop rule.
  - Memory slope returns to flat within 15 minutes of recovery; no monotonic rise during the drain (the 2024-02-22 preflight pause condition must not fire on the way down).
  - Retry storms arriving during the recovery window do not cause secondary admission failures — the service does not double-count or self-throttle after recovering capacity.
  - Deploy-pipeline rollback during a partial rollout does not strand in-flight accepted work: queued batches either continue to drain or are replayed on the previous build, and the rejected_total accounting on the rolled-back build reconciles.

NEXT STEP

If Wes still wants the freshness behavior, have him prototype the age-based admission reject (option above) on a single tenant in staging and rerun the same load harness. Compare freshness numbers against the eviction prototype. If age-based reject matches freshness without breaking ordering or accounting, that is the shape worth promoting — eviction never is, because it would force us to add post-admission signaling for displaced callers, which is a strictly larger change than tightening the admission boundary.

Diagnosis first: the foot skates because you load the sidepull before you load the smear. Pulling harder just unweights it more. Order has to change — feet first, body second, reach last.

Try this sequence on the next attempt:

1. Place the left foot on the smear slowly — big-toe pad flat, no scraping noise. Load weight onto it BEFORE you load the right hand. If the smear skates, weight almost always arrived after the hand did.

2. Drive the left hip INTO the wall until your center of mass sits over the left foot. You'll feel the rubber "turn on" — that sticky feeling is the cue that you're ready to move.

3. Right foot: point the toe toward the wall (or down-and-in), keep the leg active as a rudder. A passive right foot = a falling right hip = a skating left foot.

4. Brace the sidepull, don't pull it: right elbow drives toward the right hip (in and down), not straight down. Tension without peeling off the wall.

5. Reach from the hip, not the arm: eyes to the high left edge, rotate the left shoulder to the wall, keep the left arm straight until the last instant. The hand goes where the shoulder goes.

If the foot still skates after that, the smear is genuinely bad and the fix is mechanical — flag harder with the right leg or try a right-foot heel/toe hook on that low outside hold — not more arm pull.

Draft for Support — ingest-edge 429 handling (production ingest-edge v2.19.4+)

What the customer is seeing
  Production ingest-edge returns Retry-After in the 1–3 second range on 429
  responses. That value is randomized per response, is the minimum delay
  before the next retry attempt, and is not a guarantee that the next
  attempt will succeed.

What the client must do
  1. Treat each Retry-After header as the minimum delay for THAT retry.
     - Read the header on every 429 response. Do not cache the first value
       and reuse it for later retries.
     - Do not assume a constant value across responses — values are
       randomized 1–3s and will differ between 429s.
  2. Preserve an overall retry budget per request.
     - Cap total retry attempts (a small number, e.g. 3–5).
     - Cap total wall-clock retry time so a single request cannot retry
       indefinitely.
     - Once the budget is exhausted, stop retrying and surface the
       failure upstream rather than looping.
  3. Avoid synchronized immediate retries even after honoring the header.
     - Add client-side jitter on top of the server-provided Retry-After.
     - If no header is present, jitter an exponential backoff instead of
       using a fixed interval.
     - The server randomizes Retry-After to break up retry storms; clients
       must still avoid lockstep retries of their own.
  4. Treat each request independently.
     - A successful retry does not authorize ignoring later 429 responses.
       Each request sees its own backpressure state.

What NOT to tell the customer
  - Do not promise a retry will succeed. The randomized Retry-After
    reduces contention; it does not eliminate it.
  - Do not imply the server-side change removes the need for client
    backoff. Client backoff (jitter, retry budget, cap on attempts) is
    still required. The server-side randomization and the client-side
    backoff work together — neither is sufficient on its own.

Why this matters
  Fixed-second client retries against this endpoint previously produced
  visible retry-storm sawtooth patterns. The randomized 1–3s Retry-After
  on the server, combined with client-side jitter and a bounded retry
  budget, is what keeps accepted throughput stable under load.
Acknowledged — no further action needed.

TONIGHT — in this order

1. Photograph with scale. Take 2–3 more shots: one with a coin or ruler beside the patch for size, one wider shot showing where it sits in the ceiling, and one close-up of the edge. Confirm your phone is stamping the time on the image itself (Settings → Camera → "EXIF / timestamp" or similar).
2. Mark the edges. Lightly trace the outer edge of the darker area on the paint with a pencil. If the stain grows past your line overnight, that's a clear signal it's still active, not just a residual shadow from earlier rain.
3. Stage containment now, not after it drips. Place a flat tray, baking sheet, or wide bucket directly under the patch — even though nothing is dripping yet, a wet ceiling can start dripping without warning if it sags or more rain comes. Lay a towel under the tray in case it overflows.
4. Do not press, push, or drill the ceiling. Drywall holds more water than it looks like it can, then fails suddenly. Probing it now is how a stain becomes a collapse.
5. Keep Kibo and foot traffic clear of the area. If the surface releases, water and drywall debris fall straight down.
6. Check periodically. Every hour or two tonight, glance at the patch and the ceiling around it. Note any new spots, drip start, bubbling, sag, surface change, or smell.
7. Write down the rain timing. Note when the rain started and when you first saw the patch — building management or a roofer will want this. The Friday 4/5 riser-valve work is also worth flagging in your message as a second candidate cause, in case it isn't purely weather-driven.
8. Send the management message below now, Saturday night. Even if maintenance is closed until Monday, the message goes into the queue and you have a written, timestamped record.
9. Stage your escalation numbers where you can grab them fast: building super, building management emergency line, and (NYC) 311 for HPD non-emergency.

EMERGENCY ESCALATION — call now, do not wait for Monday

Any one of these is enough to stop waiting on the regular maintenance queue.

- The ceiling starts dripping and the flow rate is visibly increasing, or the tray fills within an hour.
- The surface begins to sag, bulge, blister, or feel soft/spongy when you press it lightly.
- Water reaches or visibly enters any light fixture, smoke or CO detector, outlet, switch, ceiling fan, or any wiring or cord.
- You hear cracking, popping, or hissing from the ceiling, or see the surface deform while you watch.
- The original stain grows noticeably fast (clearly more area within an hour), or new stains appear elsewhere on the ceiling or walls.
- Water runs down a wall or begins pooling on the floor.
- You smell something electrical — ozone, hot plastic, burning — or a breaker trips, lights flicker near the area, or you see sparking.
- An adjacent apartment (above or next door) reports a matching stain or leak — the cause is shared and ongoing.
- Rain is continuing or forecast to continue heavily overnight — the risk is escalating in real time, not theoretical.
- The affected area becomes unusable (over a cooking surface, sleeping path, or the only exit) and you cannot safely stay in the unit.

Who to call, in order:

What I changed, briefly: removed any version of "here's what I'm proposing, do you agree?" and replaced it with an experience-mapping frame (arrives → uncertain → workaround → example). Added the explicit "decision stays with my team" line so participants don't feel recruited into a verdict. Kept the offer to decline or shorten — that protects the people who'd otherwise opt out.

Yes — I agree with the direction, with two conditions I'll name at the end. First, where the current handoff actually breaks, then whether I'd use the package.

Where the current handoff causes trouble
  1. Silent drift. Tokens authored in Figma, transcribed by hand into the engineering JSON. Every transcription is a chance for a value, a name, or a casing to shift. Nobody notices until product renders look wrong, and by then the diff is in three places.
  2. Naming is not stable across surfaces. The same concept is `color.bg.surface` in Figma and `--bg-surface-1` in code, or `spacing.md` here and `space-400` there. Reviewers can't tell whether two tokens are the same token, related tokens, or accidentally-similar tokens.
  3. Partial updates. The handoff is a person copying some tokens to some surfaces. A change goes into Figma, then half the engineering consumers get it, and the rest catch up next quarter.
  4. No version story. When did `text.body` change weight? What was it before? Who approved the new value? Without versioning, "current" is whatever the loudest surface says today.
  5. No "correct use" reference. Engineers get a name and a hex. They don't get the canonical example of where this token applies versus a near-neighbor. The semantic intent lives in someone's head.
  6. The handoff is a person, not a system. If the person who usually does the transcription is out, the loop stalls, or worse, someone improvises.

Whether I'd use the proposed package
  Yes, if it satisfies three things I'd hold the line on:
    a. Single machine-readable source, and downstream is generated from it — not "alongside" it. If a human can edit a downstream representation, the source stops being canonical within a week.
    b. Generated examples live in the same package as the values. Token name + value + canonical "this is how you use it" snippet, versioned together. The example is part of the contract, not a doc that drifts.
    c. Clear ownership of the canonical file and a merge gate. "Approved" has to mean something concrete — design review, engineering review, or both — with the gate visible in the repo.

Two conditions before I'd call it done
  1. Authoring surface. The package being canonical doesn't say where it's authored. Figma-as-source fights the "generated from one file" rule because Figma files aren't diffable like code. Pick one: code-authored JSON as source with Figma generated, or a tool that treats both as views of one store. Don't let both be editable.
  2. Migration is in the package, not after it. The first version will need to absorb whatever is in Figma and engineering JSON today. If that mapping isn't done before the package ships, the old surfaces keep getting edited in parallel and the drift returns through the side door.

Net: the proposal is right, the failure modes above are the ones it actually fixes, and I'd use it on day one as long as the canonical file is genuinely canonical and the examples ship with the values.

The current rule has("env") && label("env") != "dev" short-circuits on has("env"): when the label is missing, the right side is never evaluated and the series is excluded. That is why the "env absent" bucket (6,772) lands on the not-routed side even though the customer wants it routed. The "env=dev" bucket (2,109) is correctly excluded. The 41,208 "env=prod" series are routed in both the old and new rule, so they are unaffected by the fix.

Corrected expression

  !has("env") || label("env") != "dev"

This routes when env is absent OR when env is anything other than "dev". A re-run of the dry-run should show routed = 41,208 + 6,772 = 47,980 and skipped = 2,109.

Truth table

  env label    has("env")   label("env")!="dev"   Old rule   New rule   Customer wants
  "prod"       true         true                  route      route      route
  "dev"        true         false                 skip       skip       skip
  absent       false        (not evaluated)       skip       route      route

Optional caveat to flag if the customer asks: if any series carries a non-prod, non-dev env value (e.g. "staging", "canary", ""), the corrected rule will route those too. The outer claw shell is keratin — same as a fingernail. A split near the tip with no bleeding, swelling, heat, limp, or licking is usually a superficial crack of just the husk. Low-risk, not an emergency tonight, but worth watching and worth a vet check if it stays loose.

TONIGHT — PROTECT THE CLAW
  - Don't pull, peel, or trim the loose piece yourself. Even a small tug can extend the crack into the quick (the live part with blood supply and nerves). One wiggle and you've got a bleeding, painful claw and a much harder vet visit.
  - If the paw is dirty, dip it in lukewarm water for 30–60 seconds and pat dry. No soap, no scrubbing, no ointments.
  - Stop the snagging. A snug sock over the paw (secured with a light wrap above the wrist — never tight) keeps the loose edge from catching on blankets and discourages licking. Take it off before bed so you can recheck in good light, or leave it on overnight if you have an e-collar handy and he tends to lick.
  - If you have an e-collar, use it overnight. Persistent moisture and chewing turn a benign crack into an infection in 24–48 hours.
  - Short leashed potty trip only. No zoomies, no fetch on grass, no rough-ground walks — anything that pulls the claw.
  - Dinner and water as normal.

TO TRIM OR NOT — DON'T DO IT YOURSELF
You can't see how deep the crack runs from the outside. The quick may sit further down the claw than it looks, especially if you see a faint dark line running up the center of the claw. A vet clips the loose shell back to healthy tissue in under a minute with proper restraint and lighting — quick isn't involved, no pain. If the quick IS involved, that's still a vet job, just with a tiny bit of cautery.

  - Faint dark line visible down the center of the claw (means the crack may be closer to the quick than it looks).
  - Claw looks discolored (brown, black, or green tinge) or has any odor.
  - Mild limp develops overnight even if he looks fine right now.

URGENT OR SAME-DAY VET VISIT
  - Active bleeding from the claw or quick.
  - Swelling, redness, or heat at the toe or paw.
  - Pus or any discharge.
  - Sudden or worsening limp, refusal to bear weight, or guarding the paw.
  - Whimpering, yelping when the paw is touched, or snapping at it.

This test only proves the happy path: full → reject, drain-by-one → admit. Everything else (Retry-After, identity, counters, concurrency at the boundary) is silently accepted. Three buckets before merge.

### 1. Contract assertions (single-threaded)

- **Retry-After on the 429** — `require.NotEmpty(t, resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))` and assert it's inside the 1–3s jitter window you validated on ingest-edge staging. Same value on every call = synchronized retry herd waiting to form.
- **Identity preservation** — `q.Len() == 20000` only proves count. Add: the rejected `nextRequest` is *not* in a snapshot of queue IDs; the admitted `retryRequest` *is* present at the expected position; the original 20000 are still there in original order.
- **Accounting counters** (the durable-accept contract depends on these):
  - `rejected_total` += exactly 1 per 429, no off-by-one across N back-to-back submits at cap.
  - `admitted_total` += exactly 1 on the retry 202, and *not* on the prior 429.
  - `dropped_total` stays at 0 — this is the whole point of the design (reject at admission, never evict post-admit). If it ever goes non-zero under this test, something is wrong.
  - Reconcile counters against the debug-log line for the same request IDs.
- **No debounce on first admit after drain** — `time.Since(completeOne) < 1ms` on the retry submit. If there's a hidden tick/batching layer, this catches it before users feel it.
- **Rejection reason in body** — 429 body identifies "queue full" distinctly from generic throttle/auth/rate-limit. Support needs this to triage tenant tickets.

### 2. Concurrency assertions

- **Parallel submitters vs. slow drainer** — N goroutines submit while one goroutine completes one item every X ms. For the whole run: `q.Len() <= cap` at every checkpoint (use `atomic.Int64` snapshots, not a getter that may lag); `admitted_total + rejected_total == total_submissions`; admitted rate matches drain rate within tolerance.
- **Per-tenant ordering** — two tenants submit interleaved during fill+drain; each tenant's requests come out in submit order. (If the design intentionally has no per-tenant queues, assert *that* explicitly — don't leave it implicit.)
- **Idempotent retry in flight** — same request retried before the original completes: exactly one admission, second is 429 or coalesced. Whichever the contract is, pin it; this is the durable-accept invariant from the original review.
- **Burst at the boundary** — N+M submits with `cap-N` queued and M completions arriving "simultaneously": exactly N admitted, M rejected. No overshoot past cap, no under-admit.

### 3. Race-sensitive check around the transition below the cap

This is the one that bites you. `Len() < cap` followed by `Push` is classic TOCTOU — two goroutines both see 19999, both push, queue ends at 20001.

```go
// Run with: go test -race -run TestAdmissionTransitionRace -count=200
func TestAdmissionTransitionRace(t *testing.T) {
    const cap = 20000
    q := newQueue(cap)
    fillQueue(t, q, cap-100)              // 100 slots free

    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    var admitted, rejected atomic.Int64

    for i := 0; i < 500; i++ {           // 500 submitters hammer the boundary
        wg.Add(1)
        go func() {
            defer wg.Done()
            switch submit(req).StatusCode {
            case 202: admitted.Add(1)
            case 429: rejected.Add(1)
            }
        }()
    }
    for i := 0; i < 50; i++ {            // 50 completions race in
        wg.Add(1)
        go func() {
            defer wg.Done()
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(rand.Intn(5)) * time.Millisecond)
            completeOne(q)
        }()
    }
    wg.Wait()

    require.Equal(t, int64(150), admitted.Load())   // 100 free + 50 drained
    require.Equal(t, int64(350), rejected.Load())   // 500 - 150
    require.LessOrEqual(t, q.Len(), cap)            // never over cap
    require.Equal(t, int64(500), admitted.Load()+rejected.Load())
}
```

Two race-specific items in addition to the test above:

- **`go test -race` clean for the whole suite.** If the queue's check-then-enqueue has any non-atomic path, `-race` will surface it. Make sure the CI invocation includes `-race` for this package; if it doesn't, that's a separate gap.
- **Stress the existing recovery test.** Wrap `fillQueue → reject → completeOne → admit` in a loop and run with `-count=1000`. A flaky transition only fails 1-in-N; you want that 1 in CI, not in prod.

### Recommendation

Don't block the recovery test from landing, but block the merge until (a) Retry-After + accounting assertions and (b) the race test above are in the same PR. As written, this test would pass even if admission had no Retry-After header, no counters, and a racy `Len()` check — that's not enough signal to ship behind.

If useful, I can draft the full `queue_recovery_test.go` (contract + concurrency + race) so Wes can paste it in as a single follow-up commit rather than three small ones.

Verdict: three defects in the proposal. The direction (separate attempted/validated/active) is right, but two of the three advance points are wrong, and the fallback clause bakes in the original bug.

Defect 1 -- validated_generation advances too early
"After schema validation but before dynamic validation" leaves a window where validated_generation claims success for a config that fails semantic checks. The April 8 incident (flush_interval=0s) is exactly this case: schema-valid, semantically invalid. Schema validation does not mean reload-ready.

Defect 2 -- active_generation mutates before fan-out completes
"Changes before the configuration is fanned out to workers" is the April 8 observability defect, restated. /healthz must never report a generation as active until every worker has accepted.

Defect 3 -- the fallback clause bakes in the bug
"Old configuration remains in use even though active_generation already shows the requested generation" describes a state in which the endpoint lies about what is running. Per the April 8 patch invariant, active_generation only mutates on swap, and "swap" means every worker has accepted and committed.

Corrected semantics

Fields:
  G_attempted  last generation whose config the parser accepted (syntax-valid)
  G_validated  last generation whose config passed schema AND dynamic/semantic validation
  G_active     generation whose config is currently serving on every worker

Per-reload-attempt invariants (candidate generation N):

  1. G_attempted is set to N only after read+parse succeed. It is a parse-success counter, not a progress signal. Mutation point: end of parse.

  2. G_validated is set to N only after schema validation AND dynamic/semantic validation both succeed. Mutation point: end of dynamic validation, never before.

  3. G_active is set to N only after every worker has accepted the new config AND every worker has committed (atomic swap). Any worker rejection or partial commit aborts the swap; G_active stays at its previous value.

  4. None of the three fields roll back on failure. They only advance. A later successful reload writes a higher N. A failed reload leaves a gap (e.g., G_attempted=N, G_validated=N-2, G_active=N-2) that is itself the observability signal.

  5. /healthz status stays 200 across all reload outcomes; only G_active determines what is serving. 200 != reload success.

Failure-mode matrix (candidate generation N):

  syntax failure             G_attempted unchanged, G_validated unchanged, G_active unchanged
  schema-validation failure  G_attempted=N,         G_validated unchanged, G_active unchanged
  dynamic validation failure G_attempted=N,         G_validated unchanged, G_active unchanged
  partial worker reject      G_attempted=N,         G_validated=N,         G_active unchanged
  full accept + commit       G_attempted=N,         G_validated=N,         G_active=N

Endpoint contract:

  GET /healthz -> 200 {
    status,
    active_generation,            # what is running (G_active)
    last_attempted_generation,    # most recent parse-success (G_attempted)
    last_validated_generation,    # most recent fully-validated (G_validated)
    last_attempt_status           # parse_failed | schema_failed | dynamic_failed | fanout_partial_reject | committed
  }

  - active_generation is the only field that reflects what is running.
  - last_attempt_status names the failure mode of the most recent attempt; on fanout_partial_reject it includes the failing worker IDs and reject reason.

Operator read:

  active == validated == attempted                          in sync, swap landed
  active <  validated                                      staged, awaiting fan-out (wait or revert file)
  validated < attempted                                    last attempt parsed but failed validation; check last_attempt_status
  any of the above can be observed without any service impact -- G_active has not moved

Implementation note (not the patch): the fan-out must be two-phase prepare/commit. Prepare: every worker validates locally and returns accept/reject. Commit: sent only if every worker accepted; each worker atomically swaps on receipt. G_active is written after the final commit ACK, not when prepare is sent. This is the only shape under which "every worker has accepted" is the gate.

Recommendation: ask Wes to redraft with the corrected mutation points and remove the fallback clause. The endpoint field shape (active/attempted/validated/status) is fine -- only the advance points need fixing.

What's failing

`invalid-gzip-header` is a content-validation 400. The receiver decompresses the body before parsing it, and the first bytes do not match the gzip magic (0x1F 0x8B). The capture confirms it: the wire body is raw protobuf, not gzipped bytes. The client set `Content-Encoding: gzip` but its encoder pipeline did not actually run. This is a client-side serialization bug, not a server or transport problem. The 400 is deterministic — the same bytes produce the same error on every attempt, regardless of timing or load.

Valid corrections

The client must produce a body whose bytes actually match the declared encoding:

1. Enable compression in the OTLP exporter configuration (e.g. `OtlpHttpExporter` `compression: gzip`, or the SDK equivalent) and confirm the compressed variant is wired into the export path. Setting the configuration flag is not sufficient on its own — verify the exporter being constructed is the compressed one.
2. Validate locally before sending: pipe the request body through `gzip -t`, or read the first two bytes and assert `0x1F 0x8B`. Do this once on a sample request to prove the encoder is live.
3. Once the body is genuinely gzipped, replay the buffered points. Treat the failure as non-transient at the protocol level and replay only what was never accepted — same rule that applies to OTLP partial-success rejections (do not resend the full batch blindly; resend the points the server has not yet acknowledged).

Why retrying the unchanged body does not help

Retrying the same bytes re-sends the same deterministic 400. Each attempt wastes a request, holds the buffered data in the client's queue, and consumes server capacity with zero chance of acceptance. Backoff between attempts does not change the input. The buffer will grow while nothing drains. The retry should only happen after the encoder is verified.

Why removing `Content-Encoding: gzip` alone is not enough

If the body is uncompressed protobuf, dropping the header sends the raw bytes — closer to valid, but the OTLP/HTTP receiver still requires an advertised encoding for export, and an uncompressed batch will hit the decoded-body size limit (10 MiB on ingest-edge) on the first export well before any buffered backlog drains. Relabeling the request without compressing it trades a deterministic 400 for a deterministic 413. The fix is to compress, not to relabel.

Why 429 `Retry-After` does not apply

429 is a transient capacity signal; the server sends `Retry-After` to mean "wait at least N seconds". 400 `invalid-gzip-header` is a content error: the body is syntactically invalid for the declared encoding regardless of timing. No amount of waiting turns non-gzip bytes into gzip bytes. Applying 429 backoff loops forever with no progress, and if the client uses a shared token bucket, it also starves other traffic behind the same limiter. The right backoff for a deterministic 4xx is: fix the encoder, validate locally with `gzip -t`, then replay the buffered points once. `Retry-After` is reserved for 429/503 and is not read off 4xx content errors.

Recommendation: CAP the backfill — do not pause it, do not roll back the service.

Why cap, not pause:
- Customer write path is healthy. Ingestion write p99 = 92 ms, zero batches rejected. The service is functioning for live traffic; the degradation is localized to compaction and downstream query p99.
- Cause is identified and bounded: one tenant's backfill = 43% of compaction reads. That is a known, targeted input — not a non-transient regression.
- Pause is disproportionate. The 2024-03-14 / 2024-03-26 pattern is consistent: throttle + bounded cap with jitter outperforms both "raise the limit" and "stop entirely." Apply that here.
- Backfill is a planned, announced-window operation. Halting it fully has its own operator cost and downstream schedule cost; throttling preserves forward progress while the backlog drains.

How to cap (for Cyrus):
- Reduce the tenant's contribution to compaction reads — target ~50% of current per-instance rate, or a fixed RPS cap that brings the tenant's share of compaction reads under ~25%.
- Break the long backfill into shorter bursts with gaps (jitter, not just lower rate). This stops the backfill from synchronizing with the natural compaction cadence and amplifying the backlog spike pattern.
- Keep the cap in place; do not flip back to full rate when metrics improve — ramp in steps.

Recovery thresholds — ALL must hold for 30 continuous minutes before lifting the cap:
  1. Compaction backlog age ≤ 25 min (near the 18-min starting baseline) AND trending down over the window.
  2. Query p99 ≤ 280 ms (near the 240 ms baseline).
  3. Disk utilization ≤ 75% with no monotonic rise over the window.
  4. Compaction-read mix — tenant's share ≤ 25%, no new dominant read source.

Re-introduction plan (after thresholds hold):
- Step the cap up in increments (e.g., +25% every 15 min). Hold each step if backlog age creeps up by >5 min or query p99 drifts up by >10%. Use alert aggregation max by (service, rollout) — do not let an averaging rollup mask a single-bucket spike.

Escalation triggers — these flip the call from cap to full pause:
- Compaction backlog age keeps rising past 90 min despite the cap.
- Query p99 exceeds 800 ms.
- Ingestion write p99 drifts above 120 ms (the customer write path starts to feel it).
- Any batch rejection or non-zero dropped-write signal from rollup-service or metrics-router.

Framing for the note to Cyrus: this is a tenant-side operational throttle on a known workload, not a service rollback. The service is healthy on the customer path; the backfill needs to share the compaction budget. Roll back the cap, not the service.

The core invariants in Anya's draft (block publish on generator failure, never commit/rewrite from CI, gate publish on a clean drift check) are the right shape. They close the silent-publish and silent-rewrite paths the question is asking about, with one assumption that needs to be made explicit and a few edges worth tightening.

Edges worth tightening in the draft itself

1. Partial output on exit 0. The draft treats "exits unsuccessfully" as the failure signal. A generator can crash mid-write, recover, and return 0, or a buggy generator can return 0 after writing a truncated file. Before diffing, the check should assert the candidate is parseable, schema-valid, non-empty, and that the generator's own "complete" sentinel fired. Drift-check cannot rescue a partial that happens to byte-match the committed file — only an explicit completeness check can.

2. Determinism is a prerequisite, not a check. If the generator is non-deterministic (different key ordering, timestamps in output, locale-dependent serialization), every run diffs and the check is either always red (noise) or, worse, accidentally re-matches a stale value. Make generator determinism an explicit property with a fixture test, and consider normalizing JSON before comparing.

3. Key-level diff must include value changes. "Key-level" usually means keys added/removed/renamed. The interesting silent failure is "same key, different value" (e.g., spacing 16 → 14 with no rename). The diff contract should be value-aware per leaf, not just structural.

4. Pin by content hash, not ref. "Pinned version of the canonical package" is sound only if the pin is a content-addressable hash (git SHA, package integrity hash). A tag or branch pin can move under you; a force-pushed ref makes the pipeline reproducible against something that no longer exists. Verify the pin type in CI.

5. Record the canonical version on the published artifact. Each published engineering JSON / Figma-facing blob should carry the canonical version (or content hash) it was generated from. This is what lets a future reader tell "this drift is expected, the canonical moved" from "this drift is a generator bug." Without it, every diff is a manual investigation.

6. "Publishing" needs to be a named, atomic action. Block-on-failure only works if publishing is a single, well-defined step the same job gates. If publishing is a downstream merge, registry upload, Figma plugin pull, and Slack ping across multiple jobs, the block has to cover all of them or one will leak. Define the publish action and put it behind the same gate; if it spans systems, use a single publish token/marker that each consumer checks.

7. Diff visibility. "Uploads a key-level diff" should land where reviewers actually see it — a PR comment or a run summary, not just a CI artifact. An artifact nobody opens is functionally silent.

8. The committed representation should be write-protected, not just non-committed-by-CI. CI not committing is necessary but not sufficient: a hand-edit on the branch will not publish (drift will fail), but it will block the next legitimate publish with a confusing diff. Treat the committed file as generated-only via CODEOWNERS / branch protection, or generate into a separate artifact path that humans cannot edit directly.

9. Figma has two drift surfaces, not one. The Figma-facing JSON is one. Whatever a designer has actually imported into the live Figma file (variables, styles) is another. The pipeline catches drift between canonical and the published JSON; it does not, by itself, catch drift between the published JSON and what Figma currently holds. If the import is manual, add a separate check (or a policy) that the Figma file was re-imported from the latest published blob. If the import is plugin-driven and auto, state that and verify the plugin actually ran.

10. Structural drift ≠ semantic correctness. The drift check is structural. A generator bug that consistently produces a wrong but stable value (e.g., divides spacing by 2) will pass drift forever. Golden-output tests with hand-picked known values, plus a small set of invariants (e.g., "primary color matches brand spec", "spacing scale is monotonic") belong in the generator's own test suite, not in this CI gate.

Out of scope for this draft but worth flagging upstream

- Canonical-side governance (who can edit the canonical, change log, review requirements) is what makes the pipeline trustworthy. The drift check is a consumer of canonical integrity, not a substitute for it.
- Supply chain on the generator itself: pin generator version, code review generator changes, signed builds. A compromised generator that always produces the committed output is the cleanest silent rewrite imaginable.

Verdict

On the three failure modes you asked about:
- Generator failure: handled, as long as "unsuccessful" includes exit ≠ 0 *and* a post-exit completeness check on the candidate.
- Partial output: handled only with a completeness check added; not handled by exit code alone.
- Unexpected diff: handled — diff blocks publish and is surfaced — provided the diff includes value changes and lands in a visible place (PR comment), and the committed file is treated as generated-only so the diff signal is meaningful and not mixed with hand-edits.

The draft is close to safe. The two changes that move it from "mostly safe" to "safe" are (a) the post-exit completeness assertion, and (b) treating the committed representation as write-protected rather than just non-CI-written.

Based on what you're describing — landed on a foot, rolled inward (inversion = lateral ligaments loaded), can bear weight >4 steps, no bony tenderness over either malleolus, no deformity, no numbness, mild lateral swelling — this reads as a low-grade lateral ankle sprain (likely ATFL, the front-of-ankle ligament). The Ottawa Ankle Rules are negative here, so an X-ray isn't indicated on the basis of the exam alone. Practical plan for the rest of Sunday and onward:

REST OF SUNDAY

    MICE today (skip "protection" beyond what pain dictates; gentle movement within tolerance actually helps healing):

      Ice: 15–20 min on, 40 min off, through the afternoon. Stop after today — beyond 24–48h, ice hasn't shown added benefit and can blunt the inflammatory signal you actually want.

      Compression: an elastic bandage in a figure-8 (heel-locked) pattern, or a knit ankle sleeve. Snug but not numb — you should be able to wiggle your toes fully and not feel pins-and-needles. Take it off if you sleep.

      Elevation: above heart level when sitting/lying for the next few hours. Pillow under the calf, not the heel (heel pressure is uncomfortable and unhelpful).

    Walking is fine, but minimize unnecessary steps this afternoon. No driving if the right ankle is your accelerator foot and braking feels hesitant.

    Pain: ibuprofen 400 mg with food if you need it and have no contraindications (kidney issues, ulcers, anticoagulants). Acetaminophen 500–1000 mg is a fine alternative if you want to avoid NSAIDs in the first 48h. Either is OK; don't combine them without a reason.

    Hydrate, eat normally. Skip the bouldering / running / cutting plan for the rest of the weekend.

GENTLE MOVEMENT TIMELINE

    Tonight (Sunday evening), within a pain-free range, no forced end-range:

      Ankle alphabets — trace the letters A–Z in the air, slowly.
      Slow circles both directions, ~10 each.
      Towel scrunches — seated, scrunch a towel toward you with your toes, 2×15.
      If anything reproduces sharp pain or a "stretching" sensation over the lateral ligaments, back off.

    Monday–Tuesday: progress to seated isometric holds (push foot gently into a wall or pillow in 4 directions without the foot moving — dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, inversion, eversion; hold 5 sec, 2×10 each). Continue walking as tolerated; swelling should start trending down.

    Wed–Fri: add a resistance band (light/medium) for the same 4-way ankle work, 2×15 each direction. If you have access, stationary bike or pool walking is excellent mid-week re-entry — low load, good ROM.

    Weekend / early next week: if walking is pain-free and there's no instability, light jogging in a straight line on flat ground. Hold on cutting/pivoting/sport until you can hop on the injured foot ~10 times pain-free and have full single-leg balance ≥30 seconds with eyes open.

    Soccer return: typically 2–4 weeks for a Grade I, 4–6+ for a Grade II. Use an ankle sleeve or semi-rigid brace for the first 2–3 weeks back on the field — it reduces re-injury risk meaningfully. Don't return to full sport until you can cut, pivot, and decelerate confidently without a hitch.

URGENT EVALUATION (same-day / ER)

    Cannot bear weight at all, or weight-bearing becomes impossible over the next several hours.
    Visible deformity, a "pop" or "snap" sensation recalled after the fact, or feeling the ankle is dislocated/in the wrong position.

Two signals, one response

HTTP 429 is the request-level verdict: the server is telling the client "this batch was rejected at the rate-limit gate, come back after Retry-After." OTLP partial_success is the point-level verdict on the same response: of the 10,000 points in the batch, 1,200 are explicitly rejected and the remaining 8,800 are not. They are not contradictory — they describe two different layers of the same request. partial_success is the authoritative accounting on the wire for which points the server has decided are out, and the HTTP status is the per-request transport verdict. When both appear together, the partial_success body wins for replay logic.

Why replaying the full batch duplicates accepted points

The 8,800 points in the first response's partial_success are points the server has not classified as rejected. That means one of two things, and either way resending them is unsafe:

- They were accepted and stored on the first attempt. Resending the same 10,000 batch sends those 8,800 again, opening a duplicate-write window.
- They would have been accepted if the rate limit hadn't fired. Even in this case, the server has already done point-level admission work for them and the client has no protocol-level guarantee they were not stored before the 429 was emitted.

What the client should do instead

1. Parse partial_success on every 429 response. Identify the 1,200 rejected points — by index, by ID, or by the attribute/series set the exporter can reconstruct. The rejected count and errorMessage in the body are mandatory fields for this reason.
2. Build a new batch containing ONLY the rejected subset (the 1,200 points). Do not include the 8,800.
3. Apply Retry-After from this specific response plus client-side jitter. Retry-After is a per-response minimum delay, not a value to cache, not a guarantee of success on the next attempt, and not authorization to retry forever.
4. Maintain a retry budget: cap total attempts and total wall-clock time per logical send. Treat each 429 independently — a successful retry on this batch does not authorize ignoring 429s on later batches.
5. If the new (smaller) retry itself returns 429 + partial_success, repeat: parse, build a smaller batch, retry. Stop when the budget is exhausted or the response is a clean 200 with empty partial_success.

Direct answer to the customer question

No, they cannot count 8,800 + 10,000 = 18,800 as successfully delivered.

- The 8,800 is the "not rejected" count from the first attempt's partial_success. It is not a credit to add to the second attempt.
- The 10,000 on the second response is batch-level acceptance of the resent payload. It says the server accepted the request, not that all 10,000 of those points are new unique points relative to attempt 1.
- The actual unique stored count depends on whether ingest-edge deduped the 8,800 against attempt 1's storage. With dedup (the b-771 path: attempt 1 upstream_write_ack=true, attempt 2 dedup_result=duplicate, accepted_points=0), the stored count is 10,000 and the retry contributed only the 1,200. Without dedup, the stored count is 18,800 and the customer has a duplicate-write incident on their side.

The customer needs to verify stored-point counts at sampled timestamps (same approach used for b-771) rather than trust the wire-level acceptance number. Only that verification tells them whether they are in the dedup case or the duplicate case.

Two notes for the support framing

- The customer honored Retry-After and replayed the full batch. These are independent failures. Honoring the 2-second delay was necessary but does not excuse replaying the full payload; both need correcting in the client.
- The "200 + 10,000 accepted" on the retry is per-request acceptance, not per-point-across-requests uniqueness. The customer's integration is conflating the two. That is the bug, not the rate limit.

Here is a sanity-check of a fail-closed redesign. I am leaving the pilot design and rollout with Anya — these are engineering edges she (or her North Pier engineer counterpart) can choose to adopt, ignore, or adapt. I am not volunteering to write code, run the pilot, or push for a particular shape.

The new bug from today's exercise is in a different category from the ones your earlier draft and my ten edges covered. Earlier edges were about "two generators disagreed, which do we believe." Today's bug is "one generator wrote a real file before the other failed." That is a write-side failure, not a validation-side failure. A diff check cannot catch it, because the diff is computed against an already-mutated workspace. So the redesign needs to address two separate failure surfaces: generation itself, and any side effects of generation.

What the existing draft does well
  • Pin the canonical input (content hash, not ref).
  • Generate into a temporary directory rather than the working tree.
  • Treat publishing as an explicit action behind the gate.
  • Do not let the check commit or rewrite files on the branch.

What today's run shows the draft still lets through
  • The generator wrote into the "normal output directory" before validation failed. That means generation was not actually confined to a temp area in the way the design assumed, or the boundary between "output dir" and "temp dir" was not enforced.
  • The workspace ended up with a mixed set of old and new files. So a later human `git add -A` could capture partial output, and the partial output would look plausible.
  • The CI check passed (registry publication never ran) but the side effects did not roll back. The check protected the registry, not the working tree.

The general shape of the fix
  Fail-closed here means: no generator side effect is observable outside the CI sandbox unless the full pipeline (both generators + drift check) has succeeded end-to-end. That is stricter than "don't publish on failure." It also covers "don't leave the workspace half-mutated."

Concretely, edges worth considering for the redesign (each is optional; Anya picks):

  1. Confine every generator write to a path the CI runner owns and discards. A scratch directory under the job's working dir, an overlay filesystem, or a container with `--read-only` mounts for the repo and a writable tmpfs for output. The committed representation directory should be read-only to the generator process for the duration of the run. If the generator cannot write outside the sandbox, the bug class disappears.

  2. Make the generator a pure function over its inputs. It reads the canonical package and writes to a path supplied as an argument. It never infers an output location from CWD, environment, or config that could overlap the committed tree. This is a code-shape constraint, not just a convention.

  3. Generate into a single staging tree and only promote it on full success. If both generators succeed and the drift check is clean, atomically swap the staging tree into place (rename, snapshot, or registry pointer flip). If anything fails before the swap, the staging tree is deleted and the prior published artifact is untouched. This is the "atomic publish" pattern — partial state is unrepresentable because the swap is a single filesystem or registry operation.

  4. Run validation on the staging tree before the swap, not on the live one. The platform JSON validator runs against the generator's output in staging. A failure there discards staging; the previously published package and the committed representation both stay as they were. The "registry never ran" line from today's runbook would then read "registry was never eligible to run" — a stronger guarantee.

  5. Make the drift check a precondition for the swap, not a postcondition of publishing. "Generated output equals committed representation" is checked against staging. If it fails, staging is discarded and the committed representation is left alone, with a key-level diff posted to the PR. The check still does not rewrite the branch.

  6. Add a workspace-leakage guard at the end of the job. A short step that diffs the working tree against the commit at the start of the job and fails the run if any tracked file changed, any new untracked file appears under the output paths, or the generator's known output directories contain anything they shouldn't. This catches the class of bug that produced today's mixed workspace, even if the confinement in (1) is bypassed.

  7. Pin the canonical package by content hash and record that hash on the published artifact, as your earlier draft had. This stays. It is unrelated to today's bug but it is the prerequisite for the swap in (3) to mean anything — you cannot swap in something if you cannot identify what was swapped in.

  8. Treat the registry publication step and the workspace-mutation guard in (6) as the same gate. Either both happen or neither does. Do not let a future change split them.

  9. Recovery from today's state is a separate, manual step: identify which files in the workspace are from the new generator run vs. the prior published set, discard the new ones, and confirm the working tree matches the last good commit. This is not something CI should automate; it is the cleanup for the bug the new design is meant to prevent.

What I would not change
  • The pilot design — canonical package, generated downstream representations, drift check, version pinning, automated detection of divergence. All of that stays.
  • Anya's ownership of the proposal and rollout. The redesign tightens the engineering edges; the product call (single canonical source, generated downstream, drift-checked) is unchanged.
  • The decision that publishing is an explicit action behind the gate. That part of the original draft was right; today's bug is downstream of it, not a refutation of it.

Where this leaves you with Anya
  You are in sounding-board mode. The right next move is to send her the bug report (generator wrote before validator ran; workspace ended up mixed) plus the edges above as "things to consider," and let her decide which ones fit North Pier's existing CI shape. If she wants to walk through how her current run enforced output confinement, that is a bounded engineering question you can help with. If she wants to argue the redesign is overkill, that is also fine — today's run was recoverable and the registry was not poisoned. The fail-closed case is strong but it is her call whether the cost of the sandboxing is worth the protection against a bug class that, until today, was theoretical for this pilot.

One thing not to do: do not offer to write the patch, run the change in their CI, or contact her engineer counterpart directly. She asked for a sanity check; the sanity check is the deliverable.

DIAGNOSIS

The histogram metric `router_request_duration_seconds_bucket` is exported in **seconds** (per the `_seconds` suffix and Prom naming convention). `histogram_quantile()` returns the quantile in the histogram's native unit — seconds. The threshold literal `> 300` is annotated as "300 ms," but the comparison is performed in the histogram's unit, so the expression is effectively asking "is p99 > 300 seconds (5 minutes)?" The answer is always false.

Staging math: `histogram_quantile` returns 0.47 (s) → `0.47 > 300` is false → alert inactive, even though the real p99 is 470 ms. The dashboard renders 470 ms because it formats the quantile for display; the alert fails because it compares 0.47 (seconds) to 300 (intended as ms) — a **1000× unit error** at the comparison site, not in the histogram.

CORRECTED ALERT EXPRESSION

Recommended (convert at the comparison site — keeps the literal `300` aligned with the "300 ms" annotation):

    groups:
      - name: metrics-router-latency
        rules:
          - alert: MetricsRouterP99LatencyHigh
            expr: |
              histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(router_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) * 1000 > 300
            for: 2m
            labels:
              severity: warning
              service: metrics-router
            annotations:
              summary: "metrics-router p99 exceeds 300 ms"
              description: "metrics-router p99 latency is above 300 ms (currently {{ $value }} ms)."

Why this form:
  - The literal `300` in the expression matches the literal "300 ms" in the annotation exactly. Any future drift moves both in lockstep.
  - `{{ $value }}` reflects the post-`*1000` value in ms, so the description renders correctly (e.g., "currently 470 ms").
  - The `* 1000` makes the unit conversion explicit and auditable; future reviewers cannot silently miss it.

Alternative (threshold in the histogram's native unit):

    expr: |
      histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(router_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) > 0.3

Acceptable, but couples the literal `0.3` to "300 ms" only by reviewer discipline. Prefer the `* 1000` form.

FOCUSED TESTS (promtool)

Three tests cover the 300 ms boundary: just below (clears), just above (fires), and staging-matched well above (fires). Each uses a synthetic cumulative-count histogram whose `histogram_quantile` linear-interpolates to a known value. Save as `alerts.yaml` and `tests.yaml`, then run `promtool test rules tests.yaml`.

Lantern data-contract exception — event_time schema, validation, backfill, dedup
(Iris escalation, 2024-04-25)

Problem restated
  Producer emits `event_time` as a bare local-time string ("2024-11-03 01:24:00")
  with no offset and no zone. Records persist across the 2024-11-03 NY fall-back,
  when the 01:00 hour occurs twice — first as EDT/UTC-04, then again as
  EST/UTC-05. The downstream workflow sorts+deduplicates on
  (account_id, event_time) using the local string, so the two distinct instants
  collapse to one key and a real event is dropped.

Root cause
  The contract treats a wall-clock string as a unique instant. During a DST
  fold it is not. Fix is (a) require the producer to surface an absolute instant,
  (b) forbid downstream dedup on the local string.

Minimum safe timestamp schema (per row)

  event_time_local   STRING   NOT NULL   verbatim wall-clock string; preserved as audit
  time_zone          STRING   NOT NULL   IANA zone; for this feed must be "America/New_York"
  event_time_utc     STRING   NOT NULL   RFC3339Nano, absolute instant, offset-bearing
  dst_status         ENUM     NOT NULL   one of:
                                          "none"          ordinary date
                                          "fold_first"    repeated hour, first instant (EDT/UTC-04)
                                          "fold_second"   repeated hour, second instant (EST/UTC-05)
                                          "gap"           local time did not exist (spring-forward)
  dst_resolution     ENUM     NULL       required iff dst_status IN (fold_first, fold_second):
                                          "producer_resolved" | "producer_default"
                                          records how the producer picked the instant
  as_of              DATE     NOT NULL   vendor statement date for this batch
  last_seen          DATE     NOT NULL   freshness bound
  source             ENUM     NOT NULL   mirrors prior pattern: vendor vs Sphere-derived
  confidence         ENUM     NOT NULL   "exact" | "producer_resolved_fold"
                                          | "producer_default_fold" | "invalid_gap"

  No in-place overwrites of the local string. The verbatim column is the audit
  trail; the UTC column is the canonical key downstream.

Validation — producer side, run before admission

  Reject any row missing time_zone, event_time_utc, as_of, last_seen, source, or confidence.
  Reject any time_zone not in the IANA database.
  Reject any event_time_utc that fails round-trip:
      parse(event_time_local, time_zone, dst_resolution) == event_time_utc
  Reject any event_time_local that does not exist on the wall clock for the
      declared zone (the gap case — quarantine, never coerce to a neighbor).
  For rows in a known DST fold window for the declared zone, require
      dst_resolution. Rows without it route to the dst-needs-resolution
      subreport (see Backfill).
  Bit-identical reproducibility: a re-emit of the same vendor file must yield
      the same event_time_utc for every row. Any drift = quarantine.

Validation — room side

  Mirror the prior null→basic pattern:
    - vendor / Sphere field split enforced at the view layer
    - no raw CSV column reaches downstream workflows; named views only
    - deletion propagation ≤ 30 days, verified
  Alarms:
    - null rate on event_time_utc or time_zone > 0
    - any row with dst_status = "gap" — upstream clock bug, page on first occurrence
    - week-over-week growth in dst-needs-resolution subreport
    - any (as_of - last_seen) > contractually agreed bound

Backfill

  Do NOT silently rewrite historical rows that lack zone/resolution. Bucket them:

    A) outside any DST transition for their date → derive event_time_utc
       deterministically, dst_status="none", confidence="exact", accept.
    B) inside the 2024-11-03 fold (01:00–01:59 NY local) → quarantine to
       dst-needs-resolution subreport. Room owner names a subreport owner.
       Resolution requires producer sign-off per row, OR a documented producer
       default recorded in the contract and applied uniformly.
    C) inside any DST gap → quarantine as upstream clock bug; do not coerce
       to a wall-clock neighbor (that hides the bug).

  Forward-going: full schema required. Partial rows are rejected at admission.

Downstream deduplication

  Dedup key MUST be (account_id, event_time_utc). The local string is NOT a key.
  Sort key MUST include event_time_utc (absolute instant), not event_time_local.
  Tie-breaker: when two rows share (account_id, event_time_utc), retain both
    and surface to the workflow owner — that is a producer double-emit, not a
    fold artifact.
  The current workflow sorts/deduplicates on the local string. That change is a
  precondition for admission, not a follow-up. If the workflow owner cannot
  change the key before admission, Iris should hold admission.

Repeated DST hour — handling rule

  Preferred: producer tags each fold row with dst_resolution =
    "producer_resolved" and emits the correct fold_first or fold_second
    instant. Two real events at 01:24 on the fold date then have distinct
    UTC instants (05:24:00Z and 06:24:00Z) and dedup correctly.

2. "and eliminated drift between Figma and implementation"
   Two problems. First, the pilot detects drift via an automated check — detection is not elimination. Second, what has actually been exercised is local failure-path behavior of the CI gate (generator exits, block-on-failure, key-level diff visibility). Nothing has been demonstrated about whether drift in live day-to-day authoring has actually gone away. "Eliminated" is unverified.

3. "so teams can rely on the package as the standard workflow"
   Adoption framing again. Standardization is precisely what her manager is gating on evidence for. The update shouldn't pre-announce it.

4. "The remaining six weeks will focus on documentation and rollout polish"
   Frames remaining work as cosmetic. What is actually pending is substantive validation: a real team release cycle through the gate, live-Figma-file drift evidence, golden-output tests, version-provenance evidence, friction data from the first adopting team. None of that is polish. Calling it polish telegraphs to her manager that the risk is past, which it isn't.

Readiness assessment

8 days post-roll, no swelling, no pain with walking, stairs, single-leg calf raises, balance, two-foot hops, easy jog, and 5 controlled lateral bounds is a strong Grade I / very mild Grade II lateral ankle sprain response. The pattern (no swelling from day 1, pain-free under progressive load) suggests the lateral ligaments healed enough for daily and linear/frontal-plane loading. What is NOT yet tested is the mechanism that caused the original injury: sudden inversion under load, end-range inversion under load, hard deceleration, and unstable landings. You are roughly at the "controlled linear and frontal plane" stage of a return-to-sport ladder.

Both upcoming sports hit that final gap differently. Bouldering loads it through heel hooks, toe hooks, mantles, drop-knee foot positions, and unplanned landings. Soccer loads it through plant-and-cut, which is the textbook mechanism for the original injury. The conservative move is to keep Thursday as the sport-specific exposure it can actually serve (low end-range inversion, no hard cuts), and use Sat / Sun morning as the soccer-gating work.

Progression: Mon → Wed (gating checks before Thursday)

Add one new test per day. Each test must be clean during AND the next morning. If anything lights up — even a low-level "awareness" — repeat the prior day's level and do not progress.

  Mon (tonight or Tue AM):
    - 10 single-leg hops in place on the right
    - 3 single-leg hops for distance; compare to left, >90% is a pass

  Tue:
    - 3 jump-downs from a 12–18" box onto the right foot, controlled stick-landing (no hop)
    - 3 reps from 18–24"

  Wed:
    - Plant-and-cut at half-speed. Cones in a T or X. Jog in, plant on the right, change direction at ~70% effort. 6 reps.
    - If half-speed feels clean, finish with 3 reps at ~85%.

By Wed night you should know whether Thursday bouldering is on. If Wed's cut test produces awareness or guarding, Thursday is also a skip — bouldering alone won't gate soccer for Sunday, and going to the wall without a clean Wed is the kind of stacking you've been disciplined about avoiding.

Thursday bouldering — go/no-go and stop criteria

  Pre-session gate (at the gym, before touching the wall):
    - 5 min easy walk + 2 min easy jog
    - 10 double-leg calf raises, 10 single-leg right
    - 5 small two-foot hops, 3 single-leg hops right, 3 small jump-downs from a single gym step
    - Any dull tightness, sharpness, cramping, or guarding = skip the wall, walk and spot instead

  Allowed:
    - Vertical and slab, big holds, static movement only
    - Downclimb everything — never jump down, never drop
    - 3–4 problems max, 45 min cap, one problem short of your usual volume

  Avoid for this session (all load inversion end-range or unstable landings):
    - Heel hooks and toe hooks — hard avoid for 2–3 more weeks regardless
    - Mantles
    - Dynos and any rushed movement
    - Drop knees
    - Overhangs with sketchy downclimbs
    - High-ball problems

  Stop conditions during the session:
    - Any awareness of the right ankle (dull tightness, "something there," guard reflex)
    - Sharp pain
    - An unstable foot placement that forces mid-move correction
    - Any near-roll, even with no pain
    - Cramping

  Post-session:
    - Clean → walk out, normal evening, retest the Wed plant-and-cut Thu night or Fri.
    - Awareness during → treat Thursday as a downgrade, no stacking toward Sunday, retest Friday before committing to soccer.
    - 24h after → zero new swelling, zero new pain at walking / stairs / calf raises. If not, soccer is off.

Saturday (bridge day, only if Thursday was clean)

One controlled test of the things bouldering cannot replicate:

  - Plant-and-cut at full speed, 6 reps, last rep planting right on a folded towel or thin mat to simulate grass
  - 3 jump-downs from a 24–30" box onto the right foot
  - A short deceleration set: sprint ~15m, stop in 2–3 steps, 4 reps

Any awareness here = downgrade Sunday to flat walk and spectate. Do not play through "almost clean" — that is how the second roll happens.

Sunday pickup — go/no-go and stop criteria

  Pre-game gate (same battery as Thursday plus one plant-and-cut at 85–90%):
    - If the plant-and-cut produces awareness, you are a spectator with coffee, not a player. No negotiation.

  Warm-up: progressive. Walk → jog → easy sprints → cutting. No static ankle stretching. No barefoot grass drills if anything feels "off."

  In-game rules:
    - First 15–20 min at half-speed. No tackles, no contested 50/50s, no sprinting onto a through-ball until you've had a few clean cuts under you.
    - Pick sides if you can — avoid the worst of the uneven ground.
    - One awareness event = sit out the rest of the half. Two events = done for the day.

  Stop conditions:
    - Any roll, near-roll, or "tweaked" feeling — done, walk home, reassess tomorrow
    - Sharp pain in the right ankle
    - Swelling or warmth after a play, even without a specific incident
    - Pain or stiffness that builds during the game rather than warming out

Red flags that override the whole plan

  - New pop or sharp pain at any point
  - Visible swelling or bruising that wasn't there before
  - Pain at rest or at night
  - Numbness or tingling into the foot
  - Pain that does not fully resolve within 24h of a test

Any of these → stop the progression, treat it like a fresh injury, see someone if it doesn't quiet down in 3–4 days.
