Flushing order

Close every faucet in the apartment first. Pull the aerators on the kitchen cold tap and the bathroom hot tap before you start — grit collects in the screen and keeps the stream looking discolored even after the line clears. (Same procedure you used on the bathroom tap in March.)

Then cold side, in this order, each one fully open:
1. Kitchen cold — 3 to 5 minutes, or until it has run visibly clear for a full 2 minutes.
2. Bathroom cold — same.
3. If you have a shower or tub, run cold briefly to clear that branch.
4. Flush each toilet once so the fill valve pulls fresh water through the line.

Then hot side. The water heater is a reservoir, so this takes longer:
5. Kitchen hot, fully open, 5 to 10 minutes. This pulls from the tank.
6. Bathroom hot, fully open, 5 to 10 minutes.

A faint yellow tint after 30 seconds is normal post-shutdown iron/rust discoloration and usually clears with sustained flushing. If the bathroom hot hasn't cleared after 15 to 20 minutes of continuous flow, that's the threshold for a maintenance call rather than more patience. Reinstall the aerators only after lines run clear.

Drinking readiness

No boil-water notice from management is the key signal — there isn't one, so no mandatory boil order. The kitchen cold is fine to drink once it has run clear for 2 to 3 minutes straight. Two standing rules worth keeping:

- Always draw drinking and cooking water from the cold tap. Hot water sits in the heater and dissolves more metal from pipes and the tank lining.
- Before any glass, run the cold tap 10 to 15 seconds if it hasn't been used in a few hours, so you're drinking from the freshest water in the line.

Skip ice from the fridge or door dispenser today; the reservoir needs a few refill cycles to fully turn over.

Appliance return criteria

Wait until both kitchen cold and kitchen hot have flushed clear per above, then:

Dishwasher — run an empty Rinse cycle (or a full Normal cycle with no dishes) first. That clears the supply hose and the interior without putting grit on anything you care about. Then resume normal use.

Washing machine — flush the hot and cold supply lines by running the nearest sink for several minutes past clear, then run an empty Rinse/Spin cycle. If your model has a "clean washer" or sanitize cycle, use that empty first. First real load: towels or similar, not delicates, in case any residual sediment is still in the line.

Reporting triggers

Contact management if any of the following:
- Bathroom hot stays yellow after 15 to 20 minutes of continuous flushing.
- Visible sediment or particles in any tap.
- Unusual smell — sulfur, sewage, or fuel. (A faint chlorine smell is normal.)
- Pressure is noticeably lower than before the shutdown after flushing.
- Discoloration returns hours later after having cleared.
- The kitchen slip-joint area or bathroom cold-shutoff packing nut is damp — both have been leak-prone for you before, and disturbed sediment can shift older washers.

It's also reasonable to ask management whether the riser valves were fully opened for the whole building. If neighbors are flushing clear and you aren't, that points to your branch specifically.

Reviewed the sequence against the prior April 23 partial-write, April 30 map-ordering byte drift, and the established fail-closed redesign. The sequence is largely sound but has seven hidden risks. Two are partial-publication, four are misleading-comparison, and one is cross-cutting. Numbered below by where they hide in the sequence.

Step 1 — schema 3 support matrix is implicit
  Partial-publication risk. Before any generation, verify that generator 0.9.0 has explicit schema-3 bindings for all four targets (web CSS, iOS, Android, docs). If schema 3 introduces a construct 0.9.0 doesn't know for one target, that target may emit partial output, be silently skipped, or fall back to a default that drifts from the canonical tokens. Add a preflight that enumerates (schema_construct, target) coverage and aborts if any cell is empty. Without it, step 4's "compare to semantic fixtures" can pass against a target that never actually ran.

Step 2 — pinning surface is too narrow
  Partial-publication risk. "Pin consumer and shared CI generator" leaves the drift-checker, the diff uploader, the publication action, and any post-generation audit on unpinned or differently-pinned versions. If the drift-checker runs at a different commit than the generator, drift can be detected by one component and ignored by another. Pin by content hash, not mutable ref (per the April 27 review), and the pin must cover every process that can produce a side effect outside the sandbox. "Shared CI generator" is not the same set as "everything that touches outputs."

Step 3 — April 23 partial-write returns in a new shape
  Partial-publication risk. If the four targets run sequentially or in parallel within one process, and one target fails mid-sequence, the earlier-succeeded targets have already written files. The April 23 incident wrote CSS before platform JSON validation failed; this sequence has four targets where one failed write is enough to leave a mixed old/new set in the tree. Requirement: all four targets write to a single ephemeral staging directory, and promotion to the output directory is one atomic swap at the end of the pipeline. Confirm the "staging directory" referenced in steps 6 and 7 is the same single staging, and that it is wiped at the start of each run so stale state from a prior failed attempt cannot be picked up.

Step 4 — byte stability is not correctness, and 20 runs is a regression guard, not a defense
  Misleading-comparison risk, three parts.
  (a) Twenty runs of byte-stable output prove determinism, not fidelity. A generator that consistently emits the wrong value passes byte stability cleanly. The semantic-fixture comparison is the correctness check, but only if the fixtures are independent of the generator — i.e., authored from the canonical token spec, not derived from a previous generator run. Verify fixture provenance before relying on the green signal.
  (b) "Compare all targets to semantic fixtures" needs per-target fixtures. A single shared fixture only proves the four targets agree with each other, not that any of them matches the canonical tokens. Each of CSS, iOS, Android, docs needs its own semantic fixture with its own expected values.
  (c) The April 30 incident was 1-in-4 non-determinism. Twenty runs catches that with high probability but not certainty. The structural fix — deterministic key ordering at the source — should be in place, with byte-stability as a regression guard, not as the primary defense against re-introduction.

Step 5 — drift checker coverage is CSS-only as written
  Misleading-comparison risk. Editing one CSS variable and requiring drift failure proves the drift path for CSS. iOS, Android, and docs typically use different parsers and different comparison semantics in the drift checker. The April 27 review listed "distinguish meaningful drift from formatting churn" as a required property — that property lives in the comparison logic, which is target-specific. Either repeat the edit-and-fail test for each of the four targets, or run a cross-target fixture that exercises all four drift code paths. A green signal on CSS alone is not evidence the other three are wired.

Step 6 — schema validation timing is the load-bearing detail, and "zero publication" needs an exact definition
  Partial-publication risk, two parts.
  (a) The sequence does not say when schema validation runs. If it runs pre-generation (parsing the canonical package before any target generator is invoked), zero publication is trivially satisfied. If it runs mid-generation (after one or more targets have written), the April 23 partial-write returns. If it runs post-generation as an audit, all four targets have already been emitted into staging and may persist as observable side effects. Require: schema validation is a preflight that rejects the canonical package before any target generator starts.
  (b) "Zero publication" must match the fail-closed redesign exactly: no generator side effect is observable outside the CI sandbox unless the full pipeline (both generators and drift check) succeeds end-to-end. The test assertion needs three checks, not one: (i) no files in the published output directory matching 0.9.0 content; (ii) no registry/index/bundle entry created or updated; (iii) no external artifact emitted by the publication path (a drift-check PR comment is fine; an automatic bump-and-push is not). Asserting only one of the three leaves the other two as silent regressions.

Step 7 — "complete matrix" is underspecified, and the branch carries a schema-3 canonical against a schema-2 published artifact
  Cross-cutting risk, two parts.
  (a) "Until the complete matrix passes" is a binary decision at the end, but the matrix itself is not enumerated. REVIEW: ingest-edge#229 (bounded-decompression)

Two definite bugs the PR must fix before merge: (1) the global permit leaks when the client cancels while we're blocked in tenant.acquire, and (2) the destination buffer can grow past bodyLimit before we ever check the limit. There are also a few behavior-description issues worth fixing before merge.

1. PERMIT ORDERING & CLEANUP

1a. Global permit leaks on tenant-acquire cancellation (the bug you flagged).

defer global.release() is only registered after tenant.acquire succeeds. If the client cancels while we're blocked in tenant.acquire, we return canceled(err) and never release the global permit. This breaks the "cap == permits_held" invariant from the 2024-04-18 admission race-fix (Wes): every leaked permit permanently shrinks the global pool until global admission starts 429ing under load, and once that happens we can't tell from metrics whether the cap genuinely shrunk or we just leaked permits.

Fix: register the global release before any blocking call that can fail.

    globalPermit, err := global.acquire(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        return admissionRejected(err)   // 429 + Retry-After
    }
    defer releasePermit(global, globalPermit)

    if err := tenant.acquire(ctx); err != nil {
        return canceled(err)            // global released by the defer above
    }
    defer tenant.release()

This also forces the PR to make explicit what happens when global.acquire(ctx) itself errors. With tryAcquire semantics from the 2024-04-18 fix, that branch should produce 429 + the existing 1-3s randomized Retry-After (not a 5xx and not context.Canceled to the client). Confirm the admission-rejection path in the PR produces exactly that header set.

1b. Tenant-permit starvation convoy.

The order global -> tenant is right for global budgeting, but if one tenant's permit is scarce, all 20k global permits can end up held by requests waiting on that tenant's permit — a convoy that blocks every other tenant. Two options:

  - Make the tenant permit a tryAcquire (non-blocking) and route overflow to the existing tenant-429 lane; OR
  - Bound the time spent in tenant.acquire(ctx) with a short deadline (e.g., 250 ms) and fail fast to 429 on miss.

I'd recommend the tryAcquire route — keeps the global permit count tight and reuses the proven tenant-429 path instead of inventing a new "tenant admit timed out" envelope.

1c. defer order is fine. tenant.release() is registered before global.release(), so LIFO releases global first then tenant. Correct.

1d. Both defers must run on every return path. Audit bodyTooLarge(), decoder errors, response-write errors, and any early-return helpers — every one needs both permits released. Easiest is to keep the defers attached to a single function rather than scattered across helpers, so a future refactor can't accidentally bypass a release.

2. ALLOCATION-BEFORE-LIMIT

The current loop:

    for chunk := range decoder {
        output = append(output, chunk...)
        decompressed += len(chunk)
        if decompressed > bodyLimit {
            return bodyTooLarge()
        }
    }

append can double the backing array before we ever compare decompressed to bodyLimit. With a 10 MiB limit and a chunk that pushes len(output) from 8 MiB to 12 MiB, the next append allocates ~16 MiB before the check fires. For bodyLimit << chunk size, the buffer briefly grows to 2 * len(output), which can be much larger than the limit the PR claims to enforce.

Fix: check first, append second.

    for chunk := range decoder {
        decompressed += len(chunk)
        if decompressed > bodyLimit {
            return bodyTooLarge()
        }
        output = append(output, chunk...)
    }

Or, more defensively, gate append directly:

        if int64(len(output)) + int64(len(chunk)) > bodyLimit {
            return bodyTooLarge()
        }
        output = append(output, chunk...)

The second form avoids the cumulative-arithmetic class entirely and lets you switch to bytes.Buffer.Grow with bounded preallocation if you want to eliminate append reallocation altogether.

Either way, add a test that feeds a single chunk larger than bodyLimit (e.g., a 20 MiB gzip entry decoded as one chunk) and asserts the response is 413 with peak heap allocation at most bodyLimit + one_chunk, not 2 * bodyLimit or unbounded.

3. CANCELLATION BEHAVIOR

The cancellation branch has two additional issues beyond the permit leak:

3a. If the response has already been partially written, returning an error from the handler is too late — the client has already received 200 + partial bytes. The HTTP layer must abort the response on ctx.Err() != nil and discard the body. Confirm this happens at the framework layer, not inside the decompression function.

3b. return canceled(err) must surface an actual error to the framework (which translates to 499 Client Closed Request or surfaces context.Canceled) and must NOT swallow it as a 200 with a partial body. Only bodyTooLarge() and decoder errors should produce a response body.

4. MINIMUM REGRESSION TESTS

The PR must include at least these. Without them, the two bugs above can silently regress.

Permit accounting (the cap == permits_held invariant from the 2024-04-18 fix):

  T1.  Successful request: permits_held == 0 after completion (both global and tenant)
  T2.  Body overflow -> 413: permits_held == 0 after return
  T3.  Decoder error -> error response: permits_held == 0
  T4.  Cancel while waiting for tenant permit: permits_held == 0  (regression for §1a)
  T5.  Cancel while waiting for global permit: permits_held == 0
  T6.  Cancel during decompression: permits_held == 0
  T7.  N=20000 concurrent successful requests: permits_held returns to 0; cap == permits_held holds throughout
  T8.  N=20001 concurrent requests: exactly 1 gets 429 + Retry-After; cap never exceeded

Allocation-before-limit:

  T9.  Single chunk > bodyLimit -> 413, peak heap <= bodyLimit + 1 chunk (regression for §2)
  T10. Many small chunks summing just over bodyLimit -> 413, no doubling past bodyLimit
  T11. Body exactly at bodyLimit -> accepted (confirm `>` semantics against the historical 10 MiB / 14.2 MiB customer case)

Response headers:

  T12. Admission rejection -> 429 with Retry-After in [1, 3]s, header is randomized (not constant across N samples)
  T13. Body overflow -> 413 with NO Retry-After (matches the production contract documented with the customer on 2024-03-25: customer was told 413, no Retry-After, just batch smaller)
  T14. The two cases must not be conflated. Admission rejection is 429 + Retry-After; bodyTooLarge is 413 + no Retry-After. If the PR is intentionally changing bodyTooLarge to 429+Retry-After, that's a customer-visible behavior change — call it out in the PR description and update the support doc that previously said the limit returns 413.

Concurrency / fairness:

  T15. One tenant saturated, another tenant's requests still admitted (no cross-tenant convoy; validates §1b fix)
  T16. Cancellation storm (cancel 1000 requests mid-acquire): global permit count returns to 0; no goroutine leak

Decoder robustness:

  T17. Corrupt/truncated gzip -> both permits released, no panic
  T18. Empty body (Content-Length: 0, Content-Encoding: gzip) -> 200, zero bytes written, both permits released
  T19. Decoder stream that yields a chunk > bodyLimit on the first iteration -> 413, no allocation past limit (regression for §2)

5. OTHER NOTES

The PR description says it "preserves the production one-to-three-second randomized Retry-After behavior for overflow." That phrasing conflates two distinct paths. Production 413 (decoded body too large) does NOT carry Retry-After — that's the contract documented with the customer on 2024-03-25. Retry-After applies to admission rejection (429). Either reword the PR description or call out the behavior change explicitly, because Support will need to update the customer-facing guidance if 413 starts returning Retry-After.

Confirm bodyLimit matches the existing production max_decoded_body_bytes=10485760 exactly. The customer's batching workaround (≤ 7.5 MiB per request after decompression) was sized against 10 MiB; a silent limit change here reopens the 2024-03-25 incident.

The defer-1:1-with-admit invariant from the 2024-04-18 fix is what makes cap == permits_held hold. Every code path that admits must release, and that release must not depend on control flow reaching a particular line — which is exactly why §1a is a bug and §1d matters going forward.

Reader safety on the new path is sound for the pointer-aliasing defect that got the previous revision rejected. The epoch guard wraps active.Load, the lookup, and the match as a single critical section, and Retire defers freeing the replaced generation until all earlier reader epochs have drained. That is the right shape for EBR. Two caveats that the snippet does not prove and should be verified before merge:

  - EBR protects the pointer, not the object. gen.Lookup must be race-free on a generation that is being prepared by BuildGeneration for a future Swap. Concretely, the candidate constructor has to freeze every field a reader can reach — matchers, missing-label mode, normalizer version, and any references they capture — before the candidate is visible to active.Load. A lock inside Lookup would defeat the point of the cache; the data has to be immutable by construction.

  - The cache key in the snippet is implicit in gen.Lookup(expr). Per the 2024‑04‑25 matcher-cache spec the key is (Expr, MissingLabelMode, NormalizerVersion), and NewMatcher is pure given that key. The April‑8 flush_interval investigation and the original review both depended on MissingLabelMode and NormalizerVersion being part of identity, not properties of the surrounding gen. Flag this as a verification item; do not assume it from the snippet.

  - One smaller item: the reader uses a plain guard variable. If anything between Enter and Exit panics, the epoch never closes and every later Retire blocks. Every reader call site has to be defer guard.Exit(), or the epoch lib needs to expose a scoped helper. Worth a grep before merge.

Failed reloads still retain candidate generations indefinitely. The defect is exactly where you put your finger: generationRegistry[candidate.ID] = candidate.Matchers runs before Validate, and on the failure path candidate = nil drops the local pointer without deleting the registry entry. Every validation failure (and any error between insert and Swap) leaks one entry permanently. Two equivalent fixes:

  - Move the registry insert to after Validate returns nil and before Swap.
  - On the failure path, delete generationRegistry[candidate.ID] before returning the error.

There is a second, related leak the snippet hints at but does not state outright: on the success path, epochs.Retire(old) frees the retired generation's compiled matchers, but nothing in the snippet removes the registry entry keyed by the retired generation's ID. So the registry grows by one entry per successful reload as well. The originally agreed design was per-gen Tier 1 + bounded Tier 2; an unbounded registry diverges from that. Confirm that Retire (or a paired cleanup hook) clears the registry entry keyed by the retired ID, and that nothing else keeps the registry unbounded.

Two related points worth raising on the PR thread:

  - Because candidate.Matchers is published into generationRegistry, the registry is now what keeps the compiled matchers alive — not the active pointer. Retire has to wait for both (a) all earlier reader epochs to drain AND (b) the registry to drop its reference. Otherwise Retire under-counts and a freed generation is still reachable through the registry, which is the same use-after-free class of bug in the opposite direction.

  - Nil-ing the candidate local on the failure path does not release anything to GC; the registry still holds the matchers. Only the two fixes above actually free the entry.

On ownership, separately from the patch itself: this review is at patch scope. Wes is the author of this revision, not metrics-router's formal owner. The defects above should be fixed on this PR, but the broader questions — registry lifecycle ownership, EBR vs. RCU vs. hazard pointers, what bounded tier-2 looks like, who runs the rollback story — belong with whoever owns metrics-router, not on this thread. Keep the review comments on the patch and route owner-level questions to the owner.

Lantern security rerun matrix for the PE correction — pre-signoff. Each row is a required test case; the matrix is pass/fail and all rows must pass before signoff. Where the design is silent, the matrix states the assumption it makes.

============================================================
DESIGN POINTS UNDER VERIFICATION
============================================================

- Auth evaluation runs before any external source fetch.
- Decision is cached at (tenant_id, subject_id, resource_id, action, policy_generation). All five tuple elements must participate in the key.
- 403 / not_authorized envelope carries no preview, metadata, or existence hint. Identical across every deny path.
- On allow, only sources the policy marks permitted for this subject and resource are read. No fallback to non-permitted sources.
- A permitted source that is absent yields the field's explicit `unknown` state. Absence is not a denial and not an error.
- Authorization cache entries, including denies, are invalidated when policy_generation changes for the tenant.

ASSUMPTIONS THE MATRIX MAKES

- The 403 envelope is exactly `{status, code:"not_authorized"}` and nothing else. The design should ratify this; if it carries additional fields, T4.1 must be updated.
- `unknown` is a typed constant on the wire, distinct from null/empty/error. The design should ratify the type; T5.4 enforces it.
- Cache invalidation on gen change is eager (or at least bounded such that no stale entry is observable to the next request). T3.4 enforces this.
- `policy_generation` is monotonic per tenant. Rollback to a prior gen is a test-only operation.

============================================================
SETUP REQUIRED TO RUN THIS MATRIX
============================================================

- Multi-tenant fixtures: at least three tenants, two subjects per tenant where subject identifiers collide across tenants, and overlapping resource identifiers where the resource namespace is tenant-scoped.
- Policy-generation instrumentation: ability to bump gen atomically, roll gen back in test mode, and read current gen from the cache layer.
- Source simulator returning one of four states: data, absent, transient error, denied. Per-source configuration per test.
- Cache inspection: ability to enumerate keys, values, TTLs, and assert key presence or absence in the same backend used in production.
- Request/log capture: full request envelope, response envelope, and server-side fetch log per request.
- Revocation control plane: ability to revoke subject from tenant, subject from resource, and resource from tenant, and to assert propagation latency.

============================================================
D1. CROSS-TENANT CACHE REUSE
============================================================

T1.1  Two tenants, identical (subject, resource, action, gen)
  Setup:    tenant_A/subj_1/r_1/view/gen=G and tenant_B/subj_1/r_1/view/gen=G; both allowed.
  Action:   Issue allow request from each tenant; inspect cache.
  Expect:   Two distinct entries. Key strings differ at minimum at the tenant_id position.
            Tenant_B lookup does not return tenant_A's entry.
  Breaks:   Tenant_B receives tenant_A's auth outcome.

T1.2  Cache key serialization
  Setup:    Single request (tenant_A, subj_1, r_1, view, G).
  Action:   Inspect serialized cache key.
  Expect:   All five tuple elements present in the key. No element truncated, normalized away,
            or hashed before keying.
  Breaks:   Two semantically-different tuples hash to the same key; one shadows the other.

T1.3  Subject_id collision across tenants
  Setup:    tenant_A has subject_X with membership M_A; tenant_B has subject_X with membership
            M_B (different). Resource IDs r_A and r_B differ.
  Action:   Issue (tenant_A, X, r_A, view) and (tenant_B, X, r_B, view).
  Expect:   Each resolves to its own tenant's membership. No cross-tenant cache hit.
            If subject_X alone were keyed without tenant_id, the entries would collide —
            verify this cannot happen.
  Breaks:   Authorization outcome from M_A influences a request resolved under M_B.

T1.4  Action namespace collision
  Setup:    tenant_A allows (subj, r, view); tenant_B denies the same tuple except tenant.
  Action:   Issue both; inspect cache.
  Expect:   Two entries. Deny does not shadow allow across tenants.
  Breaks:   Tenant_A receives a deny cached under tenant_B.

T1.5  Replay attempt
  Setup:    Capture an allow tuple from tenant_A's cache entry.
  Action:   Construct a request from tenant_B with the same subject_id, resource_id, action, gen.
  Expect:   No cache hit. Request re-evaluated against tenant_B's policy. If unauthorized, 403
            with no preview. If authorized, result reflects tenant_B's policy only.
  Breaks:   Tenant_B's response is dictated by tenant_A's cached decision.

T1.6  Cache eviction does not cross tenants
  Setup:    Fill cache to capacity with tenant_A entries.
  Action:   Force eviction; issue tenant_B request and observe what is evicted.
  Expect:   Eviction may remove tenant_A entries but does not remove tenant_B entries to make
            room. Tenant_B's entries remain intact and reachable by tenant_B's keys.
  Breaks:   Tenant_A eviction cascades to tenant_B data.

T1.7  Concurrent same-tuple requests across tenants
  Setup:    Two simultaneous requests for the same (subject, resource, action, gen), one per tenant.
  Action:   Issue in parallel; inspect cache.
  Expect:   Two cache writes do not collapse. No interleaving produces a cross-tenant entry.
  Breaks:   Race allows one tenant's outcome to be written under the other's key.

============================================================
D2. MEMBERSHIP REVOCATION
============================================================

T2.1  Subject revoked from tenant entirely
  Setup:    Subject S authorized for R in tenant T. Confirm allow.
  Action:   Revoke S from T. Re-issue same request.
  Expect:   403 / not_authorized; no preview. Cache entry for (T, S, R) has been invalidated or
            was never written — verify by inspecting cache.
  Breaks:   Stale allow served from cache after revocation.

T2.2  Partial revocation (resource-scoped)
  Setup:    S authorized for R1 and R2 in T.
  Action:   Revoke S from R1 only. Request R1, then R2.
  Expect:   R1 → 403. R2 → allow. Cache state: R1 entry invalidated, R2 entry intact.
  Breaks:   Resource-scoped revocation drops unrelated resources, or fails to drop the target.

T2.3  Revocation propagation latency
  Setup:    S authorized for R.
  Action:   Issue request immediately after revocation API confirms success.
  Expect:   First post-revocation request returns 403. No "eventual consistency" window serves
            stale allows. Latency bound asserted.
  Breaks:   Stale allow served for any duration after revocation confirms.

T2.4  Revoked subject retries with new session
  Setup:    S revoked from T.
  Action:   S opens new session (new tokens, new connection) and requests R.
  Expect:   403. Revocation is not session-bound.
  Breaks:   New session bypasses revocation because it triggers a fresh cache write.

T2.5  Re-admission after revocation
  Setup:    S revoked from T, then re-added.
  Action:   Request R.
  Expect:   Allow. Prior deny is not permanently cached; membership change re-evaluates.
  Breaks:   Stale deny served because denies are immutable in the cache.

T2.6  Cache TTL interaction
  Setup:    Authorization cache TTL = T.
  Action:   Within TTL, revoke S. Request R.
  Expect:   Revocation invalidates regardless of TTL. TTL does not gate revocation.
  Breaks:   TTL extends the allow window past the revocation event.

T2.7  Revocation during an active stream
  Setup:    S has open long-poll/streaming subscription authorized for R.
  Action:   Revoke S; observe subsequent frames.
  Expect:   Connection terminates or transitions to 403. No further payload frames referencing R.
  Breaks:   Stream continues to emit data post-revocation.

============================================================
D3. POLICY-GENERATION CHANGES
============================================================

T3.1  Allow invalidated by gen bump
  Setup:    S allowed under gen=G.
  Action:   Bump policy_generation to G+1. Re-issue same request.
  Expect:   Re-evaluation. If new policy denies, 403 with no preview. Cache key under G no
            longer satisfies G+1 requests.
  Breaks:   Stale allow served under new gen.

T3.2  Deny invalidated by gen bump
  Setup:    S denied under gen=G.
  Action:   Bump gen to G+1 with policy now granting S access. Request.
  Expect:   Allow. Cached deny from G does not persist; deny entries invalidate on gen change
            as the design requires.
  Breaks:   Cached deny blocks a legitimate post-bump allow.

T3.3  Cache key includes policy_generation
  Setup:    Lookups at G and G+1.
  Action:   Enumerate keys.
  Expect:   Two distinct entries; gen is part of the key. Lookup at G+1 does not match the G entry.
  Breaks:   Gen absent from key; entries collapse; old decision returned forever.

T3.4  Concurrent requests across a gen bump
  Setup:    N concurrent requests with policy that will flip via gen bump mid-flight.
  Action:   Trigger gen bump while requests are in flight. Collect responses.
  Expect:   Every response reflects the gen in effect when the request was evaluated. No mixed
            cohort (e.g., new policy with old allow still cached).
  Breaks:   Some responses pre-bump, some post-bump, despite identical inputs.

T3.5  Gen rollback (test mode)
  Setup:    Gen G → G+1 → G+2. Allow cached at G+2.
  Action:   Roll back to G. Request.
  Expect:   Re-evaluation under G. Cached allow from G+2 does not satisfy.
  Breaks:   Cached decision from a higher-numbered gen served for a lower gen.

T3.6  Gen monotonicity guard
  Setup:    Same as T3.5.
  Action:   Inspect cache after rollback.
  Expect:   Lower-gen requests never read higher-gen entries. Implementation rejects out-of-
            order gen reads or version-pins entries to their gen.
  Breaks:   Higher-gen entry returned for a lower-gen request.

T3.7  Audit of gen bump
  Setup:    Gen bump event occurs.
  Action:   Inspect audit log.
  Expect:   Log records timestamp, prior gen, new gen, actor, and a stable reference (event ID)
            for the policy change. This is the provenance artifact for the invalidation.
  Breaks:   Gen bump occurs without an audit record; operators cannot reconstruct what policy
            was live at any moment.

============================================================
D4. DENIAL WITHOUT EXISTENCE LEAKAGE
============================================================

T4.1  403 body shape
  Setup:    S requests R; S not authorized.
  Action:   Issue; capture full body and headers.
  Expect:   Body contains only the standardized envelope fields (status, code `not_authorized`).
            No resource title, summary, owner, type, count, last_modified, tags, or preview.
  Breaks:   Body reveals anything that would confirm what R is.

T4.2  Header leakage
  Setup:    Same as T4.1.
  Action:   Inspect response headers.
  Expect:   No resource-specific headers. No ETag of R, no Last-Modified of R, no Content-Location
            hinting at a real resource URL, no X-* headers carrying metadata.
  Breaks:   Headers reveal the resource or its state.

T4.3  Timing parity
  Setup:    (a) requests to existing-but-unauthorized R; (b) requests to non-existent R'.
            Both from S.
  Action:   Measure response time over N trials per set.
  Expect:   Mean and tail latencies within a defined bound (e.g., 5% across sets).
            No statistically significant difference.
  Breaks:   Timing side-channel reveals whether the resource exists.

T4.4  Existence enumeration
  Setup:    S unauthorized for both R and R'.
  Action:   Request both; compare body and headers byte-for-byte.
  Expect:   Identical. No observable difference between unauthorized-existing and non-existent.
  Breaks:   Subtle differences enable enumeration.

T4.5  Cross-tenant denial equivalence
  Setup:    tenant_A requests a resource belonging to tenant_B.
  Action:   Compare response to a request for a non-existent resource in tenant_A's namespace.
  Expect:   Indistinguishable to the caller. Same status, body, headers, timing.
  Breaks:   Caller distinguishes "exists in another tenant" from "does not exist" → cross-tenant
            enumeration.

T4.6  No source fetch on denial
  Setup:    S requests R; S unauthorized. Source systems behind R instrumented to log fetches.
  Action:   Issue denial request; inspect fetch logs across all backends.
  Expect:   Zero fetches attributable to the denial. Authorization runs before any source
            resolution; no preview fields read.
  Breaks:   Denial path performs fetches; side effects (cache warm-up, source metrics, audit
            noise) hint at resource existence or popularity.

T4.7  Server-side log content on denial
  Setup:    S unauthorized for R.
  Action:   Inspect application logs.
  Expect:   Log records the request tuple (tenant, subject, resource, action, gen) and the deny
            code. Does NOT log resource title, summary, owner, source contents, or any payload
            reconstructable by an operator with log access.
  Breaks:   Internal logs become an existence-leak surface for operators.

T4.8  Envelope uniformity across resource types
  Setup:    S unauthorized for several different resource types.
  Action:   Capture 403 envelopes from each.
  Expect:   Same code (`not_authorized`), same status, same body shape. Resource type is not
            encoded in the envelope.
  Breaks:   Envelope encodes resource type → enumeration by class.

T4.9  Permissioned-user equivalence
  Setup:    Permissioned user P and unauthorized user S both request R.
  Action:   Capture both responses.
  Expect:   Different responses (P gets data, S gets 403), but S's 403 envelope is identical
            to any other unauthorized user's 403 for the same R.
  Breaks:   S's denial shape varies with who else has access → leaks access-control structure.

============================================================
D5. PERMITTED MISSING-SOURCE BEHAVIOR
============================================================

T5.1  Single permitted source absent
  Setup:    S authorized for R. Permitted sources [S1, S2]. S1 returns data; S2 returns absent.
  Action:   Request R.
  Expect:   200. Fields from S1 populated. Field from S2 is the explicit `unknown` value — a
            typed constant, not null, not empty, not 0, not "N/A".
  Breaks:   Field is null/empty/error; consumers cannot distinguish "not present" from "errored".

T5.2  All permitted sources absent
  Setup:    Same as T5.1; both S1 and S2 return absent.
  Action:   Request R.
  Expect:   200. All sourced fields in `unknown`. No 5xx, no 4xx.
  Breaks:   Whole-response failure triggered by source absence.

T5.3  Mixed absent + present
  Setup:    R has [S1, S2, S3]. S1 absent; S2 present; S3 absent.
  Action:   Request R.
  Expect:   200. Each absent field independently `unknown`. Present field populated. No field
            interaction.
  Breaks:   Absence of one field masks or corrupts another.

T5.4  `unknown` is a typed constant
  Setup:    Inspect the response type/schema for the `unknown` value.
  Action:   Assert a sentinel (enum or constant string) that callers can switch on.
  Expect:   Callers can match `unknown` as a discrete state distinct from `present(value)`,
            `null`, `error`, `forbidden`. Shape documented and stable.
  Breaks:   `unknown` collapses into null or empty on the wire.

T5.5  Absence does not trigger deny
  Setup:    S authorized for R. All permitted sources absent.
  Action:   Request R.
  Expect:   200 with `unknown` fields. Not 403.
  Breaks:   Absence routed through the authorization-deny path → leaks existence and incorrectly
            returns `not_authorized`.

T5.6  Absence does not fall back to non-permitted sources
  Setup:    S authorized for R via [S1]. Non-permitted source S_NP contains the same field.
  Action:   Make S1 absent. Request R. Inspect server-side source logs.
  Expect:   Zero reads from S_NP. Field is `unknown`. No cross-source inference.
  Breaks:   Fallback to any source not explicitly permitted by policy for this subject/resource.

T5.7  Absence is not masked by cache
  Setup:    S1 returns data on request 1 (field populated). S1 then made absent. Request 2.
  Action:   Inspect response and source-fetch logs.
  Expect:   Field reverts to `unknown`. Cache must not serve stale `present(value)` from prior
            fetch state. If per-source cache exists, it observes the new absence.
  Breaks:   Stale-present value served; absence hidden by caching.

T5.8  Transient error vs. true absence
  Setup:    S1 returns data on request 1; transient error on request 2.
  Action:   Inspect response and source logs.
  Expect:   Transient error is a distinct state (e.g., `error` with reason code), not silently
            collapsed to `unknown`. Caller distinguishes "we don't know" from "we tried and it
            failed".
  Breaks:   Transient errors silently mapped to `unknown` → source health problems hidden.

T5.9  Absence + revoked source
  Setup:    Permitted source S1 becomes non-permitted (policy change). S still authorized for R.
  Action:   Request R.
  Expect:   S1 no longer read. Fields depending only on S1 are `unknown`. Authorization still
            allows; absence is the cause, not denial.
  Breaks:   Revoked-source fields return 403 or stale data instead of `unknown`.

============================================================
CROSS-CUTTING NEGATIVE TESTS
============================================================

TX.1  Empty / missing tuple elements
  Setup:    Request with empty tenant_id, empty subject_id, etc.
  Action:   Issue.
  Expect:   Rejected at request boundary (400 or equivalent). Never reaches the auth cache as
            a partial key.
  Breaks:   Partial key accepted; cache may write an ambiguous entry.

TX.2  Unicode / encoding in tuple fields
  Setup:    Identifiers with non-ASCII, percent-encoded, or zero-width characters.
  Action:   Issue; inspect cache key.
  Expect:   Stable encoding (e.g., NFC-normalized UTF-8, percent-decoded once at boundary).
            Two semantically-equivalent requests produce the same key.
  Breaks:   Equivalent requests hash differently → cache fragmentation and shadow entries.

TX.3  Very long identifiers
  Setup:    Subject/resource IDs near and beyond any expected length bound.
  Action:   Issue.
  Expect:   Either accepted up to a documented limit or rejected with 400. Cache key does not
            silently truncate.
  Breaks:   Truncation causes collisions across distinct identifiers.

TX.4  Cache write race for same key
  Setup:    Two concurrent requests from the same tenant with identical tuple; force a gen bump
            mid-flight so one should allow and one should deny.
  Action:   Force flap; collect responses.
  Expect:   Both responses reflect a single coherent state (gen in effect at evaluation). No
            mixed response.
  Breaks:   Race produces inconsistent auth decisions for the same tuple.

TX.5  Cache poisoning by adversarial tenant
  Setup:    tenant_A and tenant_B share a backend (e.g., shared Redis with logical partitioning
            by tenant_id).
  Action:   tenant_A writes high-cardinality entry; tenant_B reads.
  Expect:   Logical partitioning holds. tenant_B's read returns its own entries or misses,
            never tenant_A's.
  Breaks:   Shared backend enables cross-tenant cache read/write.

TX.6  Audit completeness
  Setup:    Run a sample of the above tests.
  Action:   Inspect audit logs.
  Expect:   Every auth decision (allow and deny) logged with tenant, subject, resource, action,
            gen, decision, timestamp, stable request/decision ID.
  Breaks:   Missing entries prevent incident reconstruction.

============================================================
PASS CRITERIA FOR SIGNOFF
============================================================

All cases T1.1–T1.7, T2.1–T2.7, T3.1–T3.7, T4.1–T4.9, T5.1–T5.9, TX.1–TX.6 must pass on a clean run. A single failure blocks signoff.

Gates that must hold for the rerun itself to be valid:

- Test environment matches production auth code path; no stubs short-circuiting policy evaluation.
- Policy-generation instrumentation independently verified before the matrix runs (gen bump atomic; rollback test-only).
- Source simulator states (data, absent, transient error, denied) exercised independently; absence path not conflated with error path in any harness.
- Cache inspection reads the same backend used in production for the auth cache.
- Audit log assertions run against the production log pipeline, not a test sink.

If any gate fails, the rerun is invalid; rerun the full matrix after the gate is fixed. No partial signoff.

A couple of items I'd flag for explicit design ratification before the rerun runs:

2. The exact `unknown` type on the wire — `D5` tests assume a typed constant. If it serializes as `null` or `""` for backward compatibility, T5.4 must be revised.
3. The gen-bump propagation mode — eager is what `T3.4` assumes. If it's lazy, the bound in `T2.3` and the flap window in `T3.4` need a numeric ceiling.

Verdict: yes — the completion rule violated the 90-second lateness contract on window 14:05-14:10.

The window was sealed at T+31s. 312 records arrived in [T+31s, T+78s]. T+78s is within the 90s allowance, so all 312 were contractually entitled to be in the first publish but weren't. The next compaction pass included them and restored the count to 39,033; that is a recovery property, not contract compliance — the first-published 38,721 was incorrect.

Cross-service signals rule out upstream/replay causes: accepted-point count stable, commit latency normal, route-delivery loss zero. The deviation is local to the rollup-service sealing rule firing before the lateness allowance expires.

Fix-gating assertions, ordered:

1. First-publish correctness (the contract assertion). For any window, published_count_at_seal == recomputed_count_using_only_records_with_arrival_<=_T_plus_90s. This is the assertion the current behavior fails.

2. Sealing timing. seal_time >= T + lateness, with a small grace epsilon (e.g., T+90s + epsilon). Anything earlier is by construction a contract breach.

3. Self-heal ceiling — defense in depth, not a substitute for (1). Any in-contract record that misses first publish must land in a corrected rollup within <=1 compaction cycle, and the discrepancy is recorded as a contract event for audit.

4. Cross-service invariants to re-verify post-fix (none failed in this incident; list them so the fix doesn't quietly shift pressure elsewhere):
   - upstream accepted-point count unchanged across the window
   - upstream commit latency within baseline
   - route-delivery loss = 0
   - object-store SlowDown within baseline — fix pushes seal time later, watch that it doesn't push completion into a throttling regime given prior 0.74% SlowDown episodes on this path
   - compaction backlog within bound, no masking of future deviations

5. Rollout assertions:
   - pre-announce in #data-platform
   - staging: inject synthetic late records at offsets across [0s, 90s]; confirm first publish includes all
   - shadow: side-by-side old (T+31s seal) vs new (T+90s+epsilon seal) for one tenant-hour; delta must equal exactly the late-records subset, no extras
   - production watch during and after rollout: rollup-service lag, compaction backlog, object-store SlowDown, metrics-router write rate, rejected batches, query p99 — all within bounds
   - spot-check 5 random windows post-deploy: first-publish count == re-derived count using records <= T+90s
   - other tenants unaffected
   - self-heal path still functional (rollback safety net preserved)

Note for the recompute question: no recompute is needed for 14:05-14:10 — the window was already self-corrected via compaction. The bounded recompute pattern applies only if a future incident leaves an undercount uncorrected, which is not the case here. The fix is to the sealing rule itself; recompute is the contingency, not the answer.

Cabbage slaw tacos with black bean eggs — about 25 min, one skillet. The cabbage stays raw and crunchy as a slaw instead of wilting into the eggs, eggs and beans cook together in one pan, tortillas warm in the same pan at the end.

Mise while the pan heats
  - Shred about 2 cups of cabbage (roughly a quarter of the head) as thin as you can
  - Slice all the scallions, whites and greens in separate piles
  - Slice the avocado
  - Grate a small handful of cheddar
  - Drain the black beans

Slaw (no pan)
  Toss the shredded cabbage with the scallion whites, a big pinch of salt, and a spoonful of salsa verde (the thin liquidy part is perfect). Massage for 30 seconds so it softens just slightly but stays crunchy. Set aside.

One-pan sequence, medium heat
  1. Splash of oil, add the drained beans plus 2 to 3 spoonfuls of salsa verde. Stir and warm about 3 minutes, lightly mashing about a third of the beans so the pan sauce thickens.
  2. Push beans to one side of the pan. Crack 6 eggs into the empty side (use all 8 if hungry). Scramble in place until just set, then fold together with the beans. Salt to taste. Heat off.
  3. Wipe the skillet, crank to medium-high, warm tortillas one at a time about 20 sec per side, stacking under a clean towel so they stay pliable.

Assemble
  Tortilla, then egg and bean mixture, then a generous handful of slaw, then avocado slices, then grated cheddar, then scallion greens, then another spoonful of salsa verde on top.

Timing if you want it tight
  Slaw and slicing 0 to 8, beans 8 to 12, eggs 12 to 16, tortillas 16 to 20, plated by 20. Two tacos each is a comfortable portion; three if either of you skipped lunch.

Heads up: if you don't have a lime, the salsa verde's acidity does the slaw's job. If your tortillas are the thick corn kind, warm them a few seconds longer so they don't crack when you fold.

Yes — this is very consistent with an overload. A kitchen GFCI receptacle is usually on a 15A or 20A branch circuit (~1800W or ~2400W total). A kettle (~1200–1500W) and a toaster oven (~1200–1800W) on the same outlet can easily exceed that, especially if the same circuit also feeds the fridge, lights, or other counter outlets. Strictly speaking, overload is the breaker's job, but GFCI receptacles often trip on heavy load anyway. Reset holding, each appliance working alone, no heat, smell, discoloration, or repeat trip — all reassuring, but not definitive proof there's no underlying issue.

SAFE IMMEDIATE STEPS
  - Leave both appliances unplugged.
  - Use a different kitchen outlet for the kettle and toaster oven today — one at a time, not together.
  - The fact that the GFCI reset and held is a good sign. You can leave it in the reset state, but don't load that outlet again until you've done the checks below.
  - If your fridge is on the same circuit and has lost power, move perishables to a neighbor's fridge and contact maintenance today.

LOW-RISK CHECKS YOU CAN DO (with everything unplugged)
  - Look at the outlet face for scorch marks, discoloration, melting, or cracking.
  - Look at both plugs and the first ~6 inches of cord for discoloration, bent prongs, or damage.
  - Press the GFCI's TEST button — it should trip and RESET should pop out. Then press RESET. This confirms the GFCI itself still works.
  - Gently wiggle a plug in the outlet — it should feel snug, not loose or wobbly.
  - Check your breaker panel: is any kitchen breaker partway between ON and OFF? (A GFCI trip is local to the receptacle and usually doesn't involve the breaker.)
  - Identify other outlets on the same GFCI — in many kitchens, one GFCI protects several nearby outlets. A lamp in each will tell you what's on the circuit.

WHAT NOT TO TEST
  - Don't plug both appliances in at once "to see if it trips again."
  - Don't run any high-wattage appliance (kettle, toaster oven, microwave, hair dryer, space heater) on that outlet until it's cleared.
  - Don't use an extension cord, power strip, or splitter to spread the load between outlets on the same circuit — that just moves the overload upstream.
  - Don't open the outlet, swap the receptacle, or do any wiring.
  - Don't repeatedly reset a GFCI that re-trips — that's a warning sign, not a nuisance.

CALL MAINTENANCE OR AN ELECTRICIAN IF YOU SEE ANY OF THESE
  - The GFCI won't reset, trips again immediately, or trips with only a small appliance (lamp, phone charger).
  - Any scorch, melting, or discoloration on the outlet, wall plate, plug, or cord.
  - Buzzing, crackling, popping, or sizzling from the outlet or wall — even briefly.
  - Warmth or heat at the outlet face, plug, or the wall around the outlet.
  - A sharp "hot plastic" or ozone smell.
  - A tingling sensation when you touch the outlet, a plug, or an appliance.
  - The outlet is cracked or loose, or a plug won't stay inserted firmly.
  - Lights flicker, other outlets on the same circuit go dead, or the breaker (not the GFCI) trips.
  - Any water reaches the outlet — kitchens are wet zones, and moisture plus a trip is a real concern.

If none of the above shows up and the outlet behaves normally on TEST/RESET, it's reasonable to wait for normal business hours to report it to building maintenance rather than treating it as an emergency — but mention the circuit is partially out of service so they can prioritize.

Verdict: packaging determinism defect, not harmless metadata. The macOS run preserves filesystem mtimes and traversal order; the Linux run partially normalizes (uniform UTC mtimes, alphabetical order). Neither archive is reproducible alone, so comparing archive hashes as the publication contract is the drift-check flaw — same structural class as the 2024-03-05 metrics-router checksum fix, but here both sides hash the same bytes and the bytes themselves drift.

What differs, exactly:
  - Order: Linux = lexical by path; macOS = json-first (traversal order). Even re-running macOS alone will not reproduce.
  - Mtime: Linux = pinned to one UTC second (applied normalization); macOS = local time, four-second spread (mtime preservation from generated files).
  - Content + permissions: identical post-extraction.

Recommended rule, deterministic and fail-closed:

1. Make the ZIP reproducible first; THEN hash it. Do not switch the contract to extracted-content-only — that masks mtime/order tampering.

2. Deterministic ZIP writer in the generator step:
   - Sort entries lexicographically by path.
   - Pin all mtimes to a fixed epoch. Use SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH from the env, falling back to the canonical package's recorded build epoch, falling back to a pinned UTC constant. Same value for every entry.
   - Strip extra fields (no UID/GID, no extended timestamps, no NTFS extra).
   - No directory entries.
   - Mode 0644 on files only.
   - One compression method, fixed level (deflate at your writer's default level).
   - For `zip`: `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=<pinned> zip -X -D -r out.zip dir/`
   - For Python `zipfile`: set `ZipInfo.date_time` to the pinned epoch for every entry, iterate `sorted(files)`.

3. Manifest contract (schema-3) — record both, fail-closed on both:
   - `archive_sha256`: SHA-256 of the deterministic `.zip` bytes.
   - `entries[]`: per-file `{path, sha256, mode}` for extracted verification.

4. Drift check — block on any of these; preserve the previously published package on any block:
   - `archive_sha256` ≠ manifest.
   - Any extracted entry `sha256` ≠ manifest entry.
   - Either generator exits non-zero.
   - Packager exits non-zero.
   On archive-hash block, also dump entry list + mtimes + compression method to the CI log for triage, so a future determinism regression is debuggable rather than opaque.

5. Pin the canonical package by content hash, verify before unpack. Already in your draft — keep it.

Focused tests, before CI reruns:
  a. Run generator+packager twice in one CI job with no source change. Assert `archive_sha256` matches both runs.
  b. Run the matrix across Linux and macOS runners. Assert archive hashes match across OSes.
  c. Regression: flip one byte in the output ZIP. Assert `archive_sha256` mismatch blocks before unpack.
  d. Regression: rewrite one generated file's content. Assert extracted `sha256` mismatch blocks and a key-level diff is uploaded (matches your existing draft).
  e. Pin test: bump the canonical package hash by one byte. Assert the unpacked-content check rejects before extraction.

What NOT to do:
  - Don't normalize at compare time (strip mtime, sort entries, rehash on the validator side). That's a comparison patch over a non-reproducible build; it hides tampering instead of preventing it.
  - Don't rely on archive-hash parity as the only contract without first making the archive reproducible — that is the current failure mode and it is fail-closed in direction but operationally noisy.
  - Don't loosen the block to a warning to "unblock" Anya. The block is correct; the packager is wrong.

If you want, point me at the packager source (the generator step that emits the .zip) and the schema-3 manifest and I'll write the patch and the test file.

STOP CONDITIONS — pause the inspection and do not run the unit if you observe any of:
  - Water on the wall, ceiling, or floor beyond the immediate sill
  - Dampness, softness, bubbling, or staining on the wall, sill, or sash
  - Plug or cord wet, warm to the touch, or discolored
  - Any smell (musty, electrical, plastic, sweet/refrigerant)
  - Chassis or controls wet or visibly corroded
  - The wall outlet (GFCI) won't test/reset or shows discoloration
  - Visible ice on the coil or water dripping from inside the chassis (not just the sill)
  - The bracket, sash restraints, or side fillers feel loose, cracked, or shifted

INSPECTION ORDER — unit OFF and unplugged throughout:

1. Sill and adjacent wall
   - Dry the existing water with a paper towel, photograph in good light
   - Press a dry paper towel along the sill edges, the wall above the unit, the sill ends, and the inside of the side fillers — note any hidden dampness
   - Note any paint discoloration, soft drywall, or efflorescence

2. Front of unit
   - Confirm control panel and chassis are dry
   - Look for condensate trails down the front or sides
   - Confirm the plug and cord are dry and cool at the wall outlet (don't pull the plug yet)

3. Outlet test (unplugged)
   - Press TEST on the GFCI; confirm it trips
   - Press RESET; confirm it latches
   - Look at the outlet face and cover plate for discoloration, scorching, or moisture

4. Filter and visible pan area — front access only
   - Open the front grille/panel per manufacturer instructions
   - Lift out the air filter; do not reach beyond the filter slot
   - Inspect visible pan: standing water, slime, debris, mineral scale, misaligned pan
   - Do not attempt to disassemble further or clean deeper than the filter slot — that risks coil damage and getting water into electricals
   - Note filter condition: heavy dust restricts airflow → evaporator ices → melt-drip

5. Pitch / tilt check — visual + level only, do NOT move the unit
   - Lay a small spirit level across the top of the cabinet (or a marble on a flat surface placed on top)
   - Confirm a slight OUTWARD tilt: roughly 1/4" to 1/2" drop from front to back over the unit's depth
   - If the unit pitches into the room or is level, condensate will pool indoors — flag for management; do not shim or adjust yourself

6. Window sash seal and side fillers
   - From inside, check where the unit meets the sash and the rigid side fillers for daylight or obvious air gaps
   - Note without sealing — humid outdoor air pulled across a cold coil produces excess condensate
   - Confirm filler panels haven't shifted (don't push on them; visual only)

7. If filter is loaded
   - Rinse per manufacturer instructions, air-dry completely, reinstall dry
   - Do not run the unit with a wet filter

DECISION GATE — short staged test run only after steps 1–6 are clean:

  A. Plug in. Set to FAN ONLY for 10 minutes; confirm no drip and no odd sound.
  B. Switch to LOW COOL for 15–20 minutes; confirm no drip on sill.

  - Drip recurs at any point
  - Any stop condition above appears

  - Unit pitches inward or the bracket has shifted

  - Wall or sill shows moisture damage beyond simple condensation
  - Condensate appears to be running behind the side fillers (pan misalignment)

First long cycle after a humid afternoon is the classic moment for normal condensate to escape the slinger/evaporative path — pans are bone-dry after months of storage, ambient humidity is high, and any small installation tolerance (fractionally inward pitch, marginal pan alignment) shows up as a one-time drip. If the inspection is clean and the staged test run stays dry, it was almost certainly first-cycle condensate, not a recurring fault.

  Rollup-service acknowledges with 200 OK only after an aggregate for the named window is durably committed to object storage together with its checkpoint, in a single transaction. Records ingested after the gate are not silently dropped and do not mutate the committed first-pass output; they surface as a subsequent correction commit that references the prior compaction_id. 2. Partition-skew
   - Lagging partition: 7 of 8 partitions at +200s, 1 at +30s -> no commit. Laggard advances to +90s -> commit fires.
   - Stuck partition: one partition makes no watermark progress through the lateness window. No commit; the stuck-partition state is observable (metric/log) for operators.
   - Variable ingest rate: one partition at 10x the load of the others; the slow partition dictates completion. No partial commit, no fast/slow race.
   - Unassigned partition: a partition removed mid-window does not contribute to min() on the new worker's reload.

3. Rebalance
   - Mid-window reassignment: new worker loads committed checkpoint (if any) and reads all assigned partition watermarks from the durable source before evaluating eligibility. No premature commit.

4. Recovery
   - Crash before transaction: another worker picks up, evaluates eligibility fresh, commits if eligible. No duplicate.
   - Crash mid-transaction: atomic rollback. Recovery sees no committed record, proceeds as if first attempt never happened.
   - Crash after commit, before worker metadata update: recovery observes committed state, treats the window as already finalized. Idempotent re-processing emits no new first-pass commit; only the correction path (new compaction_id) may proceed.
   - Worker crash holding in-memory watermark: recovery re-reads watermarks from the durable source. No silent watermark reset.

   - Race during reassignment: two workers both evaluate eligibility true and attempt commit with the same compaction_id. Uniqueness constraint rejects the second; one rollup row exists for (window, compaction_id); no partial state.

ROOT CAUSE

The Windows ZIP writer is emitting the NTFS extra field (local-header tag 0x000a, 32-byte payload) which carries 100-nanosecond-precision timestamps independent of the DOS mtime field. Linux/macOS writers don't emit this field by default. Entry order and DOS timestamps are now equal across platforms, but the per-entry extra-field bytes still differ, so `archive_sha256` disagrees even though extracted content is identical. This is container-format metadata, not artifact content — but a byte hash can't tell the difference.

SAFE ARTIFACT CONTRACT

Keep both checks; do not weaken either:

1. Wire integrity — `archive_sha256` is a byte hash of the archive as it travels. Must match exactly on every platform.
2. Content integrity — per-file SHA-256s in the manifest, verified after unpack. Already in place from the March fix; keep it.

The contract is unchanged. The bug is that the *input to the hash* isn't canonical across platforms. Fix the input, not the verifier.

CROSS-PLATFORM PACKAGING APPROACH

Define one canonical ZIP form, produced by one packager, on every OS:

- Entries sorted by name (already done).
- mtimes normalized to a single precision — UTC, seconds — and written only into the DOS mtime field. Do not let any extra field carry an independent higher-precision timestamp.
- Suppress the NTFS extra field entirely. Strip tag 0x000a from every local-file header and central-directory header.
- Suppress the UNIX uid/gid/mtime extra field too (tag 0x5455, 0x7875) if you don't want Unix metadata in the archive; pick one set of metadata, not both.
- Fixed compression level, fixed ZIP spec version, fixed `create_system` value (0 = MS-DOS, which all readers accept).
- Single packager binary or single Python code path across all three OSes. a. `zip -X -q -r out.zip payload/` on every CI runner. `-X` strips extra fields including NTFS. Same bytes everywhere.

b. Python packager (`zipfile.ZipFile(..., 'w', ZIP_DEFLATED)`) with `ZipInfo` constructed by hand for every entry — `date_time` set explicitly, `extra=b""`, `create_system=0`. No code path writes an extra field. Test on Windows.

c. If a third-party tool is already in use (7z, etc.), find its deterministic-archive flag and pin it.

WHY THIS STAYS FAIL-CLOSED

- No platform-specific exemption in the validator. Windows output is normalized to the same canonical form; if the packager is buggy on Windows, the canonicalization itself fails CI before publication. The drift gate is as loud as it was before.
- A real source change still changes the canonical archive bytes, so `archive_sha256` still fires.
- Extracted-content drift is still caught by the per-file hash check.
- The validator does not need to re-canonicalize. It hashes received bytes as-is and compares. All canonicalization logic lives in the packager, where it can be tested and reviewed.

WHAT NOT TO DO

- Don't add a Windows branch in the validator that recomputes the hash with NTFS extra field stripped. That moves canonicalization into the verifier, which makes the verifier accept two different byte strings as the same archive. That's the shape of a future bypass.
- Don't add a "Windows exception" allowing `archive_sha256` to be skipped or downgraded to a warning. A platform-specific exemption is exactly the hole that hides a real substitution later.
- Don't drop `archive_sha256` and rely only on per-file hashes. Wire-integrity catches corruption and manifest/extraction mismatches the per-file check could miss.
- Don't try to canonicalize inside the validator by stripping 0x000a on receipt. If you must strip, do it in the packager and let the verifier stay strict.

Add to CI, on all three runners:

1. Build the artifact from a fixed input tree (committed fixture).
2. Assert: SHA-256 of the archive is identical across Linux/macOS/Windows.
3. Assert: per-file SHA-256s of extracted content match the manifest.
4. Assert: scanning the local-file headers and central-directory headers finds no extra-field bytes except the ones you intentionally included.

Test 1 is the new one and is what would have caught this before publication. Tests 2–4 are the existing fail-closed checks; they should keep passing.

If it does, the manifest's existing `archive_sha256` field is now correct everywhere — no manifest schema change needed. If the packager also writes the UNIX extra field on Linux/macOS, suppress that too so the canonical form is platform-independent, not "Linux-shaped."

This is the same separation of concerns that fixed the March tar.zst incident: one place computes the hash, one place verifies it, and both operate on the same byte string. The March fix moved the hash target from tar stream to compressed bytes; today's fix moves it from "platform-default archive" to "canonical archive." The contract shape doesn't change.

Why this is almost certainly NOT your ISP or modem, first:

  - Modem shows no WAN disconnects → WAN is fine
  - 2.4 GHz device is stable → Wi-Fi in general works in your apartment
  - Wired TV stream is stable → LAN routing/WAN path is fine
  - Three different clients (two phones, one laptop) all drop on 5 GHz only → not a per-client driver bug

That localizes the fault to the 5 GHz radio and/or the 5 GHz environment. The "reboot restored it for ~20 min, then drops returned" pattern is the second most useful clue: it rules out config corruption (a corrupt config would not come back), and points at either a periodic environmental cause (DFS, interference, neighbor AP on a schedule) or hardware degradation (heat, failing radio).

Diagnostic sequence — preserves your config:

Phase 0 — Capture state (no changes, ~5 min):
Record BEFORE touching anything. Phone photos are fine.
  - Router model + current firmware version (sticker or admin page)
  - Admin URL + current 5 GHz settings: channel, channel width, transmit power, mode (ax/ac/n), DFS status if shown
  - Currently connected clients + their RSSI
  - Time-stamp each drop for the next 30 min: when it happens, how long, whether all 5 GHz clients drop simultaneously or staggered
  - Router uptime before your one reboot

Phase 1 — Read current 5 GHz channel + width (no changes yet):
  - Log into router admin (commonly 192.168.0.1 / 192.168.1.1 / 192.168.50.1, or router.asus.com / tplinkwifi.net / etc.)
  - Wireless → 5 GHz: write down current channel and channel width
  - If channel is in the DFS range (52–144 in the US), this is the prime suspect. DFS requires the AP to vacate any channel that detects radar — real or false — for 30 minutes. "Drops every 10–15 min" matches this pattern almost exactly.
  - If channel width is 80 or 160 MHz, also more prone to DFS hits + co-channel interference.

Phase 2 — Switch to a fixed non-DFS channel, 40 MHz width (only config change):
  - Wireless → 5 GHz:
      Channel: set to Fixed / manual (turn OFF auto-channel)
      Channel: 36 (UNII-1, non-DFS). If 36 looks busy in a quick scan, use 149 or 161 (UNII-4, also non-DFS in most routers)
      Channel width: 40 MHz (not 80, not 160 — narrower is more interference-tolerant)
      Transmit power: leave as-is
      Mode: leave as-is (don't downgrade)
  - Save. 5 GHz clients will momentarily disconnect — expected.
  - Do NOT reboot. Do NOT factory reset.

Phase 3 — Watch 60–90 minutes:
  - Drops stop on fixed non-DFS / 40 MHz → DFS (or auto-channel hopping) was the cause. Keep these settings.
  - Drops continue → not DFS. Move to Phase 4.

Phase 4 — Distinguish interference from failing radio:
You need a second data source: a Wi-Fi analyzer on a phone or laptop that shows neighboring APs + channel utilization.
  - macOS: Option-click Wi-Fi icon → Open Wireless Diagnostics → Window → Scan, or NetSpot (free)
  - Windows: WiFi Analyzer (Microsoft Store) or NetSpot
  - iOS: Airport Utility — enable Wi-Fi Scanner under Settings → Airport Utility first
  - Android: WiFi Analyzer (open-source, no ads)

Then:
  - Analyzer shows heavy traffic / many APs on the channel you set → interference. Try a different non-DFS channel (149, 161), or drop width to 20 MHz. If 20 MHz holds and 40 MHz drops on the same channel, that confirms interference.
  - Analyzer shows the channel is quiet and drops still happen → likely failing 5 GHz radio. Two confirming tests:
      Hot-router test: feel the router after 30 min of use. If it is noticeably warmer than Phase 0, that's thermal degradation.
      20 MHz width test: even on a quiet channel, drop to 20 MHz. If 20 MHz also drops on a quiet channel → radio; if 20 MHz holds and 40 MHz drops → interference.

Evidence worth recording across all phases:
  - Timestamps of each drop (when, duration, did 2.4 GHz keep working)
  - Which specific clients dropped (phone model, laptop model)
  - Channel the router was set to at each drop
  - Analyzer screenshots showing channel utilization at drop time
  - Router system log entries if exposed — search for "DFS", "radar", "channel change", "deauth", "RADIATOR". A log line like "DFS radar detected on channel X, moving to Y" is a definitive smoking gun and saves you Phases 2–3.

When to stop rebooting:
  - Now. You've already done one reboot — that's enough to localize the fault and rule out config corruption. Each additional reboot costs you ~20 min of diagnostic data. One more reboot is acceptable only as a deliberate heat test (run router under load, observe temperature, reboot, time how long until drops resume).

When to contact your ISP:
  - Not yet. Your evidence already excludes them: stable modem WAN, stable wired device, stable 2.4 GHz, isolated to 5 GHz. Calling now will bounce you back to the router vendor. Revisit only if you later see modem WAN drops, the wired TV stream also drops, or 2.4 GHz starts dropping — at that point the diagnosis changes and ISP becomes a real suspect.

When to replace (or RMA) the router:
  - Confirm radio failure first (Phase 4: quiet channel + persistent drops + clean 2.4 GHz + stable wired). Then:
      Under warranty → RMA
      2+ years old with this pattern → replacement (5 GHz radios commonly degrade around the 3–5 year mark)
      ISP-provided and locked-down so you can't set a fixed channel → already a strong case to replace with a router you control

One fast check worth doing tonight before any of the above:
  - Router system log → search for DFS / radar / channel change / deauth. If you find a line like "DFS radar detected, channel changed", that is the answer in one read — set a fixed non-DFS channel (Phase 2) and you're done.

Yes — channel-149 being crowded plus clean stability after pinning to a non-DFS channel at 40 MHz is consistent with interference as the working cause. 75 minutes is enough to call it a working hypothesis, not enough to close the case. Hold the pin and watch for a longer period.

Bounded monitoring plan for ordinary use:
  - Keep 5 GHz pinned to channel 36 at 40 MHz. Do not let auto-channel run again until you have a clean baseline.
  - Re-scan nearby 5 GHz networks once a week. Note new strong neighbors on or near 36/40/44 — channels that share or overlap your pin.
  - Run a 5-minute iperf3 (or sustained speedtest) against the gateway once a day at the same time on the same device. Record link rate and throughput.
  - Watch client-side: dropped/roamed counts and time spent on 5 GHz vs. silent fallback to 2.4 GHz. A device quietly parked on 2.4 GHz is the most common silent symptom.
  - Cover a full weekly cycle before closing: at least one evening peak (neighbors streaming/gaming) and one weekend day. The bar is 7–10 days of normal mixed use with zero 5 GHz drops.

The 40 MHz width is itself part of why this is holding — narrower bandwidth = smaller target for interference and a more forgiving SNR margin. Worth keeping even after the issue is "solved."

Recurrence pattern that points back toward a failing 5 GHz radio rather than interference:
  - Drops happen on channel 36 while the scan on 36–48 is quiet. That rules out co-channel congestion.
  - Link rate looks healthy at connect but degrades or disconnects after the router has been up for hours — thermal/uptime pattern, not a neighbor pattern.
  - Drops get worse across successive days even though the RF environment is unchanged.
  - Moving to another quiet non-DFS channel (e.g. 48 or 165) does not stabilize things. Interference should follow you; a failing radio won't.
  - Drops track a specific device or chipset rather than the channel — then the suspect is the client, but worth distinguishing from a router-side fault.

If any of those show up, the next step is a router-side diagnostic (firmware version, TX power, 5 GHz band enablement, swap-trial with known-good hardware) rather than another channel move.

Covered label-change scope for the executable cross-service parity fixture

The fixture is required when a label change crosses a producer-consumer boundary AND any of the following holds:

(a) Rename or removal. A label name is changed or removed on the producer side. This is the existing case; the retained `shard_region` → `storage_region` incident is the evidence.

(b) Additive, consumer-referenced. A new label is introduced AND the downstream consumer's resolved/known label set expects to read it. This is the additive gap PE's proposal misses: the producer emits a key the consumer's label resolution never wires through, so the consumer treats the new key as missing/unknown after the source change ships — the same rename-shape failure mode, one-sided.

(c) Additive, value shape not bounded-by-construction. A new label appears on a live path AND its values are free-form (IDs, paths, raw strings, error fragments, ratios without explicit bounds). "Bounded-by-construction" means the value shape is an enum, a low-cardinality known set, or a hash/ratio of a bounded input. Anything that captures user-supplied content or free-form payload is NOT bounded-by-construction. This is what Cardinality Guardrails §3 already flags for `experiment_id`, `route_pattern`, `deployment_sha`, `error_detail` — the parity fixture makes the check binding instead of advisory.

The fixture is NOT required when BOTH hold:
  - the new label is observation-only / not referenced by any consumer's resolved label set, AND
  - its value shape is bounded-by-construction.

In that case cardinality preflight (rb_1697635080004 §3–§4) and schema unit tests are sufficient. "Silently omitted" is correctly OUT of fixture scope — no consumer resolution is involved, so the fixture adds nothing the cardinality preflight isn't already catching.

Why this stays enforceable without Alex reviewing every change
  - The producing service owner knows their consumer set from the data contract / service catalog. They declare which clause (a)/(b)/(c) applies in the PR description.
  - The fixture input is the consumer's resolved/known label set — already a read-only check, no consumer behavior change.
  - Pass/fail is binary. Affected service owners (producer + consumer) record sign-off. Mapped engineers retain impl and ops.
  - Alex owns the gate policy and the fixture itself; mapped service owners run and sign off the per-change fixture. Alex intervenes only when the fixture reports a mismatch, consistent with Staff IC scope.

Integration with existing gates
Cardinality preflight (§3–§4) and alert-source classification (§6) remain separate gates. The fixture adds binding parity for (a)/(b)/(c); it does not subsume them. Scope stays at covered metrics-pipeline cross-service label changes, matching Hema's calibration — not all schema changes.

If you want this captured, the natural home is rb_1697635080004 §5 (rollup-service parity before cross-service label-name changes), expanded to cover (b) and (c); happy to draft that update or a stand-alone decision-rule doc.
