Plan: Low-cleanup salmon dinner for two — sheet pan veg, pot of orzo, cold yogurt-dill sauce, salmon seared last.

Total active time: ~35 min
Safe hold at room temp: salmon up to 45 min before the sear; everything else holds covered/warm for the same window
Serves: 2

WHAT YOU'RE USING
  - 2 salmon fillets (skin on if you have it)
  - ~6 oz green beans, trimmed
  - ~2 cups cherry tomatoes, halved
  - 1 cup dry orzo
  - 1 lemon
  - A small handful of dill
  - 1/2 cup plain yogurt
  - 2-4 slices bread
  - Olive oil, salt, pepper

EQUIPMENT
  One sheet pan, one pot, one small bowl, one skillet (skillet is only used at the very end for the salmon).

PHASE 1 — SET THE CLOCK (T-0 to T-5)
  Pull the salmon from the fridge. Set the fillets on a plate, skin side up, light sprinkle of salt. Leave them on the counter. This is your 45-minute holding window — they will temper, which is exactly what you want.
  Preheat the oven to 425°F.
  Put a pot of water on to boil for the orzo.

PHASE 2 — VEG ON THE SHEET PAN (T-5 to T-10)
  On the sheet pan, toss the green beans and halved cherry tomatoes with about 2 tablespoons of olive oil, a generous pinch of salt, and pepper. Spread in one layer, cut sides of the tomatoes facing up. Into the oven. Roast 18-20 min total.

PHASE 3 — ORZO + SAUCE (T-10 to T-20)
  When the water boils, salt it and add the orzo. Cook per package, usually 8-9 min.
  While it cooks, make the sauce in a small bowl:
    - 1/2 cup yogurt
    - zest of half the lemon, plus a small squeeze of juice
    - 1 tbsp chopped dill
    - pinch of salt
    - glug of olive oil
    - loosen with a teaspoon of warm water if it's thick
  Stir, taste, adjust salt and lemon. Set aside on the counter — sauce holds fine at room temp for 45+ min.

PHASE 4 — DRAIN, REST, HOLD (T-20 to T-25)
  Drain the orzo. Return it to the pot off the heat. Add a small knob of butter or a drizzle of olive oil, a squeeze of lemon, and a pinch of the remaining dill. Stir, cover. The covered pot holds at room temp up to 45 min with no quality loss — when you restart it, splash in 1-2 tbsp hot water and stir to loosen.
  Check the sheet pan: tomatoes should be blistered and collapsing, beans tender with a few brown spots. Pull the pan.

PHASE 5 — THE HOLD (up to 45 min)
  Three safe options here, pick whichever matches when Devika is up:
    A. She's up within 15 min — leave everything as-is. Orzo covered, veg on the pan, sauce on the counter, salmon still tempering.
    B. She's 30-45 min — turn the oven to its lowest warm setting (170°F if you have it). Slide the sheet pan back in, loosely tented with foil. Splash the orzo with hot water and re-cover. Sauce and salmon stay put.
    C. If she texts she's out another 90 min, abandon the sear and flake the now-room-temp salmon cold over the orzo with the yogurt sauce — it becomes a salmon-orzo bowl, and no one eats dried-out fish.

PHASE 6 — SEAR THE SALMON (only when you're ready to eat)
  Pat the salmon fillets dry with a paper towel — this is what gets you a crust instead of steam.
  Heat a skillet over medium-high with a tablespoon of olive oil until it shimmers.
  Lay the salmon in skin-side down. Press gently for 30 seconds so it doesn't curl. Cook 4 min skin-side down without moving it — skin should be crisp and release cleanly when you nudge it.
  Flip. Cook 2-3 min more for medium (pull at 125°F internal; it'll coast to 130°F). Off the heat, squeeze a little lemon over the top.
  Total cook time on the salmon: 6-8 min. This is why it goes last — any earlier and it dries out while you wait.

PLATE
  Orzo on warm plates or straight from the pot.
  Spoon the roasted tomatoes and beans alongside.
  Salmon on top, skin side up so it stays crisp.
  Big spoonful of the lemon-dill yogurt over the salmon or onto the orzo.
  Warm bread on the side for sweeping up sauce.

DON'TS
  - Don't cover the roasted veg tightly — they'll steam and go limp. Foil tent or low oven only.
  - Don't rinse the orzo — you want the surface starch to hold the sauce.
  - Don't put cold salmon straight from the fridge into a hot pan. The whole point of the 45-min hold is that room-temp fish sears; cold fish steams.
  - Don't overcook the salmon. Pull at 125°F; carryover heat finishes it.

If she naps through and you eat at 8 instead of 7, nothing changes — that was the design.

RANKED PLAUSIBLE CAUSES (high → low)

1. Downstream dependency latency spike inside the handler.
   - Handler duration typically aggregates downstream calls (auth lookup, schema/registry, batch commit, object storage, IDP). A 12‑min slowdown in any one of them inflates handler time without moving queue wait, accepted-point continuity, or dropped counters. This matches the evidence best: capacity was free, queueing was low, accepted points flowed, work got slow.
   - Trace signal: per-call latencies on outbound HTTP/gRPC inside the handler span during the burst vs. adjacent windows; downstream service dashboards for the same window.

2. Connection-setup / authentication phase eating the deadline before "handler" measurement starts.
   - If "handler duration" excludes TLS handshake, mTLS, token validation, JWKS fetch, or IP allowlist, the 2.0s budget may be consumed before the handler timer starts. The 504 would then come from the client (or an intermediate proxy) before handler work even registered fully.
   - Trace signal: span breakdown for setup vs. handler vs. response phases; whether failed requests carry a valid auth span at all; auth-specific timing on failed vs. successful pairs.

3. Response delivery / egress blocking after handler completes.
   - Handler finishes inside the deadline but cannot flush: TCP receive buffer pressure on the client side, intermediate proxy queue, asymmetric routing, response-size spike, or TLS session-resumption cost on the write side.
   - Trace signal: gap between handler-end span and response-flushed span; response-write duration; client-region network metrics for the window.

4. Per-payload slow path triggered by the affected client's traffic shape.
   - "One ingest path" hints at a specific route, content-type, schema version, header combination, or payload size/structure that hits a slow code path (regex, large nested object, decompression near a limit, per-tenant validation branch). Would not move global queue metrics if only that path is hot.
   - Trace signal: per-request attributes (route, content-type, body size, schema version, tenant) on failed traces; CPU profile correlation with the same attributes during the burst.

5. Intermediate proxy / load balancer timing out before ingest-edge.
   - The 504 may originate from an LB, CDN, or WAF in front of ingest-edge whose configured timeout is shorter than 2.0s. ingest-edge never sees deadline pressure; the client still sees 504.
   - Trace signal: did the failed request actually reach ingest-edge (look for ingest-edge trace IDs vs. client trace IDs); LB/proxy access logs for the same client IPs and time window; configured timeouts at each hop.

6. Runtime pause window (GC or runtime stop-the-world).
   - Plausible only if memory was near a threshold during the burst. Memory was steady in adjacent recent incidents, but is not measured for this window. A 12-min continuous pause is unusual; more likely to be a correlated allocation burst.
   - Trace signal: long blank gaps inside otherwise normal traces; runtime GC / stop-the-world metrics; allocation rate.

7. Recent code change that introduced a slow path for the affected input pattern.
   - A deploy within hours of the burst that added a downstream call, extra validation, or new branch triggered by a specific request attribute.
   - Trace signal: deploy timestamps vs. burst start; CPU profile diff vs. baseline; new function frames on the stack of failed traces.

Explicitly ruled out by the evidence (recorded so they are not relitigated):
- Admission permit exhaustion (eligible capacity remained in use).
- Per-tenant waiting cap (affected requests never reached it).
- Dropped accepted points (counter stayed at zero; permit release-on-completion path was clean in prior fixes).
- CPU saturation, memory pressure, or pod restarts (would also have moved queue wait; nothing in the evidence suggests it).
- Note this is a different class from the May 2 burst (429s, admission-driven) and the June 3 ramp (request-p99 blip, admission clean). 504s with handler near the deadline point downstream of admission, not at the admission layer.

DISTRIBUTED-TRACE EVIDENCE NEEDED

For at least ~10 failed requests during the burst, plus a matched sample of successful requests in the 10 min before and after:

a. Per-phase spans (separate, timed):
   - TCP / TLS connection setup.
   - Authentication (token validation, key/JWKS lookup).
   - Handler work (decompression, validation, downstream calls as nested spans).
   - Response serialization.
   - Response flush / network write to client.
   - End-to-end time as observed at the client.

b. Per-span attributes:
   - Trace ID that maps to a specific accepted_point counter increment (and confirms no increment for failures).
   - Route, content-type, body size, schema version, tenant ID.
   - Downstream call target and per-call latency.
   - HTTP status observed at each layer (edge → LB → client).

c. Failure-mode localization:
   - For each failed trace: identify the LAST span that completed and the FIRST span that did not complete. This is the single highest-value piece of evidence — it directly says which phase crossed the deadline.
   - Same localization on a successful trace, to show what "normal" looks like.

d. Downstream correlation:
   - Hop-to-hop traces from downstream services for the same window.

CLIENT-DEADLINE EVIDENCE NEEDED

a. Where the 2.0s clock starts:
   - TCP connect? Request-write start? First byte sent? Response first byte?
   - The starting point changes whether setup time is counted against the deadline.

b. What the client actually observed:
   - Whether the 504 was generated by the client (its own deadline expired) or by an intermediate proxy.
   - Client logs: time-to-first-byte, time-to-last-byte, exact time the 504 was logged, exact deadline the client enforced.

c. Client HTTP library and config:
   - Connect timeout vs. request timeout vs. response timeout.
   - Any client-side retries inside the 2.0s window that consumed budget before the real request completed.
   - TLS session-resumption behavior; any full-handshake spikes on failed vs. successful pairs.

d. Network path evidence:
   - RTT client → ingest-edge during the burst.
   - TLS handshake time on failed vs. successful pairs.
   - Any path change or routing event in the client region at burst start.

e. Intermediate proxy logs:
   - LB / CDN / WAF access logs for the same client IPs / trace IDs in the window.
   - Configured idle, request, and response timeouts at each hop.
   - Whether 504s in client logs match 504s at the LB, or whether the LB saw a different status (e.g. a successful 200 that the client gave up waiting on).

WHAT THIS EVIDENCE WOULD (AND WOULD NOT) JUSTIFY CHANGING

- Time inside handler downstream calls → investigate downstream service; do not change ingest-edge scheduling or limits.
- Time in setup / auth → investigate auth path and TLS; do not change ingest-edge scheduling or limits.
- Time in response write / network → investigate egress and LB configuration; do not change ingest-edge scheduling or limits.
- Time in a per-payload slow path → code fix or input-shape guard; do not change admission caps or waiting caps.
- LB / proxy timeout shorter than 2.0s → adjust that timeout; out of scope for ingest-edge limits.
- Handler genuinely slow because of CPU/memory/runtime pressure on this path only → consider per-path capacity isolation, but only after confirming global admission metrics still showed free capacity (which they do here, so this remains a tail-end option).

Do not change on this evidence:
- Per-tenant waiting cap — affected requests never reached it.
- Admission permit count — capacity remained in use and accepted points were continuous.
- Drop policy — no drops were happening; not the lever.
- Retry-After distribution — these are 504s, not 429s; Retry-After does not apply to 504s, and changing the 429 distribution does not touch the path the affected client is on.

Holding limits and scheduling constant until trace and deadline evidence localize the phase is the correct call here: every lever in the limit/scheduling family is contradicted by the metrics you already have.

  - Numbness, tingling, or any locking/clicking

The trace tells me three things.

1. Authorization span is correctly tenant-scoped (request=A vs request=B). Auth is doing the gating.

2. Adapter span has a tenant-correlation gap — it carries service_id=checkout only, with no field linking back to the auth request. Any downstream tool that groups on service_id alone would co-mingle the two tenants' adapter work. Not an auth regression, but an observability hole that would matter once customer access opens.

3. Deploy-card cache-key components are not recorded in spans, so cross-tenant cache reuse can't be diagnosed from instrumentation after the fact. Consistent with the bounded-cache-key discipline, but means a card anomaly later can't be traced to its key inputs.

Customer access flag held disabled throughout — boundary respected. So this is instrumentation findings on top of the July-22 rehearsal, not a re-opening of the auth decision.

Decision: the actual tenant-isolation rehearsal remains blocked.

Reason: two rendered outputs do not prove tenant isolation. With a shared service identifier in the adapter spans, no tenant correlation on the trace path, and the deploy-card cache-key components unexposed, the dry-run trace cannot distinguish "tenant A and tenant B were processed independently with tenant-scoped adapter and cache activity" from "the same code path produced different outputs under a single shared evaluation." Observable success requires the relevant state changes to be visible; here, neither the tenant-scoped adapter call nor the tenant-scoped cache key is observable, and the /healthz principle applies analogously (different output ≠ correct isolation).

Required instrumentation for the next dry run:

  1. Tenant correlation field on every request-path span.
     - Field: tenant_id, value = synthetic tenant identifier (test fixture).
     - Carried via trace context propagation (e.g., W3C traceparent baggage or a span attribute) from the ingress span through authorization, cache lookup, adapter invocation, and response composition.
     - Same tenant_id must appear on ingress, authorization evaluation, cache lookup, cache decision, adapter call, and response for any given request, so the dry-run report can group all activity per tenant.

  2. Authorization context on spans.
     - On the authorization evaluation span: subject_id, resource_id, action, policy_generation, decision (allow | deny), tenant_id.
     - On denial: span records decision=deny and reason enum only. No source-existence or field-value data is recorded on the span.

  3. Cache-key decomposition on the cache lookup span.
     - cache_key_components: ordered list of named components actually used to build the key. For the auth cache: (tenant_id, subject_id, resource_id, action, policy_generation), with tenant_id first, matching the AUTH-2 spec.
     - cache_key_hash: assembled key value (or stable hash of it).
     - cache_outcome: hit | miss | deny-cached | invalidated.
     - For the deploy-card cache: cache_key_components must expose whatever dims the deploy-card key actually uses (e.g., deploy_id, service_id, deploy_generation, and tenant_id where the card is tenant-scoped). The exact dim list should match the deploy-card key spec; the dry run must surface the values used, not just the assembled key.

  4. Adapter invocation span.
     - tenant_id, subject_id, resource_id, action, source fetched (or none), source_response_state (data | absent | transient_error | denied).
     - Must show a separate adapter invocation per synthetic tenant whenever authorization or policy_generation differs by tenant. Sharing an adapter span across both tenant contexts is itself a failure signal.

  5. Response composition span (or terminal span).
     - tenant_id, response envelope shape, field states (typed constants only: data | unknown | denied).
     - On authorization denial: 403 not_authorized envelope, no preview fields.
     - On authorized-absent permitted source: field state unknown.

  6. Cache invalidation events.
     - When policy_generation changes (or any cache-key dim changes for that tenant), emit an event: prior_key, new_key, triggering_generation, tenant_id.
     - Eager invalidation must be visible in the trace, not just claimed.

  7. Tenant-safe only.
     - Synthetic tenant IDs are test fixtures; no real customer identifiers in any trace attribute on the rehearsal path.
     - No customer source IPs, no internal production hostnames. Stable pseudonyms are fine and must be used consistently across both tenant contexts so the two contexts are distinguishable in the trace.
     - Internal lane only; customer access remains closed throughout.

Acceptance criteria for the next dry run (gating the actual rehearsal):

  - authorization context, cache key, adapter call, and response are all correlated to the same synthetic tenant_id end to end for each request.
  - the two synthetic tenants produce distinguishable trace trees: different tenant_id on every span, separate adapter invocations, separate cache lookups with tenant-prefixed keys.
  - the cache_key_components attribute explicitly shows tenant_id as a component on the auth cache, and the deploy-card cache_key_components show the deploy-card dims.
  - a policy_generation bump (between the two tenants, or within a tenant across two requests) produces an invalidation event and a miss on the next request under the new generation.
  - response envelopes for authorized-absent vs denied are distinguishable and match the 403 not_authorized and unknown-state contracts.
  - no tenant A identifier appears on any tenant B span; no shared tenant_id between the two contexts.
  - no real customer identifiers, IPs, or internal hostnames leaked into any span attribute.

If the next dry run satisfies all of the above, the actual rehearsal can proceed, still internal lane with customer access closed. If any item fails, the actual rehearsal stays blocked and the specific gap is fixed before another dry run is attempted.

     fetch defaults, 1.8 s sync RPC defaults, or a per-tenant timeout
     that hasn't been tuned to current handler cost) the most likely
     culprits. This is also the explanation that requires the least
     from ingest-edge.

  2. Upstream proxy / LB with its own ≤ 2 s timeout firing on a path
     whose real cost routinely equals or exceeds 2 s. The trace's
     "gateway boundary=2000 ms" phrasing is ambiguous as written — it
     could be the server's own outbound write deadline or an upstream
     timeout the server is observing. Distinguishing (1) from (2) is

    - Compare against the server-observed handler-start and the
      predicted handler-end (handler_ms P50/P95/P99 at admit time).
      If client_deadline − deadline_start < server_predicted_response,
      that's the cause, and the gap tells us by how much.

  Connection-timing evidence:
    - TLS handshake completion relative to request issue, on the same
      failed requests. Need to know whether connection setup itself
      was eating into the budget, or whether the client had a clean
      connection before sending.
    - The exact instant the server observed "request fully received"
      versus "client cancellation observed." If that gap is zero or
      negative (client cancels before the server has the full request),
      the cause is connection-path, not handler.
    - Whether the cancellation arrived as a clean FIN or an RST, and

Containment and shutoff — in this order:

  1. Stop using the cold tap entirely. Every open cycle is feeding the leak.
  2. Close the local cold-water stop valve (angle stop) under the sink, handle clockwise until it seats. Hand pressure only — no tools. If the drip stops, you're contained; bowl catches the residual drips while the line empties. Open the cold faucet briefly to confirm depressurization, then close it again.
  3. If the local valve closes but the drip doesn't slow, the leak is above the valve (at the valve body or the supply line connection to it). Find the apartment main — usually under the kitchen sink, near the water heater, in a hall closet, or behind an access panel. Close it clockwise. You'll lose water to the whole apartment until the super comes; fill a couple of jugs first if you need them overnight.
  4. If neither valve reduces the flow, the leak is between the meter and your apartment. That's the building's problem and a 24/7 call regardless of the time of day.

What NOT to touch:

  - The chrome braided supply line itself — don't bend, kink, or "tighten" the line as a whole. A line with a bulged braid or rust bloom is a same-day replacement, not a tweak.
  - The compression nuts at either end of the supply line. If you suspect the fitting, a very small 1/8 turn by hand with a proper wrench can sometimes reseat a ferrule, but stop the moment resistance firms up. A quarter turn past seat cracks the ferrule or the valve port and turns a drip into a stream. If it doesn't stop with a light snug, leave it for the super.
  - The packing nut behind the stop-valve handle. Backing it off is what fixed the 2023 bathroom leak, but only as a last resort and only in tiny adjustments. If the packing is the source, fiddling can break the stem.
  - Anything on the wall side of the valve. That's the building's riser/branch.
  - No Teflon tape, no plumber's putty, no epoxy, no rubber-band-and-hose-clamp fixes on a pressurized supply leak. They don't hold pressure and they make the real repair harder.

Emptying and drying the cabinet — be more thorough than it looks:

  - Pull everything out of the cabinet: cleaning supplies, trash bin, anything stored below. Wipe each item dry before setting it on the floor; wet plastic bottles trap moisture against the cabinet base.
  - Towel the base dry, then push a dry towel into the back corners and along the wall seam. Leave it 10 minutes — if it comes up damp, repeat. Particleboard and MDF wick from the corners first, even when the visible surface looks dry.
  - Wipe the valve, supply line, and connections dry so any new drip is obvious.
  - Leave both cabinet doors open. Point a fan into the cabinet if you have one. A small space heater a few feet away at low setting helps in a cool room.
  - Check the floor in front of the cabinet and the toe-kick — water migrates under the baseboard and into adjacent rooms without being obvious.
  - Empty the bowl regularly. Standing water in a closed cabinet is mold in 24-48 hours.

Escalate to a 24/7 plumber tonight if any of these appear:

  - The local stop valve won't close, won't stay closed, or closing it doesn't slow the drip.
  - Water reaches any electrical outlet, switch, appliance cord, or under the dishwasher/stove/fridge — including outlets in adjacent rooms, since water travels along the wall cavity.
  - Drip rate visibly worsens past the current ~8-sec interval, becomes a steady trickle, or you hear water moving with no fixture on.
  - Water shows up on a ceiling below, on the floor in another room, or seeping out from under the wall behind the cabinet.
  - The valve body, supply line, or any fitting shows a crack, bulge, green/white corrosion bloom, or wetness that wasn't there an hour ago — these fail without warning.
  - The leak produces rusty water, sewage smell, or discolored flow (none of which you've described, but flag if it changes).
  - The water meter (if accessible in your unit) keeps turning with every fixture off and both valves closed.

If none of those apply — slow drip, valve seats, no electrics in the path, no migration, hot side and drain still dry — this is a Monday-morning super visit, not a midnight call. Keep the cold tap closed until then.

1.  Check the valve and locate the hiss

    Start with the tube still inflated enough to feel firm. The hiss gives you a strong clue already - in many "no visible damage" flats the leak is at the valve or at a thorn you can feel but not see.

    a.  Schrader valve (the car-style one with a pin):
        - Confirm the valve cap was on and tight; a missing cap lets grit into the core and the core can slowly leak.
        - With the cap off, drip or brush soapy water around the base of the stem where it meets the tube. Bubbles there mean the stem-to-tube seal has failed - the tube is unrepairable, replace it.
        - Push the pin in briefly to release any remaining air, then release. If air keeps escaping around the pin after you release, the core is bad. Schrader cores are removable with a core tool and can be replaced in a good tube; if the tube is old, replace the whole tube.

    b.  Presta valve (the slim one with a knurled locknut):
        - Unscrew the cap, then unscrew the locknut fully (it should turn freely; you should be able to press the tip to open the valve).
        - With the tube reinflated, drip soapy water down the stem. Bubbles at the top of the stem = the core isn't seating (try tightening the locknut back up against the rim later; if it still leaks, replace the core or tube).
        - Bubbles at the base of the stem where it meets the tube rubber = same outcome as Schrader - stem pull-out, tube is done.
        - Common Presta failure: the stem is too short for a deep-section rim, so the locknut clamps above the rim hole instead of at it, and the tube pulls through under pressure. This is a fit problem, not a patch problem.

    c.  If no bubbles at the valve: rotate the inflated tube slowly with your ear (or a stethoscope, or your lips) a few centimeters away. Soapy water over the whole tube is faster and reliable.

2.  Remove the tube and find a small puncture

    a.  Deflate fully. For Presta, unscrew the locknut and push the valve up through the rim.

    b.  Push one bead of the tire off the rim opposite the valve. To do this, squeeze the tire together at the top and work your thumbs under the bead on the far side, pushing it toward the rim's center channel (the rim well is deeper in the middle for exactly this). Once one bead is loose all the way around, pull the tube out - start opposite the valve and finish at the valve so the stem doesn't get torn.

    c.  Reinflate the tube until it's barely firm, not taut. Submerge sections in a basin of water, or pass a wet hand slowly along it. Bubbles mark the hole. Note both the position relative to the valve (distance and which side of the tube) and the orientation - inside (rim-side) or outside (tread-side). Mark with a pen or remember the position.

    d.  If you can't submerge: in a quiet room, pass the tube close to your cheek/lip - you'll feel a tiny stream of air. Rotate slowly.

    e.  Side tells you the cause:
        - Outside puncture = something came through the tread; it may still be lodged in the tire.
        - Inside puncture = rim tape shifted, spoke nipple protruding, or a rim defect; very rarely a manufacturing defect at the seam.

3.  Inspect the tire casing and rim tape

    a.  Tire casing (inside): with the tube out, run a fingertip carefully along the entire inside surface, slowly. Feel for anything embedded - glass splinters, wire, thorns, staples, grit. A thorn head can sit in the tread with the tip just barely pressing on the tube; it punctured once and will do it again. Run a damp cloth over the outside tread too - if it snags, you've found it.

    b.  Tire casing condition: look for cuts, slashes, exposed casing threads, bulges, separated plies. A small hole matching the tube puncture is normal; a long cut or a bulge means the tire is compromised.

    c.  Rim tape: with one bead still on the rim, look at the tape covering the spoke nipples. Confirm it runs continuously around the well (no gaps, no shifted sections, no torn patches). Press along it - any hard bump under the tape is a nipple protruding, which will pinch the tube. Tape that has slipped off-center is the most common cause of repeated rim-side punctures.

    d.  Rim: check the rim well for sharp burrs around spoke holes, and confirm the rim is straight. A small bend can be the culprit; a significant bend means a new wheel.

4.  Patch vs. replace

    Patch is adequate when:
        - The puncture is small (under ~2-3 mm), round or near-round, and not a long slash.
        - It is not within ~2 cm of the valve stem (patches don't hold where the rubber flexes against the stem).
        - The tube is otherwise sound - no dry-rot, no cracking, no thin spots, no prior failed patches in the same spot.

    Replace the tube when:
        - The puncture is at the valve stem or the stem is torn at its base.
        - The hole is a long cut, a blowout patch, or larger than ~5-10 mm.
        - The rubber is aged (brittle, micro-cracked, sticky, or visibly rough). Shelf life is roughly 5-7 years; heat and UV shorten it.
        - Multiple patches or repeated failures in the same area.

    Replace the tire when:
        - Tread is worn through (road: visible casing threads; MTB: lost or rounded knobs).
        - A sidewall cut that exposes casing threads, or any cut longer than ~2-3 mm.
        - A bulge, blister, or separated ply (impact damage or age).
        - Repeated flats at the same spot even with a sound tube and correct rim tape - the casing is failing.
        - A field "boot" (a patch on the inside of the tire, or a folded dollar bill/energy bar wrapper taped over a cut from the inside) is a get-home repair only; replace the tire as soon as you can.

    Replace the valve (or the tube) when:
        - Schrader core won't seal after cleaning and re-seating - replace the core, or the tube if the body is corroded.
        - Presta core leaks and reseating the locknut doesn't fix it - replace the core; if unavailable, replace the tube.
        - Stem is the wrong length for the rim (too short for a deep rim, too long to clear a deep rim safely).
        - Stem rubber is torn at the base - tube is unrepairable.

    Replace the rim tape when:
        - It is torn, has shifted, has gaps, or is the wrong width (too narrow to cover the nipples, or so wide it interferes with the tire bead seating in the rim hooks).
        - Spoke nipples sit above it - the tape has compressed, shifted, or was never the right size.

5.  Before you ride, verify each of these

    - The tire is seated evenly on the rim, both beads, all the way around. Look across the rim: the tire should sit at a uniform height on both sides. A misseated bead will let the tube blow out under inflation.
    - The valve is perpendicular to the rim and the locknut (Presta) is finger-tight only - not torqued, which can distort the stem.
    - Pressure is within the range printed on the tire sidewall. Under-inflation invites pinch flats; over-inflation risks blowout, especially if the tube was just patched.
    - The tube holds pressure over time. Re-check at 10 minutes, at 30 minutes, and ideally after an hour or overnight. A patch that passes an immediate leak test can still seep slowly. Soap-test the patch again before riding.
    - No foreign object remains in the tire casing - finger-test the inside and visual/damp-cloth test the outside.
    - Spin the wheel and check true - no rim wobble hitting the brake pads or frame. Reinstalling a tire can shift the rim tape and cause the wheel to sit unevenly.
    - Quick-release or thru-axle is correctly closed and tensioned. For rim brakes, the brake is re-engaged and the wheel is centered in the dropouts so the brake doesn't rub.
    - A short stationary or low-speed test before a full ride - inflate, sit on the bike in a stand or hold the bike upright and load the tire with your weight briefly, then ride around the block before committing to distance.

    Air holding for ten minutes is not the same as a repaired tire. The verification above is what lets you ride with confidence, and any failure in that list means staying off the road until it's fixed.

- Authorization span — stop if the span lacks a tenant tag, or the tag does not match the synthetic tenant that issued the request. Without this, the auth decision cannot be tied to A or B.
- Normalized cache tuple — stop if the cache entry for the shared service identifier is not cleanly partitioned by tenant: missing tenant partition field, cross-tenant key collision, or the same tuple served to both tenants. The cache is the most likely isolation leak vector, so this stop is non-optional.
- Adapter span — stop if the upstream/downstream adapter call lacks a tenant tag, or if the same adapter invocation is reachable from both tenants without a partition boundary visible in the trace.
- Rendered response — in addition to the existing content-contains-other-tenant stop, stop if the response cannot be traced back through auth → cache → adapter to a single tenant. Correct content with broken correlation is not evidence of isolation; it is a coincidence.
- Auth-before-lookup order — stop if the trace shows cache lookup preceding the authorization span. The order is what this rehearsal exists to confirm; a trace where auth follows cache is a stop regardless of whether rendered output happens to look right.

2. Missing per-phase access-verification ownership

The sheet says "verify customer access disabled before setup." That is a single point-in-time gate, not a per-phase one. Customer-access state can change between phases (deploy-card → ownership → incident-summary → explicit-unknown), and a one-shot check at setup cannot catch a flip mid-run.

What needs to be in the sheet:

- A named individual, not just a role. "Rehearsal lead" alone is insufficient — single-checker access verification lets a setup bug pass undetected. Expect a named executor plus a named independent verifier (two-party check at each phase boundary).
- The named verifier signs off at the START of each phase, not only before setup. Each of the four phase boundaries gets its own "customer access disabled" attestation.
- The verifier has direct read access to the access-control surface (flag / config / guard), not a screenshot or a secondhand confirmation from the executor.
- A named escalation path: if access is found enabled mid-rehearsal — who pages, what gets rolled back to, and whether the rehearsal pauses or aborts on that finding. Without this, "stop" has no defined behavior.

Without a named per-phase verifier with direct access-control read, the "customer access remains closed" boundary is being asserted on trust rather than evidenced per phase, which is the same gap the security rerun's matrix checks were designed to prevent.

3. One adjacent item worth naming in the sheet

For each stop condition above, specify the response: pause, abort, or roll back to the last clean phase. The stops are currently defined but the abort behavior is not — so a stop firing mid-rehearsal leaves the lead improvising the recovery, which is when evidence integrity usually degrades.

If those four changes (per-layer correlation stops, named per-phase verifier with direct access-control read, named escalation path, and stop-response per condition) are filled in before the rehearsal runs, the execution sheet meets the bar set by the prior security rerun's evidence requirements.

Pre-install checks (do these before touching the new tube):

  - Casing: run your fingers inside the tire all the way around, both beads, in good light. You already cleared the obvious debris — now check for embedded wire, glass slivers, or a casing wire poking through the casing that wasn't obvious from outside.
  - Rim tape: continuous, centered over the spoke holes, no wrinkles, no exposed nipple heads, no torn section near the valve hole.
  - Valve hole: clean rim hole, no burr, no sharp edge. The old tube failed at the stem, so the rim-side cut surface here is the prime suspect — run a finger around it.
  - Tire stem-hole area: with the tire unmounted or with one bead off, inspect the tire's valve hole for a sharp molding flash or wire that may have cut the old stem.
  - Rim bed: wipe clean. Dust, dried sealant, or old grit can cause slow leaks that look like tube defects.

Tube prep:

  - Unroll/unkink the new tube. Do not stretch it. If it's folded from the package, lay it flat for a few minutes.
  - Add just enough air to give it shape — roughly a handful of pumps on a floor pump, or 2–3 seconds of breath on a Schrader. The tube should hold its own round shape but still be soft enough to squeeze flat between two fingers. Rule of thumb: under 5 PSI / 0.3 bar. This is the "pre-seat" air the question asked about — it stops the tube folding under the bead and getting pinched.
  - Skip talc unless you have clean talcum powder on hand. Not required.

Valve first, then tube:

  - Insert the valve stem through the rim hole from the inside of the tire outward (or per the rim's design — Schrader/Presta straight through, no twist). The stem must come out straight, perpendicular to the rim, not tilted. A tilted stem is a guaranteed slow leak at the rim hole.
  - With the stem through, work the tube into the tire starting at the valve, going around both directions. Keep the tube down in the rim well (the center channel), not up under the tire bead.
  - If the tube has a nut, thread it on finger-tight now to hold the stem straight while you finish mounting. If it's a Presta, leave the locknut open.

Seating the bead without pinching:

  - Use thumbs only for the last 6–12 inches of bead on each side. The tube wants to escape under the bead edge — that is the pinch point. Keep your thumb between the bead and the tube as you press the bead over the rim flange, so the tube can't migrate up.
  - Tire levers: only on the bead, never with the tube anywhere near the lever tip. If you need a lever at all, lever the bead only and keep the lever tip facing the rim, not the tube.
  - As you go, every few inches press the mounted bead inward with your free hand so the unseated section sits in the rim well — this leaves slack in the tube where you still have to seat the bead, so it isn't stretched tight.

Initial inflation to seat the bead:

  - Inflate to roughly 20–30 PSI (road) or 5–10 PSI (MTB / gravel / wide tire) — just enough to pop both beads against the rim flanges. You should hear distinct snaps as each section seats.
  - Stop and spin the wheel. Look at both sides all the way around. The bead line should be a continuous even ring just inside the rim edge. No high spots, no dips, no tube visible between bead and rim.
  - If a section isn't seated, deflate fully, push that section of bead back into the rim well with your thumbs, re-inflate. Do not inflate higher trying to force a stubborn bead — that is how you explode a tube on a misseated tire.

Inflation to operating pressure:

  - Check the tire sidewall for the pressure range, e.g. "60–80 PSI" or "35–65 PSI". Inflate to the upper end of your normal range for the first ride, then adjust after you confirm no leaks.
  - Use a separate pressure gauge to confirm — floor pump gauges are routinely off by 5–10 PSI.
  - Presta: open the locknut fully to inflate, close it finger-tight after.
  - Schrader: cap off during inflation is fine; cap on afterward.

Hold and wheel checks before riding:

  1. Valve: stem is straight (perpendicular to rim, no tilt), nut snug if used, cap on. A tilted stem under full pressure will hiss and may slip down into the rim.
  2. Bead line: spin the wheel slowly, both sides, all the way around. The bead should sit as a uniform ring. Any visible tube between bead and rim — deflate and reseat.
  3. Squeeze test: press the tire sidewall with your thumb all the way around on both sides. Pressure should feel uniform. A soft spot means a pinch / fold of tube under the bead — deflate that section and reseat.
  4. Wheel true: spin in the frame/fork. Side-to-side wobble at the rim = either tube unevenly seated (often fixable by re-squeezing and re-inflating) or a true issue that pre-existed. Up-and-down hop = spoke tension / rim, pre-existing, not caused by the tube.
  5. Axle / quick release / thru-axle: closed, torqued to spec, wheel centered and seated fully in the dropouts or fork ends.
  6. Brakes: rim brakes — pads clear the tire, full lever pull without the pads diving into the tread. Disc brakes — rotor centered in the caliper, lever firm (no sponginess suggesting a caliper got bumped).
  7. Sit test: bike on the ground, sit on the saddle with normal weight, look at the tire profile from behind. No asymmetric bulging, no tire visibly deforming more on one side.
  8. Roll test: helmet on, walk the bike forward 3–4 meters while listening. No hiss, no irregular tick, no rubbing.

Pre-ride verification (first 50–100 m on the road):

  - Ride slowly in a straight line. No hop, no pull to one side, no hiss.
  - Brake test at walking speed — both levers, full pull. No dive, no rub, no fade.
  - Gentle lean each way — no rim touching the frame or fork crown, no brake pad contact on the rim where there wasn't before.
  - After 5 minutes of riding, stop and pressure-check again. A small drop (1–3 PSI) is normal as the tube settles and stretches. Anything more, stop and re-inspect.

Stop conditions on the first ride — dismount immediately if:

  - Any hiss or pressure loss you can feel by squeeze.
  - Visible bulge in tread or sidewall.
  - Wheel no longer tracking straight.
  - New brake rub that wasn't there at install.
  - Any vibration or hopping you didn't see in the static checks.

That sequence covers the pre-seat air (just enough to round the tube), the pinch avoidance (thumbs only, tube in the well, never lever near the tube), and the hold/wheel checks (valve straight, bead line, squeeze uniformity, true, axle, brakes, sit test, roll test) before you commit any real speed to the wheel.

Reading your symptom: "drags once per revolution" is a single high spot, not continuous contact. Continuous rub = wheel off-center laterally in the frame. Single-spot rub = lateral rim wobble, or axle seated unevenly (one end farther into its dropout than the other). Run both checks before you touch the brake.

Assumption: rim brake (your wording — "rim drags against one brake pad" — fits a rim brake). If yours is actually a disc brake, the brake-side of this sequence changes (caliper alignment over the rotor, not pad centering); the wheel-side checks are the same.

PHASE 1 — RELEASE THE BRAKE
  Open the brake's cable quick-release (or back off the cable barrel a few turns) so the pads clear the rim. Spin the wheel to confirm clear.

PHASE 2 — LATERAL RIM TRUENESS (the safety gate)
  1. With brake open, spin the wheel slowly. Watch the braking surface pass a fixed reference — the stationary pad, or a finger held ~2 mm from the rim.
  2. If the rim moves toward and away from you (side-to-side wobble) as it rotates → rim is laterally untrue. STOP. Centering the brake here only shifts the rub to the other pad. The wheel needs truing or replacement. Do not ride.
  3. If the rim's lateral position is steady → rim is laterally true in this plane. Continue.
  4. Local kink check: run a finger along both braking surfaces looking for a single dent or step. A small lateral kink can ride fine on its own but will rub intermittently. If found, the wheel needs work, not brake adjustment.

PHASE 3 — WHEEL CENTERED IN FRAME
  1. Loosen the QR (or thru-axle) just enough that the axle can settle laterally but is still captive in the dropouts.
  2. With the bike on the ground, bounce it gently once or twice so the wheel settles by gravity into the dropouts. Do not push the wheel to one side while tightening.
  3. With QR still loose, sight the gap between rim and seat tube and between rim and the non-drive chainstay. Gaps should be visibly equal on both sides.
  4. Close the QR firmly (torque the thru-axle to spec). Recheck gaps — they should remain visibly equal.
  5. If gaps are unequal after settling → frame misalignment or bent axle. Stop and inspect.

PHASE 4 — AXLE / QR ENGAGEMENT
  For QR:
    - Cam must close with firm resistance; the lever should leave a slight imprint on your palm. If it snaps shut with light force, the skewer is wrong-length, the nuts are backed off too far, or the cam is worn — adjust and retry.
    - Both axle ends must sit equally recessed into their dropouts. A QR pulled sideways will under-clamp the opposite dropout.
  Thru-axle:
    - Confirm full insertion before clamping; torque to frame spec.
  Lift test (both systems): with the closure tight, grab the top of the tire and try to lift the wheel. The wheel must not shift up off the dropouts. If it does, the axle isn't fully engaged.

PHASE 5 — HUB BEARINGS
  1. Try to wobble the rim side-to-side by hand — no detectable play.
  2. Spin with QR tight — smooth run, no roughness, no grinding, no clicking.
  Any play or roughness → hub needs servicing. A loose cone lets the hub shift under braking load, which can re-introduce mid-ride rub even after brake centering.

PHASE 6 — RE-SPIN WITH BRAKE STILL OPEN
  Spin freely, several revolutions, no contact. If yes → wheel is true, seated, and centered; original rub came from a shifted wheel or a misaligned brake. Proceed. If no → return to Phase 2; you have a rim or seating issue brake centering will not fix.

PHASE 7 — CENTER THE BRAKE (only after Phases 2–6 pass)
  1. With wheel spinning, identify which pad contacts first.
  2. Single-pivot side-pull: use the centering screw (typically at the back of one arm or on the bridge). Quarter-turn at a time.
  3. Dual-pivot: small centering-screw adjustment.
  4. V-brake / linear-pull: use the spring tension screws at each arm. Tighten the screw on the side that is NOT rubbing — that pulls the opposite arm in and equalizes clearance.
  5. Re-spin after each adjustment.
  6. Pad alignment: each pad should contact the braking surface flat, not the tire, not below the rim. Slight toe-in (front of pad hits first, rear trails ~1 mm) prevents squeal.

PHASE 8 — PRE-RIDE GATE (all must pass before riding)
  - Wheel spins freely for at least 5 full revolutions with brake closed, no pad contact at any point.
  - QR / axle: fully closed; lift test passes; wheel does not shift vertically or laterally.
  - Brake lever firm; pads engage squarely and release fully when the lever is released.
  - Pad material above the wear line; no oil contamination on the braking surface.
  - Tire bead evenly seated all around.
  - Tire pressure holding (you've already verified overnight).
  - Final slow spin, brake closed: clearance visibly even on both sides, no rub anywhere in the rotation.

If any item fails, do not ride. The chain is only as strong as its weakest check.

WHY THIS ORDER MATTERS
  - Phases 2–6 diagnose the wheel. Phase 7 diagnoses the brake. They are independent. Conflating them is how a warped rim gets masked by a recentered caliper and ridden on.
  - Once-per-revolution contact specifically demands the lateral-trueness check (Phase 2) before anything else — that symptom is exactly what an untrue rim produces.

Three-hour ajar with a final reading of 24°F in the freezer and 39°F in the fridge. The fridge held, so anything in there is fine. The freezer is warmer than it should be (0°F target) but is already recovering. Here is the item-by-item call.

ICE CREAM — discard
Soft at 24°F means it thawed enough that the emulsion has broken; when you refreeze it you get an icy, grainy block that weeps whey. Dairy is also the most temperature-sensitive item you had in there, and we don't know the peak temperature during the 3 hours the drawer was open, only that it ended at 24°F. The conservative call is the same one you made in February: it goes in the trash. If you wanted to bend the rule you could refreeze and discard later if it separates or smells off, but the texture loss is guaranteed and the safety margin is the only real upside.

CHICKEN BREASTS — refreeze, or cook promptly if you want to use them this week
Sealed, still showing firm ice crystals, 30°F at the surface — that's a meat that never crossed 40°F, so perishable-pathogen growth didn't start. USDA says refreeze is fine when ice crystals are still present and the food has stayed below 40°F. Either path works:
  - Refreeze now: quality will be slightly drier than fresh but safe.
  - Cook tonight or tomorrow and then freeze the cooked meat: best texture outcome, same safety.
Pick by when you actually want to eat them.

BERRIES — refreeze for cooked use, or cook now
Partly thawed at 34°F with no leak is still inside the safe zone, and berries' acid + sugar make them less hospitable to pathogens than the other two items. Two options:
  - Refreeze for later: usable in smoothies, oatmeal, baked goods. Expect mushier texture than fresh-frozen.
  - Cook now into a quick compote, jam, or pie filling: best use of partly-thawed fruit, and freezing the cooked result is fine.
Do not eat them raw/thawed and refrozen as a "fresh-frozen" snack — the texture will be disappointing and that path offers no upside over cooking them.

HOUSEKEEPING
  - Recheck freezer in 1–2 hours, again at 4 and 6 hours. Target is a steady drop back toward 0°F.
  - Fridge at 39°F is on the high side of normal — keep an eye on it for the next day; if it climbs, the door seals may have been stressed too.
  - If the 1–2 hour reading is flat or rising, or the 6 hour reading is still mid-teens or warmer, treat this as an appliance problem and move the chicken and any other frozen food to a neighbor's freezer or a cooler with ice.

  - Lukewarm water rinse on the right front paw, 30–60 sec. No scrubbing or picking at the flap.

  - Short leashed potty trips only — no real exercise walks.

- Collapse, stumbling, sudden weakness, pale/white/blue or yellow gums.
- Rapid or labored breathing, severe lethargy, or dehydration signs (sticky gums, skin tent that doesn't snap back).

DRYWALL ANCHOR PATCH (later-ready, no paint today)

What you're dealing with: 2 ordinary drywall anchors (the plastic expansion
or self-drilling threaded kind). After removal each leaves a hole about 1/4
to 3/8 inch wide with maybe a scuff of torn paper around the rim.

Materials:
  1 small tub of lightweight spackle (DAP DryDex pink-to-white is handy
    because it self-tells you when it's cured). A few dollars.
  1 plastic putty knife, 1 to 1.5 inch wide.
  A square of 220-grit sandpaper.
  A damp rag or paper towel.

Steps (about 10 minutes for both holes):
  1. Pull or back out the anchors fully. If a head is flush and just spins,
     push the anchor into the wall cavity and patch over it. Small loss.
  2. Press down any raised paper around the hole using the handle of the
     putty knife or a clean fingernail. Torn paper sticking up will
     telegraph through paint later.
  3. Wipe the area with a dry cloth so spackle bonds to clean wall.
  4. Press a small amount of spackle firmly into each hole, then smooth it
     flat so it's just barely proud of the wall surface. A thin film haloing
     past the hole is fine. A thick mound means more sanding.
  5. Let dry - 1 to 2 hours for these small holes, longer if the room is
     cool or humid. DryDex turns from pink to white when fully cured, so no
     guesswork.
  6. Lightly sand with 220-grit in a small circle until flush with the wall,
     then wipe the dust with the damp rag.

You are done. No paint today, no primer needed before the move. The patches
are flat, sealed, and ready for paint whenever you do touch-up later. Two
weeks is plenty of runway before the Sept 30 handoff.

Storage tip: keep the spackle tub, putty knife, and leftover sandpaper in a
labeled zip bag. You'll hit more anchor holes between now and the handoff
(curtain brackets, picture hangers, over-the-door hooks) and the kit is
ready for the next one.

If the block runs short, the only must-do today is getting the 8 medium
boxes under 35 lb. The drywall patch can happen any evening this week - the
holes aren't going anywhere - and the "live" row can be a partial decision
today (just the cookbooks or just the reference shelf is fine).

A few things worth knowing first, then the plan:

Kibo is showing mild-to-moderate stress signals (following, pacing during box movement) but he's not in crisis. No panting at rest, eating/drinking/walking normally, settles when his bed comes back. That's a good baseline. The "settles only when bed is returned to the usual corner" pattern is the most important fact in your message — that corner and his food/water station are the single highest-leverage things you can protect. Your instinct to skip sedation and avoid moving the anchors is correct; sedation would mask signals you'd actually want to see, and shifting bed or food mid-packing usually makes this worse, not better.

STABLE SAFE AREA
Pick one room that's not on the packing list and lock it for the duration — bathroom, laundry, or a small bedroom. In that room:
  - Bed stays in the usual corner. Don't shift it even a few feet.
  - Food and water station stay where they are.
  - Close the door or put up a baby gate so he can't wander into packing traffic.
  - Drop in a worn t-shirt or a blanket that's been on your lap (scent anchor), a long-lasting chew (a Kong with his normal kibble plus a little low-sodium broth, frozen), water, and a familiar toy or two.
  - Run white noise or a low, familiar radio/playlist to mask tape guns, wrap crinkle, and door slams from other rooms.
  - Stage boxes in hallways or the garage, not in his space.

ACTIVITY TIMING
  - Pack during his off-hours. Best windows are 30–60 minutes after a walk and 1–2 hours after a meal. Tired and fed is calm.
  - Do the loudest, box-heaviest blocks (tape, packing paper, emptying drawers) when he's already in his safe area and ideally just back from a walk.
  - Feed on his normal schedule. Don't shift meals to "fit" packing — predictable feeding is itself a calming anchor.
  - Two decompression walks a day on familiar quiet routes. Short leash; front-clip harness if you have one. Avoid construction, busy blocks, dog parks.
  - One short, calm pre-bed wind-down walk at the same time each night.
  - No packing in the 60–90 minutes before bed — give him quiet to settle.

DURING PACKING BLOCKS
  - Boxes only move through his room when he's on a walk or briefly elsewhere.
  - When he follows you out of a room, calmly say the same short cue every time ("back to bed" or similar) and walk him back. No picking up, no treat-luring with something novel, no scolding, no slammed doors.
  - If he lies at a distance watching packing happen with ears neutral, that's information-gathering, not distress — let him observe.
  - Keep packing-room voices low.

SIGNS THAT WARRANT A VET CALL (or at least a phone consult)
  - Vomiting (one episode could be incidental; two in 24 hours or any with blood = call).
  - Diarrhea, especially with blood or black/tarry stool.
  - Refusing food 12+ hours, or refusing water 6+ hours.
  - Panting at rest that doesn't resolve within ~30 minutes of leaving the packing area.
  - Hiding for hours and refusing to come out, trembling, or freezing.
  - Tucked tail, ears pinned, whale eye, or repeated lip-licking/yawning for >30 minutes straight.
  - Snapping, growling, or guarding (a real change for him).
  - House soiling after being clean.
  - Excessive licking at one spot (paw, leg, flank).
  - Lethargy that doesn't lift after a good walk and a meal.
  - Swollen or firm belly, hunched/"prayer" posture, whimpering when belly touched.
  - Limping, stumbling, or sudden weakness.
  - Pale, white, blue, or yellow gums.
  - Any suspicion he got into packing materials (tape bits, ribbon, eraser bands) — bring the packaging if you go in.

WHEN TO ESCALATE FROM "WATCH" TO "CALL TONIGHT"
Any one of the above, OR a sustained behavior shift that doesn't return to baseline within ~24 hours. Right now his baseline is: following, settling on cue, eating, walking normal. If tomorrow morning he's still pacing during a quiet moment, won't take a treat, or hides when boxes are stationary, that's worth a vet call even if the specific symptoms are mild.

ONE NOTE ON THE MOVE ITSELF (9/27–9/28)
Don't move his bed and food station the day of the move. Set them up first in the new place before he arrives, ideally in a corner with the same orientation (e.g., if the bed faces the doorway now, keep it facing the doorway there). That anchor is the most reliable stability cue he has and it should travel intact.

Lower-back stiffness after weekend lifting, no neuro symptoms — this looks like ordinary mechanical muscle soreness, not a structural issue. But because Saturday's packing block is the real priority, the right framing is: protect Saturday, treat today's session as a graded exposure, and let the back's response in the first 15–20 minutes decide the rest of the hour.

PRE-SESSION GATE (5–10 min, at home or in the parking lot)

Do these in order. If any step reproduces or sharpens symptoms, skip the session and reschedule — don't push through.

  1. Walk easily for 3–5 minutes. Stiffness should stay stable or warm up; it should not sharpen.
  2. Standing gentle back extensions: hands on lower back, lean back 5–8 times, just to comfortable end-range. No bouncing.
  3. Supine knee-to-chest, one leg at a time, 30 sec each side. Should feel like a stretch, not a pinch.
  4. Cat-cow x 8 slow reps on hands and knees.
  5. Two body-weight squats, slow. Just confirming full-range comfort.

Pass = mild stiffness only, no pain, no change in sensation.
Fail = radiating pain, numbness, tingling, sharp local pain, pain with any of the above → don't climb.

WARM-UP ON THE WALL (15 min)

  - 5 min easy traversing on jugs, horizontal. Big feet, slow hands. Get blood in.
  - Two gentle back-bend pauses between traverses (hang straight arms, let the spine open, 15 sec each).
  - One easy vertical route, footwork-only, big holds. Find your three points before every move.
  - Two-three progressively harder problems on big holds, each one move harder than the last, all static.

MAIN SESSION (35–40 min, then walk out)

Volume cap:
  - 4–6 problems total
  - 2–3 attempts per problem
  - 10–15 min of total rest across the hour (sit, hydrate, let the back relax between burns)

Choose:
  - Vertical or slab
  - Holds you can hold with an open, neutral hand
  - Footwork problems where the hands are easy
  - Anything you've already done at the same or easier grade

Avoid for today:
  - Dynos, deadpoints, jump-offs
  - Heel hooks and toe hooks (loads the lumbar under hip flexion)
  - Mantles (loaded spinal extension with shoulder load)
  - Campus moves, big reaches on overhangs
  - Anything that twists the torso under load (cross-through, big drop-knees)
  - Reachy problems that pull you out of alignment
  - Any move where you find yourself holding your breath and bracing hard

Downclimb everything. If a problem is awkward to downclimb, it's the wrong problem for today.

MOVEMENT LIMITS IN PRACTICE

  - Two points of contact at all times during weight shifts; no committing before the next hold is found.
  - Keep the core quiet. Brace lightly, breathe through every move. If you notice yourself holding your breath, the problem is too hard.
  - Bend at the knees and hips to reach low holds, not the lower back.
  - Twist with the whole body, not just the spine.
  - If a problem makes the back talk at all on the first move, downgrade or skip.

STOP CRITERIA

Back off / change the problem (yellow):
  - Mild ache or tightness that builds during a problem rather than warming out
  - Local guarding, or feeling like you're protecting one side
  - Stiffness that's noticeably worse than at the start of the session
  - Any sensation that wasn't there at the gate

Stop the session (red):
  - Pain that radiates down the leg, into the buttock, or around the hip
  - Numbness, tingling, or "pins and needles" anywhere in the legs or feet
  - Weakness in a leg or foot (can't push off a foot you'd normally trust)
  - Sharp local back pain, especially with a specific movement
  - Pain at rest between burns, or pain triggered by coughing/sneezing
  - Pain that makes you change how you walk

Stop means stop for the day — no "one more easy one."

POST-SESSION (next 18–24 hours)

  - Walk home at an easy pace. Notice whether the back feels the same, better, or worse at the end of the walk.
  - Tonight: skip any loaded lifting, bending, or twisting. No packing, no box work.
  - Optional: heat (warm shower, heating pad 15 min) if stiffness is annoying. Ice is fine if anything feels inflamed. Either, not both, not long.
  - Sleep priority. A back that's been loaded tolerates the next day much better after a real night of sleep than after a short one.
  - Gentle mobility tomorrow morning: cat-cow, knee rocks, short walk. No new exercises.

DECISION RULE FOR SATURDAY

Saturday's packing block stays in the plan unless:
  - Tomorrow morning is worse than this morning (more stiffness, new soreness, any neuro symptom).
  - Tonight's sleep is broken by back pain.
  - Walking, bending to put on shoes, or sitting-to-standing is noticeably guarded.

DEFAULT CALL
Given the joint is solid, there is no wobble, the assembled piece fits the doors, and you have no screw extractor, the safer default is BRACE AND MOVE INTACT. Force-disassembly past the safe attempts below trades a likely cosmetic-damage risk (further rounding of the socket, finish crushing around the bolt hole, or splitting the substrate) for a benefit (one panel off) that the move does not actually need. Only run the attempt ladder if the loose panel would prevent a piece from fitting through a doorway, would risk finish damage in transit, or otherwise blocks the move.

ATTEMPT LADDER (least to most aggressive; stop and reassess after each step)

  1. RECHECK THE FIT. Try rocking the panel by hand. If it cannot move more than a hair at the joint, the piece is already stable enough for the move and you can skip straight to bracing.

  2. PAINTER'S TAPE + NEXT-SIZE-UP BIT.
     - Press a layer of painter's tape firmly into the socket (use a fingernail to seat it).
     - Set the next-size-up hex bit into the taped socket.
     - Apply steady hand pressure straight down (so the bit bottoms in the socket, not on the rim) and try to back the bolt out CCW.
     - Stop condition: any slip, any "mushroom" of the socket rim, or zero rotation after one clean try. Do not retry this step on the same socket.

  3. RUBBER BAND + NEXT-SIZE-UP BIT.
     - Lay a flat rubber band across the socket, press the bit through it into the hex.
     - Same downward pressure, same CCW back-out.
     - Stop condition: any slip. A rubber-band slip rounds the socket worse than a clean failure.

  4. LOCKING PLIERS ON THE BIT, NEVER ON THE SOCKET.
     - Seat the next-size-up bit fully (tape or rubber band for grip).
     - Grip the bit SHANK with the locking pliers. Clamping the bolt head directly will crush it.
     - Use the pliers as a slow lever. Stop at the first "tock" of movement OR the first sign of slip.
     - Stop condition: any rounding sound, any fiber crush around the bolt, no rotation after ~5 seconds of firm effort.

  5. MANUAL SCREWDRIVER AS A PUNCH — DO NOT DO THIS ON FURNITURE.
     - Wedging a flat-blade into the hex socket permanently mushrooms the bolt head. On furniture bolts (typically steel into MDF or particleboard) the head will shear or spin in the substrate, leaving a panel you cannot remove AND a piece you cannot properly reassemble. Skip this method.

HARD STOP RULE
Switch to bracing immediately if any of the following:
  - The bolt does not rotate after one clean attempt at each step above (about 5 minutes of total work).
  - The socket visibly rounds further between attempts.
  - The bolt "wants" to spin without backing out (stripped shank threads or loose substrate).
  - Any crack, crush, finish pop, or hairline split appears at the bolt hole.
  - The panel begins to rack, gap, or wobble.

BRACING THE PARTIALLY ASSEMBLED BOOKCASE FOR THE MOVER
Goal: immobilize the last side panel relative to the rest of the frame so it cannot swing, rack, catch a doorframe, or load the one remaining bolt during a carry.

  1. Wipe the area around the joint clean so tape will hold.

  2. Cut a CARDBOARD SLEEVE that wraps the panel-to-frame seam with at least 4 inches of overlap onto each side of the joint, on both faces. Fold it snug.

  3. Tape the sleeve with PAINTER'S TAPE (it will not lift the finish). Wrap at least three bands: one above the joint, one across the joint, one below. The cardboard should feel rigid when you wiggle the panel.

  4. Add a STIFFENER STRIP across the seam — a flat piece of cardboard or a small wood offcut taped perpendicular to the seam so any racking force transfers to the brace, not to the bolt.

  5. Tape a small patch over the bolt head itself — keeps the bit pocket clean for the mover and keeps the bolt from vibrating loose in the truck.

  6. WIGGLE TEST. Any visible movement at the panel = add another band of tape or a second stiffener. No movement = ready to move.

MOVER HANDOFF

  - Tag the piece with painter's tape and a marker: "BOOKCASE — 1 JOINT NOT DISASSEMBLED, BRACED — KEEP UPRIGHT, DO NOT TILT ON THIS SIDE."
  - Tell the crew lead verbally at pickup that the bookcase is intentionally braced, not damaged. The crew should carry it upright (not on its side) and not set the braced face down on the truck floor.
  - If the second bookcase ends up with the same issue, use the same brace-and-move approach rather than pushing through a stripped fastener.

ONE NOTE FOR REASSEMBLY AT SOUTH SLOPE
When you reassemble, do not reuse the bolt that stripped. The mating hex on the bolt head is now deformed and will strip again on the first re-drive. Plan to replace it with a fresh hex-socket bolt of the same thread and length (bring one to the new place, or pick one up locally before final reassembly).

What you're describing — bilateral soreness across shoulders and thighs, worse with stairs, eased by warmth, no focal sharp pain, swelling, weakness, numbness, radiating pain, or systemic symptoms — fits generalized muscle soreness from two consecutive days of unaccustomed load, not an injury. The "better after a warm shower" line is exactly the pattern you'd expect from sore muscle, not from a strain.

  - No more lifting. Anything still in boxes stays in boxes tonight.
  - Warm shower is fine and useful; a second short one before bed is reasonable.
  - Hydrate steadily through the evening — water, plus a little sodium/potassium if you were sweating during the moves. Move-day dehydration is what tips borderline soreness into the bad zone and is also the input that raises rhabdomyolysis risk, so this one actually matters tonight.
  - Normal dinner with protein + carbs. Recovery fuel, not a diet moment.
  - Gentle movement only: walk around the apartment, light stretch to tolerance of quads, hamstrings, hip flexors, and the shoulder girdle. Don't force any of it — deep static stretching of sore muscle tends to worsen next-day ache rather than help.
  - Sleep on your normal schedule. Sleep is the single biggest recovery input you control.
  - Pain relief if you want it: acetaminophen 500–1000 mg as needed, or a topical NSAID/menthol on the worst spots. Oral ibuprofen or naproxen are fine for tonight's comfort.
  - Position: pillow under the knees if thighs dominate, small pillow supporting each forearm if shoulders are barking.

Sunday pickup soccer

Conservative read: sit this one out.

Two back-to-back move days is a meaningful unaccustomed load on the same muscle groups soccer stresses most — quads, hamstrings, calves, hip flexors — and playing through significant DOMS is a known injury-risk setup. Sore lower-body muscles alter landing and change-of-direction mechanics in ways that raise ankle and knee injury risk, sprint output is going to be poor, and it's unlikely to be fun. Your last clean logged session was a controlled 45 min on Sept 12 with no symptoms; one week off after a heavy move week is exactly the pattern you've used successfully before.

If you really want to go anyway: attend, warm up, cap yourself at 15–20 min of easy play, no sprints, no hard tackles, no contested headers, and stop at the first hint of guarding or any sharp focal pain. But the cleaner call is to skip this Sunday and return next week with a normal warm-up and your usual 30-min cap. That's the call I'd make.

Warning signs that should prompt medical evaluation

The most important one for your specific situation is at the top — read it.

Go to urgent care or ER for any of the following:
  - Dark, cola-, tea-, or reddish-brown urine, OR a clear drop in how much you're urinating. Rhabdomyolysis is the real concern after sustained heavy lifting, especially paired with under-hydration. This is the single most important item on this list for you tonight.
  - Unilateral calf pain, swelling, warmth, or tightness that doesn't match the other side, or a tender cord in the calf. DVT risk after heavy exertion, particularly if you were dehydrated.
  - Chest pain, shortness of breath, sudden sharp pain with breathing, coughing up blood, lightheadedness, or passing out. Pulmonary embolism shares the same risk factors.
  - Focal sharp pain, visible swelling, deformity, or bruising at one specific joint, or inability to bear weight on one leg / use one shoulder normally. That pattern is an injury, not soreness.
  - New numbness, tingling, or true weakness in a specific limb distribution (one hand, one forearm, one foot) — nerve compression or stretch from lifting.
  - Fever above about 38°C / 100.4°F with a focal hot, red, swollen muscle — could indicate a compartment issue or infection, both rare but both urgent.
  - Sudden severe headache, vision change, confusion, or new seizure.

For anything borderline, your primary care's after-hours line is the right first call; for dark urine, chest symptoms, focal neuro deficit, or focal weakness, go straight to the ER.

If none of those show up, expect the worst of the soreness to fade over 48–72 hours from the second move day, and reassess Wednesday or so for whether you want to do anything before next Sunday's session.

## 2024-05-30 — Active vs retired generations, epoch drain, matcher cleanup, STW cleanup pauses

The existing entry covers CPU, memory, queue depth, route-delivery divergence, dropped series, and restarts. This section adds the checks that are missing from that surface: generation lifecycle, epoch drain, matcher cleanup, and stop-the-world (STW) cleanup pauses.

### Signal set — what to compare by pod

For each canary pod, alongside the existing p99 reading, capture:

1. Active generation count on the pod (`active_generation` per the /healthz state model — active only changes on swap, never on a failed apply).
2. Retired generation count on the pod (generations no longer active but not yet reaped).
3. Epoch drain state (in-flight reloads/workers that have not yet acknowledged the active generation).
4. Matcher cleanup state (matcher cache size, and how many retired-generation matchers remain).
5. STW cleanup pauses (GC pause durations, especially anything tagged cleanup / mark / sweep on the matcher and generation caches).

Compare p99 against active and retired generation counts and against cleanup pause durations — not against CPU alone. A pod with normal p99 but a growing retired count or rising STW pauses is signaling leak pressure, not steady state.

### Pause thresholds — when to halt further configuration pushes

Pause additional configuration pushes when ANY of the following hold:

- Retired objects accumulate above four per pod (retired generations, retired matchers, or any combination). This is a leak-shaped signal, not a warmup blip.
- Cleanup pauses exceed 100 ms per occurrence, or show a sustained upward trend over the pause window.

When pausing, do not roll back by default. Hold at the current cohort, capture the evidence below, and page the on-call owner before any further push or rollback.

### Verification set before resuming pushes

All of the following must hold before resuming additional configuration pushes:

1. Active-generation consistency across all canary pods (every pod reports the same `active_generation`; partial worker-apply failure is not allowed to leave pods on divergent active generations).
2. Route parity between canary and control (route-delivery counters match within the existing alert tolerance).
3. Dropped series at zero across canary pods.
4. Reload failures at zero during the pause window.
5. Restarts at zero during the pause window.

### Evidence to capture during the pause

Capture and attach to the incident / pause note:

- Per-pod generation evidence: `attempted_generation`, `validated_generation`, `active_generation`, and retired-generation count, sampled at pause start and at 5-minute intervals.
- Per-pod heap evidence: heap in-use, matcher cache size and key count, generation cache size, and the top STW pause duration during the pause window.
- The p99-by-pod comparison the thresholds above are keyed off.

### Rollback clarification

Responders must NOT roll back solely because a transient p99 spike recovered. A recovered p99 spike by itself is a hold-and-verify signal, not a rollback trigger.

Rollback IS warranted for any of:

- Active-generation inconsistency across pods (including any partial worker-apply failure that leaves divergent active generations).
- Route divergence between canary and control beyond tolerance.
- Dropped series above zero on canary pods.

In all other cases — including transient p99 spikes that recovered, elevated CPU that compresses, or retired-object counts that stay at or below four — hold, capture evidence, and verify against the signal set above. Do not auto-rollback on those signals alone.

## 2024-07-25 — Owner-led-window rule (supersedes 2024-06-18 bounded single-push model)

The 2024-06-18 bounded single-push model treated each push as needing its own drain-and-verify approval. That framing is superseded. The accepted operating model is an owner-led window: Alex opens a window with a fresh decision, and mapped operators may push single files within it under the conditions below. The 2024-05-30 signal set, pause thresholds, verification set, evidence capture, and rollback clarification remain in force and are referenced by name.

### Window opening

Each window requires a fresh opening decision from Alex. No mapped operator opens a window on their own. The opening decision is what converts the prior hold into push permission; a prior approval does not carry forward to a later window.

### Pushes during the window

Once a window is open, mapped operators may make single-file pushes while ALL of the following hold on every canary pod:

1. Retired generations remain at four or fewer — the same threshold the 2024-05-30 signal set uses.
2. Cleanup pauses remain at or below 100 milliseconds — the same threshold the 2024-05-30 signal set uses.
3. The full health set returns to baseline after every push — active-generation consistency, route parity, dropped series at zero, reload failures at zero, restarts at zero, and p99/heap inside the pre-canary band.

A push that disturbs the full health set does not, by itself, stop the window — but until the full health set returns to baseline, no further pushes are permitted. Baseline is the pre-canary p99 band and the pre-canary heap band, not a downward trend.

### Threshold exceedance stops the window immediately

Exceeding either threshold — retired generations above four, or a cleanup pause above 100 ms — stops the window immediately. There is no warmup exemption and no grace period. When the window stops, mapped operators hold further pushes, capture the evidence set from the 2024-05-30 section, and page the on-call owner.

### After recovery

After recovery:

- A fresh decision from Alex permits exactly one fully observed push.
- After that push returns the full health set to baseline, another window requires a separate fresh decision from Alex.

A single fully observed push after recovery is not, on its own, the start of a new window. The window only reopens with another fresh decision from Alex; prior approval does not carry forward.

### Rollback conditions (unchanged)

The following remain rollback conditions regardless of whether the window is open, whether p99 and heap look healthy, or whether the retired-generation and cleanup-pause thresholds are clean:

- Active-generation inconsistency across canary pods (consistency).
- Route divergence between canary and control beyond tolerance (parity).
- Dropped series above zero on any canary pod.
- Reload failures during the pause window or through any push.
- Restarts during the pause window or through any push.

A clean resource surface does not offset any of these five. Any one is sufficient on its own to roll back, and rollback remains an explicit decision routed through the deploy pipeline.

### Ownership (unchanged)

- Primary owner: Alex.
- Practical backup: Wes.
- This rule does not make Wes the primary owner. Wes remains the practical backup under the existing practical backup rules. The owner map is unchanged.
