  - A faint high-pitched squeal on the first stops after bedding is normal and usually fades as the pad layer equalizes.
  - New pads on a new rotor typically need 40–60 total loaded stops to fully equalize. Treat the next 1–2 rides as part of the bedding process — favor easy braking, avoid long descents.

The crack is in the cast clamp body adjacent to the desk-tightening bolt. That bolt is a stress concentration point, and the surrounding casting is what resists both the clamping load and the cantilever load from the arm. A crack in cast metal at that location is a structural defect, not a cosmetic one. Castings tend to fail in fatigue without prior warning deformation, and failure tends to be sudden rather than gradual. Cyclic loading from arm movement is enough to propagate a hairline crack over time, and the propagation rate is not predictable from a photo.

The 14.2 lb on a 22 lb arm is paper headroom. Headroom does not arrest a fatigue crack. A clamp failure under load would drop the monitor onto the desk and anything underneath it. Beyond the safety issue, mounting it would convert a clear manufacturing-defect return into a dispute, since you would be the first party to apply load to a part that was already cracked on arrival. There is also no safe way to verify whether the crack is benign without loading it, so you gain nothing by trying.

Evidence to include in the return request:

1. Timestamped photos (you have the subjects; ensure each shot is timestamped by your phone):
   - Close-up of the crack with a scale reference — a ruler or coin placed next to it so the ~18 mm length is verifiable in the image, not just stated.
   - The same close-up lit at a low angle (raking light) so the crack's depth is visible. Hairline cast cracks often photograph as faint lines straight-on but are obvious under oblique light.
   - A wider frame that places the crack in context — the whole clamp body with the desk-tightening bolt visible, so the reviewer sees the crack is adjacent to the load-bearing bolt, not somewhere inconsequential.
   - The model and serial number label (you have this).
   - A whole-unit photo so the part is unambiguously identifiable.
   - The outer carton: all four sides plus the shipping label. The intact carton is itself evidence — it argues against in-transit damage and supports a casting-defect claim.

2. Written description in the return message:
   - Date the unit was received.
   - Date the defect was noticed.
   - A clear statement that the unit has never been mounted and no load has been applied.
   - Location of the crack: cast clamp body, adjacent to the desk-tightening bolt.
   - Approximate length: ~18 mm.
   - That all original packaging, manuals, hardware bags, and included parts are retained and will be returned in full.

3. Order record:
   - Order confirmation or receipt with the order number, purchase date, and the seller's stated return window.
   - This anchors the claim inside the return window and confirms the item was sold by them.

4. Retain everything until the return is closed:
   - Box, foam, manuals, hardware bag, all accessories. Do not discard until the refund or credit has posted. A complete kit removes any "missing parts" deduction.

5. Filing:
   - Submit today rather than waiting — most windows are 30 days from delivery, and a prompt claim with photos is harder for a seller to dispute than a delayed one.
   - If the seller offers a "defective / damaged on arrival" or "arrived damaged" path distinct from a standard change-of-mind return, use that path. It usually routes to a different queue, waives return shipping, and skips any restocking fee.
   - Keep the carrier tracking for the return shipment and the refund or credit confirmation once it posts.

If the seller pushes back on the casting-defect framing, the intact outer carton plus the photo showing the crack adjacent to the bolt boss is your strongest pair of evidence — together they argue the defect was present at manufacture rather than introduced during shipping or by you.

Verdict: this is a client-interpretation problem, not accounting loss. Sphere's numbers reconcile exactly (11,760 + 240 = 12,000), so no points are unaccounted for on our side. The 240-point gap is real — those points were never stored — but the dashboard is treating "attempted" as "sent," which is wrong whenever a partial-success response is in play.

Why it is a client-interpretation problem

  1. The OTLP partial_success response is authoritative at the point level. It explicitly partitions the 12,000 attempted points into 11,760 accepted and 240 rejected (invalid attributes). Both buckets are server-decided and sum to the attempted total.
  2. The SDK upgrade changed how the client reads the response. Pre-upgrade behavior treated partial_success as a soft signal; post-upgrade behavior is collapsing accepted+rejected into a single "sent" count and dropping the rejected bucket.
  3. There are no duplicate request IDs and no retries, so this is not a dedup-stored-once / attempt-counted-twice scenario (which is the trap with received-batches panels). It is purely a count-model mismatch.

How the client should represent the three counts

  - attempted:  12,000  (points the client submitted in the export)
  - accepted:  11,760  (points ingest-edge stored; listed as success in partial_success)
  - rejected:     240  (points ingest-edge refused; per-point error in partial_success.errorMessage / rejected_points)

  "Sent" must equal "accepted," not "attempted," when a partial_success body is present. The dashboard should surface all three: attempted (volume submitted), accepted (delivery success), rejected (delivery failure with reason). The 240 rejected points should not be carried forward as "in flight" or "pending" — they have a terminal reject from the server.

What the client should do operationally

  - Stop counting the 240 as delivered. They are not stored and will never appear in queries.
  - Inspect partial_success for the per-point errorMessage; here it is "invalid attributes."
  - Correct or omit only those 240 points in the next export and resend. Do not replay the full original batch — the 11,760 are already stored and replay would double-write them.
  - If the SDK upgrade itself is swallowing partial_success, that is the SDK bug to fix, not something to paper over in the dashboard.

Two weeks symptom-free with unloaded, low-velocity, sagittal-plane activity is real progress, but it is not the same demand as soccer. Walking tests tolerance to walking. The graded field test below tests tolerance to the actual loads you'll apply — fast eccentric calf work, lateral direction change, deceleration, repeated jumps. Anything that reproduces the original high-calf tightness or surfaces a new symptom is information to stop, not push through.

GRADED PRE-SOCCER FIELD TEST

Do this Saturday or Sunday morning well before kickoff, on grass or turf, in the cleats you intend to wear. Each step is a gate. If a step reproduces the original tightness, sharp pain, grab, swelling sensation, fatigue asymmetry, or any new symptom, stop at that step and do not advance. The test is the answer — passing it earns clearance, failing it tells you to sit out another week and re-test in 7 days.

  0. Baseline (already passed): 10-min easy walk, stairs, cycling, 10 slow single-leg calf raises each side. No pain, no tightness, no asymmetry.
  1. Faster tempo calf raises: 15 single-leg raises each side at a 2-sec up / 1-sec down cadence. Watch for tightness or fatigue asymmetry.
  2. Repeated hops in place: 20 submaximal two-foot hops, then 10 single-leg hops each side. Submaximal first, max only if submax is clean.
  3. Straight-line jog: 3 × 40 m at easy pace with full rest between. Note any tightness onset — distance, speed, or fatigue-dependent.
  4. Lateral shuffle: 4 × 20 m at moderate pace, both directions. This is the movement that previously made the tightness noticeable. Clean shuffle = biggest gate cleared.
  5. Forward accelerations: 4 × 30 m builds to roughly 70–80%. Testing, not maxing.
  6. Controlled lateral cut: jog-into-plant-and-cut, 4–6 reps each direction. Plant foot should feel stable; calf should not grab or guard.
  7. Repeated bounds: 3 × 5 two-foot bounds, then 3 single-leg landings each side.
  8. Backpedal and decel: 3 × 20 m backpedal, then jog-forward stop. Tests eccentric load, which is where calves get re-injured.

If all eight steps pass with zero recurrence and symmetric performance, you've earned a graded return. If step 4 (shuffle) or step 6 (cut) reproduces the original sensation, the answer is no for Sunday.

CONSERVATIVE CRITERIA DURING PLAY

Green — play as planned, but still graded
  - Test was fully clean, calf feels "forgotten" during the warm-up jog, push-off is symmetric in warm-up cuts.
  - Operational: full participation is fine, but still honor the time cap below.

Yellow — modify, do not push through
  - Mild tightness that only appears at the end of a rep or in the final 15 min of a half.
  - Calf feels "there but not painful," or a subtle awareness that wasn't there in warm-up.
  - Operational: play only the first half, no extra-time, sub yourself before it compounds. Stay wide, no repeated sprints down the line, no contested 50/50s, no jumping headers. Hard cap: 30–40 min total pitch time.

Red — stop immediately
  - Sharp pain, pop, grab, or sudden tightness that doesn't fully resolve within 2–3 min of walking.
  - Pain that builds during a rep instead of settling.
  - Swelling, warmth, or visible asymmetry appearing during play.
  - Calf feels weak on push-off vs the other side, limping gait, or guarding.
  - Operational: walk off, ice 15–20 min, compression sleeve optional, re-evaluate tomorrow before any follow-on activity.

Black — same-day medical evaluation, skip the game
  - Sudden sharp pain with an audible pop or sensation of something giving.
  - New swelling, redness, warmth, or focal tenderness — especially along the medial calf or behind the knee. These can indicate DVT or a partial tear and shouldn't be self-managed through a pickup game.
  - Calf pain at rest or pain that wakes you, color change, numbness, or pins-and-needles in the foot.
  - Calf visibly swollen, hot, or tender compared to the other side.

SUNDAY EXECUTION NOTES

  - You're committed to Devika in the afternoon. That's a second reason to be conservative — a minor setback doesn't just cost the sport, it costs the day. Treat the afternoon plan as a constraint on risk, not a separate decision.
  - On arrival, run a structured 15-min warm-up: easy jog, dynamic mobility, gradual accelerations, lateral shuffles, two-foot hops. Skipping the warm-up means skipping the game.
  - Pre-decide your exit. Tell yourself now: at first yellow, you come off. "One more point" is how the afternoon gets wrecked.
  - If you play: ice 15–20 min after, gentle straight-knee calf stretch if pain-free, hydrate, re-check tomorrow morning before deciding on any follow-on activity.
  - If the field test on Saturday or pre-kickoff Sunday fails at any step: stay out, re-test in 7 days. The two-week symptom-free window you've built isn't wasted — it's the foundation that makes the next attempt safe.

What you described is a textbook microwave-vs-2.4 GHz Wi-Fi interaction, and it does not call for moving equipment or buying anything. The pattern you observed (drops only on 2.4 GHz during microwave run, instant recovery when it stops, 5 GHz and wired untouched, modem and provider path healthy) is already strong evidence. Here is the why, the lowest-touch verification, and the stable setup you already have.

WHY THIS HAPPENS

A microwave oven's magnetron oscillates at roughly 2.45 GHz, which sits inside the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi band. Even a well-sealed microwave leaks a small amount of RF through the door gasket while it runs; a worn, dirty, or compressed gasket leaks more. The 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi channel layout in North America:

  Channel 1 center  2.412 GHz  (farthest from 2.45 GHz, most resistant)
  Channel 6 center  2.437 GHz  (closest, most affected)
  Channel 11 center 2.462 GHz  (close on the high side)

5 GHz Wi-Fi operates an order of magnitude higher in frequency and is unaffected. Wired Ethernet uses no RF at all and is unaffected. The modem staying online and the provider status page being clean both confirm the ISP path is fine — the failure is purely between the laptop's 2.4 GHz radio and the router while the magnetron is firing.

This is not a router defect. Your router already proved itself on 5 GHz at channel 36 / 40 MHz during the June work, and that performance is intact. Replacing or repositioning the router or modem would not change this.

LOWEST-DISRUPTION VERIFICATION (no equipment changes)

The pattern is already strong. To make it bulletproof and have something to refer back to:

1. Temporal coupling. Run the microwave for 30-60 seconds on three to five separate occasions while the work-room laptop is connected only on 2.4 GHz and doing something that exercises the link (a continuous ping to the router, an active download, a video call). Note whether the link drops within the microwave window. Then run it once with the laptop forced to 5 GHz — should not drop. Then run it once with the laptop on wired Ethernet — should not drop.

2. Wi-Fi analyzer snapshot. Stand near the work-room laptop with a phone running a Wi-Fi analyzer (iPhone has built-in Wi-Fi diagnostics; Android has apps like WiFi Analyzer). Capture:
   - The router's 2.4 GHz channel the laptop is associated with
   - The 2.4 GHz RSSI just before, during, and after a microwave run
   The channel the laptop is on matters; if it lands on 6 the drop will be sharpest, on 1 it should be smaller or absent.

3. Visual check of the microwave door gasket. Look at the seal around the door. Is it compressed, cracked, gummy, or visibly dirty? A failing gasket is the most common cause of unusually severe interference. Visual inspection only; do not disassemble anything.

Per-run log to keep (one line per microwave run):

  - Timestamp microwave started
  - 2.4 GHz channel and RSSI just before
  - Pattern of failure (full disconnect, association lost, pages stalled, etc.)
  - Timestamp microwave stopped
  - Timestamp link restored

Three to five runs is enough. You don't need to share this with anyone — it is a self-contained environmental fact — but the log is the artifact if you ever want to show it to a landlord, building management, or microwave manufacturer.

THE STABLE SETUP YOU ALREADY HAVE

A. Wired Ethernet for the work-room laptop when you are doing anything that cannot tolerate a hiccup. The wired path is the most robust, does not touch Wi-Fi, and DNS has been verified clean since the Oct 8 fix. This is your primary setup for focused work sessions.

B. 5 GHz for everything else mobile. You have already verified it stable on channel 36 at 40 MHz. It is not affected by the microwave at all. Use it for browsing, video calls, downloads, and anything else that is not currently running over Ethernet.

C. 2.4 GHz only for devices that genuinely need it (smart-home gear, anything that does not speak 5 GHz). If a specific device you care about uses 2.4 GHz and you want to harden it, pin the router's 2.4 GHz channel to 1 — this is a single setting change, no equipment swap. You do not need to do this for the laptop; it has the 5 GHz and Ethernet options above.

OPERATIONAL HABITS THAT MAKE THIS A NON-ISSUE

- Do not start the microwave mid-call. Run it before or after, or pause briefly.
- If you are on 2.4 GHz by accident (some clients fall back from 5 GHz when the signal is weak), check the band the laptop is actually connected to before assuming the network is down. The laptop will auto-rejoin within seconds of the microwave stopping, which is what you are already seeing.
- If microwave interference grows noticeably worse over weeks or months, the gasket is the first place to look — clean the seal as a zero-cost first step, replace the microwave as the only durable fix. The network gear is not the problem.

WHAT NOT TO DO

- Do not replace the router. The 5 GHz performance proves the radio is healthy.
- Do not move the modem. It is not in the path of the interference.
- Do not buy a mesh system, a Wi-Fi 6E upgrade, or shielded cabling. None of these address in-band RF noise from a microwave.
- Do not open a provider ticket. The provider path is up, the status page is clean, and the failure is inside your apartment between the magnetron and the 2.4 GHz radio.

Memory saved (99% — near ceiling; future saves should consolidate before adding). Now the assessment.

## Classification

The five temporary 503s are a **warmup-window availability defect**, not a serving-safety one. The interval (180–240 ms post-lease-acceptance, pre-cache-ready flag) sits entirely inside the lease-transfer warmup window, before the new holder has any opportunity to misroute — exactly the slot the previous evidence (8/22 drill, 9/11 supervised verification, 10/23 1,200-transfer observation, 42- and 20-transfer worksheets) had classified as "availability degraded, serving safety clean." The patch (publish cache-ready before admitting routed requests) closes the gap directly; if it holds, the defect is eliminated at its source rather than papered over.

That said, the evidence supports a bounded 5% canary but does **not** justify expanding past it on the staging result alone. Three reasons:

- 10k staging transfers is large for a load test, but the previous warmup outliers that produced the 503s (1.8 s warmup max, 8.6 s total-transfer max) were rare-tail events. Canary should be sized to actually exercise the tail.
- Staging doesn't carry production traffic mix; the 503 frequency in prod was 5/10 min on the paused rollout — the team needs to see at least comparable wall-clock exposure with comparable request rates, not just higher transfer counts.
- The patch changes ordering, which is the class of fix most likely to interact with the existing fail-closed gate on lease loss (#197). The interaction isn't visible in "no temporary 503s / no stale / one holder" — those are necessary but not sufficient. The relevant assertions are still the serving-safety ones.

## Sufficient for 5% bounded canary — with these conditions

The data platform team may proceed to a **fresh 5% canary** if and only if:

1. **Bounded**: hard cap at 5%, auto-pause configured (the existing rollback guard that fired on the original rollout stays), no manual expansion without another cross-service read.
2. **Wall-clock, not just count**: minimum observation window should be long enough to capture warmup-tail behavior — the 10/23 observation used 24 h; for a 5% canary a multi-hour window with the same per-minute request rate as the paused 10% is the minimum that produces a fair comparison.
3. **Pre-fix evidence retained as baseline**: keep the original 5×503 trace panel accessible so any new temporary 503 can be compared against the same interval shape. If a new temporary 503 falls inside the same 180–240 ms pre-cache-ready window, that's a partial fix or ordering regression, not a fresh class — and it's a pause + look, not a proceed.
4. **No changes to other knobs**: the seven-second timeout change stays disabled; the lease format stays unchanged for rollback; #197 fail-closed gate stays in place.

## Safeguards to retain

- **Rollback guard** that auto-paused on the original 5×503 — same threshold, same shape. Pause is the correct first action on the original signal; the team's choice to pause rather than expand was correct and should be the documented response, not an ad-hoc one.
- **#197 fail-closed serving gate** on lease-loss. The patch and #197 interact on the same ordering axis; the gate must stay as the backstop in case the patch's publish-before-admit ordering is bypassed by any path (e.g., a future code path that admits without going through the new readiness gate).
- **500 ms lease-validity poll** as backup detector — unchanged. The user's September staging rehearsal note already classified the sub-poll-interval exposure as acceptable, but it remains a backstop the patch doesn't replace.
- **One-holder invariant** on every transfer, and **old gate closed before later routing** on every transition — these are the serving-safety assertions and continue to be authoritative.
- **Stale-read / data-loss indicators** at zero. Any non-zero pause; any look is a regression.
- **Lease format unchanged** so a rollback is a deploy, not a data migration.

## Rollback signals the team should retain (authoritative stop conditions)

- **Any temporary 503 inside the warmup window** — pause. Even one is enough to revisit; the original signal was five, but the team is patching the cause, so a single reoccurrence means the patch didn't actually close the gap or there's a second path the patch missed.
- **Any stale response** — pause and full stop until characterized.
- **More than one serving holder observed at any instant** — pause and full stop.
- **Gate-close regression**: any trace showing a later routing response from the old holder after its gate was supposed to be closed — pause and full stop.
- **Sustained error-rate movement** (the team's existing error baseline + the 15-min monotonic rise rule from the preflight playbook already in memory).
- **Any process restart** during or attributable to a transfer — pause.
- **Lease epoch non-monotonicity** — full stop; this is a correctness signal, not an availability one.

The decision and ownership of the rollout stay with Cyrus's team. The read here is: the patch targets the right defect, staging evidence is consistent with the fix, and a bounded 5% canary with the existing guard + stop conditions retained is a reasonable next step — but the team should not interpret "no 503s in 10k staging" as "patch proven in production." The 5% canary exists to do that translation under the same wall-clock and traffic-mix conditions that produced the original signal.

The rollup queue being deep is a data-platform condition; whether `metrics-router` is scrape-able is an Infra condition. Coupling them via `unless` means the alert vanishes exactly when both are bad at once — which is precisely the case the data-platform team needs to be paged on.

Why the `unless on() up{job="metrics-router"} == 0` is wrong here:

1. Conflates two failure domains. Rollup lag and `metrics-router` scrape health are owned by different teams and have different remediations. `up == 0` on a metrics-router target tells you nothing about whether the rollup workers are draining.
2. Hides the worst correlated case. If `metrics-router` publication stalls, upstream points back up, and rollup's input queue grows — the `unless` swallows the very alert that would tell data-platform their drain path is degraded.
3. `unless on()` with an empty label list is "suppress whenever the right-hand vector has any series." One down target anywhere in `metrics-router`'s scrape set silences the whole rollup alert.
4. Treats scrape absence as service absence. `up == 0` fires on DNS/auth/sidecar blips too. A real backlog gets muted because a probe couldn't reach the exporter.
5. Violates the principle the alert condition should be self-contained on the owned service. The alert belongs to data-platform; its firing predicate must read rollup-service signals only.

Safer formulation — keep it pure on the owned service, let upstream health live in context:

    max_over_time(rollup_queue_age_seconds[5m]) > 300

That's the entire expression. The annotation can carry the upstream context the responder needs without making it load-bearing on firing:

    summary: "rollup-service queue age exceeded 5m (data-platform owned)"
    description: "max queue age over 5m is {{ $value }}s. Check rollup worker concurrency and compaction backlog. If metrics-router is also down, that is a separate Infra-owned alert — correlate on the dashboard, do not treat as suppression."

If data-platform wants co-occurrence to escalate severity rather than suppress, do it as a sibling rule with a severity label, not as a suppression:

    # Same condition, tiered
    labels { severity: "warning" }
      expr: max_over_time(rollup_queue_age_seconds[5m]) > 300
    labels { severity: "critical" }
      expr: max_over_time(rollup_queue_age_seconds[5m]) > 300
        and on() up{job="metrics-router"} == 0

That keeps the data-platform condition firing on its own merits and lets Infra's `metrics-router` alert fire independently — both pages land, the responder sees the correlation in the dashboard or the severity tier, and no one has to guess who owns the page.

On ownership: this alert stays with data-platform (Cyrus's team). The expression reads only `rollup_*` metrics; Infra's contribution is the parallel `metrics-router` alert and the dashboard panel showing both signals side-by-side. That's the boundary that held through the Oct 25 incident — rollup queue at 11m while metrics-router, ingest-edge, and point accounting were all healthy, and the rollback lived entirely on the data-platform side.

Cyrus's team handled both incidents with the kind of ownership discipline that's easy to miss in a busy week. On the October rollup backlog, the data platform team owned the compaction-worker flag end-to-end — they were the ones who reduced rollup concurrency, and they were the ones who rolled it back; the freshness recovery from eleven minutes to under forty seconds was the work of that side, and pulling in Infra for a narrow cross-service health read was the right scope rather than a transfer of ownership. On the shard-keeper prefetch rollout, the team stopped exactly when the configured 503 guard said stop and then traced the activation to a 180–240 ms admit-pre-cache-ready gap using its own patch and ten thousand staging transfers before any resume conversation. That's the pattern worth naming: own the change, let the guard do its job, and bring in adjacent evidence only where the boundary genuinely needs it.

Given that the bathroom hot side is normal and there was daytime plumbing work in the building, the most likely causes are (in order): the kitchen hot shutoff was closed during the work and not fully reopened, the aerator is partially clogged on the hot-side passage, or work debris got into the hot branch serving the kitchen only.

DIAGNOSTIC SEQUENCE (no supply-line disconnects):

1. Look under the kitchen sink. Identify the hot-side shutoff (typically on the left, marked red). Turn it gently counter-clockwise by hand until it stops, then leave it fully open. Hand pressure only — no tools.

2. Note the faucet type:
   - Two-handle: independent hot/cold cartridges and stops
   - Single-handle (mixer): one cartridge blends both, so a cartridge issue is also possible

3. Test hot flow with the aerator removed:
   - Unscrew the aerator at the spout tip (hand, or pliers wrapped in a rag if stuck)
   - Keep parts in order on the counter
   - Run hot only at full blast into a basin for 15 seconds
   - Compare to cold at the same handle position

4. Interpret:
   - Hot normal without aerator -> aerator was the cause. Clean it: brush with an old toothbrush under running water, soak in white vinegar 20 min if mineralized (you've seen grit in fixtures here before), reassemble.
   - Hot still weak without aerator -> problem is upstream of the spout. Stop and call management.

STOP AND CONTACT MANAGEMENT IF:
- The hot shutoff won't open fully, is stuck, or shows corrosion
- Aerator removal does not restore normal hot flow
- Hammering, whistling, or vibration when you run hot
- Water suddenly scalds at the normal handle position (anti-scald failure)
- Any new drip, moisture, or cabinet dampness appears during testing
- Pressure continues to drop over the next 24 hours
- Discoloration, sediment, or unusual odor shows up at any point

DO NOT:
- Use tools on the shutoff valves
- Disconnect supply lines or open the wall
- Force a stuck handle
- Dismantle the cartridge yourself

Why this is safe to scope to the kitchen: the bathroom hot is normal, so the building's hot supply and your apartment's main hot branch are fine. The fault is isolated to the kitchen faucet's hot-side path — shutoff, supply stub, or spout-side components only.

WET-ONLY SQUEAL — WHAT'S HAPPENING

A thin water film on the rotor lowers the friction coefficient and makes pad contact slightly unstable, so the pad face oscillates micro-scopically and you hear it as a high-pitched squeal on the first few stops. Heat from braking and airflow evaporate the water, friction stabilizes, the noise goes away. This is normal on a fresh rotor and on older ones alike. None of your other observations contradict that:

  - Lever firm and stopping straight -> caliper is centered, hydraulics/mechanical cable are healthy.
  - No pulse -> rotor is still true, no thickness hot-spot (your shop measured <0.05 mm runout on 2024-10-26).
  - No scrape -> pads are clearing the rotor.
  - No discoloration or debris -> no contamination, no overheating.

The clue that this is water, not contamination: it self-resolves as the rotor dries. Contamination or glazing would keep squealing on a dry rotor.

CLEANING SEQUENCE (next dry day, before riding)

  1. With the wheel in place, wipe both rotor faces with a clean lint-free cloth dampened with 90%+ isopropyl alcohol. Rotate the wheel as you wipe so the entire swept track is covered. Don't drip solvent into the hub or caliper piston area.
  2. If the pads look shiny or feel slick to the touch, remove them (note orientation), scuff the friction surface lightly with 120-220 grit sandpaper in one direction, then wipe the dust off with isopropyl on a fresh cloth. Reinstall in the same orientation.
  3. NEVER use on rotors or pads: WD-40, chain lube, degreaser, soap, Simple Green, or a water rinse. Only 90%+ isopropyl alcohol or a dedicated bike brake cleaner (Park Tool CM-5, Finish Line, or similar).
  4. Re-spin the wheel in the air. No rub, no scrape, no audible lateral runout.
  5. Squeeze the lever at standstill (walk-bike). Firm, even, lever does not bottom.

TEST SEQUENCE BEFORE THE NEXT RIDE (traffic-free, dry pavement)

  1. 5 min easy spin: confirm no rub, no pulse, no pull.
  2. 5 progressively firmer stops from ~10 mph to walking pace: lever firm, straight, no pulse, no fade.
  3. If all quiet, normal use. If squeal returns on a DRY day after cleaning, the rotor or pads are likely contaminated -- re-clean or replace pads.

SIGNS TO STOP RIDING

  - Lever feels soft, spongy, pulls to the bar, or gets worse during the ride
  - Any fluid (wet or oily) on rotor, caliper, or near the lever -- assume hydraulic leak until proven otherwise
  - Rotor: visible crack, deep groove you can catch with a fingernail, blue/purple heat discoloration, or thickness below the MIN stamp on the rotor (commonly 1.5 mm)
  - Pads: friction material at or below the wear line on the pad backing, or a shiny/slick surface that won't scuff clean
  - Persistent rhythmic rub or scrape after the caliper has been recentered and bolts are at spec
  - Bike pulls to one side under front braking, or lever pulses rhythmically (suggests a rotor thickness/parallelism issue, not water)
  - Squeal that continues even after the rotor has been fully dry for 10+ minutes AND alcohol-wiped -- that's contamination, not water
  - Any grinding or metal-on-metal sound, or a burning smell that doesn't fade after a stop

When in doubt, walk the bike home. A rotor or pad failure under hard braking is a much bigger problem than a short walk.

Current state matches the "fast-clearing, no smell, no leak" pattern from your May 21 valve-replacement event, which is the safer of the two outcomes. Your sequence is: finish cold-side flush systematically, then hot-side flush, then bring appliances and the filter back. Stop at any trigger below rather than push through.

Phase 1 — Cold-side flush (finish what you started)
  Goal is to clear sediment from the branch lines, not just the faucet spout. Aerators catch sediment first and will re-stain the stream even when the pipe is clear.
    1.  Close every other fixture.
    2.  Run kitchen COLD at full flow for 3–5 min total. You saw clear in 20 s; the extra time is for the branch line.
    3.  Run bathroom COLD at full flow for 3–5 min.
    4.  Run shower/tub COLD for 1–2 min (lift any flow-restrictor).
    5.  Flush each toilet once, then a second time.
    6.  Unscrew the aerators on the kitchen and bathroom cold taps. Rinse the screens under the cleared stream. Run both taps 30 s without the aerator, then reinstall.
    7.  Eyeball under the kitchen sink (the Aug 2024 cold-supply drip area) and around the toilet base — any new dampness, shut the local stop valve clockwise by hand and contact management.

Phase 2 — Hot-side flush (untouched since the shutdown)
  The water heater / hot riser held water the entire outage. Hot is where persistent discoloration and any sediment is most likely to surface.
    1.  Run kitchen HOT at full flow for 5–10 min.
    2.  Run bathroom HOT at full flow for 5–10 min.
    3.  If either tap goes brown or yellow and does NOT clear within 15–20 min, stop the flush and contact management.
    4.  Listen for hammering/banging — air in the lines after a shutdown is normal and quiets in a few minutes. Persistent or severe hammering is a stop-trigger.

Phase 3 — Appliances and filter return
  Only after Phase 1 AND Phase 2 are both fully clear:
    •  Drinking-water filter: do NOT run existing cartridges — trapped sediment will pass through. Bypass or replace the cartridge, then flush ~2 L through the new filter before drinking.
    •  Dishwasher: run an empty rinse/normal cycle. First real load: towels or items you don't mind re-washing.
    •  Washing machine: flush the supply hoses by running the nearest sink (bathroom or kitchen) hot+cold for 30 s with the washer supply valves open. Then run an empty rinse/spin (or clean-washer) cycle. First real load: towels.

STOP and contact management if ANY of these appear
  •  Brown/yellow returns after clearing, or hot-side doesn't clear within 15–20 min of flushing.
  •  Visible sediment in the stream, aerator screen, or toilet tank after lines have run clear.
  •  Smell: sewage (possible cross-connection), sulfur / rotten-egg (anaerobic water), fuel or oil (cross-connection), strong chlorine (over-dose).
  •  Pressure noticeably lower than before the shutdown and not recovering after 10–15 min of flushing.
  •  Any leak at a supply line, stop valve, or packing nut — particularly the kitchen cold supply (Aug 2024) or bathroom cold-shutoff packing nut (Jul 2023). Close the local stop valve clockwise by hand only.
  •  Persistent pipe banging, water heater popping, or hot-water scalding temperature swings.
  •  Management posts a boil-water notice at any point, even later in the day.

If none of the above appear by the end of Phase 2, the cold tap is safe for drinking and cooking within your standing rules: draw from cold, run 10–15 s if the tap has been idle for hours, skip the fridge ice and door dispenser today.

Comparison using the 99.6 / 0.4 distribution across three clients.

OPTION 1 — Hard 2,000-point client cap (permanent)

Operational failure modes
  - 88% peak local queue utilization is modeled, not observed. The 14-day run peaked at 82% (third client, 11-min drain, no drops, no retry storm). 88% is +6pp into headroom that has not been tested under live load.
  - Client-side queue-cap interaction. Under the 8-waiting-request client cap and 4-per-pod / 2-per-tenant ingest admission, a transient retry spike at 88% local utilization could overflow the client-side queue and reproduce the immediate-retry pattern from the 2024-07-16 incident.
  - No server-side enforcement. A client that regresses its batcher, runs an unmigrated code path, or sends raw events for a new code path reintroduces the prior latency path with no signal at the edge.
  - Permanent policy is enforced by clients we don't control; one client's compliance is one client's compliance.

Evidence gaps
  - Single-burstiest-client model. 88% is one client's projected peak. No dose-response at 2,500 or 3,000; no fourth-client data. The cap is fit to three observed workloads; a fourth workload profile could push different headroom.
  - Server-side fallback behavior uncharacterized. We accept oversized batches today; we have no telemetry on how often that happens because clients are complying with the temporary config.
  - 14 days at 2,000 does not establish multi-week or seasonal stability of the modeled 88% peak.
  - Aggregate 0.97 s p99 vs. burstiest-client 88% are different signals; we don't have the burstiest-client p99 under a permanent cap, only its modeled utilization.

OPTION 2 — Documentation-only guidance

Operational failure modes
  - No enforcement. The previously reproduced latency path remains reachable by any client that doesn't read, follow, or correctly implement the guidance.
  - Silent drift: clients optimize for throughput and may regress batching without our visibility. We see the symptom (tail latency, queue build) only after it manifests.
  - Multi-tenant fairness unchanged. An oversized batch from one tenant still consumes admission slots for its full duration under the 4-per-pod / 2-per-tenant bounds.
  - Point-accounting semantics remain undefined for oversized arrivals: we accept them or reject them on terms nobody has specified.

Evidence gaps
  - No positive evidence that documentation changes client behavior. The original incident presumably came from clients who either lacked or didn't follow guidance.
  - No telemetry on client compliance; cannot measure adherence until something breaks.
  - No way to distinguish accidental oversized batches (a regression we could detect) from deliberate oversized batches (a workload profile we need to support). The distribution does not separate these.

OPTION 3 — Ingest-edge soft rejection above 8,000

Operational failure modes
  - 0.03% rejection rate is low in aggregate but concentrated at the worst moments. For the burstiest client, rejections arrive precisely when their send-queue is most stressed — the very burst that triggered rejection is the burst most likely to be retried badly.
  - Partial-delivery semantics are undefined in the proposal. A 9,000-point batch: rejected wholesale (9,000 points lost client-side, no Retry-After contract on the lost points) vs. first-8,000 accepted / last-1,000 rejected with retry. Each implies a different point-accounting contract; no client has committed to either.
  - Client retry-contract gap. The 2024-07-16 trace shows at least one client issues three immediate retries before inspecting Retry-After. Under the existing admission pathway (retryable429 with Retry-After, per the 2024-04-18 admission fix), a non-compliant client produces a retry storm at exactly the moment we rejected its batch.
  - 8,000 is below the largest observed burst (9,600). The maximum-observed workload is incompatible with this option as proposed; any client whose legitimate peak sits above 8,000 must change their batching contract.

Evidence gaps
  - No production data at the 8,000 threshold. The 14-day run was at 2,000; zero runs at 8,000. The 0.03% figure is from recorded requests under the temporary config — we don't know what the rejection count looks like under Option 3 enforcement.
  - Partial-delivery contract undefined. Implementing this requires specifying and negotiating the contract with each participating client before deployment; that work has not been done.
  - Threshold placement unmodeled. 8,000 vs. 9,600 is a hypothesis about the workload mix that hasn't been tested. Of the 0.4% burst population, ~7.5% sits above 8,000 (0.03 / 0.4); the other ~92.5% of bursts are between 2,001 and 8,000 and would not be affected by this option.
  - No data on whether clients above 8,000 are the same clients whose retry behavior is non-compliant, or whether they could honor the partial-delivery contract we haven't written.

WHAT THE DISTRIBUTION DOES AND DOES NOT SAY

The 99.6 / 0.4 split is a workload description, not a policy justification.
  - 99.6% tells us a 2,000-point cap affects a small minority of requests. It does not tell us what the right cap is.
  - 0.4% tells us the burst population is real and material — across three clients and 30 days, the burst tail extends to 9,600 points and represents a workload we have not yet decided to support, throttle, or reject.
  - The 0.03% figure (vs. the 0.4% burst population) tells us only ~7.5% of bursts sit above 8,000; Option 3 affects roughly one in thirteen burst requests, not the burst population as a whole.

The distribution bounds the three options; it does not select among them:
  - Option 1 changes behavior for 100% of the 0.4% burst population (if clients comply).
  - Option 2 changes behavior for 0% of requests.
  - Option 3 changes behavior for ~7.5% of bursts (those above 8,000), conditional on a partial-delivery contract that hasn't been written.

WHAT THE COMPARISON SURFACES

Strongest evidence case: Option 1's temporary configuration as a *floor*, not a *policy*. 14 days, 0 accepted/rejected discrepancy, 0 duplicate IDs, error rate at baseline, p99 0.94 s on the affected class — that is real evidence across three clients. It supports "2,000 works for these three clients under these conditions." It does not support "2,000 is the right permanent threshold for all clients in all conditions," and the 88% modeled peak is one client's worst case, not a measured equilibrium.

Weakest evidence case: Option 3. The proposal requires three things we do not have — production data at 8,000, a partial-delivery contract, and a retry-compliance commitment from the burstiest client whose retry behavior is already characterized as non-compliant under the 2024-07-16 incident. Of the three options, this one has the largest gap between proposal and evidence.

Option 2 is the most defensible as a baseline — it preserves status quo while evidence is gathered — and the most likely to be wrong if the question is "should we do something." Doing nothing leaves the original latency path reachable in the system. It is the right choice only if the owners explicitly accept the latency path as a known, monitored risk with a detection signal and a runbook.

WHAT THE OWNERS STILL OWE BEFORE A PERMANENT DISPOSITION

For Option 1: server-side fallback behavior characterized; dose-response data at 2,500 and 3,000; a fourth-client or future-workload headroom analysis; explicit acceptance of the modeled 88% peak (or rejection of it as a policy floor).
For Option 2: an explicit decision that the latency path is acceptable as a known risk, with a detection signal (latency alert, queue-depth alert) and a runbook for when it fires.
For Option 3: a specified partial-delivery contract agreed with the three participating clients; a focused shadow or canary run at the proposed threshold with retry-behavior telemetry; threshold-placement analysis (why 8,000 and not 9,600 or 6,000).

The temporary experiment setting should not become the permanent disposition by default. It is evidence; the disposition is a separate question, and the three options as stated each carry a failure mode or evidence gap the owners have not yet resolved.

Current picture (one bite, dropped leaf, no confirmed swallow, breathing normal, no swelling, just brief lip-licking) is consistent with minimal or no actual ingestion. Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) is toxic to dogs via calcium oxalate crystals, but it is primarily a local oral and GI irritant; systemic effects are uncommon with small exposures. You are right not to have induced vomiting or given anything — that is the correct first move. Same general pattern as the 2024‑03‑30 episode the vet poison line already triaged as a local‑irritation case.

Immediate handling, in order:

  1. Gentle mouth decontamination. Wipe the gums, tongue, and inside of the cheeks with a damp cloth or offer a small amount of water in a bowl. Do not syringe or pour water into the mouth.
  2. Leave water available. Let him drink on his own; do not force.
  3. Hold food for about 30–60 minutes if lip‑licking or any drooling continues, then offer a normal or slightly bland meal.
  4. Keep him where you can see him for the next few hours and continue your checks.

Do NOT:
  - Induce vomiting (no hydrogen peroxide, no salt, no other method).
  - Give any medication (Pepcid, Benadryl, activated charcoal, etc.) without veterinary direction.
  - Force food or water.
  - Pull at any plant material in the mouth — from your description there is none.

When to call animal poison control:
  - Now, if you want professional confirmation for peace of mind, or if any symptom develops. ASPCA Animal Poison Control 888‑426‑4435 (fee may apply). Pet Poison Helpline 855‑764‑7661. They can also tell you whether the specific plant material you kept warrants escalation.

When to call your regular vet (within the day):
  - Repeated vomiting or retching.
  - Refusing food or water, or any signs of dehydration (dry gums, skin tenting).
  - Soft stool or diarrhea lasting past 24 hours.
  - New lethargy or appetite loss.
  - Persistent lip‑licking, drooling, or pawing at the mouth beyond the next hour or two.

Go to urgent care / ER immediately if you see:
  - Any facial, lip, tongue, or throat swelling.
  - Labored, noisy, or rapid breathing.
  - Repeated vomiting, especially with fresh blood or coffee‑ground appearance.
  - Pale, blue, yellow, or tacky gums.
  - Collapse, severe weakness, or inability to stand.

The shape of the night is one you know well — food, shower, quiet, presence without demand. What's different tonight is the patient death, so the three pitfalls you named are worth being deliberate about.

**When she walks in**
One line that names the night without opening it. Something close to: *"That sounds like an awful night. Food's on the counter, I'm right here. Take whatever time you need."* Then stop.

Hers. Don't knock, don't ask "are you okay?" when she comes out. *"Food's there if you want it"* is enough.

She decides if tonight is a talking night. If she talks, listen. No fixing, no reframing, no pivot to "at least you..." or "you did everything you could." If she doesn't, that's a complete answer. Sit with her, watch something, go to bed.

**Holding the three pitfalls**
- *Interrogation*: the only useful question tonight is *"what do you need right now,"* and she's already answered it — shower, food, quiet hour, then her call on talking. Trust that.
- *Minimizing*: the patient was a person and tonight was hard. Don't compare it to other shifts, don't reach for silver linings, don't tell her this gets easier with time. Even gently, those tell her grief is the wrong shape.
- *Diagnosis*: one patient death after a long shift is grief, not a sign something is wrong with her. Don't suggest debriefing, a therapy referral, or "you should really process this." If she brings it up, follow her lead. If she doesn't, ordinary grief after a hard shift doesn't need a clinical frame tonight — and probably not at all.

The loss did not occur in the transport. It occurred in the client's point-accounting layer, which only recorded the HTTP status and never inspected the OTLP partial-success body.

What actually happened:

- 600 OTLP requests reached ingest-edge and were forwarded to the collector. Both hop counters agree at 600, and every response was HTTP 200. Transport delivery was complete.
- The collector's responses carried a partial_success object reporting 240 rejected points with reason "timestamp is too far in the future" (the client host clock is ~7 minutes ahead of real time; this is the point-validity class of rejection, not a transport class — same family as the 2024-02-05 collector-clock and 2024-03-08 time_unix_nano unit-mismatch cases).
- Because the test client's logger records only the HTTP status, those 240 points were never decremented from the sent-side total. The dashboard counts them as delivered, the collector never persisted them, and the visible "four-minute gap" is the time range covered by the rejected timestamps rendered against a wall-clock axis that the collector never saw points for.

Transport success vs point acceptance:

- Transport success = HTTP exchange completed: request reached collector, response returned to client. Both sides can agree on this with request counters alone, and they do (600/600).
- Point acceptance = the collector's point-validity verdict, authoritative source is partial_success in the response body. Per the OTLP contract, HTTP 200 with a non-empty partial_success means the batch was not fully accepted; rejected_data_points is the only reliable count of what the collector did NOT persist.

Smallest diagnostic corrections:

1. Have the test client log the full OTLP response body, not just the HTTP status, for every export in the failing window. Surface partial_success.rejected_data_points, the error.type, and the error.message verbatim.
2. On the client host, run an NTP comparison and capture offset between the host clock and a known-good source (chronyc tracking / ntpdate -q). "7 minutes in the future" is far outside the normal sample-timestamp skew tolerance; confirm whether it is monotonic host-clock drift, a VM time-sync pause, or a milliseconds-vs-nanoseconds unit error in the exporter's time_unix_nano encoding (the latter would also present as "future" on the same scale).
3. Confirm the rejected-point reason is the timestamp class and not a coincident second cause by checking that rejected_data_points + accepted_data_points == attempted_data_points for the window.

Client-accounting corrections (aligns with the go-otlp-client#88 model already approved 2024-11-14):

- Attempted = outbound batch size (sum of data points the client tried to send). Do not decrement this on the wire; it is the denominator.
- Accepted = attempted - rejected, where rejected is read from partial_success.rejected_data_points on a successful HTTP response.
- Rejected = the rejected_data_points value, reported separately, with the rejection reason attached.
- Delivery state: complete only when rejected == 0; partial when rejected > 0; failed when the HTTP exchange did not return a parseable partial_success body.
- Stop counting rejected points as delivered. The four-minute gap closes once the dashboard's "sent" series is recomputed against (attempted, accepted, rejected) instead of against HTTP 200s.

Why this is not an ingest transport failure: every request crossed the edge-gateway, was accepted by the collector, and produced a well-formed OTLP response; request counters on both hops reconcile at 600; error rate, latency, and queue depth on ingest-edge and the collector are not implicated. The rejection is a per-point validity decision against the client's timestamps, surfaced through the normal partial-success channel that the client chose not to read. There is nothing to roll back or reroute — the fix is on the client side (parse the body, fix the clock, correct the counters).

DECISION: A 4 mm surface tread cut with no casing threads visible, no tube visible, no bulge, and the tire holding pressure for 30 minutes is permitted to ride locally — but ONLY after a tire boot is installed at the cut from the inside. Without a boot, the conservative call is replacement. Reasoning and the inspection order below.

WHAT THE STATED CONDITIONS MEAN
- "Surface cut" with no casing visible: the cut is in the tread cap (the cosmetic/wear rubber on top), not in the structural cord plies. That is the key fact.
- No tube visible: the inner liner is still intact; no herniation risk right now.
- No bulge: the casing plies are not severed (a bulge under load is the sign that cords are cut).
- 30-min pressure hold: reassuring for slow leaks, not conclusive at speed/load; do not rely on it alone.
- A boot is what converts "structurally OK today" into "structurally OK for the next ride."

SAFE INSPECTION SEQUENCE (do in order; stop and replace if any step fails)

1.  Outside visual, second look
    -  Re-confirm the cut is in the center tread, not creeping toward the shoulder or sidewall.
    -  Look for hairline extensions running circumferentially from the cut ends — those propagate under load.
    -  Replace if the cut reaches the tread shoulder or enters the sidewall at all.

2.  Flex / squeeze test — the check you have not yet done, and the most diagnostic one
    -  Deflate to roughly half pressure so the casing can move.
    -  Press thumbs firmly inward on either side of the cut, simulating a rider's load.
    -  Watch and feel: does the cut gape? Do white threads, nylon cords, or a darker woven layer show? Does the tire bulge at that spot under thumb pressure?
    -  Any of those = casing damaged → replace. This is the test that catches cuts that "look fine" until loaded.

3.  Inside check
    -  Push the bead away from the cut on both sides and look at the inner liner at that spot.
    -  Liner should be smooth rubber with no threads showing through and no pinhole.
    -  Threads visible from inside = cut goes through casing → replace.
    -  Pinhole visible from inside = the tube is likely already nicked; treat as a slow leak in progress → replace tire (or at minimum, fit a new tube and watch pressure closely).

4.  Re-inflate to the tire's marked pressure and re-hold
    -  Inflate to the sidewall rating, then wait another 30 minutes and confirm pressure is stable. Your first 30-min check was at unknown pressure; this is a confirmation at full pressure.

5.  Install a tire boot — mandatory for the ride-home call
    -  Boot goes on the INSIDE of the tire, centered over the cut, extending at least ~10 mm past the cut on every side.
    -  Acceptable materials: a commercial boot (Park Tool TB-2 etc.), a piece of old tube, a swatch of tough synthetic fabric, or a folded high-denier note as a one-ride field boot.
    -  Re-seat the tube, re-seat the bead with thumbs only (no lever on the cut side), inflate, confirm the boot has not shifted.
    -  A boot does two things: keeps the tube from being pushed into the cut under load, and prevents the cut from propagating circumferentially from road vibration.

6.  Reinstall the wheel (same procedure as before)
    -  Axle fully seated in the dropouts, quick release closed with firm resistance, lever oriented away from the drivetrain.
    -  Spin and confirm rim clears both brake pads through a full rotation. Do NOT recenter the brake to mask rub — that hides a real rim/wheel problem.
    -  Both brake levers engage, no rub, no wobble, no hiss on re-inflation.

7.  Low-speed test ride, traffic-free
    -  10–15 minutes, easy pedaling, a couple of moderate brake applications.
    -  Stop and inspect if any of these appear: hiss, sudden pressure loss, bulge forming at the cut, wobble, braking pull, or new rub.

REPLACE-NOW CONDITIONS (skip the boot, fit a new tire)
- Cut extends into the shoulder or any part of the sidewall.
- Squeeze test exposes casing threads, makes the cut gape, or produces a bulge.
- Inner view shows threads or a pinhole through the liner.
- Pressure does not hold on the second 30-min test at full pressure.
- Any bulge at the cut under load or under the squeeze test.
- The tube is already nicked at that spot.
- You will not or cannot install a boot — in that case replacement is the only acceptable answer.

LOCAL-RIDE IS PERMITTED ONLY IF ALL OF THE FOLLOWING ARE TRUE
- The squeeze test passes (no casing, no gape, no bulge).
- The inner view passes (no threads, no pinhole).
- The second pressure hold passes.
- A tire boot is fitted at the cut before the wheel goes back on.

Treat "local" as low-speed, low-traffic, near home — not a commute, not a descent, not a loaded ride. Re-flag if any of the stop conditions from step 7 appear.

WEDNESDAY EVENING PREP (Nov 27)

BAKE THE PIE
The oven is free tonight — bake the pie now. Pumpkin/typical fruit: 375 F for 45-55 min from raw, or 325 F for 10-15 min if pre-baked. Cool to room temp, cover, refrigerate. Serve Thursday at cool room temp, or warm 10 min at 300 F just before dessert.

CRANBERRY RELISH
Combine and refrigerate covered. Overnight rest deepens the flavor and saves counter time Thursday.

VEGETABLES
  Potatoes: peel, halve or quarter to uniform size (1.5-2 inch pieces). Submerge in cold water in a sealed container, refrigerate. They will not brown in water for 24 hrs.
  Carrots: peel, cut into 1.5-inch batons or 1-inch rounds. Submerge in cold water in a sealed container, refrigerate.
  Green beans: trim stem ends. Store DRY in a zip bag or container, refrigerated. Do NOT submerge — moisture plus time promotes bacterial growth and sogginess.
  Aromatics for gravy: chop 1 small onion, mince 2 garlic cloves, refrigerate in a small container.
  Fresh herbs (if using): wash, dry, wrap in damp paper towel, refrigerate.

CHICKEN (already in the fridge)
  Confirm fully thawed. If you froze it recently: fridge thawing takes ~24 hrs for 4.5 lb (about 5 hrs/lb). Fastest safe alternative is cold-water submersion in the sealed package, 1 hr/lb, changing water every 30 min — cook immediately after. Never thaw on the counter.
  Optional dry-brine (recommended): rub 1.5 tbsp kosher salt + 1 tsp sugar all over and under the skin. Place uncovered on a sheet pan in the fridge overnight (12-24 hrs). Skin dries out and crisps far better in the oven. Skip the brine and you'll still get a good bird, just less crackling skin.
  Remove the giblet bag from the cavity. Reserve the neck and back for a quick stock simmer if you want richer gravy.

THURSDAY DAY-OF TIMELINE (Nov 28)

2:00 PM  Pull chicken from fridge, set on counter to lose chill for 30 min. Whole-bird tempering is safe and shortens oven time slightly while evening out the cook.

2:45 PM  Preheat oven to 425 F with the roasting pan and rack on the lower-middle rack.

3:00 PM  Anya arrives. Pat chicken thoroughly dry with paper towels. Rub with 1 tbsp olive oil or softened butter. Season cavity and outside generously with salt and pepper. Tuck wing tips under, tie legs loosely with twine if you have it. Place breast-up on the rack.

3:00 PM  Chicken into the oven. Plan 75-90 min total at 425 F (roughly 18-20 min/lb unstuffed). Do NOT open the oven for the first 45 min — every opening drops the temp ~25 F and adds real cook time.

3:00-4:00 PM  While chicken roasts (an hour of relaxed time with Anya):
  - Drain prepped potatoes/carrots, pat dry on a clean towel.
  - Stage gravy ingredients: 1.5-2 cups stock (carton or Better Than Bouillon + water), 3 tbsp butter, 3 tbsp flour, salt, pepper. If using the neck/back, simmer it in 2 cups water on a back burner for 30 min, then strain.
  - Pull pie from fridge to lose chill.
  - Set the table, pour drinks.

4:00 PM  Start temp-checking. Insert an instant-read thermometer into the thickest part of the thigh without touching bone. At 160 F it is nearly done and carryover will finish it. At 165 F, pull immediately.

4:15 PM  Pull the chicken. Tent loosely with foil. The whole bird sits safely on the counter — its mass keeps the interior above 140 F for 30+ min, so the rest period is well within the safe window. Do NOT carve yet; sliced meat loses heat fast.

         CRANK the oven up to 425 F for the vegetables.

4:20 PM  Sheet pan of vegetables:
  - Toss potatoes and carrots with 2 tbsp olive oil, 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp pepper. Spread in a single layer on a sheet pan (parchment underneath for easy cleanup).
  - Slide into the oven (425 F, upper rack is fine). 25-30 min total.

4:25 PM  Gravy on the stovetop (one front burner):
  - Pour pan drippings into a fat separator, or skim off all but ~3 tbsp of fat.
  - In a saucepan over medium heat, melt 3 tbsp butter, whisk in 3 tbsp flour, cook 2 min without browning.
  - Slowly whisk in 1.5-2 cups of warm stock plus the drippings. Simmer 3-5 min, whisking, until silky. Season.
  - Hold on the lowest burner setting, stirring occasionally, or transfer to a slow cooker on WARM.

4:50 PM  Green beans (one burner):
  - Bring 1 inch of salted water to a boil in a wide pan.
  - Blanch the beans 3-4 min until bright green and tender-crisp.
  - Drain, return to the pan with 2 tbsp butter, salt, pepper, optional slivered almonds. Toss and cover.
  - Hold covered on the lowest burner setting, or transfer to a warm serving bowl covered with foil.

5:00 PM  Carve the chicken at the table or just before. Plate everything while hot: sliced chicken, roasted potatoes and carrots, green beans, cranberry relish, gravy on the side. Serve pie for dessert.

FOOD SAFETY REFERENCE

Thawing chicken
  Fridge: 5 hrs per lb, so ~24 hrs for a 4.5 lb bird.
  Cold water (sealed, submerged): 1 hr per lb, change water every 30 min. Cook immediately.
  Microwave: cook immediately after.
  Never thaw on the counter.

Cooking chicken
  165 F internal at the thickest thigh, no bone contact.
  Carryover during rest brings it to ~168-170 F.

Resting chicken (whole, tented with foil)
  15-20 min is the target. Whole bird stays safely above 140 F for 30+ min because of thermal mass. Do not carve during rest — sliced meat cools fast.

Hot holding (target 140 F or above)
  Gravy: lowest burner or slow cooker on WARM.
  Roasted vegetables: oven at 200 F, door closed, up to 30 min safe.
  Green beans: covered pan on lowest burner or warm oven (200 F).
  Never hold any cooked food at room temp for more than 2 hrs total. In this plan, nothing sits more than ~15 min before serving.

Reheating (relevant only for the pie)
  Previously cooked and refrigerated items reheat to 165 F internal. For pie: 300 F for 10 min covers this. Served at room temp is also safe for fruit/custard pies.

HOLDOVER CONTINGENCY (if Anya runs 5-15 min late, or the bird needs longer rest)

  Chicken: keep tented with foil. The whole bird is safe for 30-40 min total rest.
  Potatoes/carrots: leave in the oven, drop to 200 F, door closed. Re-crisp 3 min at 425 F just before serving if they soften.
  Green beans: refresh in a covered pan with 1 tbsp water over low heat 2-3 min.
  Gravy: stays on the lowest burner; thin with a splash of stock if it tightens up.
  Pie: serve at room temp, or 300 F for 5-10 min if you want it warm.

NOTES ON THE NO-ROOM-TEMPERATURE RULE

The whole plan avoids the danger zone (40-140 F) by keeping everything either actively hot (gravy on a burner, veg in the oven at 200 F, beans covered on low) or moving it directly from heat to plate within minutes. The chicken is the only thing that "rests" at room temp, and the rest window is 15-20 min on a whole bird — well inside the 2-hr rule and well above 140 F internally for that whole period. Slicing happens at 5:00 PM, immediately before plating, so no carved chicken sits out.

What the evidence supports

The 170,600 cumulative patched transfers across 5%, 25%, and 50% hold up as cross-service evidence for the patch's core claim. Three signals matter:

Two-track plan: decouple the breast from the heat so it coasts safely, finish the dark meat on its own, and stage the sides so nothing drifts below 140°F.

PART 1 — FINISH THE DARK MEAT

The breast at 162°F only needs a brief rest — carryover will take it to roughly 167-169°F on its own. Pushing it back into the oven is what dries it out. Best move is to separate the two leg quarters now and finish them apart from the breast.

1. Pull the bird, breast-up on the cutting board. Let it sit 2-3 min so juices settle.
2. With kitchen shears, cut along both sides of the backbone from tail to neck and lift the backbone out (save it for stock). You now have the breast half still attached to the two leg quarters.
3. Find the soft cartilage line where each leg quarter meets the breast half (roughly under where the wing joins). Cut straight down through that line with shears or a boning knife. Result: one intact breast half and two leg quarters (thigh + drumstick each).
4. Tent the breast half loosely with foil and leave it on the counter or a warm plate. It will coast to a safe 167-169°F over the next 10-15 min with no further heat.
5. Set the two leg quarters skin-side up on a sheet pan or roasting pan, ideally on a rack. Into a 375°F oven.
6. Roast until the deepest part of each thigh reads 165°F — about 12-18 min depending on size. No basting; you want the skin to re-crisp.
7. Pull at 165°F, tent loosely, rest 5 min while you carve the breast.

Simpler alternative if you'd rather not break the bird down: tent only the breast area with a doubled sheet of foil and return the whole bird to a 375°F oven for 10-12 min. Pull the instant any thigh probe hits 165°F. Less precise than separating, but it works.

PART 2 — HOLDING THE SIDES (40 min to plate)

Target: keep everything ≥140°F. Below that, the 2-hour room-temp clock starts.

Potatoes and carrots: leave them in the roasting pan, uncovered, in the oven dropped to 200°F. Stir once around the 20-min mark so the bottom pieces don't over-brown. If the oven is busy at 375°F with the legs, transfer the veg to a covered dish set over a pot of barely-simmering water on the back burner — a makeshift bain-marie. Cover tightly and check the water level once.

Gravy: keep on the smallest burner at the lowest setting. Stir every 10 min — skin forms fast and fond on the bottom scorches easily. Better option: pour it into a small slow cooker on "warm," or a thermos pre-warmed with hot water. Both hold above 140°F for over an hour without babysitting.

Green beans: don't start them yet. At the 10-min-to-serve mark, blanch 3-4 min in salted boiling water, shock briefly under cold to hold the color, then sauté 2 min in butter with salt and pepper. Hold covered on the lowest burner until you walk the plates out. About 7 min of active work at the end.

PART 3 — SERVICE SEQUENCE

T-40 (now): separate leg quarters, breast tented, sides held as above, legs into 375°F oven.
T-25: legs approaching 160°F — start probing every 2 min.
T-20: legs at 165°F, pull, tent, rest. Drop oven back to 200°F if you want to push the veg back in for a final warm-through.
T-15: carve the breast against the grain, ~½-inch thick, leave skin intact on top pieces for the platter.
T-10: separate drumsticks from thighs if you want a cleaner presentation, or leave whole.
T-5: green beans into boiling water.
T-0: plate, pass the gravy.

If anything slips by 5+ min: gravy stays on warm, veg stay in oven at 200°F, tent the breast tighter — a tented, just-cooked bird holds safely above 140°F for 30-40 min before food safety becomes a real concern.

KIBO PAW PLAN — FIRST SALT EVENT OF THE SEASON (2024-11-30)

PRE-WALK (5 min, at the door)
- Wipe each pad and interdigital space with a barely damp towel to remove any overnight residue, then pat dry.
- Apply a thin layer of paw balm to pads and between toes; let it absorb 2-3 minutes so it isn't a slippery mess on pavement. Balm acts as a barrier against direct salt contact.
- Trim or brush out any long fur between the pads if needed; longer fur traps granules that sit against skin.
- Stage a damp clean towel and a small bottle of lukewarm water by the door for the return wipe.
- Use a standard-length leash on treated sections for quick lift-and-carry or sidestep control; the front-clip harness is fine.

ROUTE (quieter loop, salt-aware)
- Keep the same quieter loop but AVOID the visibly granulated stretches entirely — detour one house over to a treated-but-drier block, cross at a clean apron, or cut through the closest untreated stretch.
- Walk on the DRYEST pavement available: mid-block concrete beats curb edges, where salt pools with meltwater. Avoid metal grates and storm drains (salt cakes there).
- Stay clear of the grass strip if it's been treated; curbside concrete is usually less loaded than the strip directly in front of buildings.
- Shorten the loop to ~15-20 min for the first salted outing; build back to full length after a clean walk confirms tolerance.
- If you can't route around a fresh-granule patch, lift Kibo over it or carry him across — short carries on quiet blocks are fine.

PAW-CLEANING (at the door, ~5 min)
- Damp-towel wipe FIRST, before stepping inside, to lift the bulk of granules and grit.
- Lukewarm soak 30-60 seconds per paw in a shallow bowl or cupped hand; swish the paw gently so the water gets between pads. Do one paw at a time so the others aren't dripping on the floor.
- Pat dry thoroughly between every pad and around each nail bed — moisture left between toes is what causes the irritation cycle.
- Recheck each pad and interdigital space under good light: cuts, cracks, redness, swelling, foreign grit wedged in fur.
- Optional: a second thin layer of balm after the paws are fully dry if pads feel chalky.
- Distraction (treats, a moment of training) so Kibo doesn't lick the wet paws and undo the drying.

MONITORING (next 24-48 hours)
- Gait recheck immediately on return, again at ~30 minutes, and once before bed.
- Visual paw check at the next outing (morning and evening) for 48 hours.
- Track which block segments looked freshly granulated so you can route around them next walk.
- Watch during the walk and after for: licking, weight-shifting, stopping to look at a paw, shaking a paw, shorter stride on one side.

END THE WALK EARLY IF YOU SEE
- Sudden favoring or lifting of a paw
- Repeated stopping to lick or chew
- Shaking a paw more than once or twice
- Shortened stride or reluctance to keep moving
- Whimpering, yelp, or visible startle when a paw touches down
- Shivering combined with paw attention (cold-pain combo)

CALL THE VET (or message the clinic) IF YOU SEE
- Persistent focused licking on one paw beyond ~30 minutes after cleaning
- Redness, swelling, heat, or tenderness in any pad or between toes
- Any visible cut, crack, split pad, bleeding, or discharge
- Limping or weight-bearing loss that doesn't resolve within an hour of rest
- Pad color change (white blanching, deep red, bruising) or unusual odor
- Cracked or flaking pads
- Foreign body wedged in a pad or toe web that you can't gently wipe free
- Behavioral changes: hiding, refusing food or water, lethargy, restlessness
- GI signs after a walk — vomiting, repeated retching, diarrhea (especially with blood or black stool), bloated/firm belly, excessive drooling, hunched posture (these suggest salt ingestion from paw-licking, not just paw irritation)

QUICK REFERENCE FOR THE FIRST WALK OUT
- Balm on before leaving.
- Damp towel + lukewarm bottle staged by the door.
- Loop the quiet side streets but skip the visibly salted patches; mid-block over curb; ~15-20 min.
- Wipe at the door, then 30-60 sec lukewarm soak per paw, pat dry between pads, light, recheck, optional second balm layer.
- Gait recheck at 30 min; full paw visual at the next outing.

If the first salted walk goes clean, you can keep the quieter route indefinitely with just the wipe-soak-dry routine at the door. Booties can come later for the heavy-grit weeks; they aren't required as long as the rinse-and-dry habit holds.

Failure boundary: the client wrapper that emits OTLP/HTTP. Production is unaffected because it still runs the prior wrapper. The collector is not in scope — it never saw any of the 120 gzip requests because the edge-gateway rejected them before forwarding. Other shapes (uncompressed HTTP, gRPC) passed, so the receiver path is healthy and the gateway's encoder-validation is doing its job, not failing. This is a malformed outbound header, not an ingest outage.

Why HTTP 415: the gateway logs show `Content-Encoding: gzip, gzip` — a duplicated content-coding in the value list. Per RFC 7231, Content-Encoding is a comma-separated list of codings; `gzip, gzip` is a malformed identity (two of the same coding with no defined "decode twice" semantics), and the OTLP/HTTP receiver path treats it as an unsupported payload format and returns 415. The body is presumably valid gzip (otherwise we would expect different surface evidence), so the encoder ran but the header was set twice. The collector's absence on the receipt side is the consequence of the gateway's correct rejection, not a forwarding failure.

Smallest wrapper correction:
  - In the OTLP/HTTP gzip sender, treat Content-Encoding as a single-valued header. Replace, don't append: any pre-existing Content-Encoding value must be overwritten, not merged.
  - Make the encoder idempotent across retry/redirect — a re-send of the same logical request must not re-add the header on top of an existing one.
  - Add a pre-send assertion: the outgoing header value must parse as a comma-separated coding list with no duplicate tokens, and the first two body bytes must be 0x1F 0x8B when the header advertises gzip.

Bounded staging replay, no production movement:
  - Deploy the corrected wrapper to staging only. Production wrapper stays put until staging clears.
  - Replay the same three shapes against the same staging collector: 120 valid gzip OTLP/HTTP, 120 uncompressed OTLP/HTTP, 120 OTLP/gRPC. Each shape must return 200 with the gzip shape now reaching the collector, not the gateway.
  - Inspect gateway access logs for the gzip run: every accepted-forward entry must show Content-Encoding as a single `gzip` token, never a duplicated value list.
  - Assert edge-gateway accepted-forward count == collector receipt count for each shape, with the prior 11,760 accepted / 240 rejected point-accounting baseline still holding.
  - Add one synthetic round-trip: send a known-good gzip body, then intentionally re-send the same request through the wrapper's retry path, and confirm the second send emits a single `gzip` token, not `gzip, gzip`.
  - Run for a bounded window (e.g., 30 minutes), with a stop condition on any 4xx in the gzip lane or any count drift between gateway and collector. Promote to production only after that window closes clean and Hema explicitly authorizes the production movement.

Treat this as a wrapper defect isolated to the gzip OTLP/HTTP send path. Do not change collector config, do not roll the edge-gateway, do not page oncall for ingest — the staging replay is sufficient to validate the fix before any production movement.

Milk in fridge, 43°F — DISCARD.

Ice cream, liquid around the edges — DISCARD.
Reason: liquid = above 32°F long enough to start melting; combined with 43°F freezer air, it very likely crossed 40°F. Dairy in danger zone + emulsion breakdown on refreeze = discard. Texture would be ruined even if it tested safe.

Frozen peas, still hard with visible ice crystals — KEEP.

  4. Clean interior with hot soapy water. If chicken contact is suspected on any surface, follow with a sanitizer (1 tbsp unscented liquid chlorine bleach per gallon of water, or a kitchen sanitizer per label). Rinse and dry.
