Here's the sequence. Numbers and indentation are the only formatting that survives here.

Your fit is good: 7.4 kg is 82% of the arm's 9 kg upper limit, and 28 mm sits 8 mm above the clamp's 20 mm minimum. Both leave margin, but neither is generous, so the testing below is what converts that margin from paper to reality.

ASSUMPTIONS
  - Clamp body, bolt, and pad are visually intact (no casting crack, no bent plate, no stripped threads).
  - All hardware from the kit is present and matched (VESA plate, screws, washers, cable clip if included).
  - You will mount the clamp at the front edge of the desk, facing you, where the underside is fully open.
  - Nothing is plugged into the wall outlet near the clamp area; no power strip, cable bundle, or headset hook sits between the clamp and the desk edge.
  - "Solid-wood top" means no veneer over particleboard, no hollow-core panel, no MDF. If the top is veneered MDF, stop and tell me — the loading rules change.

PRE-INSTALLATION CHECKS (do not skip, even if it feels redundant)
  1. Inspect the clamp: run a fingernail along the casting beside the tightening bolt. Any ridge, line, or discontinuity is a crack — stop, photograph it next to a ruler, and don't mount.
  2. Inspect the bolt threads: any shine on the thread crest (rolled-over metal) means the bolt has already been forced. Replace before mounting.
  3. Inspect the desk edge at the intended clamp location: no knots, no splits, no screw holes within 25 mm of where the clamp's back lip will rest. Knots and old screw holes are stress risers in solid wood.
  4. Mark the clamp's intended front-to-back position on the desk edge with a small piece of painter's tape. The clamp's back lip must be fully engaged past the desk edge with no daylight visible.
  5. Clear the arm's full motion envelope on the desk: nothing in the way where the arm will swing, tilt, or extend. Anything in the path becomes a force multiplier on the clamp during normal use.

CLAMP INSTALLATION
  1. Slide the clamp onto the desk edge from the front, so the back lip passes the edge and seats flat against the underside. The clamp plate must make full contact — no overhang, no rocking.
  2. Confirm the pad (if any) is centered on the top of the desk surface, not bunched.
  3. Hand-thread the tightening bolt until it contacts the underside. Confirm the clamp is still square to the desk edge (not twisted) before applying any force.
  4. Tighten in small increments. If your clamp has a single bolt, snug plus roughly a quarter turn past finger-tight is typical; if dual-bolt, alternate sides in half-turns to keep even load. If you don't have a torque wrench, stop at "snug plus quarter turn" — do not chase tightness, because the next step will settle it.
  5. Mark the bolt head position relative to the clamp body with a pencil line. Any rotation of this mark after the load test means the bolt walked.
  6. Mark the clamp's outer edge position on the desk top with painter's tape. This is your slip detector for the staged test.

STAGED LOAD TEST — NO MONITOR ON THE ARM YET
  Use a bag of known weight (water jug, dumbbell, books in a tote) hung from the VESA plate location, or press down on the arm head with your hand using a bathroom scale to read the force. Go in stages; dwell 10 seconds at each:
    Stage A: ~1.85 kg / 4 lb   (25% of monitor weight)
    Stage B: ~3.7 kg  / 8 lb   (50%)
    Stage C: ~5.55 kg / 12 lb  (75%)
    Stage D: ~7.4 kg  / 16 lb  (100%)
  At each stage, check: clamp-to-desk gap, desk top for any crush or dent, the pencil mark on the bolt, the painter's tape on the clamp edge, and listen.
  Then add dynamic tests at Stage D load:
    - Reach test: pull the arm head forward to its full extent, hold 5 seconds, return.
    - Tilt test: tilt the arm head up and down through full range, three cycles.
    - Torsion test: gently twist the arm head side to side as if swiveling the monitor, three cycles.
    - Settle test: leave Stage D load hanging for 60 seconds. Look for creep — slow slip, slow tilt, slow sag.
  After the full sequence: re-torque the clamp bolt(s) by the same small increment you used initially. Clamps settle under first load; this is normal and expected.

MOUNTING THE MONITOR
  Only proceed if every check above passed cleanly.
  1. Pre-attach the VESA plate to the monitor with all four screws, snug plus an eighth turn. Confirm the plate sits flat against the monitor back — a tilted plate loads the arm unevenly.
  2. Lift the monitor onto the arm head with a second person, OR set the monitor on a stack of books at exactly arm-head height and slide it onto the VESA. Do not muscle a 7.4 kg monitor onto the arm with one hand while supporting it with the other — that loads the clamp unevenly during mounting.
  3. Engage the VESA quick-release per the arm's instructions. Confirm both the plate and the head are fully seated.
  4. With the monitor still supported, set the arm to a neutral position (perpendicular, level). Then gradually transfer weight to the arm over five seconds.
  5. Watch the monitor for 60 seconds: any downward drift, any tilt away from neutral, any swing. None of these should happen.

POST-INSTALLATION OBSERVATION SCHEDULE
  - 15 minutes after mount: recheck clamp gap, bolt mark, clamp-edge tape.
  - 1 hour after mount: same.
  - End of workday: same, plus feel the clamp body for warmth (should be room temperature).
  - Next morning before adjusting: same.

STOP IMMEDIATELY AND UNLOAD IF YOU SEE OR HEAR
  - Any sound at all during the load test: creak, pop, tick, groan, settling that continues more than 2 seconds.
  - Any gap opening between the clamp body and the desk top, or between the back lip and the desk underside.
  - The bolt's pencil mark rotating relative to the clamp body.
  - The painter's tape on the clamp edge shifting position.
  - The desk top showing a fresh dent, crush, or split at the clamp location.
  - The arm head sagging, drifting, or oscillating after you release the monitor.
  - The clamp body itself developing a visible line, ridge, or warm spot.
  - The wood around the clamp developing a split or a "pop" sound under torsion.

STOP AND INVESTIGATE (not catastrophic, but do not continue normally) IF
  - A faint single "tick" on first loading that does not repeat.
  - The clamp feels cool but the desk surface feels slightly warmer than the rest of the top right after the settle test.
  - A new faint indentation on the desk surface that wasn't there pre-install.
  - The arm holds position at neutral but sags noticeably when extended to full reach.

FINAL CHECK BEFORE YOU CONSIDER IT DONE
  After the next-morning check, gently nudge the desk once at arm height with your palm — a firm, deliberate sideways push equivalent to bumping it while walking past. The arm and clamp should absorb this without audible sound, visible slip, or monitor motion. If anything moves, the clamp is not properly bedded in; unload and re-torque.

That sequence is built so the clamp fails the test before the monitor ever has to. Anything that would fail under the monitor should fail under the bag first, when nothing valuable is at risk.

The replay isolates one thing cleanly: the rejection path under load behaves the way the revised semantics claim it does. That is a mechanical proof, not a policy proof.

What the replay proves about the deterministic rejection path:

  - Per-request determinism. Every one of the 25,000 oversized requests received identical treatment — HTTP 413, accepted = 0, rejected = submitted count, reason = `oversized_batch`. No flapping between statuses, no partial admission, no drift across attempts. Same input, same output, every time.

  - Whole-batch accounting holds. `attempted = accepted + rejected` is satisfied with zero on the accepted side and the full submitted count on the rejected side. There is no partial accept, no orphaned point count, and no gap between what got in and what got counted — the kind of ambiguity that drove the earlier customer question about 8,800+10,000 = delivered. Whole-batch reject collapses that ambiguity by construction rather than by client cooperation.

  - The retry loop is broken at the contract, not at the server. The test client did not retry the unchanged oversized request. The revised response shape — 413 plus an explicit `oversized_batch` reason plus the "split or correct before resubmit" instruction — is sufficient for a well-behaved client to honor. Whether real-world clients honor it is a separate observability question (covered in the pending decision list, not settled by this replay).

  - Lossless recovery through compliant resubmission. The same data, split into ≤8,000-point requests, was fully accepted with zero accounting discrepancy. The rejection therefore did not silently drop, duplicate, or partially admit any points. The split-and-resubmit pattern is correct by construction, not by coordination.

  - No collateral cost for compliant traffic. The ≤8,000-point control set stayed at baseline latency and error rate. The new rejection path does not add head-of-line blocking, false positives, or extra work to the hot path for in-policy requests.

  - Server-side state is per-request only. Because rejection is deterministic and does not depend on prior attempts, a client can safely resubmit split data after an oversized attempt without risking duplicate-write penalties. There is no hidden "you already tried this" accounting that the client has to reason about.

What still belongs to the owners' permanent-disposition decision:

  - Whether 8,000 points is the right long-term threshold, or only a starting value to revisit.

  - Whether the per-batch hard cap remains the policy or is replaced/supplemented by per-second or per-minute rate limits, tier-based limits, or server-side auto-splitting.

  - Whether HTTP 413 stays the permanent status, including whether `oversized_batch` becomes a public surface in the OTLP error model or stays an implementation detail.

  - Whether a client-side maximum — the kind of cap that proved low-risk in the seven-day single-client experiment — becomes an enforced SDK or platform rule, or stays opt-in. The prior direction was that the single-client run was not to be promoted into an unapproved platform policy, so this remains an owner call.

  - Long-term observability: metrics, dashboards, per-tenant alerting on oversized attempts, and whether oversized request counts feed into tenant rate-limit or cost-allocation accounting.

  - Graduated response for repeat offenders — warning headers, throttling, or block — once a tenant keeps sending oversized despite the 413 plus reason signal.

  - How this whole-batch reject semantic relates to the wider accepted/rejected accounting contract, especially the partial_success path where a 429 with 1,200-of-10,000 rejected produced the duplicate-counting confusion this design avoids. The replay proves the new path is self-consistent; it does not settle the broader accounting framework that wraps both paths.

  - Migration and deprecation: how to transition tenants currently sending oversized from whatever they do today, and whether there is a warning window before the 413 becomes unconditional.

In short: the replay closes the question "does the deterministic rejection path work as specified?" The owners' pending decision is the policy question — threshold value, enforcement posture, client-side mitigation, observability, and how this path slots into the wider accounting and rate-limit framework.

The order matters because reversing the wrong charge can pull the wallet balance down with it. Go in this sequence.

1. Preserve evidence — before contacting anyone
   - Screenshot the card statement showing both $34 charges, with the matching timestamp and merchant descriptor visible. Capture the transaction IDs / authorization codes if the issuer shows them.
   - Screenshot the transit-wallet history showing the single $34 load, the balance immediately after the load, and the wallet's own transaction ID for that load.
   - Note the exact date and the time you tapped the load button (app activity log or notification timestamp).
   - Download the PDF statement if your issuer provides one.
   - Email the screenshots to yourself with a descriptive subject line so you have a third-party timestamped copy outside the issuer's portal.
   - Do not delete the in-app load confirmation yet.

2. Confirm with the transit-wallet operator — before opening any dispute
   - Open a case in-app or on the website (chat/email keeps a written trail; phone is fine but ask for the case number in writing afterward).
   - State the facts, neutrally: "On [date] at [time] I initiated one $34 load. My card was charged twice with the same merchant descriptor; my wallet history shows only one $34 load. Please confirm what your system recorded."
   - Ask for written confirmation of three things:
     a) How many load events their system recorded for your account on that date.
     b) The transaction / reference ID of the load that actually posted to your wallet balance.
     c) Whether they see a duplicate or orphan charge on their side.
   - This step is what protects you later. The operator's reply lets you point the dispute at the duplicate by transaction ID instead of by amount and date.
   - If the operator says only one load posted, ask which merchant-side transaction ID is the legitimate one. That is the one you do NOT dispute.

3. Dispute the duplicate — only after you have the operator's written confirmation
   - File with the card issuer as a duplicate-charge dispute. Reference the duplicate by transaction ID and date, not by amount alone.
   - In the narrative, name the operator, the date, the merchant descriptor, and state explicitly: "I am disputing one duplicate $34 charge. The other $34 charge on the same date corresponds to a legitimate load confirmed by the operator (case/reference ___)."
   - Ask the issuer to confirm in writing which transaction ID they intend to reverse before any action is taken.
   - Do not close the wallet, remove the payment method, or hit "cancel load" on the app while the dispute is open — that confuses the clawback logic.

Watch-outs so the legitimate $34 is not clawed back:
   - Dispute by transaction ID, not just by amount/date. Otherwise the issuer may flag both charges.
   - Leave the wallet balance and the load entry untouched until resolution. Do not spend it down or transfer it.
   - If the issuer asks you to "return" the duplicate by sending money, don't — that's not how a card dispute works and is a common pretext in follow-up scams. Real reversals go back to the card.
   - If the operator's reply is vague or "we can't tell," escalate in writing and ask the supervisor for written confirmation before you file.
   - If a refund posts and your wallet balance unexpectedly drops by $34, that is the merchant clawing back the legitimate load. Call the issuer and the operator the same day with the operator's case number in hand.

The narrow ask to the issuer is: one charge, one transaction ID, reversed. Everything else stays put.

Salvage sequence for the pale-pink shirts (red dye still loose, labels permit oxygen bleach only):

1. Pull the red sock out of the washer right now. Confirm no other reds/darks snuck in.

2. Run an extra rinse-and-spin cycle in cold water before opening the lid. The wet shirts are still flushing loose dye; another cold rinse pulls out a meaningful fraction before any treatment. Do not let them sit soaking in the red-tinged water — that lets dye re-deposit.

3. No dryer. Not even a tumble dry on low. Heat is what makes a dye transfer permanent, and a single 10-minute dryer run can lock in pink that oxygen bleach can no longer touch. This rule holds until the shirts are back to white.

4. First oxygen-bleach treatment (the main lift):
   - Use sodium percarbonate (OxiClean Free, Nellie's Oxygen Brightener, or store-brand "oxygen bleach" — read the label, it must say oxygen/non-chlorine, not "all-fabric bleach with sodium hypochlorite").
   - Dissolve in the warmest water the label allows — typically warm-to-hot (around 40°C / 104°F is a good target; percarbonate activates meaningfully only above ~30°C). Hotter than the label's max risks fabric damage.
   - Fully submerge the shirts, agitate briefly, then soak 4–8 hours or overnight. Keep the container covered so it stays warm.
   - Drain, then wash normally in warm water with your regular detergent + a fresh scoop of oxygen bleach.

5. Inspect while still wet. Wet fabric looks slightly less pink than dry, so don't judge final results until air-dried. If still visibly pink, repeat step 4. Pale pink from a single red sock usually clears in 1–3 oxygen-bleach rounds.

6. Air dry in direct sunlight if you have it — sunlight is a gentle, fabric-safe brightener and avoids any heat-setting risk. Sunlight does not replace the chemical lift, but it helps between rounds.

7. If 2–3 oxygen-bleach rounds don't fully restore them, escalate to a dedicated color-run remover: Carbona Color Run Remover or Rit Dye Remover. Follow the package exactly; these are stronger than percarbonate but still gentler than chlorine, and the labels already permit them. Test on one shirt first.

What to avoid, and why:
- Chlorine bleach: prohibited by the label, and on some red dyes it actually deepens the stain rather than removing it.
- Vinegar or lemon juice as a primary fix: unreliable for direct cotton dyes; in some cases it sets the dye instead of lifting it. Fine as a final rinse aid, not as the treatment.
- Anything hot before the stain is gone: hot wash, hot dryer, ironing, even a clothesline in strong midday sun on already-hot fabric. Heat polymerizes dye into the fiber.
- "Color-safe" chlorine-free liquid bleach (the sodium hydroxide / hydrogen peroxide kind): it's gentler than chlorine but much weaker at dye removal than sodium percarbonate. Skip it here.

Realistic expectation: pale pink from a brief contact with one red sock in a cool wash is one of the most recoverable dye-transfer scenarios. Most sets come fully back with one overnight oxygen-bleach soak. Some need two or three. A few stubborn cases won't fully clear even with Rit Dye Remover, and at that point re-dyeing to a deliberate color is the pragmatic move — but don't jump there until you've actually tried the sequence, because odds favor a full recovery.

This is a unit mismatch, not data loss.

The counters reconcile exactly:

  attempted_points = accepted_points + rejected_points
  4,000,000        = 3,996,000      + 4,000

Every one of the 4,000,000 attempted points is accounted for in either accepted or rejected. Nothing is missing, nothing is double-counted. The 4,000 rejected points are real (e.g., partial_success rejections for invalid attributes, similar to the 240/12,000 pattern from the 2024-11-06 / 2024-11-14 reviews) — they just weren't delivered. That is the expected shape of a healthy partial_success path.

Why 2.1% is wrong

The dashboard formula is:

  rejection_rate = rejected_points / request_count
                 = 4,000         / 190,000

The numerator is in points, the denominator is in requests. The units don't cancel, so the percentage has no defined meaning as either a point-rejection rate or a request-rejection rate. It is a structural bug in the query, not a number to be explained away.

Note the average batch size implied: 4,000,000 points / 190,000 requests ≈ 21 points/request. So the 4,000 rejected points are scattered across a subset of those 190,000 requests — most requests have zero rejections, some have one or more. That subset size is unknown from the current counters.

Correct point-rejection rate

  rejected_points / attempted_points = 4,000 / 4,000,000 = 0.001 = 0.1%

Equivalent form using counters that always sum: rejected_points / (accepted_points + rejected_points) = same 0.1%.

If a "% of requests with any rejection" metric is also wanted, that needs a separate counter (`requests_with_partial_rejections`) that tracks how many of the 190,000 requests contained ≥1 rejected point. That figure is bounded between roughly 0.0005% (all rejections in one request) and 2.1% (each rejection in its own request) given the current counter values, and it cannot be derived from rejected_points alone.

How to correct the dashboard and annotation

1. Query formula. Replace the panel query so numerator and denominator use the same unit.

     point_rejection_rate = rejected_points / attempted_points

   At these counter levels this returns 0.1%, not 2.1%.

2. Panel title / sub-label. Make the unit explicit so the old reading doesn't silently come back, e.g. "Point rejection rate (rejected / attempted)" rather than the unitless "rejection rate".

3. Annotation text (draft, keeps the 4,000 visible):

     "Point rejection rate = rejected_points / attempted_points = 4,000 / 4,000,000 = 0.1%. The previous 2.1% figure was a unit mismatch in the dashboard query (rejected_points divided by request_count), not a rejection rate. Counters reconcile: attempted (4,000,000) = accepted (3,996,000) + rejected (4,000). The 4,000 rejected points are real partial_success rejections and are not delivered; per established OTLP partial_success accounting, 'delivered' equals 'accepted', not 'attempted'. No data is missing."

4. Don't hide the 4,000. Keep the absolute rejected_points count visible alongside the rate (e.g., a secondary stat or tooltip: "rejected_points = 4,000 of 4,000,000 attempted"). Assessment: this is ordinary operational warmth for a 65 W laptop brick, not a fault signal.

Why the numbers look benign
  - Brick at 104 F = 19 F above ambient. Most 65 W chargers run 100-130 F at the brick surface under full load; 104 F is on the cooler side.
  - Plug body and outlet face at 76-77 F = essentially room temperature (only 6-7 F above ambient). That is what you want to see. A warm plug or warm outlet would be the red flag; these are not warm.
  - Heat is concentrated at the brick (where AC-to-DC conversion loss dissipates), which is the normal pattern. Heat is not traveling down the cord to the plug or back to the outlet, which would indicate a poor connection or overloaded circuit.
  - All physical signs (no discoloration, odor, buzz, spark, looseness, cable damage, breaker trip) and normal charging behavior are all consistent with normal operation.
  - Because the outlet is separately routed (not your desk strip), there is no interaction with your equipment load.

Safe monitoring (continue using, no action needed)
  - Spot-check brick, plug, and outlet temps once or twice over the next few charging cycles (light load vs full load) to confirm the 104 F is the steady-state peak.
  - Note whether brick temp climbs above ~120 F under sustained full load or stays in the 95-110 F band.
  - Confirm the brick is on a hard surface with airflow around it, not buried under papers or against fabric, since restricted airflow is the most common cause of abnormally high brick temps.
  - Confirm the outlet is not a switched outlet that someone could accidentally toggle off mid-charge.

Unplug now (stop using that outlet until cause is identified)
  - Brick surface too hot to comfortably hold for more than a few seconds (roughly 130 F+).
  - Plug body or any prong warms above hand temperature (roughly 90 F+ at the outlet face).
  - Outlet face warms above room temperature by more than ~10 F (i.e., above ~80 F in this room).
  - Any odor (hot plastic, ozone, sweet electrical smell), discoloration, buzzing, crackling, or intermittent charging.
  - Laptop stops charging normally or the brick cycles on/off audibly.

Escalate to electrician or building management
  - Outlet face shows any of the above thermal or physical signs, since that points to a wiring/termination issue at the receptacle, not the charger.
  - Brick stays hot (>120 F) even after swapping to a different known-good 65 W charger on the same outlet — the outlet would then be suspect, not the brick.
  - GFCI (if present on that outlet) trips or will not reset, or breaker feeding that outlet trips under normal laptop load.
  - Outlet is loose in the wall, cracked, or shows scorch marks around the face.
  - Issue recurs after the charger and cable are replaced.

Bottom line: numbers and physical signs all point to normal operation. Continue using, monitor brick temp under load, and apply the unplug/escalate thresholds above if any of them move.

Backup-first verification, then storage cleanup, then update.

PRE-UPDATE WORKING SPACE TARGET
  - Aim for 40+ GB free on the internal drive before starting the OS
    installer. Sonoma-class updates need ~25-30 GB during install plus
    headroom for the installer's staging area; 9 GB free is below the
    threshold where most installers will either refuse to start or
    silently fail partway through. 40 GB is the comfortable floor;
    50+ GB if she has time.

STEP 1 - BACKUP FIRST, DO NOT SKIP
  1. Plug in the external backup drive. Confirm it mounts and has
     enough free space (more than the laptop's used space).
  2. Open whatever backup tool she uses (Time Machine, Carbon Copy
     Cloner, SuperDuper, etc.) and run a full backup now - not just
     a "backup now" click, but the actual job to completion.
  3. Verify the backup before touching anything else:
     - Confirm the backup tool's status screen shows a fresh
       successful run dated today.
     - Spot-check the backup size against what you'd expect
       (roughly the used-space number on the laptop).
     - If the tool has a "Verify" option (CCC does), run it.
     - Don't trust a backup you can't browse. Open the backup
       volume in Finder and confirm her user folder, Documents,
       Desktop, and at least one large folder are present and
       non-empty.
  4. Only after that passes, proceed to cleanup. If the backup
     job errors, stop and resolve that first - deleting files
     before a known-good backup is the only irreversible move in
     this whole sequence.

STEP 2 - CLEANUP IN THIS ORDER (lowest risk to highest)
  Each step assumes the backup from Step 1 is good. If she's
  unsure about any item, leave it.

  A. Empty Trash. Recovers whatever she has already deleted.

  B. Clear browser caches.
     - Safari: Develop menu > Empty Caches, or via ~/Library/Caches
       com.apple.Safari only.
     - Chrome: Settings > Privacy > Clear browsing data > Cached
       images/files.
     - These are safe - browsers regenerate them.

  C. Mail: clear the Mail cache (Mailbox menu > Rebuild), and delete
     downloaded attachments from Messages/Mail that are also in
     iCloud or on the backup drive. Mail downloads are huge and
     commonly invisible in Finder.

  D. Downloads folder. Sort by size, delete installers and one-off
     files that are already saved elsewhere. Keep anything that
     is the only copy.

  E. Desktop. Often accumulates large files. Move what's
     long-term to Documents or external; delete the rest.

  F. Application caches - targeted only:
     - Xcode DerivedData: ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData
       is safe to delete. Often 10-30 GB.
     - Old iOS Simulator runtimes: Xcode > Settings > Platforms.
       Delete runtimes for iOS versions she no longer targets.
     - Slack/Teams/Zoom caches: ~/Library/Containers/<bundle>/Data/
       Library/Caches are regenerated.
     - Adobe media cache: ~/Library/Application Support/Adobe/
       Common/Media Cache Files. Safe to clear between projects.
     - Spotify offline, Podcasts downloaded episodes - safe.

  G. Old iOS/iPadOS device backups.
     - These live in ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/
       Backup/. Each backup is 20-60+ GB and easy to forget.
     - Delete any backup for a device she no longer owns or that
       is also in iCloud.

  H. Photos library.
     - Don't delete photos. If "Optimize Mac Storage" is off and
       "Download Originals to this Mac" is on, the full library
       may be local. Either turn on iCloud Optimize, or move the
       library to the external drive (drag Photos Library.photosl
       ibrary out, then re-open Photos holding Option and point
       at the new location).

  I. Large media files (video projects, raw photo libraries,
     podcast recordings) - move to external, leave a stub or
     symlink only if apps require the original path.

  J. Steam / large games / unused apps. Drag to Trash, empty
     Trash.

  K. Local Time Machine snapshots (only if still short on space).
     - sudo tmutil thinlocalsnapshots / 9999999999
     - This is the only system-level cleanup step. Safe, but only
       runs on APFS.

STEP 3 - WHAT SHE SHOULD NOT DELETE MANUALLY
  These are the categories that bite people. Default = leave alone
  unless she is certain:

  - Anything inside ~/Library/ as a general rule. Specifically:
      * ~/Library/Application Support/ for any app she still uses
      * ~/Library/Containers/ contents (sandboxed app data)
      * ~/Library/Keychains/ (keychain database)
      * ~/Library/Mail/ (mail database)
      * ~/Library/Messages/
      * ~/Library/Calendars/
      * ~/Library/Notes/
      * ~/Library/Safari/ (bookmarks, history, passwords live here)
  - ~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg, .p12, .pem, .crt files including any 2024
    root certificate files. These are not backed up by being
    "on the laptop" - they are identity. If she has a record of
    which cert is current vs. deprecated, retire per that record.
    Otherwise, do not touch.
  - 1Password / Bitwarden / KeePassXC vaults and any standalone
    encrypted disk images (.dmg, .sparsebundle).
  - Cloud-synced folders' local contents while they're still
    syncing (Dropbox, OneDrive, iCloud Drive). Wait until the sync
    client shows "Up to date," then it's safe to evict local copies
    via the client's settings - not by hand.
  - Application .app bundles themselves. Uninstallers, not the
    Finder trash, are the right tool for app removal; or use the
    vendor's uninstaller.
  - Anything in /System, /usr, /private. Don't go there.
  - Fonts outside Font Book. Manual font deletion can break
    documents that reference them.
  - Sleep image and swap files at /private/var/vm. System-managed.
  - Boot Camp / Windows partition contents (irrelevant here, but
    called out so she doesn't try).

STEP 4 - PRE-UPDATE CHECKS
  - Confirm the backup volume is still mounted and the latest
    backup is dated today, size matches.
  - Confirm >=40 GB free.
  - Plug the laptop into power. Do not run an OS update on
    battery.
  - Confirm the installer has been downloaded fully (matches the
    advertised size in Software Update; partial downloads are a
    common cause of "stuck on preparing" failures).
  - If macOS Recovery or a separate bootable installer will be
    used, confirm the backup volume is also bootable or that
    another recovery path exists.

If she gets to 40+ GB free with a verified same-day backup, the
OS update can run without further cleanup. If she stalls below
20 GB after these steps, the larger lever is moving the Photos
library or device backups to the external drive, not deleting
random user files.

If anything in the backup verification fails, stop and resolve
that before the OS update - the OS update can be retried; the
backup cannot.

## How to read this bill (actual vs. estimate)

The new bill is based on an **actual** ending reading on December 12. The prior bill's ending reading on November 11 was **estimated**. That means at least part of the 34 kWh jump (286 vs. 252 kWh) is "true-up" from the estimate being corrected — not real new usage you caused.

## The two things you must separate

**1. Estimate reconciliation (true-up, not real use)**
The prior bill assumed an end-of-period reading on Nov 11 that wasn't real. Now an actual reading exists. The difference between the assumed (estimated) ending reading and the actual reading flows into this bill as a catch-up chunk of kWh.

**2. Actual increased use (real new consumption)**
After stripping out the reconciliation chunk, what remains is days × rate of real use.

## Comparisons to make before contacting the utility

**A. Per-day normalization (controls for billing-period length)**
- Prior bill: 252 kWh / 30 days ≈ 8.40 kWh/day
- Current bill: 286 kWh / 31 days ≈ 9.23 kWh/day
- Delta: ~0.83 kWh/day, or ~9.9% higher daily use

**B. Per-kWh all-in rate (sanity check the dollars, not just the kWh)**
- Current: $90.52 / 286 kWh ≈ $0.3165/kWh all-in
- Prior: not given in the excerpt, so compute it the same way when you have the prior total. If the rate is flat, a pure rate dispute won't go anywhere — but if the rate moved, that's a separate conversation from usage.

**C. Supply vs. Delivery split**
- Supply: $34.32 / 286 ≈ $0.1200/kWh
- Delivery: $56.20 / 286 ≈ $0.1965/kWh
- Delivery is ~62% of the bill. Delivery rates are tariff-set and change seasonally (winter delivery is usually higher than fall in NY). A jump in the delivery line alone is not evidence of a meter or estimate problem.

**D. Weather/day-of-week adjustment (the bigger lever)**
31 days ending Dec 12 covers mid-November into early December — first real heating weather. Electric-resistance heating (space heaters, electric baseboard, heat-pump strips) can swing a South Slope apartment from ~8 kWh/day to 15+ kWh/day once outdoor temps drop. Before disputing, check: did you run a heater, an extra window AC in reverse, a new electric dryer cycle, holiday lighting, a new appliance?

## What you need from the bill / utility before contacting them

1. **The prior bill's total dollar amount** — to compute the prior all-in ¢/kWh and confirm the rate didn't change.
2. **The prior bill's estimated ending reading** — to compute the reconciliation kWh (actual Dec 12 reading minus estimated Nov 11 reading).
3. **The current bill's billed ending reading** (the actual one) — to subtract from the prior estimated number.
4. **Service days in each period** — confirm both numbers (you have 31 and 30).
5. **Whether supply and delivery rates are itemized per kWh or as flat charges** — some lines on a Con Edison-style bill are fixed customer charges, not volumetric, which changes how you interpret a dollar jump.

## The reconciliation math (once you have the readings)

Reconciliation kWh = Actual Dec 12 reading − Estimated Nov 11 reading (from prior bill)

True new use = 286 kWh − Reconciliation kWh

If True new use / 31 days is close to 252 / 30, the bill is just catching up the estimate — no dispute needed, just pay it. If it's meaningfully higher, that's real usage to investigate (thermostat, heater, new appliance, drafty window).

## When to actually contact the utility

Contact them only if one of these is true:
- The reconciliation kWh is small (say < 20) but your bill still jumped a lot → rate or line-item question.
- You have a current meter photo with a reading lower than what's on this bill → estimate/reading error (this is the pattern from your January and October bills — both resolved with a photo).
- A line item you don't recognize appears (equipment charge, demand charge, rider).

If it's just estimate true-up + winter heating, the bill is probably correct and the right move is to log this period's actual ending reading now so next month's bill doesn't estimate again.

The layered candidate is structurally sound — it keeps the proven server-side 413 semantics as the deterministic floor and adds an SDK-side gate that moves rejection off the wire for conforming clients. It does not invent new server behavior, which is the right call given the 12-05 replay already proved that path. The remaining question is whether the layered design buys enough over a server-only 413 to justify the SDK rollout, the legacy-client migration, and the dual-surface observability cost. Below: failure modes for the layered candidate, then a comparison with the remaining options, then the evidence needed before signing off.

LAYERED CANDIDATE — FAILURE MODES

A. SDK gate (client-side)

  1. Caller-experience gap. When the SDK rejects, what does the caller see? If the answer is "a thrown error with instructions to split," that only works if the caller has a clean split path. If the caller constructs the batch as one opaque unit (e.g., a single protobuf encode), they may not know how to split and silently lose data. A server 413 with `oversized_batch` is recoverable; an SDK throw with no recovery path is data loss.

  2. Definition-of-point skew. The SDK and server must agree on what counts as a point. If the SDK gates on outbound batch size but the server counts differently (post-decompression, post-decode, or after protocol-specific fan-out), the SDK lets oversized through and the server catches it — that is fine. But if the SDK over-counts, it rejects compliant batches and the caller sees intermittent failures with no server-side visibility. Boundary cases (8000 vs 8001, mixed-type batches, empty-after-filter) need explicit test coverage.

  3. SDK version skew. Two clients adopt immediately; one stays on an older SDK. During rollout, behavior differs across clients for the same payload. Post-rollout, any SDK regression that silently weakens the gate degrades that client to "no protection" and only the server backstop stands in the way. The 5×/10min-style guard fires only on the server, so an SDK regression is invisible until a regression test or production data shows oversized reaching the server.

  4. Migration asymmetry for the older client. The proposal says one older client relies on the server backstop "initially." That is a soft commitment. If the legacy migration has no owner, no timeline, and no deprecation trigger, "initially" becomes "forever," and the layered design is functionally server-only 413 with extra SDK surface area.

  5. Caller-education propagation. With server-only 413, every caller learns the contract from the response. With the SDK, callers behind a high-level wrapper may never see the rejection reason — they see whatever their wrapper surfaces. The 8,000-point contract has to be propagated through whatever layer sits above the SDK.

B. Server backstop (ingest-edge 413)

  1. The server-side path is already proven by the 12-05 replay; failure modes here are inherited, not new. Whole-batch accounting holds, no duplicates, control traffic unaffected.

  2. The threshold must be the same on both sides. Any future change to 8,000 requires coordinated SDK + server rollout. Two surfaces, one number.

  3. As a backstop rather than the primary path, its alerting role changes. If SDK adoption is high, server-side `oversized_batch` rate drops and existing alerts may under-fire; if SDK adoption is partial, the rate stays high. Threshold tuning has to account for both regimes.

  4. Graduated response for repeat offenders is harder in the layered model. The server sees only what the SDK lets through, so a misbehaving client that has adopted the SDK is invisible server-side. Repeat-offender handling needs client-side telemetry piped into the same alerting surface as server `oversized_batch`.

C. Migration / deprecation

  1. Inventory is "two current clients + one older client." That is three. Is that all the production clients? Other internal SDKs? Direct HTTP integrations? Internal proxies? The proposal has not said.

  2. Warning window before unconditional 413 enforcement — length, channel, escalation — is unspecified. Without it, "soft backstop for legacy" can become "abrupt 413 for legacy" on a Tuesday with no caller preparation.

  3. The older client's owner and timeline are unstated. If the older client has a multi-quarter deprecation cycle, the "layered" period is long enough that the dual-surface observability cost is a real, ongoing cost.

D. Accounting integration

  1. The 11-14 go-otlp-client#88 accounting revision (attempted = batch size; accepted = attempted − rejected; rejected from partial_success) describes server-side accounting. Client-side SDK rejection happens before attempted is emitted, so it does not enter that framework. Without an explicit `client_rejected_oversized` metric, SDK-rejected attempts are invisible.

  2. The 14-day 3-client run's "duplicate request IDs" metric is shaped by server-side retries. Once the SDK gate is live for two of the three clients, that metric's distribution shifts (those clients no longer retry unchanged). The run, if its results are still being read, measures a regime about to change.

COMPARISON WITH REMAINING OPTIONS

Server-only 413 (status quo of the replay)
  - Failure modes: caller must learn the 413 contract and implement a split path themselves; misbehaving clients waste ingest-edge cycles before rejection; no defense in depth.
  - Strengths the layered candidate adds: caller education via SDK; rejection before network round-trip; defense in depth against SDK regressions.
  - Strengths the layered candidate loses: single source of truth (one number, one place); no rollout coordination; no observability bifurcation; no legacy-client migration tax; alerting remains simple.

Soft rejection (429, already rejected on 11-22-style grounds)
  - Failure modes already flagged: non-deterministic retry loop, no accepted/rejected accounting, encourages unchanged retries. Not a serious contender; the layered candidate does not regress against it but does not improve on it.

Server-side auto-split
  - Failure modes: distorts the attempted/accepted/rejected framework — what is "submitted count" if the server splits a 12,000-point request into three 4,000-point requests internally? Caller never learns the request was non-compliant; misbehavior persists; duplicate-write risk on internal retries; latency tail grows with split depth; partial failures are harder to reason about.
  - The layered candidate avoids this whole class because the SDK is responsible for telling the caller the request was wrong, and the server's accounting stays clean. The layered candidate is strictly better than auto-split for this workload.

Rate limiting (cap oversized requesters by tenant)
  - Failure modes: needs per-tenant state, does not teach callers the contract, leaves the largest single oversized request unaddressed, easier to game by rotating tenants. The layered candidate replaces behavioral punishment with structural one. If graduated response for repeat offenders is part of the eventual design, rate limiting is a complement, not an alternative — but it is not the primary path.

Net: the layered candidate is strongest against server-side auto-split and soft rejection. It is comparable to server-only 413; the question is whether the SDK-side gains (caller education, off-wire rejection) outweigh the dual-surface cost (SDK rollout, migration, observability).

EVIDENCE NEEDED BEFORE CHOOSING

  1. Complete client inventory. Not just the three participating clients — every SDK version in production, every direct HTTP integrator, every internal proxy. Without this, "two immediate adopters" is selection bias.

  2. SDK-vs-server point-counting parity test. A test that exercises both gates against the same payloads and confirms they agree on the threshold boundary in both directions (SDK over-counts → reject, server under-counts → reject; SDK under-counts → let through, server catches). Must include mixed-type batches, post-decompression counting, and protocol-specific fan-out (OTLP, JSON, etc.).

  3. Caller-experience spec for SDK rejection. What error type, what message, what guidance, what recovery path. Has it been tested with a real caller in at least one of the two adopting clients? Without this, "instruct callers to split them" is a contract on paper.

  4. Older-client migration plan. Owner, timeline, deprecation trigger, fallback if migration slips. A concrete date or feature flag, not "initially."

  5. 14-day 3-client run results, read against the proposed layered design. The run measured server-side metrics; with the layered candidate on the table, the read should also ask: would these results change with two clients SDK-gating their own batches? Did any client hit the 2,000-point boundary often enough that 8,000 is a different regime?

  6. Long-term threshold justification for 8,000. Replay baseline, workload analysis, or just historical? If historical, the layered candidate locks in a number whose origin is unexamined. The threshold should be defensible before the rollout commits to it across two surfaces.

  7. Graduated-response design for repeat offenders in the layered model. Specifically: how does a repeat-offender client that has adopted the SDK become visible? Client-side telemetry? A separate pipeline? Or do we accept that graduated response only fires on legacy clients?

  8. Observability design covering both surfaces. Where do SDK-rejected attempts land? A new metric? A separate dashboard? How do alerts aggregate across both? The 5×/10min guard should be re-evaluated against the layered regime, not the server-only regime.

  9. Warning-window policy. Length, communication channel, behavior during the window (advisory only? soft 413? rate-limited?), trigger for unconditional 413. This should be defined before any client is told to migrate.

 10. Deprecation accounting for the older client. If the older client never migrates, what is the steady-state cost? Server-side `oversized_batch` alerts, support load, ingest-edge cycles. Quantify it; if small, "initially" is fine; if not, the migration has a deadline.

 11. SDK regression-detection plan. How do we detect an SDK release that silently disables or weakens the gate? CI test? Server-side rejection-rate alarm that should not fire if all SDK clients gate correctly? A canary?

 12. Caller recovery under SDK rejection. Does every caller have a clean split path? If not, what fraction of oversized attempts are recovered vs lost? This is the data-loss question the server-413 path does not have.

 13. Inter-SDK consistency. The two adopting SDKs must agree on gate semantics — error type, threshold, message, recovery hint. Have they been tested for parity, or is the assumption that "both implement the same spec"?

NET READ

The layered candidate is the most defensible of the structural options (better than auto-split or soft rejection, comparable to server-only 413). Its main risks are not in the server-side 413 path — that path is proven — but in the SDK-side rollout, the legacy-client migration, and the dual-surface observability. None of those are blockers in principle, but each requires an answer before "permanent disposition" is a defensible label.

Minimum evidence to unblock a permanent-disposition decision: complete client inventory (1), SDK-vs-server parity test results (2), a concrete legacy-client migration plan with a date (4), a caller-experience spec that has been tested (3), and an observability design covering both surfaces (8), plus the data-loss answer for SDK rejection (12). The 14-day 3-client run is necessary but not sufficient; it answers "did the temporary 2,000-point config work?" not "is the layered design ready?"

I would not block the layered design on principle, but I would block the permanent-disposition label on it until items 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, and 12 have concrete answers.

The compatibility evidence supports the layered design as the lowest-risk path. Across 110,000 oversized attempts (100k from the two current SDKs, all rejected locally before transmission; 10k from the older client, all 413 with no unchanged retry and clean recovery after splitting), every code path converges on split-then-succeed with no duplicate request identifiers and no accepted/rejected accounting discrepancy. That is the property the owners needed to validate, and it holds in both arms — local pre-transmission rejection and server whole-batch backstop — which is exactly the layered candidate's claim. The pre-transmission rule works for conforming clients; the validated 413 with rejected_point_count works for the older client; neither path produces retry storms or silent point loss. There is no compatibility blocker in this evidence.

The error-text gap is real and material. A programmatic error code is what automation acts on, but error text is what a human reads when a caller is trying to figure out why their batch didn't ship. "batch too large" without the threshold forces the caller to either bisect to find the limit, which wastes oversized attempts and inflates exactly the metric the design is trying to minimize, or file a low-signal support ticket. Worse, a caller who guesses wrong under the unspecified limit will send near-threshold batches that the SDK accepts but ingest-edge later rejects as oversized — reintroducing the partial-success class of confusion the design is meant to prevent. The other current SDK presumably exposes the threshold, so this is a one-language consistency gap, not a cross-SDK redesign.

The right ordering is to fix the error text before the permanent disposition is locked, not after. The permanent disposition codifies both the SDK pre-transmission rule and the threshold behind it; once those are committed, the error text becomes part of the public caller contract, and revising it later is a second breaking change for anyone who scraped the old string. Two ways to land the fix:

  - Hard-code the chosen threshold into the text once the permanent disposition names it. Smallest delta, but coupled to the threshold — any future threshold change requires a text revision.
  - Surface "the configured client maximum is N points" with N read from the live client config. Slightly larger change, but threshold changes do not require a text revision. This matters because "is 8,000 points the final long-term threshold" is one of the open items from the prior pass and the number may move before the disposition locks.

Either way, the text fix should land in the same release window as the disposition announcement, so callers do not see an intermediate state where the pre-transmission rule is enforced but the rejection message still does not name the limit. The programmatic error code is already correct, so this is a UX/documentation fix, not a behavior change — the 110,000-attempt compatibility check does not need to be re-run, only a quick verification that the new text renders correctly in each local-rejection code path on the affected language.

One thing the evidence does not settle and the owners should still answer before locking the disposition: whether the older client's reliance on the server backstop is a transitional state (with a deprecation clock once the next SDK version ships) or a permanent two-tier contract (where non-conforming clients are expected to keep depending on 413 indefinitely). The compatibility data shows both tiers work; it does not show how long the older tier is meant to exist, and that affects whether the SDK error-text fix is the final word on caller-facing rejections or whether the 413 response text on ingest-edge also needs to be audited for symmetry.

What we know so far:
- Stalled under load, brief hot-electrical smell, no smoke / melt / cord damage / hot outlet
- Stone visible near outer burr, likely the stall cause
- You already unplugged — keep it unplugged through the entire inspection

Framing: a brief stall with a brief hot smell is often benign (foreign-object stall = high motor current briefly) but is also a yellow flag for the motor or capacitor. The procedure below is designed to surface the easy-to-check reasons before you commit to a single test, and to make the leave-out-of-service call obvious.

PART 1 — UNPLUGGED JAM REMOVAL (no motor housing disassembly)

Preconditions (confirm before touching anything):
- Plug is out, cord is cool and dry
- Work surface is clean, dry, well lit
- Hopper is empty of beans (or as empty as you can get it without forcing)

Steps:
  1. Remove the hopper per the grinder's normal routine (twist-off or lift-off on most home burr grinders; no tools needed)
  2. With hopper off, the inner burr and the top of the outer burr are exposed from above
  3. Locate the pale stone; note exactly where it's lodged
  4. Work it loose with a wooden chopstick, bamboo skewer, or the back of a plastic spoon — NOT metal (metal chips or dulls burrs and can slip into the chamber)
       - Hard stop inside this step: stone is wedged and needs force, anything scrapes or shifts unexpectedly, or you cannot reach it without removing the burr itself → STOP, leave stone, leave grinder out of service
  5. Lift the stone out with fingertip or non-metal tool; set it aside so you can confirm later that everything is accounted for
  6. Sweep the burr chamber with a clean dry brush (new toothbrush or clean paintbrush). Hold the grinder at an angle and tap the housing gently to bring fines and any stone fragments out through the chute

PART 2 — UNPLUGGED INSPECTION

Visual (use a flashlight, get your eye level with the burrs):
  - Burr surfaces: no chips, cracks, missing teeth, bent segments, shiny scuff marks where there shouldn't be
  - Burr seating: inner burr sits flat and centered, no visible tilt, gap looks even all the way around
  - Plastic inside the burr chamber: no tan/brown discoloration, no warping, no glossiness that suggests heat
  - Motor housing exterior: no discoloration, no deformation, no smell
  - Chute and grounds path: clear of debris

Smell:
  - Nose close to the chamber and the motor housing — any residual hot-electrical or burnt odor? If yes, that smell should have aired out by now; a lingering one is meaningful

Mechanical (still unplugged):
  - Rotate the inner burr by hand from above. It should turn smoothly with the normal light magnetic/brush resistance
  - No scraping, ticking, catching, or rhythmic clicking
  - No vertical play beyond a fraction of a millimeter
  - No horizontal wobble — the shaft should run true

PART 3 — DECISION GATE

Leave out of service if ANY of the following is true:
  - Stone could not be removed without force or is still in there
  - Any visible burr damage: chip, crack, missing segment, bent tooth, polished wear line
  - Burr does not turn freely by hand, or turns with scraping, ticking, or catching
  - Any wobble or play in the shaft
  - Burr appears misaligned, tilted, or has uneven gap
  - Any discoloration, warping, or glossiness on plastic in or near the chamber
  - Any residual hot-electrical or burnt smell on close inspection
  - You find fragments you can't account for, or any other anomaly
  - Anything feels wrong and you can't name it — this counts

You may run one controlled test only if ALL of the following hold:
  - Stone removed cleanly and the chamber is clear of debris
  - Burrs visually intact and properly seated, gap even
  - Burr turns smoothly by hand, no scraping, no play, no wobble
  - No discoloration anywhere, no residual smell
  - You are comfortable proceeding

PART 4 — IF YOU TEST: a single controlled run

Setup:
  - Use a different outlet than the one where it stalled (rules out an outlet anomaly cheaply)
  - GFCI-protected outlet preferred
  - Empty hopper — no beans for the first run
  - Nothing flammable nearby; cord routed so you can pull the plug instantly (not buried behind furniture)
  - The grinder on a stable, visible surface so you can watch and smell it

Sequence:
  1. Plug in
  2. Run empty for about 5 seconds — use pulse / short-run mode if the grinder has one; otherwise hold the power button briefly
  3. Stop and immediately assess: any grinding, scraping, ticking, sizzle, or hot smell? → UNPLUG, leave out of service
  4. If clean: leave it powered off, wait 3 minutes, then touch the motor housing — any warm spot? Warm under no-load is a bad sign → leave out of service
  5. If still clean: load a small dose (~5 g) of beans, run a single short pulse
  6. Stop, assess: normal startup hum + grind sound = proceed. Anything off (squeal, drop in rpm, smell, hesitation) → unplug, leave out of service
  7. If all clean: discard that first dose (may carry fine debris), then resume normal use

PART 5 — IF YOU LEAVE IT OUT OF SERVICE

  - The hot-electrical smell is the reason this is not a clean "clear the stone and go" situation. Even with a perfect inspection, a stall that produced a smell has stressed the motor windings or capacitor in a way that visual inspection cannot rule out
  - For consumer burr grinders, manufacturer service is often not economical; replacement is usually the right call
  - If you want to pursue service: contact the manufacturer with model + serial, describe the stall and the brief hot-electrical smell, and ask whether they'll inspect. Do not run it again before that conversation

Summary of the two questions you asked:

  - Removal: unplug, empty hopper, work the stone loose with a non-metal tool, brush and tap out fines, no force, no motor housing
  - Inspection: burrs intact and seated, no discoloration, no residual smell, smooth free rotation, no play or wobble
  - Test once: only if every inspection item is clean; use a different outlet, run empty first, then a small dose, with an unplug-and-stop rule on any anomaly
  - Leave out of service: any damage, misalignment, play, scraping, discoloration, residual smell, or the test producing anything off — or simply the hot-electrical smell itself making you uncomfortable, which is a legitimate reason on its own

Today's pattern matters more than the absolute number. The flexors were quiet at rest and on open-hand holds (low isometric demand), then reproduced 3/10 on the first undercling (the grip that loads the flexors hardest in climbing — fingers resist as the wrist is pulled into extension). That points to a still-sensitive flexor strain, not a new injury. No red flags present (no pop, swelling, bruising, neuro symptoms, focal bony tenderness), and stopping immediately was the right call.

Loading pause (next ~5–7 days)
- No climbing, no hangboarding, no dead-hangs, no heavy one-handed carries (groceries, luggage, water jugs), no tough jars, no white-knuckle driving.
- Light daily hand use is fine (typing, cooking, coffee).
- Skip forearm stretching, foam rolling, or "test it" curls.
- Optional: 10–15 min ice if you notice a low background ache. Skip if you're sitting at 0/10.
- Expected trajectory: 24–72 hours of relative rest should bring you back to a clean baseline at rest.

Morning self-check (Day 1 and Day 2 after today)
Same six-criterion framework as the 12/10 plan, score each 0–10:
1. Resting awareness — any baseline ache at the desk?
2. Full wrist and finger ROM — comfortable in all directions?
3. Everyday grip — mug, doorknob, phone — clean?
4. Resisted wrist flexion (other hand pushes your palm down, you resist) — any pain?
5. Light finger curls with a soup can or light dumbbell — any pain at end range or under load?
6. 20–30 sec open-hand hang from a pull-up bar or doorframe — clean or does it light up?

Decision rule:
- All six at 0/10, or only #1 at 1/10 that fades with movement → proceed to return progression.
- Any score ≥2/10, or pain that lingers >60 sec after the test → another 2–3 days of rest and re-test.
- Anything that worsens over 48 hours instead of improving → see criteria below.

Return progression (over ~2 weeks, conservative)
Stage 0 (gate): symptom-free at rest, all six checks clean. Don't rush.

Stage 1 (~3–4 days after Stage 0):
- 5–10 min warm-up + arm swings.
- Easy bouldering only on big holds (jugs, large slopers, big pinches). Open-hand grip only — no crimps, no underclings, no small edges.
- Cap session at 30–45 min. Stop with margin.

Stage 2 (if Stage 1 was completely clean):
- Add gentle half-crimp on positive holds, easy vertical/slab. Still no underclings. Still capped.

Stage 3:
- Reintroduce pinches and small edges. Open-hand → half-crimp → full crimp progression on easier moves.

Stage 4:
- Reintroduce underclings LAST. Start with bodyweight-only positions on large holds, short duration (one or two moves per problem, not sustained).
- If any 3/10 returns on Stage 4, drop back to Stage 2 for another week.

Stage 5:
- Normal session variety.

Stop-symptom criteria during any return session
- Pain that returns during a move
- Dull tightness that builds across the session
- Sharp or cramping pain
- Guarding or "I'm protecting it" instinct
- Post-session ache that lasts >24 hours

Red-flag criteria → urgent evaluation (sports med / ER)
- New pop or snap
- Visible swelling, bruising, or deformity
- Persistent numbness or tingling in the hand or fingers
- Loss of circulation (cold, pale, blue fingers)
- Severe pain at rest
- Focal bony tenderness over the ulna or radius

Routine sports-medicine / PT evaluation criteria
- Pain that doesn't fully resolve within 7–14 days of relative rest
- Pain that returns at progressively lower loads (getting worse, not better)
- Pain at rest or at night
- Grip weakness that isn't recovering in parallel with the pain
- Loss of motion that doesn't return with gentle use
- A third recurrence on this same tissue — at that point a PT assessment of forearm flexor loading, grip technique on underclings, and any contribution from the medial epicondyle region is worth booking even if you feel fine
- If Stage 3 or Stage 4 reproduces symptoms, that's a sensible threshold to book now — two episodes in 11 days on the same flexor group earns a formal look

Note on undercling technique when you do return
- Underclings are the highest-load position for forearm flexors in climbing because the hold pulls the wrist into extension while the fingers resist — the flexors are doing the dominant pull.
- Keep the grip open (no thumb wrap, no full crimp on the undercling), keep duration short, and try to drive with the legs so you're not hanging statically on the flexors.

Here's the play for the next ~10 minutes.

Read on what you've got
- Thin section at 145°F is at the USDA safe mark for salmon — it's done.
- The two thick sections (126°F and 133°F) need active heat. Carry-over alone from where they are won't reach 145°F in any reasonable time.

Step 1 — Separate by thickness
Cut between the thin section and the two thick ones. They are now two different jobs:
- Thin section: keep warm only, do not return to heat.
- Thick sections: low-oven finish to 145°F internal.

Step 2 — Finish only the thick sections
Put the two thick pieces on a small sheet pan or in a small oven-safe dish, skin-side down if there's skin. Oven at 275°F, probe in the thickest part of the slowest piece.
- Pull at 142–143°F. Carry-over will land them at 145–146°F.
- Estimate from your reads: ~5–8 min from 126°F, ~3–5 min from 133°F, depending on thickness.

Why 275°F and not 400°F: a hot oven overcooks the exterior while the center is still climbing. 275°F is gentle enough that the outside stays moist and the center catches up without a steep gradient. Don't go by time alone — probe.

If both burners and oven are full, a covered skillet on medium-low works in a pinch: 3–4 min lid-on, flip once, probe. Less precise.

Step 3 — Hold the thin section
Plate it now, tent loosely with foil. It will coast to ~148–150°F from residual heat over the next 10 min — still good texture for salmon. Do not put it back in the oven.

Step 4 — Hold the vegetables during the delay
Short delay (under 15–20 min), pick one:
1. Best: 200°F oven, loosely covered with foil. Stays well above the 140°F USDA holding line.
2. Stovetop on the lowest burner, tight lid. Works for most veg; stir once.
3. Tented on the counter is only fine if the delay is under ~10 min and the veg went on the plate hot.

The 200°F oven is the cleanest answer and pairs naturally with finishing the salmon at 275°F — drop the temp when the thick sections come out.

Step 5 — Plate and serve
Pull thick sections at 142–143°F, plate next to the thin section, spoon any pan juices over. Total added time from now: about 10 min.

One safety note: don't skip the probe check on the thick pieces before pulling. 142°F is not 145°F — the carry-over is what closes the gap.

CHRISTMAS EVE DINNER — 6:30 PM SERVICE
4-lb unstuffed chicken + roasted potatoes + sautéed green beans

CURRENT TIME: 1:10 PM → 5h 20m runway

THE PRINCIPLE
- 4-lb unstuffed chicken at 425°F: 75–90 min total
- Pull at breast 160–163°F and thigh ≥165°F; carryover adds 5–8°F during rest
- Safe rest = 15–20 min tented (stays above 140°F); can extend to 30 min if needed
- Potatoes ride the oven the whole time. Green beans wait until T‑15m. That is how the vegetables stay hot instead of getting held for an hour.

TIMELINE

1:10 PM (T‑5h20m) — TEMPER + SALT THE CHICKEN
- Pull chicken from fridge, set on counter on a tray or in its roasting pan
- Pat dry inside and out with paper towels (dry skin = browning)
- Salt: 1 tsp kosher salt per pound, all over skin and inside cavity
- Leave uncovered on the counter; 45–60 min temper is food-safe (under the 2-hr room-temp limit) and reduces the breast-thigh gap

1:15 PM — VEGETABLE PREP (after handling raw chicken, wash hands and board)
- Potatoes: cut into ~1.5" chunks, toss with 2 tbsp olive oil, 1 tsp salt, ½ tsp pepper in a separate roasting pan
- Green beans: trim stem ends, hold in a bowl at room temp (no need to refrigerate)
- Measure 2 tbsp butter + 2 cloves minced garlic into a small dish for the bean finish

2:00 PM (T‑4h30m) — PREHEAT
- Oven to 425°F, rack in lower third
- If you have a second rack, set it one position up for the chicken

2:15 PM (T‑4h15m) — IN THE OVEN
- Chicken on upper rack, breast-up, on a rack inside the roasting pan (air under the bird = even browning)
- Potatoes on lower rack in their own pan
- Set a timer for 60 minutes. Do not open the oven door before this.

3:15 PM (T‑3h15m) — FIRST PROBE
- Thermometer calibration check first: stick it in a glass of ice water; should read 32°F ±2°. If not, adjust your target temps by the offset.
- PROBE 1 — BREAST: thickest part is the upper-outer area near the wing joint. Insert horizontally from the front, parallel to the roasting rack, going into the meat. Stop halfway through. You must NOT be touching the ribcage bone. If you hit bone, angle up slightly and re-probe in a fresh spot.
- PROBE 2 — THIGH: deepest part is the inside of the thigh where the leg meets the body, NOT the outside (outside is closer to surface and reads higher). Insert from the body-side, pushing in along the femur until the tip is buried, then pull back ½ inch so it isn't grazing bone.
- Expected at 60 min: breast ~145°F, thigh ~155°F. If both tracking normally, set timer for 15 more min.

3:30 PM (T‑3h) — SECOND PROBE
- Target now: breast 158–162°F, thigh 162–165°F.

3:40–3:50 PM (T‑2h40m to T‑2h50m) — PULL DECISION
Pull the bird when ANY of these is true:
  (a) breast 160–163°F AND thigh ≥165°F (ideal)
  (b) both at 160°F (carryover will carry both to safe; rare on a 4-lb bird)
  (c) breast 163°F and thigh 162°F (close enough — both finish via carryover)

DO NOT wait for the breast to hit 165°F — by then it will be dry. Pull at 160–163°F breast; the rest window is where the breast finishes cooking safely without losing moisture.

3:50 PM — CHICKEN OUT, POTATOES CHECKED
- Move chicken to a cutting board, tent LOOSELY with foil
- Internal temp will rise 5–8°F over the next 10 min (carryover)
- Potatoes: probe a chunk with a fork or paring knife — should slide in with no resistance and the edges should be golden. If yes, cover the pan with foil, lower oven to 200°F. If not, give them 5 more min at 425°F first.

HOLD WINDOW — 3:50 PM to 6:00 PM (T‑2h40m to T‑30m)
- Chicken: tented on the counter. Stays above 140°F for at least 30 min, often 40–45 min in a tented roast. Fully safe.
- Potatoes: covered pan in a 200°F oven. Stays hot indefinitely.
- Green beans: still raw in their bowl at room temp. No safety issue — they go in last.

IF THINGS DRIFT (contingencies):
- Breast hit 162 but thigh is still 158–160 (rare on a 4-lb bird): tent the breast tightly with foil, return the bird to the oven tilted breast-down for 5–7 min so the thighs face more heat, then re-probe thigh only.
- Everything is ahead of schedule: chicken can tent on the counter up to 30 min; potatoes can sit in the 200°F oven as long as needed. Only the green beans are time-sensitive.
- A guest is late: do not carve yet — leave the bird whole and tented. Everything holds for you.

6:00 PM (T‑30m) — CARVE + POTATO RE‑CRISP
- Carve chicken: legs/thighs off first, then slice breast against the grain on the bias
- Potatoes: uncover, blast at 425°F for 5 min to re-crisp the edges
- Pile carved chicken on a warmed platter, tent again

6:15 PM (T‑15m) — GREEN BEANS (the hot-at-service move)
- Hot pan, medium-high, melt the 2 tbsp butter, drop in the garlic, 30 sec until fragrant
- Add green beans, salt, toss 4–5 min until just tender, bright green, with a few charred spots
- Off heat: pepper, optional squeeze of lemon
- Transfer immediately to a warmed serving dish

6:25 PM (T‑5m) — PLATE AND TABLE
- Pull the potato pan, the chicken platter, the bean dish, all within 2 min
- Everything on the table within 2 min of leaving its heat source

6:30 PM — SERVE

VERIFICATION CHECKLIST (read once while the chicken is in the oven)
[ ] Thermometer reads 32°F in ice water before first probe (calibration sanity check)
[ ] Breast probe inserted HORIZONTALLY from the front, midway through the thickest part, not touching ribcage
[ ] Thigh probe inserted from the BODY-SIDE along the femur, deepest interior point, not the outside surface
[ ] Both probes used before each read; if readings disagree, trust the lower one and pull
[ ] Pulled at 160–163°F breast (not 165°F — the rest window finishes it safely)
[ ] Rest tent is LOOSE foil, not sealed; 15–20 min minimum
[ ] Potatoes never sit covered on the counter for more than ~1 hr; the 200°F oven is the safe hold
[ ] Green beans are cooked AT T‑15m, not before

FOOD SAFETY NOTES
- Carryover from 160°F pull = ~5–8°F during rest → breast settles at 167–170°F, thigh at 170–175°F. Both well above the 165°F safe minimum.
- Whole bird tented stays above 140°F (the hot-holding floor) for 30–40 min.
- Cooked potatoes held in a 200°F oven stay safely above 140°F indefinitely.
- Cooked vegetables left at room temperature are only safe for ~2 hr total; do not start the bean sauté until T‑15m.

TOTAL ACTIVE TIME: ~85 min chicken + ~5 min beans across the afternoon. The rest is waiting and probing.

Classification: bounded consumer-capacity backlog. The 31% input rise on a holiday burst pushed queue age up only because consumer throughput held flat at its provisioned ceiling while accepted points temporarily exceeded drain rate. Flat throughput is the load-bearing signal: workers did not slow, error, restart, or shed. They kept working at capacity and absorbed the surplus as queue depth, then drained when input normalized. Rollup errors=0, metrics-router and ingest-edge at baseline, and the symmetric decline of queue age once input returned to normal rule out upstream publication lag, labelset divergence, or worker fault. This belongs to Cyrus's data-platform team; nothing in the evidence triggers an Infra hand-off under the routing rule (upstream publication stale / metrics-router input lag / labelset mismatch).

Pre-close checks before signing off as bounded:

  1. Per-worker queue age, concurrency, and restart count during the 6-min peak. Confirms saturation was uniform across workers, not one shard dragging the service average.
  2. Drain completion: queue age returned to the pre-burst baseline and held there, with no residual tail or late-window compaction work.
  3. Input accounting parity: accepted+rejected in window vs. consumer input vs. rollup output. The 31% extra must be present in downstream output, not silently dropped or stuck.
  4. Retry, dedup, and partial-write counters at zero. Errors=0 is necessary but not sufficient; some paths swallow errors and retry instead.
  5. Producer vs. consumer labelset parity for the burst window. Divergence here is one of the three conditions that adds Infra, so verify it explicitly even when it looks fine.
  6. Deployment.environment label and rollout slice unchanged through the burst. A canary/stable churn during the window would invalidate the burst interpretation.
  7. Time-boundedness: spike window length and that queue age resolved within a small multiple of input-normalization time.
  8. Prior-baseline comparison: same pattern at prior comparable bursts (Thanksgiving, Black Friday in past years)? If yes, this is a known operating regime, not a regression.

Data Platform follow-up (Cyrus's side, do not move to Infra):

  - Alert tuning. The current rule `avg by (service) (queue_age_seconds) > 15` for 5m masks slice-level saturation. With 36 stable pods near zero and a few rollup workers at 6 min, the service-wide average understates the worst case and may even under-trigger if only a small fraction of workers spike. Move to a per-shard or high-quantile signal so a saturated spool pages while the stable slice stays clear. This holiday burst is the right test case; it produced real saturation and the rule's averaging hides the shape.
  - Capacity sizing. Workers held flat throughput during a 31% surge. The question is whether provisioned concurrency was sized for peak burst or for steady state. If steady-state sizing is intentional (cost), the alert needs a known-burst lane. If peak sizing is intended, surface the gap.
  - Burst-aware routing. If a 31% surge is a recurring holiday pattern, consider a tier that fires only when the surge matches a known calendar event so the page goes to a known handler and not the on-call rotation's lap.
  - Per-worker visibility. Today the alert only sees the service-wide average; per-worker queue age and concurrency make future saturation easier to attribute and triage.

Infra: nothing required for this event. metrics-router, ingest-edge, and labelset routing stayed at baseline; producer and consumer labelsets aligned; no upstream publication lag. The routing rule (default data-platform; add infra only when upstream publication is stale, metrics-router input lag present, or producer/consumer labelsets differ) is satisfied with no Infra branch. Preserve the time-stamped evidence (input rate, queue age, throughput, errors, metrics-router and ingest-edge health, labelset parity) so the next burst compares against a clean reference and Infra involvement stays opt-in.

Yes — the combined load fully explains the trip. There is nothing in what you described that points to a wiring fault.

The math:

  15 A × 120 V = 1,800 W circuit capacity
  80% sustained-load ceiling = 1,440 W

  Kettle alone:  1,500 W ≈ 12.5 A  (already above the 1,440 W ceiling)
  Toaster alone: 1,450 W ≈ 12.1 A  (right at the 1,440 W ceiling)
  Both together: 2,950 W ≈ 24.6 A  — 64% over the 1,800 W rating, 105% over the sustained ceiling

A 15 A breaker trips somewhere in the 125–150% range after a short delay (and instantly on a hard short). 24.6 A into a 15 A breaker is comfortably in its trip band. The fact that the breaker reset cleanly with nothing plugged in, and that you've confirmed no heat, odor, discoloration, buzzing, sparking, or loose fit at the receptacle, means this was an overload event, not a fault. Nothing to mask.

Safe reuse, without masking anything:

1. One high-load appliance at a time on this 15 A circuit. Solo, both devices sit at or just over the 80% sustained-load ceiling, so don't run either on long or repeated duty cycles back-to-back on this circuit (e.g., several kettle reboils in a row while the toaster is also warming).
2. If you genuinely need both at once, they must be on different circuits. Kitchen counter receptacles are usually split across two or more branches (often left/right halves of the run). Map yours by tripping the breaker and noting which receptacles go dead — don't guess. The fridge, microwave, or dishwasher receptacle is often a separate circuit and may be the right home for one of them.
3. Both appliances plug directly into the wall, fully seated. No extension cords, splitters, or power strips on this circuit — they don't add capacity and they add resistance (heat) at every joint.
4. Leave the breaker in its reset state with both appliances unplugged. If the wiring were compromised, you'd see a symptom at the outlet or at the panel under no load, and you've already checked.

Involve South Slope management (or an electrician) if any of the following shows up — these are the markers that the trip was no longer just an overload:

  - Breaker re-trips with only one appliance running, or with nothing at all plugged in
  - Breaker won't reset, or feels warm to the touch after resetting
  - Heat, discoloration, scorching, or melting at the outlet, plug, or cord
  - Hot-plastic or ozone smell
  - Buzzing, crackling, popping, or sizzling at the outlet or panel
  - Loose-fitting plug (won't stay seated, falls out, or the receptacle wobbles in the wall)
  - Lights on the same circuit flicker or dim when an appliance runs
  - Tingling when touching the appliance, plug, or outlet
  - Any water reaching the outlet

You have none of these right now. Don't test by re-running both together.

One thing worth doing regardless: this is the third overload trip you've logged on a 15 A branch from high-wattage appliances (May 26 kitchen GFCI, hair-dryer + heater bathroom GFCI, now this one). That is a pattern, not bad luck. The proper fix is building-side — either a 20 A small-appliance branch to the counter, or splitting the existing 15 A so the kettle and toaster land on different breakers. South Slope management should be looped in not because anything is broken today, but because the load you want to run cannot be run simultaneously on the wiring you have, and "one at a time" is a habit that will eventually slip.
