2. Look at what the synthetic probe actually calls — which route, which downstream. A 500 from a single probe against a back-end that briefly 503'd, or against an auth path that requires a synthetic-only header, is the most common cause.
3. Check the probe's retry policy. Seven attempts in five minutes from one ID is consistent with a tight retry loop (e.g., 1s/2s/4s/8s backoff or a fixed-interval probe) that ran head-on into a transient. Confirm in the probe config or in logs.
4. Re-verify the "zero errors" claim on adjacent intervals isn't a 5-minute-window blind spot — pull the underlying counter (not the rate) and confirm the bucket boundaries actually contain the retry storm.
5. Re-confirm latency p99, egress reconciliation, drop, dup, and queue depth at baseline. If any of those have moved even slightly, the assumption "synthetic only" is wrong and you re-escalate. If they haven't, you're done.
6. Quick check whether the synthetic target had a known blip around the same timestamp (downstream health, dep rollout, DNS hiccup). If yes, root cause is identified and no runbook entry is even needed beyond a one-line note.

Safer alert formulation

The current rule (`error_rate > 1%` over 5m) is correct in shape but missing a volume floor — every percentage-only alert has this blind spot at low traffic. Replace with a two-condition or two-rule formulation. The cleanest options:

- Rate + floor (single rule, recommended):
  `sum(rate(http_5xx_total{service="metrics-router"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="metrics-router"}[5m])) > 0.01 AND sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="metrics-router"}[5m])) > 100`
  The denominator floor of ~100 req/5m (≈0.3 RPS) eliminates the near-idle regime while still catching a real 1% once traffic picks up. Tunable: 50 if you want even more sensitivity at very low volume.

- Absolute floor (parallel rule, catches real failures during genuinely quiet windows where the rate ratio is meaningless):
  `sum(increase(http_5xx_total{service="metrics-router"}[5m])) > 50`
  A burst of 50+ actual 500s is worth a page regardless of denominator.

Run both as OR'd page conditions. Each alone has a hole; together they cover both regimes.

Two additional hardening steps worth considering, in order of value:

- Exclude the synthetic source label from the error-rate query (`source!="synthetic"`) so a probe failure cannot page at all, and add a separate, lower-priority alert for synthetic-probe health that pages the probe owner rather than the on-call. This is the right architectural fix; the rate+floor is a band-aid.
- If you keep the synthetic traffic in the metric, also add a minimum unique-request-IDs dimension check: `count(count by (request_id) (rate(...))) > N` — a single ID producing most of the failures is itself a signal to suppress, not page.

Optional follow-up

This is a textbook near-idle false positive and the runbook rb_metrics_router_canary currently doesn't have an example for it — only the replay-mirror and live-vs-canary cases. Worth adding a short entry in the same evidence-entry format, owner alex / backup wes, so the next on-call doesn't repeat the verification dance. Let me know if you want me to draft and append it.

The 2 mm gap is a small visible sign of a real internal failure: gas from electrolyte breakdown inside the cell. With your current observations (cool, no odor, no vapor, no discoloration, no puncture), nothing is actively wrong yet, but the cell is in a failed state and the question is when, not whether, it goes further. "Older" makes this more concerning, not less — the chemistry has had time to degrade.

Principles, in order of priority:
  1. Do not charge, discharge, press closed, puncture, or heat the cell.
  2. Isolate it on a non-combustible surface, away from anything flammable.
  3. Get it out of the apartment via a vehicle you control, not transit.
  4. Hand it to a facility that accepts damaged lithium-ion batteries — never household trash, never the recycling bin, never a drop-box that only takes intact cells.

1. ISOLATE IT IN THE APARTMENT (do this now)

  - The best location is bare concrete, ceramic tile, or a metal surface, with nothing flammable within roughly 1 m (no wood, paper, fabric, carpet, plastic, curtains, bedding). A bathroom or kitchen floor is usually acceptable; a carpeted room or near a wooden bookshelf is not.
  - Ideal container: a metal pot, metal bucket, or ammo can. Even better: the same with a bed of sand (or clean kitty litter) underneath and around the battery, with the lid resting on loosely so pressure can vent. Sand smothers a fire if the cell ignites.
  - Orient it so the swollen side faces up — the cell vents upward, and you don't want that vent blocked by a surface pressing back.
  - Cover the USB ports with a piece of electrical tape if you can do so without pressing on the case. This prevents an accidental short across the port pins if it brushes against something conductive.
  - Keep it out of direct sun and away from radiators, heaters, and appliances that run warm.
  - Do NOT put it in water, in a sealed plastic bag, or in any airtight container.
  - Keep it out of sleeping areas and away from your exit path. If you have a balcony or concrete stoop at moderate temperature (roughly 5–25 °C / 40–77 °F), an outdoor spot away from the building, vehicles, and vegetation is the safest single choice — cold is better than warm for a compromised lithium cell, and any fire stays outside.

2. HANDLING AND TRANSPORT (without carrying it loosely on transit)

  Your instinct is right. If a swollen cell vents or ignites in a subway car or bus, you cannot safely isolate it and you put many people at risk. Drive it instead.

  - Drive yourself, or use a taxi / car service. Place the metal container with sand in the trunk, not the cabin. Crack a window for ventilation in case of vapor. Go directly to the drop-off — no side errands. Do not leave the battery in a closed car in the sun, even briefly.
  - If you have no vehicle and must use transit, the same container (metal, sand, loose lid, ports taped, swollen side up) in a bag you can set down and step away from is the minimum. Tell the operator. But this is genuinely a "drive or borrow a car" situation if at all possible.

3. DISPOSAL (not household trash)

  NYC and New York State prohibit lithium-ion batteries in both trash and curbside recycling. Swollen cells in garbage trucks and materials recovery facilities are a documented cause of facility fires, and this is the explicit scenario those rules exist to prevent.

  Reliable options, roughly in order of preference for a visibly swollen cell:

  - NYC Department of Sanitation Household Special Waste Drop-Off. Call 311 or check nyc.gov/dsny for the current permanent sites and event schedule. This is the right channel for damaged/defective lithium.
  - Best Buy, Home Depot, or Lowe's — many locations accept lithium batteries, but policies on visibly damaged cells vary. Call ahead and ask: "Do you accept swollen lithium-ion batteries?" If no, ask where they refer people.
  - Apple Store — accepts lithium batteries for recycling regardless of brand, including damaged ones, at most locations.
  - Call2Recycle (call2recycle.org) locator — their standard drop-off sites are for intact cells. For damaged ones they will direct you to a specialized handler.
  - The manufacturer (Anker, RAVPower, Aukey, Belkin, Mophie, etc.) — for damaged cells they typically route you to a certified handler rather than a mail-back envelope.

  Bring it in the same metal container with sand, hand it to staff directly, and don't leave it on a counter unattended.

4. EMERGENCY SIGNS THAT CHANGE THE IMMEDIATE RESPONSE

  Any of these means the cell is entering or about to enter thermal runaway. Stop handling it, leave the room, close the door behind you to contain any fire, and call 911 from outside. Do not re-enter for the battery.

  - The case warms above room temperature, or its temperature rises over time. Brief edge-touch only; do not put your face over it.
  - A sweet, chemical, or ether-like odor — distinctive electrolyte vapor.
  - Any hissing, popping, whistling, or cracking sound — the cell is venting.
  - Any visible vapor or smoke, even a wisp.
  - The swelling increases, or the case softens, bulges further, or splits.
  - Discoloration on the plastic near the swelling, or any liquid on the case (electrolyte is corrosive and flammable).
  - Sparks or flame — full thermal runaway.

  If a small flame starts while you are still at a safe distance and have an ABC dry-chemical extinguisher or a source of large amounts of water: a single power-bank-sized lithium-ion fire in early ignition can be knocked down that way. (Note: this is lithium-ION, not lithium-metal — water is appropriate here, not contraindicated.) If the fire is more than a small flame, or there's heavy smoke, evacuate and call 911. NYC firefighters are equipped for lithium-ion fires, but the smoke is toxic — do not breathe it.

  The transition from "looks fine" to "actively venting" can happen in minutes, and a runaway once started is hard to stop. Treat every hour with this battery in the apartment as a window where it could change, and let that urgency drive the disposal timeline — same day if you can arrange it, next day at the latest.

- Appetite drops or he turns away from the bland food.
- Mild lethargy extends past this morning.

Classification: bounded maintenance behavior, not an incident.

Evidence shape matches prior bounded precedents (the 2024-04-22 resolver-latency / renewal-deadline burst, the 2024-05-08 follower-catchup closure, and the 2024-12-23 Data Platform node replacement): brief excursion, bounded shard count, single signal, every other safety indicator clean, and the metric is already moving in the expected direction. Snapshot age rising while compaction workers are active is expected — compaction can briefly defer snapshot emission while a merge or write is in flight. The 4-6 minute excursion above the 15-minute warning line is small, the shard count is 3 of 480, and the slope is declining. Lease convergence complete, zero read and write errors, client latency at baseline, no split-generation or stale-write signal. That combination is consistent with maintenance, not failure.

Verification conditions required before treating this as bounded maintenance:
  (1) Snapshot age for all three shards returns below the 15-minute warning line within one expected compaction cycle; verify the trend is declining, not just the most recent sample.
  (2) Per-shard exactly one serving holder throughout the window; lease epochs monotonic; no overlapping-leader, duplicate-generation, or stale-owner message in logs for the three shards across the alert window and one cycle after.
  (3) Zero write errors and zero read errors across the window and the following compaction cycle; client p99 stays inside the baseline band with no short-burst excursion.
  (4) Compaction workers for the three shards show active progress — not stalled, not errored — and emit a new snapshot within the expected cadence.
  (5) Disk utilization stays below the safe threshold with no anomalous climb (currently <61%, confirm slope is flat or falling).
  (6) No companion alert in the same window: no lease-renewal-exceeded, no resolver-latency alarm, no replication-lag warning, no disk-latency alarm, no leader-election burst.
  (7) Affected shard IDs and their lease epochs preserved on file (matches the record-keeping from your 2024-12-02 cache-readiness rollout and the 2024-12-23 node-replacement precedent).

Escalation conditions — any one of these pages the shard-keeper owners (Alex / Nadia primary, Wes backup) and reclassifies the alert as an incident:
  (a) Snapshot age does not return below 15 minutes within two expected compaction cycles, or returns and then rises again inside the same maintenance window.
  (b) Any write error, stale-write indicator, split-generation, or duplicate-leader message appears in logs for the three shards or any other shard.

Triage rule of thumb for Anya
  web matches canonical AND iOS is stale  →  generator/cache problem (iOS-side stale artifact)
  web drifts AND iOS matches canonical  →  generator-version drift on the web side (the inverse of what we saw in the Node 22.4 case; don't confuse the two)
  web and iOS both disagree with canonical on the same token, both disagree in the same direction  →  canonical-package problem

Smallest diagnostic sequence (no manual edits to generated iOS, fail-closed publication, Anya's lane preserved)

0. Freeze publication. Don't delete anything yet; record the current state of canonical, the web artifact, and the iOS artifact (file SHA-256 + parsed semantic dump). This is the baseline against which every later claim is checked.

1. Read all three sides without running anything. From the versioned machine-readable canonical package, pull (a) the canonical content hash, (b) the canonical version + schema_version, and (c) the resolved token's intended value and full path. From the just-generated web artifact, pull (d) the token's emitted value, the path, and any generator/version metadata embedded in the file header or surrounding build log. From the iOS artifact on disk, pull (e) the same token's emitted value and the iOS generator's recorded version + schema_version. Compare (c) vs (d) vs (e). At this point you already have one of three outcomes and can stop early in the common case:
   - (c) = (d) ≠ (e): iOS is stale. Go to step 2.
   - (c) = (e) ≠ (d): web is wrong; iOS is fine. Go to step 3.
   - (c) ≠ (d) and (c) ≠ (e), and (d) and (e) agree with each other on the same wrong value: canonical-side. Go to step 4.

2. Stale iOS test (distinguishes on-disk cache vs per-target cache inside the generator). Do not touch the existing iOS file. Run the generator with a clean output directory and an explicit, recorded invocation: same canonical, same generator version, same Node runtime as the original run. Diff the freshly written iOS artifact against the on-disk iOS artifact byte-for-byte and semantically. Two sub-results:
   - New iOS matches canonical and disagrees with the on-disk iOS: the on-disk file is stale generated output (build cache or stale staging directory), not a generator bug. Resolve by re-running generation into a clean staging dir; the fail-closed gate then has a chance to publish a correct iOS artifact. No change to canonical or to the generator.
   - New iOS also equals the old on-disk iOS and disagrees with canonical: it is not a cache issue; the iOS target itself is reading from something other than the canonical you think it is. Step 3 picks this up.

3. Generator-version drift test (distinguishes per-target generator binaries from a single shared generator). Force the shared CI to resolve and record the exact generator version actually used for the web target and for the iOS target in this run. Pin both to the same recorded version, then re-run with a clean staging dir. If the iOS artifact now matches canonical and web, the asymmetry was per-target generator drift; pin them together and re-run the matrix. If iOS still disagrees with canonical, the iOS target is reading from a state that is not the canonical package — go to step 4 with that framing.

4. Canonical-package test (only after 2 and 3 have not resolved it). Re-resolve the canonical package from scratch by content hash (not by mutable ref), re-parse it, and recompute the token's intended value from the re-parsed canonical. If the recomputed canonical value matches what the package file claims, the canonical package itself is not the problem; the generator is producing a wrong value from a correct canonical and the fix is a generator bug, owned by Anya's lane. If the recomputed canonical value is itself wrong (e.g., a stale alias, a case-normalization collision like Surface.Muted / surface.muted, or a per-platform suffix leaking in), then the canonical package is the source of truth and is broken. Either way, do not edit the generated iOS file by hand to "fix" it — that is a Figma-first-style shortcut and violates the canonical-versioned-source rule. The fix lives in the versioned machine-readable package or in the generator; the iOS file is regenerated from it.

5. Sanity check that the matrix still fails-closed. Whatever the diagnosis, run the full matrix once with the diagnosis fix in place: semantic fixtures on web/iOS/Android/docs, 20× byte stability on each, and confirm a deliberate edit still fails the drift check. Hold publication until that passes.

What this sequence is doing, and what it is not doing
- It is the smallest sequence because step 1 already resolves the common case (stale iOS) without running anything; steps 2 and 3 are evidence tests, not fixes; step 4 is only reached when the first three have not converged.
- It does not recommend touching the generated iOS file by hand. The iOS file is treated as derived state; if the generator and canonical cannot reproduce the right value, the answer is to fix whichever of those two is wrong, then regenerate.
- It preserves Anya's ownership: the generator, the canonical-versioned-source rule, the fail-closed gate, and the design-system / engineering-handoff decision all stay in her lane. The sequence is diagnostic, not prescriptive about which generator fix or canonical correction she chooses — that is the readout she owes the pilot.
- It is consistent with prior pilot practice: same clean-staging-dir regeneration pattern as the second-team migration matrix, same generator-version pinning that closed the 0.8.4 / 0.9.0 schema-2 mismatch, same content-hash canonical pinning that resolved the Linux/macOS ZIP hash divergence, and it explicitly avoids the Figma-first-style shortcut Anya already ruled out for the Friday-demo case.

One thing worth flagging to Anya, not fixing
The asymmetry you described — web fresh, iOS stale — is the inverse of the 3.14.2 / Node 22.4 case, where web was the only target that drifted and iOS/Android were byte-identical. Worth recording in the pilot readout that the same shape of failure (one target drifts, others don't) has now been observed on both web and iOS, and that the diagnostic that distinguished generator-iteration-order from canonical in that earlier case is the same diagnostic that distinguishes cache from canonical in this one. That is the kind of pattern the six-week pilot readout should be capturing.

OFF-BIKE INSPECTION SEQUENCE FOR SMALLEST-COG CHAIN SKIP

Why the smallest cog is the canary: it has the fewest teeth (typically 10–12), so each tooth transmits the highest torque per pedal stroke. Four causes are most likely; each has a distinguishing sign. Run the sequence in order; stop at the first positive finding and proceed to the corresponding remedy or shop threshold.

PREPARATION
  - Bike on a work stand, or flip it upside down resting on bar tops + saddle (pad the hoods/bar tape with a rag).
  - Wipe the chain and cassette with a dry rag so tooth profiles are visible.
  - Good direct light; magnifier if available.
  - Have a chain wear gauge, hex keys, cassette lockring tool (if you have one), flashlight ready.

PHASE 1 — STATIC VISUAL: DRIVETRAIN
1.1 Smallest cog. Look down at the smallest cog from above and from behind the derailleur. Compare each tooth to its neighbor. Flag any of:
    - "Shark-fin" shape (leading edge hooked/thinned instead of symmetrical)
    - Asymmetric tooth (one tooth visibly thinner or leaning)
    - Tooth tipped forward in the direction of pedaling
    - Chipped, broken, or missing tooth
    Even ONE worn tooth on the smallest cog causes skip under load. Smallest cog wears first because it sees the highest tooth load and gets used most under hard pedaling.
1.2 Other cogs. Same check on the 2nd and 3rd smallest. If wear shows up across multiple cogs, the cassette is generally worn.
1.3 Chainrings. Same shark-fin check on the front ring(s), especially the small chainring if you have a double.
1.4 Derailleur hanger. Sight down the chainstay from behind the cassette. The hanger body should be in line with the cassette cogs. Any twist/bend will affect small-cog behavior and can masquerade as skip.
1.5 B-tension screw (rear derailleur). The upper jockey pulley should clear the largest cog by ~5–6 mm. In the smallest cog the pulley must NOT be close enough to the cassette that the chain binds. If the pulley is sitting too close, the chain can climb the cog teeth under hard pedaling — looks like skip, is actually clearance.

PHASE 2 — CHAIN FLEX / STIFF LINK
2.1 With the chain on the smallest cog, rotate the cranks slowly backward by hand and watch the chain run across the top of the cassette. The chain should flow smoothly; any spot that hesitates or pops over a link is a stiff link.
2.2 Pinch the chain between two fingers about 6 inches apart on the bottom run. Flex it side-to-side link by link by walking your fingers along. A stiff link won't articulate freely; you can usually see the bind.
2.3 If you find a stiff link: count it from a master link or known reference, drip chain lube directly onto it, then flex that link 10–20 times by hand. Re-check. If it frees up, the skip is likely resolved — confirm with a controlled low-load test in the smallest cog before returning to full effort. If it does not free, replace the chain (Phase 3 reading will tell you whether to replace cassette at the same time).

PHASE 3 — CHAIN WEAR (CHAIN STRETCH)
3.1 Use a chain wear gauge. Drop the pins into the chain at the 0.5% side first:
    - Gauge drops in fully at 0.5% → chain is worn, replace chain.
    - Gauge drops in fully at 0.75% but not at 0.5% → chain is at the upper limit, replace soon (and the cassette is at risk).
    - Gauge won't drop in at either → chain is within spec.
3.2 Without a gauge: pull the chain straight at the front of the chainring. If the chain lifts off the chainring teeth by more than half a tooth height, it is stretched.
3.3 Important interaction: a NEW chain on a WORN smallest cog will often SKIP because the new chain's rollers no longer match the worn tooth profiles. If your chain is at 0.75%+ AND the smallest cog shows any wear, plan chain + cassette together.

PHASE 4 — CASSETTE PLAY (LOOSE LOCKRING OR WORN FREEHUB)
4.1 Grab the smallest cog with your fingers and try to rock it fore-aft and side-to-side. There should be ZERO perceptible movement. Any rocking means the cassette lockring is loose, or the freehub splines are worn.
4.2 Grab each cog from largest to smallest. If only the smallest cogs rock, the lockring is loose and the small cogs are sliding on the splines. If every cog rocks, the freehub body itself is worn.
4.3 Lockring check: the lockring is the largest visible ring on the cassette, with a 12-tooth spline (or matching interface). If you have the tool, torque to spec — typically 40 Nm for Shimano road cassettes, 40 Nm for many MTB cassettes. If you don't, this is a shop trip.

PHASE 5 — WHEEL AND AXLE (LOOSE WHEEL)
5.1 Lift test. Grab the front of the saddle and rock the bike fore-aft. No clunk should come from the rear. Any clunk = wheel/axle likely loose in the dropouts.
5.2 QR (quick release):
    - Open the lever, confirm both cone springs are present.
    - With the wheel in the dropouts, finger-tighten the adjusting nut until the QR closes with firm palm pressure at ~half-closed. The lever should END pointing backward, roughly opposite the drive-side chainstay, NOT pressed against the chainstay.
    - If you can flip it past closed with one finger, it is not tight enough — re-open, make sure the axle ends are fully seated in the dropouts, and close again.
5.3 Thru-axle:
    - Should torque to spec (typically 12–15 Nm for road; check frame spec).
    - If it rotates freely or you can wiggle the wheel in the dropouts, it is loose.
5.4 Axle seating. Look at the non-drive-side dropout. The end of the QR rod or thru-axle should sit flush with or slightly inside the dropout face. If it is protruding, the wheel is not fully seated — re-seat before any other diagnosis.
5.5 If the wheel was loose: re-seat and retighten, then re-test skip with the bike upside-down using the Phase 6 load test before riding under power.

PHASE 6 — LOADED PEDALING TEST (BIKE IN STAND OR UPSIDE-DOWN)
6.1 Shift into the smallest cog. Pedal by hand with moderate force on the cranks. Watch the chain at the cassette and listen.
6.2 Try to reproduce the skip pattern:
    - Hard pedal stroke in smallest cog — does it skip?
    - Light pedal stroke in smallest cog — does it skip?
    - Hard pedal stroke in middle cogs — does it skip?
    - Hard pedal stroke in large cogs — does it skip?
6.3 Mapping of findings:
    - Skip ONLY under hard load + ONLY in smallest cog → most consistent with worn chain + smallest cog (cause 3).
    - Skip under all loads in smallest cog → indexing/cable, B-tension, or stiff link more likely.
    - Skip in multiple cogs under hard load → worn drivetrain OR loose wheel/cassette.
    - Skip accompanied by a clunk at the rear → wheel/axle is loose in the dropouts.

DISTINGUISHING SUMMARY

INDEXING ISSUE
  Hallmarks: slow or sloppy shift feel; skip at the SHIFT TRANSITION rather than steady pedaling; behavior changes with a quarter-turn of the barrel adjuster.
  Found in: Phase 1.4 (hanger), Phase 6 (multi-gear pattern).
  Off-bike remedy: cable tension tweak at barrel adjuster. Persistent = shop.

STIFF LINK
  Hallmarks: a specific link hesitates under Phase 2.1 / 2.2; often appears after storage, after rain, or after a fresh chain install.
  Found in: Phase 2.
  Off-bike remedy: lube + flex. If it doesn't free, replace chain.

WORN CHAIN OR COG
  Hallmarks: skip only in smallest cog under hard load; chain wear gauge reads 0.5%+; shark-fin teeth on the smallest cog.
  Found in: Phase 1.1, Phase 3.
  Off-bike remedy: not feasible at home — chain breaker, cassette lockring tool, and matching chain/cassette are needed. Shop trip.

LOOSE WHEEL OR CASSETTE
  Hallmarks: cassette rocks by hand; wheel clunks on lift test; QR / thru-axle not at spec.
  Found in: Phase 4, Phase 5.
  Off-bike remedy: re-seat and torque. If the cassette still rocks after lockring is torqued, the freehub body is worn — shop trip.

SHOP-TRIP THRESHOLDS — DO NOT RIDE UNDER LOAD UNTIL SHOP INSPECTS

Take the bike unridden (walk it, or roll it slowly on flat ground without pedaling) to a shop if ANY of the following is true:
  - Cassette shows any play in Phase 4.1.
  - Chain wear gauge reads 0.5% or more.
  - Smallest cog has any shark-fin tooth, asymmetric tooth, missing or chipped tooth.
  - Derailleur hanger is visibly bent or twisted, or the derailleur body is bent.
  - B-tension is mis-set and you cannot correct it with the screw.
  - Axle / QR / thru-axle cannot be made fully tight and properly seated in the dropout.
  - Phase 6 reproduces skip in any cog under hard load.
  - You cannot identify the cause from Phases 1–6.

Stay off the bike under load (no commuting, no traffic riding) if:
  - Skip recurs after any off-bike remedy.
  - Any new symptom appears — chain noise under steady pedaling, derailleur not returning under load, chain falling off the cassette, crank or bottom-bracket play.

Safe-rolling rule: walking the bike or rolling it slowly on flat ground without pedaling, to a shop, is acceptable. Do not ride under power until one of these is true: skip is eliminated and confirmed by a controlled low-load re-test, OR the shop has inspected and signed off on the drivetrain.

The fact that a reseat bought an hour of stability points to a marginal cable or marginal connector contact, not yet a port or ISP fault. The sequence below keeps the current configuration intact, changes one variable at a time, and only escalates once evidence justifies it. Plain-text outline:

  Phase 0 — capture baseline before changing anything
    Modem (Arris S33, 192.168.100.1):
      - downstream SNR, downstream power, upstream power, correctable/uncorrectable codewords (today's values + ranges across the past 24 h)
      - event log entries for the drop window (T3/T4 timeouts, CM resets, "LAN link" changes)
      - confirm optical/Coax status light and Online light stayed normal across the drop
    Router:
      - WAN port status page: negotiated speed, duplex, link up/down count, uptime since last flap
      - system log entries around 13:40 ET: every "WAN link up/down" / "speed changed from 1000 to 100" line, with timestamps
      - 5 GHz status (still pinned to channel 36 / 40 MHz from 2024-06-04 — confirm no regression there; the simultaneous 5 GHz stall suggests WAN loss, not radio)
    Save a screenshot of each page and a one-line summary per metric so the values are comparable later.

  Phase 1 — cable substitution (single-variable test, highest signal)
    Use a factory-terminated Cat6 cable, ≤ 2 m, from a sealed bag. Swap only the modem-to-router lead; leave everything else untouched.
    Note the wall time of the swap and run ≥ 24 hours, ideally through one of Devika's normal charting sessions and one of your heavier-use windows.
    What to record:
      - any new "WAN link" or "speed changed" lines in the router log
      - modem event log entries
      - whether drops recur (recurrence → cable was not the only contributor; stability → cable was the root cause)
    Do not reseat, reboot, or change Wi-Fi settings during this window. One variable at a time.

  Phase 2 — port and connector check, only if a fresh Cat6 still flaps
    Inspect both RJ45 ends of the original cable under a light: bent or recessed pins, crushed jacket near the boot, kinked run, parallel run alongside a power cable or microwave-side outlet. The Arris S33 typically exposes one Ethernet port; if yours has a second (some S33 variants carry a 2.5 G + 1 G pair), try the spare. On the router, the WAN port is usually the only one labeled WAN, so port isolation has to come from the modem side or by temporarily testing the router's WAN port with a laptop (link speed only — no need to bring the laptop onto the internet).
    Recheck the same logs from Phase 0; identical flaps on a different port or a known-good cable point to the device, not the lead.

  Phase 3 — environment and signal recheck
    Router and modem temperature (warm is fine, hot to the touch is not), recent moves, any new appliance on the same circuit or near the cable run. Re-pull downstream SNR and upstream power from the S33 to confirm they are still within the provider's accepted range (the September 24, 2024 install readings are your reference).

  Evidence threshold for contacting the ISP (XG-8)
    The modem's optical/Online indicator was normal across the drop, so the link under suspicion is the customer-owned segment between the S33 and the router. Contact XG-8 only if at least one of the following appears with a known-good Cat6 on a confirmed-good port:
      - S33 event log shows T3/T4 timeouts, CM resets, or downstream SNR / upstream power excursions outside the install-day range
      - S33 event log shows the modem's own Ethernet port flapping or downshifting (rare but worth checking)
      - WAN disconnects begin to appear on devices that are not on the customer-owned cable path
      - Drops persist across a different router on the same modem
    Bring the Phase 0 screenshots, the post-swap log excerpts, and the timestamp of the reseat recovery. With those, XG-8 can scope their side (line, node, CMTS) rather than dismiss it as inside wiring. If the new Cat6 holds for 48 hours and the original cable is the only thing that flapped, the fix is to retire that lead; the ISP does not need to be involved.

Two things to deliberately not do while the sequence runs: do not reboot the modem or router to "clear" the issue (a reboot masks whether the cable is still marginal), and do not open an ISP ticket speculatively — a ticket opened without the evidence above tends to bounce back as "customer equipment, not our problem," which burns the credit path.

Good call holding the laptop at the screen and not entering anything. A recovery-key prompt after an overnight firmware update can be legitimate (TPM re-measure or BIOS/firmware changes often force a recovery boot), but the recovery-key screen is also a well-known phishing/social-engineering lure, so you treat it as untrusted until IT verifies.

Here's the safe order:

1. Stop and leave the laptop at the screen. Do not type anything. Do not photograph the screen with the recovery key if one appears and send it anywhere — only enter it on the laptop's own screen after IT confirms it's expected.
2. Power the laptop off (hold power ~10s) so the prompt isn't sitting there indefinitely. Don't try to "boot around it."
3. Identify Sphere IT through an out-of-band channel you already trust, not from the recovery screen, not from a link in an email, not from a web search result. Use one of:
   - The phone number on your Sphere badge/intranet page, or the IT helpdesk address you have used before
   - Slack #it-help (typed, not via a link)
   - The corporate portal page you normally reach by typing the URL
   Give them the asset tag SPH-LT-4431 and say: "Post-overnight-firmware-update BitLocker recovery prompt on a Sphere-managed laptop. No input entered, no bypass attempted, no third-party recovery site used. Need verification and the legitimate recovery key through a verified channel."
4. IT will normally do one of:
   - Confirm the firmware update was scheduled and provide your recovery key from Sphere's MDM (Intune/Entra or equivalent) through the verified channel — you enter it on the laptop's own screen

Here's a concise note that flags the discrepancy and asks which record controls without conceding the longer shift:

  Hi [scheduler name],

  Quick clarifying question on my Saturday, January 18 hospitalist assignment — my issued January block schedule shows 8:00 AM–5:00 PM, but the staffing portal is displaying 7:00 AM–7:00 PM. Neither version is labeled as overnight coverage, and I haven't agreed to an extension. Could you confirm which record controls?

  Thanks,
  Devika

A few notes on why it's shaped this way:

- Opens as a clarifying question, not a refusal or a complaint — keeps the tone collaborative and avoids framing it as a dispute.
- Names both records verbatim (issued block vs. portal) so the scheduler can immediately see the conflict you're asking about.
- Explicitly notes "neither version is labeled as overnight coverage" and "I haven't agreed to an extension" — this is the key guardrail. It anchors the conversation to the issued 8–5 block until the scheduler responds, rather than implicitly accepting the 7 AM–7 PM range by, say, asking about a specific portion of it.
- Doesn't volunteer partial coverage, an alternative date, or a reason (e.g., childcare, Kibo walks) — keeps the question tight and prevents the reply from drifting into negotiation.
- Doesn't request a specific outcome, just "which record controls" — that's the only thing she needs answered before any further conversation.

If the scheduler replies that the 7 AM–7 PM portal entry is correct, she'd then need to decide whether to accept, decline, or counter — but that's a separate message and shouldn't be pre-decided here.

Repair accepted. The diagnosis matches the symptom cleanly: chain at replacement threshold plus a visibly hooked smallest cog is the classic combination — the smallest cog wears fastest because fewer teeth share the chain load, and once a cog tooth hooks a chain won't seat properly under hard pedaling. Replacing chain and cassette together (rather than chain alone) is the right call; a new chain on a hooked cog would have skipped again and would have worn the new chain faster.

New chain and cassette don't need a special bedding procedure like rotors do — normal riding is fine, and the drivetrain will settle over the first few rides as the chain plates and cassette teeth polish in. No need to baby it.

No-riding restriction closed. Re-flag only if skip returns — under load in any cog, under light load in the smallest cog, or as new noise/grinding that doesn't fade after a few rides.

The principle: messages and device settings are the data at risk — photos are already safe because they're syncing independently. So the sequence below captures those locally and verifies them BEFORE any cloud-side change, so that even if the cloud side goes wrong, nothing important is lost.

0. Preconditions (don't skip — these are what make the backup trustworthy)
   - Confirm the computer has real free space, not just claimed. ~40 GB free is a safe target; encrypted iPhone backups routinely run 10–40+ GB depending on apps and Messages.
   - Mac: use Finder on a recent macOS. Windows 10/11: use the Apple Devices app. Older Windows: iTunes.
   - Plug the phone into the computer with a known-good cable (USB or USB-C). Wired is more reliable than Wi-Fi for a first full backup.
   - Unlock the phone and stay near it. You'll be asked to "Trust This Computer" and to enter the device passcode.
   - Sign the computer into the same Apple ID as the phone (Settings → [your name] on the phone should match).
   - Plug the laptop into power. Leave both alone during the backup.

1. Make the encrypted local backup (no destructive steps yet)
   - In Finder (Mac) or Apple Devices (Windows), click the iPhone in the sidebar.
   - Under Backups, choose "Back up all of the data on your iPhone to this Mac/PC" — NOT iCloud.
   - Tick "Encrypt local backup." This is the critical checkbox. Without it, keychain, Health, Wi-Fi passwords, and most app data are excluded.
   - Set an encryption password. This is a one-way door: without it the backup is unrecoverable. Save the password in your password manager right now, and write it down somewhere secure.
   - Click "Back Up Now." First-time full encrypted backups run 30 min to a few hours.

2. Verify the backup exists
   - On the same iPhone page, "Latest Backup" should now show today's date and time.
   - Open "Manage Backups" (Mac) or the backups list (Windows). Confirm the entry is dated today and its size is in the multi-GB range. A backup in the few-hundred-MB range usually means a data class was skipped — redo it with "Encrypt local backup" confirmed.
   - Click "Show in Finder/Explorer" on the dated backup. Inside that folder you should see Manifest.plist and Manifest.db. Their presence confirms a real backup, not a half-written one.

3. Verify the right DATA is inside — this is what actually answers "are messages and settings preserved"
   - Trigger a second small backup (Settings → iCloud → Back Up is unrelated; here just click Back Up Now again in Finder/Apple Devices). It should finish in minutes and update the timestamp. A successful delta on top of a full backup proves the structure is sound.
   - For Messages specifically: with the encryption password, you can use iMazing (free trial) or any tool that decrypts a Manifest.db to confirm your most recent conversations are present. If "Messages in iCloud" was on in Settings, messages also live in iCloud independently; if it was off, the local encrypted backup is the only copy and this check matters more.
   - For settings: encrypted backups include Home Screen layout, wallpaper, accessibility, paired Bluetooth devices, VPN configs, etc. If "Encrypt local backup" was unchecked, none of this is in the backup — redo if in doubt.
   - Caveat for chat apps with their own encryption (Signal, WhatsApp, etc.): the backup container is there, but a restore still requires that app's own keys/PIN. Note which apps you'd need to re-pair on restore.

4. Save the encryption password in two places
   - Password manager entry, named so you recognize it later.
   - Paper copy stored with the backup drive or in a safe.
   - This is the single most common way local iPhone backups become useless. Do not skip.

5. ONLY NOW address the cloud side — pick one path, do not do both
   a. Make space for the cloud backup to finish on its own:
      - iCloud settings → Manage Storage → delete large unused items, old device backups from other devices, and Messages attachments you don't need.
      - In Photos, empty "Recently Deleted" — items there still count against iCloud.
   b. Shrink the cloud backup scope:
      - Settings → [your name] → iCloud → Show All → Back Up → toggle OFF apps whose data you can regenerate. Keep Messages and any data class you can't reconstruct ON.
   - Do NOT sign out of iCloud, do NOT turn off iCloud Backup, do NOT "Erase All Content and Settings" on the phone. The local backup is your safety net during this step.

6. Confirm the cloud backup now completes
   - Plug the phone into power, on Wi-Fi, locked. Settings → iCloud → Back Up → Back Up Now.
   - Verify "Last successful backup: today."
   - Only after this date is post-dating your local backup should you consider deleting the local backup folder. Until then, leave it alone.

Order matters: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 are the preservation steps. Step 5 is the first destructive step, and step 6 is the recovery check. Nothing in 5 should happen until 1–4 are confirmed.

If the phone is actually Android rather than iPhone: the same preservation-first logic applies, but the tooling is OEM-specific (Samsung Smart Switch, Pixel "Transfer files" backup, etc.) layered on top of Google One's cloud backup. Google Photos sync means photos are already preserved, freeing space = emptying Google Photos "Trash" plus pruning large Drive items, and verification means confirming the OEM export contains SMS + app data and that a fresh Google One backup completes after space is freed.

INTERPRETATION — fits a normal acute loading response, not tissue overload.

- 1/10 only in the last set = end-of-dose muscular fatigue, not a provocative reproduction.
- Settled in 10 minutes = acute fatigue pattern, not a tendon flare (a flare would persist hours or into the next day).
- No next-morning symptom = no delayed tissue reaction.
- No stiffness, swelling, grip change, or ordinary-use pain = no inflammatory or structural signal.
- Compared to 2025-01-05 (resisted wrist flexion alone reproduced 2/10), today's graded progression produced only 1/10 at the top of the dose. That is below your prior provocative threshold, not a step backward from it.

RECOMMENDATION — repeat the same level for one more session; advance only if session 2 reproduces the same clean response.

Reason: tendon-loading rehab uses a "two clean sessions" rule before stepping up. A single clean session can still be followed by a delayed flare that you would not see until tomorrow or the day after. Two consecutive clean sessions confirm the dose is reliably below your symptom threshold. The cost is one week out of a six-week plan; the upside is that you do not trade a clean start for an avoidable setback, given that the undercling pattern had already reproduced twice (2024-12-21 and 2025-01-05) before the plan started.

- No loaded underclings (the pattern that reproduced across two rest blocks; 2024-12-10 onset mechanism was overgripping).
- No hard gripping (same mechanism).
- No provocative testing beyond the prescribed progression (no extra undercling simulations, no single-shot resisted-flexion checks beyond the daily gate).

Direct answer on locking: YES, lock the card now while the $1.00 auth is pending. A small unknown-dollar authorization from an unrecognized merchant is a classic card-testing signature — fraudsters verify a stolen card with a $1 probe before running a larger charge. Locking is reversible, declines new authorizations, and the cost of locking (declined legitimate recurring charges) is recoverable; the cost of not locking (a larger fraudulent charge posting overnight) is not. The pending $1.00 auth itself will typically either post, expire in a few business days, or be declined by the issuer; locking does not retroactively cancel a pending auth, but it prevents the next one.

Proportionate steps, in order:

1. Lock the card immediately via the issuer app or website (the lock toggle is usually under Card Controls / Card Management). Do this from the official app, not from any link in a text or email.

2. In parallel, independently verify whether NORTHSTAR DIGITAL is yours:
   - Search your email (including spam/promotions) for "northstar", "northstar digital", or any subscription/trial confirmation from the last 60 days.
   - Web-search "NORTHSTAR DIGITAL charge" or "NORTHSTAR DIGITAL credit card billing" — card-testing merchants often surface in fraud reports.
   - Check any subscription manager or password manager for a service matching that name.
   - If you identify a legitimate trial/subscription, unlock the card and watch for the actual recurring charge. If unverifiable, keep it locked and continue.

3. Preserve evidence before anything rolls off the pending list:
   - Screenshot the pending auth showing merchant name (NORTHSTAR DIGITAL), amount ($1.00), timestamp (8:41 PM, Jan 17), and any authorization code or transaction ID the app shows.
   - Screenshot the full statement / pending view so the absence of other unfamiliar activity is documented in one image.
   - If the issuer app shows device, location, or merchant category for the auth, screenshot that too.
   - Note (don't just rely on the app) the exact time you first saw the auth (you said ~9:05 PM, Jan 17).
   - Save any email/text you did NOT act on — those are evidence of non-engagement, useful if a phishing follow-up appears later.

4. Contact the issuer through an independent channel:
   - Open the issuer app directly and use in-app chat or the in-app "report this charge" link, OR
   - Call the number printed on the BACK of your physical card. Do not use a number from any alert text/email.
   - Report the unrecognized $1.00 auth as suspected fraud. Specifically ask: can the pending auth be declined before it posts? What is the authorization/MCC code? Do they show merchant category or origin?
   - Mention you have already locked the card so no further auths go through.

5. Criteria for replacing the card (reissue with new number):
   - Replace by default unless you confirm a legitimate subscription. Card reissue is free, fast, and the safest move when the data is in unknown hands.
   - You can skip replacement only if the $1.00 auth expires without posting AND you can identify the legitimate source of the auth (e.g., a forgotten free trial). If the auth actually posts, that proves a working card detail set — replace.
   - Physical card is with you and account/MFA work, which suggests card-data compromise via online breach or merchant leak rather than skimming or account takeover. That still warrants reissue, but does not by itself justify rotating unrelated passwords or freezing credit.

6. After reissue:
   - Update saved payment methods wherever the old number is stored (subscriptions, retailers, transit/streaming wallets).
   - Watch the next two statement cycles carefully for follow-up activity on either number.
   - Do not delete or "clear" the pending $1.00 auth from the app view — leave it for the dispute trail.

What NOT to do right now:
- Do not call any phone number that arrived in a text or email referencing this charge. That is the most common follow-up phishing vector after a small probe auth.
- Do not click links in "fraud alert" texts/emails, even if they look like they came from the issuer.
- Do not share the full card number, CVV, or one-time codes with anyone who calls you, even if they claim to be the issuer's fraud team — hang up and call back via the number on the back of the card.

Escalation triggers that would broaden this response:
- A second unfamiliar charge appears (even small) — confirm fraud, request expedited reissue, and consider filing a police report for the record.
- Login starts failing, an unfamiliar MFA factor appears, or recovery email/phone changes — that is account-level compromise, separate from card data; rotate the issuer login password and review active sessions.
- A text or email specifically referencing this $1.00 charge arrives — treat it as phishing; do not engage, preserve it as evidence, and report via the issuer app.

## 2024-05-30 — Active vs retired generations, epoch drain, matcher cleanup, STW cleanup pauses

The existing entry covers CPU, memory, queue depth, route-delivery divergence, dropped series, and restarts. This section adds the checks that are missing from that surface: generation lifecycle, epoch drain, matcher cleanup, and stop-the-world (STW) cleanup pauses.

### Signal set — what to compare by pod

For each canary pod, alongside the existing p99 reading, capture:

1. Active generation count on the pod (`active_generation` per the /healthz state model — active only changes on swap, never on a failed apply).
2. Retired generation count on the pod (generations no longer active but not yet reaped).
3. Epoch drain state (in-flight reloads/workers that have not yet acknowledged the active generation).
4. Matcher cleanup state (matcher cache size, and how many retired-generation matchers remain).
5. STW cleanup pauses (GC pause durations, especially anything tagged cleanup / mark / sweep on the matcher and generation caches).

Compare p99 against active and retired generation counts and against cleanup pause durations — not against CPU alone. A pod with normal p99 but a growing retired count or rising STW pauses is signaling leak pressure, not steady state.

### Pause thresholds — when to halt further configuration pushes

Pause additional configuration pushes when ANY of the following hold:

- Retired objects accumulate above four per pod (retired generations, retired matchers, or any combination). This is a leak-shaped signal, not a warmup blip.
- Cleanup pauses exceed 100 ms per occurrence, or show a sustained upward trend over the pause window.

When pausing, do not roll back by default. Hold at the current cohort, capture the evidence below, and page the on-call owner before any further push or rollback.

### Verification set before resuming pushes

All of the following must hold before resuming additional configuration pushes:

1. Active-generation consistency across all canary pods (every pod reports the same `active_generation`; partial worker-apply failure is not allowed to leave pods on divergent active generations).
2. Route parity between canary and control (route-delivery counters match within the existing alert tolerance).
3. Dropped series at zero across canary pods.
4. Reload failures at zero during the pause window.
5. Restarts at zero during the pause window.

### Evidence to capture during the pause

Capture and attach to the incident / pause note:

- Per-pod generation evidence: `attempted_generation`, `validated_generation`, `active_generation`, and retired-generation count, sampled at pause start and at 5-minute intervals.
- Per-pod heap evidence: heap in-use, matcher cache size and key count, generation cache size, and the top STW pause duration during the pause window.
- The p99-by-pod comparison the thresholds above are keyed off.

### Rollback clarification

Responders must NOT roll back solely because a transient p99 spike recovered. A recovered p99 spike by itself is a hold-and-verify signal, not a rollback trigger.

Rollback IS warranted for any of:

- Active-generation inconsistency across pods (including any partial worker-apply failure that leaves divergent active generations).
- Route divergence between canary and control beyond tolerance.
- Dropped series above zero on canary pods.

In all other cases — including transient p99 spikes that recovered, elevated CPU that compresses, or retired-object counts that stay at or below four — hold, capture evidence, and verify against the signal set above. Do not auto-rollback on those signals alone.

## 2024-07-25 — Owner-led-window rule (supersedes 2024-06-18 bounded single-push model)

The 2024-06-18 bounded single-push model treated each push as needing its own drain-and-verify approval. That framing is superseded. The accepted operating model is an owner-led window: Alex opens a window with a fresh decision, and mapped operators may push single files within it under the conditions below. The 2024-05-30 signal set, pause thresholds, verification set, evidence capture, and rollback clarification remain in force and are referenced by name.

### Window opening

Each window requires a fresh opening decision from Alex. No mapped operator opens a window on their own. The opening decision is what converts the prior hold into push permission; a prior approval does not carry forward to a later window.

### Pushes during the window

Once a window is open, mapped operators may make single-file pushes while ALL of the following hold on every canary pod:

1. Retired generations remain at four or fewer — the same threshold the 2024-05-30 signal set uses.
2. Cleanup pauses remain at or below 100 milliseconds — the same threshold the 2024-05-30 signal set uses.
3. The full health set returns to baseline after every push — active-generation consistency, route parity, dropped series at zero, reload failures at zero, restarts at zero, and p99/heap inside the pre-canary band.

A push that disturbs the full health set does not, by itself, stop the window — but until the full health set returns to baseline, no further pushes are permitted. Baseline is the pre-canary p99 band and the pre-canary heap band, not a downward trend.

### Threshold exceedance stops the window immediately

Exceeding either threshold — retired generations above four, or a cleanup pause above 100 ms — stops the window immediately. There is no warmup exemption and no grace period. When the window stops, mapped operators hold further pushes, capture the evidence set from the 2024-05-30 section, and page the on-call owner.

### After recovery

After recovery:

- A fresh decision from Alex permits exactly one fully observed push.
- After that push returns the full health set to baseline, another window requires a separate fresh decision from Alex.

A single fully observed push after recovery is not, on its own, the start of a new window. The window only reopens with another fresh decision from Alex; prior approval does not carry forward.

### Rollback conditions (unchanged)

The following remain rollback conditions regardless of whether the window is open, whether p99 and heap look healthy, or whether the retired-generation and cleanup-pause thresholds are clean:

- Active-generation inconsistency across canary pods (consistency).
- Route divergence between canary and control beyond tolerance (parity).
- Dropped series above zero on any canary pod.
- Reload failures during the pause window or through any push.
- Restarts during the pause window or through any push.

A clean resource surface does not offset any of these five. Any one is sufficient on its own to roll back, and rollback remains an explicit decision routed through the deploy pipeline.

### Ownership (unchanged)

- Primary owner: Alex.
- Practical backup: Wes.
- This rule does not make Wes the primary owner. Wes remains the practical backup under the existing practical backup rules. The owner map is unchanged.

Interpretation of what changed

What you're describing is a failed tolerance check, not a structural setback. In graded tendon loading, two criteria govern whether a step-up "took":

  1. During-set pain should stay roughly at or below the prior session's peak (yours went 1 → 3).
  2. Symptoms should return to baseline within ~24 hours (yours were still 1/10 the next morning instead of 0).

The during-set number (3/10) is technically inside the "acceptable symptom" range used in tendon rehab (often capped at 3–4/10), but the 24-hour non-resolution is the more meaningful signal — it means the new load exceeded what the tendon could clear overnight, and that's exactly what progressive loading is designed to surface. Nothing about this pattern suggests tear, inflammation flare, or nerve involvement: motion is full, grip is normal, no swelling, no bruising, no numbness or tingling, no pain in ordinary use, and provocative climbing patterns (undercling, hard grip) remain excluded. So the finding is "your step-up was too big," not "you reinjured yourself."

Recommendation: return to the prior tolerated load (Progression #1)

This is the right call for three reasons:

  - Progression #1 was clean — 1/10 final set, resolved within 10 minutes, no next-morning symptom. That's a confirmed tolerated load and the right floor to consolidate on.
  - Repeating #1 for another 1–2 weeks lets the tendon adapt to that load before you try to step up again, which is how graded loading actually works: each step-up needs to be earned by stable tolerance at the prior step.
  - When you do try to step up again, make the increment smaller than this one — not "the next rung on the plan," but something closer to a 50–70% jump in load rather than the full rung. If the original plan's increments were coarse, the clinician can dial that in at the Feb 20 visit.

Pause is not wrong, but it's more conservative than necessary. Contacting the clinician before Feb 20 isn't required — the pattern is expected, the red flags aren't present, and the corrective action (step back, consolidate) is the same one the clinician would recommend.

  - Continue excluding loaded underclings and hard gripping — unchanged.

  - If a future session reproduces the 1/10 next-morning pattern again after stepping up, contact the clinician before Feb 20 to recalibrate the plan.

When to contact the clinician sooner than Feb 20

Any of these would change the picture and warrant an earlier message or visit: new swelling or bruising in the forearm, numbness or tingling, night pain or pain at rest, loss of grip strength, loss of wrist or finger motion, or pain that gets worse 48–72 hours after a session rather than settling. Direct read: not an emergency. No smoke, spark, heat, odor, or moisture at the plate, and the breaker hasn't visibly tripped — so there's no active hazard at the face. But an outlet that killed two known-good loads with no external cause is reportable on its own; the most common explanations are an upstream GFCI or AFCI trip (which won't show at the panel) or an internal failure — loose backstab, broken splice, or a failed splice — that won't read on the surface.

Permitted reset, in this order — each is one attempt, not repeated:

  1. Hunt for a GFCI elsewhere on this circuit. Bedrooms in older buildings are often downstream of a GFCI in a bathroom, kitchen, hallway, closet, or another bedroom, and a GFCI trip shows at the GFCI, not at the breaker panel. Press TEST then RESET on every GFCI in the apartment. The one whose buttons won't click or won't stay in is the tripped one.
  2. If no GFCI restores it, hard-reset the bedroom breaker: flip it firmly all the way to OFF, then back to ON. Some breakers sit in a half-tripped position that reads as ON; a deliberate full OFF→ON clears it. One pass only.
  3. If either step restores power, plug a single known-good low-draw load (phone charger or one of the lamps) into the suspect receptacle. One test, not a sequence.

What NOT to do: do not open or unscrew the receptacle, do not pull the faceplate, do not keep resetting a GFCI or breaker that re-trips, do not load-test with a heater or hair dryer, do not run the outlet tonight even if a reset appears to work — wait until it's been inspected.

Report to building management regardless of whether the reset works. The flicker-then-failure pattern with no external signs points to an internal connection issue that can recur and can overheat under load; an electrician should open the box and inspect the splice, not just the face. Frame it as: "bedroom receptacle failed with two known-good loads, no visible cause, breaker not obviously tripped — please send an electrician." This is the right call even if power comes back, because a successful reset doesn't rule out a failing splice.

Call rather than email/portal if any of these show up before management responds: the breaker feels warm, any click or buzz from the outlet, faint odor, the plate warms under a small load, or any other outlet on the same circuit starts misbehaving. Leave both lamps unplugged and the outlet unused until management or an electrician has looked at it.

The proposal inverts source-of-truth direction. Treat it as a request for evidence first; do not run the migration.

What the timestamps in the iOS file actually are
  The iOS artifact contains two timestamps because the generator writes
  generation-time metadata (typically `generated_at` plus a `generator_version` or
  per-run `mtime`). These refresh on every clean run. Newer-looking timestamps in
  a generated file mean "this artifact was generated later," not "the values
  inside it are more current than the canonical package." Without source-level
  evidence, they are not a signal that the canonical values are stale.

Why generated iOS output must not be written back into the canonical package
  1. Canonical is the agreed source; all three teams consume generated outputs
     from it. Promoting iOS to source makes canonical a derived artifact and
     breaks the consumer lockfile that pins `@northpier/tokens` by content hash.
  2. If the iOS artifact is wrong, copying it into canonical bakes the bug into
     the source instead of finding it. The next regeneration then "matches" the
     broken artifact and the drift check reports clean while the contract is
     still broken.
  3. Generation timestamps are not part of the token contract. They have no
     schema_version semantics and no consumer depends on them. Treating them as
     a value signal is the bug, not the data.
  4. The proposed write skips the compatibility gate (schema_version alignment
     between `@northpier/tokens` and `@northpier/token-generator`) and the
     key-level drift check, both of which exist to catch exactly this class of
     problem.
  5. It creates a feedback loop: future runs would diff canonical against itself
     and report clean even if the underlying token contract is broken.
  6. Anya's lane owns the canonical package and the generator pinning. A
     migration script that silently rewrites canonical from a generated file
     bypasses the change control the three consuming teams rely on.

Bounded verification sequence (read-only, no writes to canonical)
  Step 0 - Freeze and record
    - Compute and log SHA-256 of: canonical package (committed), generated iOS
      (committed), generated web (committed), generated Android (committed).
    - Save a parsed semantic dump of each. Do not run anything yet.

  Step 1 - Generator version
    - Read the `generator_version` (and any `generator_commit`) embedded in the
      iOS artifact's header/metadata block.
    - Read the consumer lockfile entry and the shared CI job's resolved
      `@northpier/token-generator` version.
    - Expected: embedded version equals resolved CI version, and both equal the
      pinned version. If they diverge, the timestamps are explained by a
      generator-version mismatch and the canonical package is innocent. Record
      the diff; do not act.

  Step 2 - Package commit
    - Resolve the canonical package by content hash from the consumer lockfile.
      Confirm the on-disk file hashes to that value.
    - Record: commit SHA, author, commit timestamp, content hash. Note that the
      canonical commit timestamp being older than the generated timestamps is
      correct, not a problem.
    - Confirm no one has hand-edited the iOS artifact (`git log -p` on the iOS
      path should show generator-driven changes only). If it shows a manual
      edit, that is the drift signal - not the canonical package.

  Step 3 - Generation logs
    - Pull the most recent generator run that produced the committed iOS
      artifact. Capture: input canonical content hash, resolved generator
      version, schema_version reported, exit status, any warnings.
    - Expected: input hash equals pinned canonical hash; generator version
      matches lockfile; schema_version matches consumer; exit clean.
    - If warnings include deprecation, missing field, or normalization notes,
      those are the candidate root cause, not the canonical timestamp.

  Step 4 - Drift check (clean regeneration, no writes back)
    - In a temporary directory only: run the pinned generator against the
      pinned canonical package. Do not touch the working tree.
    - Diff: new iOS vs committed iOS; new web vs committed web; new Android vs
      committed Android.
    - Expected: all three diffs empty (or limited to timestamps, which should
      themselves be absent if the generator is byte-stable per the prior
      pilot's fix).
    - If only iOS differs: generator or iOS target drift, not canonical.
    - If all three differ the same way: generator-version drift, or canonical
      was mutated after the last committed generation. Re-resolve canonical
      from its content hash and re-run.
    - If iOS differs in a way the others don't: iOS serializer or template is
      the suspect, not canonical.

  Step 5 - Decide
    - Clean across all four steps: the proposal is unfounded. The newer-looking
      timestamps are generation-time metadata. No write to canonical. Hand
      back to Anya's lane with the recorded hashes and diffs.
    - Drift localized to iOS: file as a generator or target bug. Canonical is
      innocent. No write to canonical.
    - Drift across all formats after re-resolving canonical from its pinned
      content hash: generator is wrong about the canonical values; canonical is
      still innocent. File as a generator bug against the pinned version.
    - Drift that disappears only when canonical is not pinned by content hash:
      someone mutated canonical locally. That's a change-control issue, not a
      reason to copy generated output back.

What to tell the migration-script author
  - "Generated" is a one-way arrow. Source-level evidence means: the canonical
    package, the generator, or the contract changed in a way that justifies a
    new value. Timestamps in a derived artifact are not source-level evidence.
  - If the iOS values are correct and the canonical values are wrong, the fix
    is a source-of-truth PR against the canonical package, reviewed by each
    consuming team, with a schema_version bump if needed and a coordinated
    re-generation. That is the lane the three teams already agreed to.
  - If a migration script writes generated artifacts back into canonical
    without that coordinated change, the next failure will be silent and harder
    to attribute. The bounded sequence above catches it before that happens.

Safeguards this sequence keeps intact
  - Fail-closed publication (no publish on any incompatibility)
  - Content-hash pinning of the canonical package
  - Key-level diff on generated vs committed
  - schema_version compatibility gate
  - Anya's lane ownership of canonical package and generator pinning
  - No manual edits to generated artifacts in the working tree

Recurrence matters here — same sink, ~8 months apart, both hair + soap at the stopper. Most likely a heavy-shedder plus a partial downstream restriction. Mechanical clean below, but tell management this is the second time; if it happens again, ask them to check the branch line or vent.

Mechanical clean (renter-level, no chemicals, no trap disassembly):

1. Lay a towel under the P-trap, paper towels, a trash bag, rubber gloves, an old toothbrush, and either a Zip-It strip or a wire hanger with a small hook bent into the last inch.
2. Pop the stopper out. Most South Slope pop-ups lift and twist; if yours doesn't lift clear, reach under and unclip the pivot rod from the lift rod.
3. Wipe hair and soap scum off the stopper with the toothbrush — this alone often restores full flow.
4. Feed the Zip-It or hooked hanger 6–10" into the drain and pull back out 2–3 times, rotating a quarter-turn between pulls. Don't push past light resistance.
5. Run warm water 30–60 seconds and watch the basin — it should clear in well under 30 seconds. Reseat the stopper and confirm.

Stop and call management — don't push past any of these:

- Hard resistance on the tool — never force it.
- Water rises in the basin instead of draining.
- New drip appears in the cabinet or at the supply valves.
- Stopper won't reseat or the pivot rod won't reclip cleanly.
- No real improvement after ~15 minutes of effort.
- Gurgling or new backup in the tub or toilet, or any sewage odor — that's a main-line or vent issue and is firmly the building's problem.

Going forward, a $3 hair catcher over the stopper will catch most of what you're pulling out. And given this is the second occurrence, a short note through the South Slope portal is worth sending — mention both dates and that cleaning restored flow both times. That's the building's cue to send someone to scope the branch line if it returns a third time.

Pattern fits a video-path or handshake issue, not a managed-policy one (dock power and Ethernet are up, direct HDMI works, no MDM banner). Run the steps in order — one change at a time — so each result points to exactly one cause. No security settings are touched.

PRE-CONDITIONS (already verified by the situation; restating so the sequence stays clean)
  - Display panel + HDMI input on monitor: OK (direct HDMI works)
  - Dock power delivery: OK (laptop charges)
  - Dock USB-C/PD data path: partially OK (Ethernet works)
  - One dock reseat already attempted; did not recover (so it isn't a one-off seating flake)
  - No MDM/compliance banner on screen
  - Unknown: dock video output stage, dock-to-monitor cable, USB-C uplink cable, OS handshake state

SEQUENCE (smallest non-destructive; one change per step)

  1. Trigger an OS-level display re-handshake. No cables move.
       - Windows:  Win+P  →  choose Extend/Second screen only once, then back to Extend.
                  Or Settings → Display → Multiple displays → Detect.
       - macOS:    System Settings → Displays → option-click "Detect Displays"
                  (or Cmd+F2 if "Detect Displays" hotkey is enabled).
     RESULT  ─  image returns: stale handshake confirmed. Stop. No further action needed.
     NOTE     ─ if OS shows the monitor listed but no image, the link layer is up; the
              failure is downstream (cable or dock output). Continue.

  2. Power-cycle the dock ONLY (do not sleep/wake the laptop again yet).
       - Unplug dock AC. Wait 30 s (lets dock caps discharge and state clear).
       - Replug AC. Wait for dock LEDs to stabilize (typically 10–20 s).
       - Trigger OS Detect again.
     RESULT  ─ image returns: dock video-state latch was stuck. Stop.
     No change yet to the USB-C uplink, so a recovery here implicates the dock's
     internal multiplexer, not a cable.

  3. Reseat + swap the dock-to-monitor cable.
       - First reseat firmly both ends; trigger Detect. If no change:
       - Swap in the HDMI cable you already confirmed works in the direct-HDMI test.
         Trigger Detect.
     RESULT  ─ image returns with the known-good cable: that cable was bad. Stop.
     This isolates the dock's video OUTPUT stage from the laptop/uplink side.

  4. Reseat + swap the USB-C uplink cable (laptop ↔ dock).
       - Reseat firmly at both ends; trigger Detect. If no change:
       - Swap for a known-good USB-C cable that is explicitly rated for
         DisplayPort Alt Mode or Thunderbolt 3/4 (NOT a charge-only or USB 2.0 cable).
         Trigger Detect.
     RESULT  ─ image returns: uplink cable was bad (DP Alt Mode pins open).
              Stop.

  5. Try a different USB-C port on the laptop, if one exists.
       - Move the uplink cable to another USB-C/Thunderbolt port. Trigger Detect.
     RESULT  ─ image returns: that port's display routing was the issue
              (some laptops wire only specific ports to the discrete GPU/dock
              controller). Use that port going forward and report to IT.
     RESULT  ─ still no image after step 5: dock video-path hardware failure.
              Stop. Hand to Sphere IT or the dock vendor with the step-by-step
              log; do not open the dock or reflash firmware.

WHAT TO LOG (one line per attempt — saves a back-and-forth with IT later)
  - step #, time, OS, what changed, OS "saw monitor?" yes/no, image yes/no,
    dock LED state, laptop USB-C port used.

DO NOT (preserves managed security and avoids masking the real cause)
  - Do not change BitLocker / disk encryption / firewall / antivirus state.
  - Do not uninstall or roll back video drivers without Sphere IT — on a
    managed asset that can flip compliance state and trigger a re-image path.
  - Do not disable MDM agent, attestation, or VPN.
  - Do not run a firmware update on the dock or laptop to "fix" this — if
    steps 1–5 don't recover it, IT should own any firmware change so the
    recovery key / boot measurement state stays clean.
  - Do not keep sleep/wake-cycling the laptop hoping it will "take"; that
    just delays the diagnosis and can fill the system log with noise that
    obscures the real fault.

STOP CONDITIONS WORTH PAUSING THE SEQUENCE FOR
  - An MDM/compliance banner appears at any point: stop, contact Sphere IT
    before continuing — policy could be intentionally disabling the dock.
  - Any heat, odor, or LED error pattern on the dock during step 2: stop,
    unplug, hand to IT/hardware support.
  - Direct HDMI also stops working at any point: stop — the failure has
    moved off the dock and into the laptop's GPU/display stack, which is
    outside this sequence.
