That's a gauge-ownership bug, not a cancellation bug. The terminal accounting (77 dispatched + 23 canceled = 100) and the empty queue confirm the cancellation path itself is doing the right work — `cancelRequest` correctly removes from `tenant.queue`, the tenant drops out of `activeRing`, and dispatch proceeds work-conservingly for the remaining 77. What's wrong is that two paths both think they own the "queue slot released" decrement.

Concretely: the cancel path decrements the pending-queue gauge the moment `cancelRequest` removes the request from `tenant.queue` (real-time, slot-owned transition). The tombstone sweep later runs and decrements again for the same 23 records because it iterates all tombstones without distinguishing "this request was canceled before dispatch" from "this request was dispatched and is now a completed tombstone." 100 − 23 − 23 = 54, which matches what you're reading.

Recommended fix: make the sweep the *only* decrement path for dispatched tombstones, and skip canceled tombstones there. Cancel tombstones already released their slot at cancel time; sweep should filter on the terminal state (or a "queue-slot-released" flag) and not touch the gauge for canceled records. Idempotency is the property you want — whoever writes the tombstone also marks whether the slot is still accounted for.

Why not invert it (cancel path doesn't decrement, sweep handles everything): the gauge then overcounts during the sweep interval, which matters for cancel-heavy workloads and breaks the real-time accepted-point accounting you've already locked in. The asymmetry is fine as long as it's explicit: cancel path owns "slot released by cancel"; sweep owns "slot released by dispatch completion." One owner per transition, both flagged on the tombstone.

Two things to verify before this merges:

1. Staging rerun with the fix — same 100/23 fixture, gauge should read 0 after sweep. Then a second fixture where cancellations happen *after* dispatch begins (cancel-mid-dispatch), to confirm sweep still correctly decrements once for those (cancel-after-dispatch doesn't touch the gauge because the request isn't in the queue anymore; sweep owns it).

2. Sweep doesn't regress on the rolled-out invariants — empty-tenant eviction from `activeRing`, eight-waiting cap, four-active-per-pod, two-active-per-tenant, `Retry-After` on queue-cap 429, accepted-point integrity. Those should all stay green; this is purely a gauge-ownership patch.

THE DEFECT

A single logical event (admit, release, or reject) drives two independent decrement paths. The authoritative state path mutates permits_held / accepted_total / rejected_total. A separate telemetry or derived-counter path observes the same event and independently decrements the same budget. The state sees "request completed, release one permit." Telemetry also sees the completion event and applies its own -1. Net effect: the available budget reflects -2 per release when only -1 actually happened. Symmetrically, an admit can increment permits_held twice, tripping the cap prematurely and rejecting work the state still believes is admissible. The visible symptom is drift between dashboard and state — rejections begin before the cap appears full, or the cap appears full when it isn't. Under concurrency the two paths race, so the bug is non-deterministic: sometimes both fire, sometimes only one, sometimes in the wrong order, which is what makes it a defect class rather than a single bug.

QUEUE-OCCUPANCY EVIDENCE REQUIRED

  - queue_depth observed at the state layer equals queue_depth reconstructed from telemetry over the same window (delta zero within rounding).
  - under a synthesized burst, queue_depth never exceeds the cap; once the burst ends, queue_depth returns to baseline within the SLO window without manual intervention.
  - permit saturation (permits_held / cap) reported by state matches the saturation reported by telemetry; any disagreement is itself the defect signature.
  - a sustained-load run shows no monotonic rise in queue_depth or permits_held; slope is flat or bounded.
  - dropped_total stays at zero unless an explicit drain-or-reject boundary was crossed — never rises as a side effect of telemetry.

TERMINAL-ACCOUNTING EVIDENCE REQUIRED

  - each rejection increments rejected_total exactly once; rejected_total is monotonic non-decreasing across the run.
  - accepted_total increments only when admission actually succeeded; it never increments on rejection.
  - permits_held is NOT decremented on rejection — a rejected request was never held, so no decrement should occur; a tracer must show the decrement branch is unreachable on the reject path.
  - reconciliation invariant over any window: accepted_total + in_flight + rejected_total == submitted_total (within the window's accounting latency).
  - every 429 carries Retry-After; rejected_total matches the 429 count in access logs over the same window.

SINGLE-DECREMENT OWNERSHIP EVIDENCE REQUIRED

  - static or dynamic trace showing that for every event class (admit, release, reject) exactly one site mutates permits_held; telemetry consumers observe but do not mutate the authoritative counter.
  - if a derived metric exists (e.g., a separately reported permits_in_use), it is computed from state deltas, not from independently observed event hooks.
  - concurrency test: N parallel admits followed by N parallel releases converge permits_held to its initial value; convergence to N-k for any k>0 means a release was double-counted; convergence to N+k for any k>0 means an admit was.
  - the original failing scenario, replayed against the fix, produces a single decrement per event in the trace.

END-STATE REGRESSION EVIDENCE REQUIRED

  - after the burst ends and the queue drains, permits_held returns to its idle baseline, demonstrating no permit leak.
  - accepted_total and rejected_total remain monotonic across the run; no counter resets mid-window.
  - in_flight converges to zero when traffic stops; no stranded work.
  - rollback (revert the fix) reintroduces the double-decrement trace; the failing test fails on the unfixed branch and passes on the fixed branch — the regression test is a real trip wire, not a tautology.
  - boundary-condition regressions — mid-flight cancellation, retry past the horizon, fill-then-drain — each show permits_held does not drift under that event.

GATING

All four categories must be produced from a single instrumented run against the canary, with the original failing pattern present as a control case. Until then, the staging-only status does not move.

Title: [BLOCKING] reload path must be fail-closed, generation-aware, and never let gen 618 silently replace active gen 621

Body:

This revision does not yet meet the bar for the reload path. Holding review until the items below are addressed. The core invariant: `active_generation` may only change as the final step of a fully validated atomic publication; any other outcome must leave serving state pinned to the prior active generation and must emit an explicit stale-bundle / failed-reload signal.

1. Generation-aware replay protection (fail-closed)
   - Reader path must observe a generation epoch, not a raw pointer. Every candidate carries its generation id; readers either observe the prior active generation or the new one, never a torn mix.
   - The watcher must detect rename-and-create atomic replacements, not just in-place writes, and must perform content-addressed change detection (hash or canonical form) before triggering reload — identical content must not produce a "reload."
   - Failure to validate the candidate (parse, schema, semantic, dynamic, or worker apply) must (a) leave `active_generation` unchanged, (b) drop the candidate pointer AND remove its entry from any process-wide candidate registry, and (c) emit an explicit `failed_reload` signal visible to /healthz and logs. A debug-only log is not a signal.

2. Separately authorized emergency rollback
   - Rollback is not a reload and must not share the reload code path. It is a discrete, authorized action (operator-initiated, audited) that swaps to a pinned prior generation with its own atomic-publication semantics.
   - Rollback must NOT be triggered by the watcher, the poller, or any reload-adjacent failure path. If the regular reload path could "roll back" by itself, the fail-closed guarantee is hollow.
   - Health endpoint must distinguish reload from rollback in `last_attempt_status` so on-call can tell them apart.

3. /healthz semantics (matches the 2024-04-08 contract)
   - `active_generation` reflects only what is currently serving, every reader.
   - `last_attempted_generation` / `last_validated_generation` / `last_attempt_status` expose the most recent reload outcome without implying that active has changed.
   - HTTP 200 must not be conflated with a successful reload — only with liveness.

4. Required regressions — must run green before merge
   - atomic_rename_publishes: filesystem rename-create swap of a valid bundle publishes gen N+1; readers see complete N or complete N+1, never both, never neither.
   - atomic_rename_failed_validation_publishes_signal: same swap but candidate fails semantic validation. `active_generation` stays at N, `failed_reload` signal fires, no registry entry for N+1 remains.
   - identical_content_no_reload: re-publish of byte-identical content produces no reload attempt and no `last_attempted_generation` bump.
   - interrupted_watching_during_swap: watcher paused across the rename; on resume it detects via content hash, validates, and either publishes cleanly or fails closed — never silently serves stale.
   - rename_only_no_write_event: rename without a write event still triggers validation (rename-aware, not write-event-only).
   - **gen_618_cannot_silently_replace_active_gen_621**: starting state active=621, a candidate bearing generation=618 is offered (stale / replay). The path must reject it on generation comparison, leave active=621, and surface a stale-bundle signal. This is the regression the prior follow-up explicitly required; its absence is a blocker on its own.
   - atomic_replacement_authorized_rollback: operator-initiated rollback from active=621 to pinned gen=618 succeeds atomically and is logged as rollback, not reload; `last_attempt_status=rollback_ok`.
   - concurrent_publish_and_failure: a successful gen=N+1 publication racing a failed gen=N+2 candidate — readers see complete N or complete N+1, never N+2 even partially; failed N+2 leaves no registry residue.

5. Open ownership question (separate from this review)
   - Per the current owner map, metrics-router mapped owners are Alex and Wes; Wes is not the formal owner. Please confirm this revision is being shepherded under the mapped-owner lane and that the separately authorized rollback path has an owner of record before approval.

Failure-mode review — shard-keeper PR #774 (stale-response fencing)

Classification: stale-response fencing defect, not split-brain. Your framing is right and the trace invariant you cite (never two serving gates open simultaneously) is the correct discriminator. That distinction matters because the fix is at the *response* layer, not the *holder* layer, and conflating the two tends to produce fixes that re-open gates or add polling intervals we deliberately removed.

What's actually happening
- Lease-loss path is clean. The epoch-811 holder closed its serving gate under the corrected fail-closed contract (the one we accepted on shard-keeper#197 and that the 50% canary validated: gate-close ≤14 ms after lease-loss notification, zero stale reads across 170,600 transfers). So the holder side of the seam is sound.
- The defect is on the client-side response application: responses don't carry the serving epoch under which they were authorized, and the client applies writes in arrival order. So an in-flight epoch-811 response that was authorized *before* lease loss can arrive *after* the epoch-812 retry's response and silently overwrite it. The client's newer routing value is older data — classic fencing-token omission, just expressed at the application layer instead of the storage layer.

Why your trace invariant is the right one
- "Two serving gates open simultaneously" would be split-brain and a holder-side defect; the rollback playbook and the fail-closed serving-gate contract already rule that out.
- "Stale write wins over newer write" is a *response* invariant failure: the client cannot tell which response was authorized under which epoch because that information is stripped at the wire format.
- The fix belongs to whoever owns the response payload — and per the Q3 ownership map, that's Cyrus+DP, with you as mapped owner for the overall service. The mapped owner should drive; you're reviewing.

What I'd want to see before approval
1. Serving epoch on the response. Every routing response carries the epoch under which it was authorized. Stale epoch-811 responses are then dropped on the client before they touch the cache. This is the minimum.
2. Or, equivalently, a monotonic sequence id on the response and an arrival-order-but-keep-newer policy on the client. Epoch is cleaner because it composes with the rest of the lease machinery and doesn't introduce a new id space.
3. A barrier test in the PR's test set that mirrors the staging fixture: revoke between authorization and response, expect the stale response to be dropped (not merely delayed), expect the epoch-812 value to be the one the client retains. The 2024-09-11 supervised run with the control-plane delay is a good template — final old-holder response 6 ms, gate close 12 ms, no later old-holder response — but it's a holder-side template; you want the response-side analogue.
4. Repeat the repeated-failover and delayed-notification cases with the wire-format change. From shard-keeper#197 we already require "exactly one active serving holder" across repeated failovers — extend that to "exactly one *applied* client-side routing value per request, regardless of arrival order."
5. Rollback shape unchanged. Per #197's contract, the lease format is unchanged so rollback is a binary flip, not a migration. Hold to that.

What I'd push back on if proposed
- A client-side "debounce / last-writer-wins-with-timestamp" patch. It papers over the same defect and creates a new failure mode where a legitimately newer response gets dropped because its wall-clock crossed a skewed boundary. Epoch-on-the-wire is the durable answer.
- Increasing the in-flight read timeout on the client to "wait longer for the retry" so the epoch-811 response is more likely to arrive first. That just shifts the race; it doesn't fence it.
- Any change that re-introduces a polling interval on the gate-close path. The fail-closed contract is event-driven (atomic close before any subsequent routing read can respond); keep it that way. Polling is a backup detector, not the primary mechanism.

Stop conditions I'd attach if this advances toward prod (consistent with the language we used approving the 50% canary expansion)
- Stale response applied: stop.
- Two holders observed at any layer (client cache included): stop.
- Gate-close regression relative to the canary baseline (≤14 ms): stop.
- Sustained error rate elevation or any restart: stop.

Recommendation
- Direction is right, scope is small, and it composes cleanly with the corrected serving-gate contract. Ask Cyrus to: (a) put the serving epoch on the response rather than rely on a client-side heuristic, (b) add the response-layer barrier test to the PR's test set, (c) confirm rollback remains a binary flip, (d) name the canary stop conditions in the PR description using the language above. Then this is approvable as the mapped owner; deployment and ops stay with Cyrus+DP per the ownership map. No prod change until the staging fixture replays clean with the wire-format fix and the barrier test is in the suite.

**The four regressions requested:**

(a) **Handoff** — a request arriving at the exact moment the lease authority reassigns the epoch is served by the new epoch; a synthetic prior-epoch response injected at the same boundary is rejected by the consumer-side identity check.

(b) **Retry** — a client retrying against a holder that has already lost its lease is rejected by identity, not by transport-level failure.

(c) **Delayed old-holder response** — an old-holder response delayed past the new holder's first accepted response (slow GC, scheduler stall, network reorder) is rejected by identity and never overwrites accepted state.

(d) **Client-cache ordering** — cached routing state is populated by identity rank, not by arrival order; a lower-rank late arrival cannot move cached state backward.

**Response identity required on every authoritative response:** live epoch + serving holder's generation bound to that epoch + a disambiguating digest/version tag. This makes "no stale old-holder responses" and "exactly one serving holder" structural invariants of identity, not empirical timing artifacts of any single drill.

This is not an emergency given no hazard signs, but a GFCI that won't reset is a real fault signal, so the goal is to isolate the cause without loading the circuit further.

Pre-check (do all of these first)
- Unplug everything from the kitchen GFCI itself.
- Unplug everything from every other kitchen receptacle on the same counter / island. Kitchen GFCIs frequently protect additional "downstream" outlets that are not labeled or are labeled only "GFCI protected." If any appliance is still plugged in downstream, the leak path is still present and the GFCI will refuse to reset by design.
- If a fridge, freezer, or any other always-on appliance is on this circuit, note it now. If it has stopped running, plan to move perishables to a working outlet or cooler today and include it in any report.

Step 1 — Try the GFCI's own reset once, with everything unplugged
- Press TEST until it clicks, then press RESET firmly. If it clicks and holds, go to Step 4. If it won't click, won't hold, or trips back immediately, do not keep pressing it. Move to Step 2.

Step 2 — Check for another upstream GFCI (yes, do this)
- Kitchen circuits in many apartments are fed from a GFCI located elsewhere: bathrooms (including any half-bath or Jack-and-Jill), the laundry area, an exterior or patio outlet, a garage outlet, or a second kitchen / dining outlet on the opposite wall. Walk the apartment and press TEST then RESET on every GFCI you find. South Slope memory notes GFCIs have shown up in unexpected spots before, so check the obvious and the not-obvious.
- If another GFCI was tripped and you reset it, return to the kitchen GFCI and try RESET once more. If it now holds, go to Step 4.

Step 3 — Reset the breaker once, only if Steps 1 and 2 did not restore it
- Breakers can trip to a middle position that looks "on." Flip the kitchen breaker fully OFF (firm click), then fully ON. Try the kitchen GFCI RESET one more time.
- This is a one-shot, not a procedure. If it still will not reset, do not cycle the breaker again. Repeated cycling on a faulted circuit is one of the common ways people cause damage that wasn't there to start with.

Step 4 — Verify only with a known-good low-draw load
- Plug in a phone charger or a small LED lamp. Leave it for a minute or two. Do not plug the blender back in tonight, and do not load-test with a kettle, toaster, microwave, or hair dryer.
- If the low-draw load holds, the GFCI itself may be failing or there may have been a transient leak from the blender's plug or cord. Use a different kitchen outlet for the blender from now on until the suspect GFCI has been inspected.

Stop and leave the circuit off — request a licensed electrician or management service if any of the following applies
- The GFCI will not reset after Steps 1–3, even with everything unplugged.
- The GFCI resets but trips again immediately, or trips again when a small known-good load is plugged in.
- The breaker trips again on its own after Step 3.
- Any new sign appears at the outlet, the plate, the cord, or the plug: warmth or heat, buzzing, crackling, popping, sizzling, ozone or hot-plastic smell, scorch mark, discoloration, melting, cracking, looseness, or moisture reappears.
- You feel any tingle or mild shock when touching the outlet, the plate screws, or an appliance plugged into the circuit.
- A reset appears to succeed but other outlets on the same counter or kitchen circuit are dead, dim, or flickering, or the fridge/freezer (if on this circuit) has been off long enough to risk perishables.
- The GFCI resets, you use it briefly, and it trips again within the same evening — that is a recurring fault, not a transient.

What not to do (consistent with prior guidance for this apartment)
- Do not open, unscrew, swap, or "push harder on" the receptacle or its face plate.
- Do not repeatedly press TEST/RESET on a GFCI that won't hold.
- Do not cycle the breaker more than once.
- Do not plug the blender, or any other high-wattage appliance, back into this outlet tonight even if the reset appears to hold.
- Do not use an extension cord, power strip, or splitter to bypass or share this receptacle.
- Do not run the suspect outlet overnight unattended.

Revision still has the same fundamental flaw. The retry-queue merge is treating "moment the envelope got emitted" as a substitute for "moment the source emitted the observation," and `source_timestamp` is the wrong field to carry that. Whether the new value is 10:19, 10:31, or `clock.Now()`, the downstream consumer can't distinguish "the source reported this late" from "ingest held this for 29 minutes." Both look identical to freshness.

What the merge needs to produce, given the inputs you described:

  source_timestamp:       10:02  (the observation's original emission — unchanged)
  retry_attempt_at:       [10:19, 10:31]  (per-attempt transport timestamps, on the envelope or per-span)
  envelope_emitted_at:    10:31  (optional, downstream-visible only — for SLO on collector latency)

`source_timestamp` must be set from the original observation's source time on first ingest and then frozen for the life of the envelope. The retry queue's job is to preserve it, not to refresh it. If the merge needs to record "this is the wall-clock time the collector decided to ship it," that goes in a separate field — never in the field freshness treats as authoritative. Same rule applies if there are multiple observations being merged: each one keeps its own source_timestamp; the envelope does not get a synthesized one.

Two things worth checking in the diff before pushing back on the thread:

1. Whether the merge path also collapses multiple observations into a shared envelope timestamp. If the collector is averaging or max-ing across the batch on emit, that's a second instance of the same bug and needs the same fix.
2. Whether `retry_attempt_at` is on the envelope, on each span, or only on internal logs. If it's only internal, downstream still has no way to see retry latency vs. source latency, and a future "freshness regressed" alert will blame the source again.

I'd push back on the PR with a concrete ask: revert `source_timestamp` to the original observation time on merge, add `retry_attempt_at` as per-attempt transport metadata, and extend the existing regression fixture so a merged-after-retry envelope asserts `source_timestamp == 10:02` and `retry_attempt_at == [10:19, 10:31]`.   2. xxd | head each → confirm the diff is exactly ordering + EOL, nothing else
  3. Inspect the canonical source as it sits on disk: is it actually CRLF? If yes, the read path isn't normalizing. If LF, the iOS writer is emitting CRLF.

Fix (layered — don't skip):

  1. Generator: deterministic key order for iOS. Sort by fully-qualified name using iOS-specific case folding (lowerCamelCase for Swift). Don't rely on map iteration order.
  2. Generator: normalize line endings. On read, canonicalize the canonical source to LF. On write, emit LF for every platform. Pick one. Don't let the platform decide.
  3. Drift check: split into two signals.

     - Byte — SHA-256 of the normalized form (LF, sorted keys, no trailing-whitespace noise). Catches unintentional drift in the writer (stray BOM, tabs vs spaces, weird newlines).

  - EOL normalization — feed a CRLF canonical source, generate, expect LF output and PASS

  - negative — key rename — rename one token, expect FAIL

The boundary has two layers and they answer different questions; collapsing them is what produced the 1-in-4 false-positive rate, and "fixing" it as a single check is the move that would weaken publication safety.

What the pass/fail decision canonicalizes (semantic leg)
  Token names, values, aliases, scopes, platform targets — after normalization
    (sorted keys, numeric format canonicalized, whitespace stripped, locale-agnostic).
  Effective value after resolver/alias expansion.
  Presence, absence, add, remove of a token — these ARE signal, never normalized away.
  Everything that's pure serialization noise (map traversal order, locale-formatted
    decimals, embedded timestamps/nonces, line endings, generator comments) gets
    stripped before the hash. Two artifacts that differ only in those layers MUST pass.

What stays available as evidence (byte leg)
  Both raw candidate artifacts, unmodified, each with its own byte-hash.
  The canonicalized form actually compared, with its hash.
  The generation manifest: runtime version, locale, deterministic-key-order flag,
    and the source-owner-supplied canonical-package version identifier
    (per NP handoff — no inference, no backfill).
  The semantic diff report (which fields changed after canonicalization).
  The byte diff report (raw delta — for post-hoc "why did this pass/fail" review).

Why both legs are required (the asymmetry that matters)
  Deterministic generation alone: removes the noise floor, but a legitimate token
    rename also produces byte-different output that has to FAIL — and you need a
    way to confirm it's failing for the right reason.
  Semantic comparison alone: catches real drift, but can't distinguish a real
    failure from a serialization-ordering failure, so reviewer trust erodes at
    ~1/4 false positives.

Title: [BLOCKING] emergency rollback authorization must be narrowly bound to current generation and target generation, with identified operator, short expiry, audit recording, single use, and regressions for reused/expired/auth-misuse paths

Body:

Holding review. The emergency-rollback path still does not meet the bar — the gap is not the existence of a separately authorized channel, but the shape of the authorization itself. The invariant: an emergency rollback may move `active_generation` backward only when an authorization token presented at decision time uniquely authorizes that exact transition, and is invalid for any other use, any other moment, or any other caller. Anything weaker lets a stale or replayed token move routing backward.

1. Authorization token shape (must hold before any rollback path is considered mergeable)

   - **Generation binding — narrow and explicit.**
     The token names exactly two generations: `current_generation` (the generation the system is in when the token is presented) and `target_generation` (the generation to move to). Both must appear in the token, and both must match the live state at decision time. The token does not encode a generic "rollback to version X" capability — it authorizes exactly one transition (current → target) and nothing else.
   - **Operator identity.**
     The token is bound to a single identified operator (handle + auth principal). The decision path must verify the principal presenting the token equals the principal named in the token; mismatch fails closed. Operator identity must be recorded with the audit event regardless of outcome.
   - **Short expiry.**
     Expiry is a duration, not a date. It must be short enough that an issued-but-unused token does not outlive the incident response (≤ 30 min from issue is a sensible default; justify anything longer in the PR description). Expiry is checked against a monotonic clock, not wall-clock — clock skew must not be used to extend a token.
   - **Single use.**
     The token carries a nonce that is consumed atomically on use. "Consumed" means recorded-as-used in durable storage in the same critical section that performs the rollback; an attempted second use, or an attempted use after a partial rollback that left state inconsistent, must fail closed. A token that was issued and never used must still expire; a token that was used once must fail on every subsequent presentation.
   - **Audit recording.**
     Every authorization decision — success, failure, replay, expiry, operator mismatch, generation mismatch — emits an audit event that records: token id, presenting principal, named principal, current_generation at decision, target_generation at decision, decision, monotonic timestamp, and outcome (applied / rejected / partial). Audit events are durable, append-only, and observable to /healthz or equivalent status surface. A debug log line is not an audit event.
   - **Decision placement.**
     The full token check (generation binding AND operator identity AND expiry AND single-use nonce consumption AND audit emit) runs inside the same critical section that performs the rollback. No partial check, no lazy check, no "we'll log it but still roll back."

2. What the emergency path is NOT

   - It is not triggered by the watcher, the poller, the reload path, or any reload-adjacent failure signal. If the regular reload path can "rollback by itself" when given `allow_rollback=true`, the authorization model is decorative.
   - It is not a fallback for an ordinary reload that failed — a failed reload leaves active pinned and emits a failed-reload signal; it does not silently transition to a rollback.
   - It does not share the reload code path's state mutation. The rollback transition is a discrete, audited atomic publication that replaces active with target_generation and records the prior active as the new "last rollback from."

3. /healthz and status surface

   - `last_rollback` exposes: target_generation, source_generation, operator principal, monotonic timestamp, audit event id.
   - `last_attempt_status` continues to distinguish reload from rollback so on-call can tell them apart.
   - An authorization failure (any kind) is visible in status counters and logs as a distinct event type from a failed reload.

4. Required regressions — must run green before merge

   Each test below starts from a known live state and an explicitly issued token. Token shape, expiry, and consumption rules are exercised; no test relies on internal luck or timing.

   - **emergency_rollback_to_named_target_succeeds.** active=621, issue a token for (current=621, target=618, operator=alex, expiry=15min, single-use). Present it. Expect: active=618, audit event recorded, token consumed, counters move, /healthz reports new active and last_rollback with source=621 and target=618.

   - **reused_authorization_cannot_move_routing_backward.** active=621, issue a token for (current=621, target=618). Use it once successfully → active=618. Re-present the same token (or any replay of its nonce). Expect: rejected, active unchanged at 618, no second rollback, audit event recorded as `replay_rejected`, no state mutation.

   - **expired_authorization_cannot_move_routing_backward.** active=621, issue a token for (current=621, target=618, expiry=1ms). Advance monotonic clock past expiry. Present the token. Expect: rejected as `expired_rejected`, active unchanged at 621, audit event recorded, no state mutation.

   - **authorization_for_other_generation_cannot_move_routing_backward.** active=621, issue a token for (current=618, target=610) — i.e. a token that named a *different* current generation than the live state. Present it. Expect: rejected as `generation_mismatch_rejected`, active unchanged at 621, audit event recorded naming both the token's named current and the live current, no state mutation. This test is the regression for "an old rollback-enabled bundle cannot move routing backward" — the bundle the token names must not be honored when the live state has moved past it.

   - **old_rollback_enabled_bundle_without_valid_token_cannot_move_routing_backward.** active=621, an attacker / operator hands the rollback path an old bundle that itself carries `allow_rollback=true` but no current token. Expect: rejected as `missing_authorization`, active unchanged, audit event recorded. The presence of `allow_rollback=true` on the bundle is not authorization.

   - **partial_rollback_consumes_token_and_fails_closed.** Force a rollback that mutates some state but fails before completion (e.g. audit write succeeds, target matcher install fails). Expect: token is consumed regardless, active is left in a recoverable pinned state (not at the partial target), audit event recorded as `rollback_partial_failed`, retry requires a fresh token.

The distinction (per-field vs envelope-only)

- Per-field: each field carries its own absence reason. A mixed response (some restricted, some source-missing, some present) keeps each field's cause distinct.
- Envelope-only: one top-level label collapses all fields into a single reason.

Recommendation: per-field is the source of truth; envelope is a derived summary.

Per-field is right because customers act on the specific field — "request access" vs. "report a data gap" are different remediation paths; support-admin attribution needs the field-level signal to route correctly (access-control ticket vs. data-pipeline ticket); and envelope-only forces a misleading single label onto mixed responses. Envelope is still useful as a fast filter, but it summarizes per-field, never replaces it.

Customer-facing wording Iris can use

Two short labels, one per absence reason:

- Permission denied → "Not available — access restricted. Ask your account manager to request access."
- Source data missing → "Not available — data not yet collected."

If the in-product UI only has a one-line slot: "Restricted" / "Awaiting data."

Structured payload (recommended shape):
- field.value: null
- field.absence_reason: "permission_denied" | "source_data_missing"
- envelope.status: "all_present" | "partial" | "all_restricted" | "all_missing"

The process serves generation N+1 while disk holds N+2 for up to one full poll interval, with no signal that a generation was skipped. The previous revision's rename/create handling and failed_reload emission do not close this — the underlying defect is a close-then-open TOCTOU window between the old watcher and the new one, and a single-file watcher cannot recover from a rename that lands inside that window.

Required changes:

1. No watch gap during swap. The reload path must establish the new watch (file-level on the new inode, or parent-directory on routes.yaml's parent directory) before closing the old one. Close-after-open, not close-then-open.

2. Parent-directory Create/Rename watcher is required, not optional. A watcher on the directory containing routes.yaml captures every Create/Rename on the file regardless of file-level watch state, including renames that land mid-swap. The 60-second content-hash poll is a consistency check, not a real-time detector — do not rely on it for prompt correctness.

3. Prompt signal on missed-and-recovered generation. When the hash poll (or any out-of-band detector) finds the on-disk generation ahead of active_generation, emit an explicit missed_generation_recovered signal carrying both generation numbers and the elapsed time. Today nothing is emitted during the gap.

4. Generation-sequence invariant. Every generation observed by either detector (fsnotify or hash poll) must be either published to active_generation or rejected with an explicit failed_reload / missed_generation_recovered signal. Silent skip of an intermediate generation is not acceptable, regardless of how fast the next event arrives.

- rapid_back_to_back_atomic_replace_publishes_both: two atomic replacements 11 ms apart; both generations reach active_generation in order, OR the second emits failed_reload / missed_generation_recovered. Never silent stale serving for the duration of a poll interval.
- watch_continuous_during_swap: invariant test asserting the parent-directory watcher captures every Create/Rename on routes.yaml even while a swap is in flight. Must hold across N concurrent swaps.
- hash_poll_recovers_with_signal: when the poll detects on-disk generation ahead of active_generation, missed_generation_recovered is emitted with both generation numbers and a non-zero elapsed-since-observation field.
- generation_sequence_no_silent_skip: across any interleaving of fsnotify events and hash-poll observations, every generation the process sees is either published or rejected with a signal; active_generation is never silently older than the latest observed generation.

Remaining blocker — restart recovery:

When the exporter is killed mid-stream (after N chunks written), the partially-written object stays in the shared object-store prefix until the normal 24-hour retention sweep runs. That leaves a window where:

  - An object containing rows committed before the kill is addressable by its object key.
  - Any signed URL or cache entry issued for that object before kill (if not already invalidated by the chunk-recheck path) can still serve partial data until it expires independently.
  - Cleanup is decoupled from the failure event — it depends on a periodic sweep, not on the exporter's recovery path.

Two acceptable fixes, either of which closes the window without changing the 24h retention policy for completed exports:

  1. Recovery hook on exporter startup: scan the object-store prefix for objects lacking a "complete" marker (or stamped with an in-progress marker) and delete them synchronously before accepting new work.
  2. Atomic write: stream chunks to a temp key, then rename to the final key on successful completion; the temp key never appears under the final export URL, and a startup sweeper cleans any orphaned temp objects.

The drift check is the right place to make the semantic-vs-byte split, but the line has to be drawn by the canonical schema, not by the generator. Here is where engineering stops being the decision-maker and becomes the executor of what the schema says.

Safe to normalize for semantic comparison (pure serialization noise):
  - key ordering inside maps and structs (sort deterministically)
  - numeric representation where the value is mathematically equal (1 vs 1.0, trailing zeros)
  - whitespace between structural elements (indentation, line endings)
  - locale-agnostic decimal separator
  - generator comments and metadata blocks not part of the token value
  - embedded timestamps, nonces, build IDs

Rule of thumb: if the change does not alter the token name, the token value, the alias path, the scope, or the platform target as defined by the canonical schema, it is serialization noise. Anything that touches those four is a semantic call and belongs to the schema, not the generator.

Not safe to silently normalize:
  - whitespace inside a token value, e.g. "Prod " vs "Prod"
  - case, e.g. "Prod" vs "prod"
  - zero-width or invisible Unicode
  - empty string vs absent string
  - aliases, scope paths, platform suffixes

These are identity-bearing by default. The schema is the only thing that can declare any of them insignificant, and the declaration has to be explicit per field.

Why whitespace must not be trimmed by default:
  The collector's current behavior — reject "Prod " as malformed — is correct, and the fix lives on the producer side, not in the normalization layer. If TrimSpace runs before the allowlist, the malformed value slips through as valid "Prod" and the rejection signal that lets the producer catch and fix its bug is destroyed. The same logic applies to case: trimming "Prod " to "Prod" silently and then lowercasing to "prod" is two compounding identity changes that mask the defect. Either the schema defines whitespace and case as insignificant for that field — in which case the canonical source reflects it and the comparison layer applies the rule — or the schema does not, and the value is malformed input that must be reported and rejected.

  Empty vs missing is the same shape of bug. Missing = omit. Empty or malformed = reject. Treating empty as "unknown" or as a synonym for absent collapses two distinct signals and hides a producer defect.

Evidence to retain:
  - raw candidate artifact, with its original byte hash
  - canonicalized form and its hash (so the comparison is reproducible)
  - generation manifest: generator runtime version, locale, deterministic-key-order flag, and the canonical-package version the source owner supplied
  - semantic diff report (what the comparison concluded as equivalent)
  - byte diff report (what serialization noise was stripped)
  - the schema version the comparison ran against

The byte hash on the raw input matters because the semantic decision ("these are equivalent" or "these are not") is only defensible if you can show what was actually compared. Without the original bytes, a later "why did we accept this?" question is unanswerable. This is the artifact set that lets you tell the 2024-04-30 map-ordering case apart from a real semantic regression.

Boundary:
  Engineering owns the generator, the deterministic-key-order flag, the comparison engine, the artifact retention, and the manifest. We do not decide that "Prod " and "Prod" are equivalent, that lowercase folding is safe, or that empty equals absent — those are schema decisions and live in the canonical source Anya owns. The comparison rules themselves should live in a documented spec owned by engineering but reviewed against the schema, so when a future field asks "is whitespace significant here?" the answer points to one place.

  If the schema is silent on whitespace or case for a field, the default is to preserve the producer's exact bytes and treat any deviation as a defect — that is the fail-closed behavior that caught the April 30 incident and that has to stay in place until Anya explicitly relaxes it in the canonical source.

[BLOCKING] Follow-up on metrics-router#1920 — generation/operator/expiry/audit bindings are correct, but single-use is broken; "consumed only after publication" lets two workers both publish under one grant. Require atomic claim before publication; invert the concurrency regression.

Generation/operator/expiry/audit fields are now in place (621 to 618, operator bound, 5-min, audit ID) — those match the prior blocking review. The single-use requirement is not met. Marking the grant consumed only after publication opens a validate-then-publish TOCTOU window. The owner's own concurrency regression is the smoking gun: two workers both validate "unused," both publish, both complete the rollback path. Single-use means single-use — the second worker must not reach the publish step.

Required fix:

  1. Atomic claim, not consume-after-publish. Validation that the grant is unused and the transition to claimed (or in-flight) must be a single operation that completes before publication begins. The first worker to claim proceeds; the second observes a non-"unused" state and fails before any state change on the routing side.

  2. Publish-failure policy — pick one and document it:
       - Fail-closed: a successful claim consumes the grant regardless of publish outcome. Audit the failure but do not return the grant.
       - Release-on-failure: a failed publish returns the grant to "unused" with an audit event. Only safe if the publish path is fully idempotent and the rollback can be cleanly retried.
     Recommend fail-closed unless there's a concrete reason otherwise; this is the safer default for an emergency mechanism.

  3. Expiry semantics with the claim. The 5-minute clock should anchor at claim time (or issuance time — pick one and document it). If expiry is issuance-based, the claim must re-verify the grant hasn't expired at the moment of claim, not only at issuance. Otherwise a slow claimer can use a stale grant.

  4. Generation binding under churn. If a parallel authorized promotion moves the active generation away from 621 between claim and publish (e.g., to 622 via the ordinary path), the grant must fail-closed at publish: target 618 no longer matches the now-current generation. Add a regression for this — it is not covered today.

  5. Audit ID lifecycle. The audit ID must be emitted at claim time, not only at final state. The audit trail needs:
       - claim: operator, grant_id, audit_id, claimed_at, observed_active_gen, target_gen
       - publish outcome: success/fail, final_active_gen, completed_at
       - release event (only if release-on-failure is chosen)
     Audit events for two separate publications under one grant are not acceptable.

Regression requirements — the current concurrency regression documents the bug, so it must be inverted:

  - concurrent_claim_only_one_proceeds: two workers race the same grant; exactly one reaches publish, the other is rejected at the claim step with grant_already_claimed. Assert no second rollback publication and exactly one publish-path invocation.
  - concurrent_claim_publish_failure_fail_closed: worker A claims, publish fails; worker B's claim attempt is rejected (grant_already_claimed); audit shows the failure, grant stays consumed, routing unchanged.
  - concurrent_claim_publish_failure_release_path (only if release-on-failure is chosen): worker A claims, publish fails, grant returns to unused; worker B can then claim and publish successfully; audit shows the release event.
  - claim_after_active_gen_changed: grant bound to 621, claim succeeds, an authorized promotion moves active to 622 before publish completes — publish must fail-closed and audit must record the generation mismatch with no routing change.
  - reused_authorization_cannot_move_routing_backward: existing test must still pass after the fix.
  - expired_authorization_cannot_move_routing_backward: existing test must still pass; expiry check must run at claim time, not only at issuance.
  - old_rollback_enabled_bundle_rejected: existing test must still pass.
  - reload_path_does_not_invoke_rollback: existing test must still pass.

Out of scope (do not couple to this PR):

  - Health-z "active" / last_attempted / last_validated semantics (separate thread).
  - NewMatcher lifecycle and per-gen Tier 1 / bounded Tier 2 caching (separate thread).
  - Metrics-router cap+drop admission policy (separate thread).

PR 309's estimator is a sample-mean approximation: refused_requests × average_points_per_request only equals the true refused-point sum when the mean batch size of refused requests equals the mean batch size of all attempted requests. Replay A satisfies that by accident — the four refused batches average 40,000 / 4 = 10,000, which happens to equal 1,000,000 / 100. It's a mean-equality coincidence, not a correctness property.

Replay B breaks it for two reasons that compound:

  1. Variance. Even if refused batches were a random sample of attempted
     batches, the estimator has variance ≈ |R| × Var(batch_size). With
     four refusals and heterogeneous batch sizes, the realized estimate
     can easily be off by tens of thousands of points on any given run.

  2. Selection bias. Refused batches are not a random sample of
     attempted batches. Request-granularity refusals (memory_limit,
     queue_full, payload_too_large, downstream_unavailable) skew toward
     sizes that don't match the population mean — small batches hit
     tight limiters, large batches hit payload caps. The estimator
     assumes a symmetry the refusal paths don't provide.

The estimator also can't separate the two refusal paths:
  - Path A (whole-request refusal): the batch was never opened, so
    requested_points at refusal time is the only direct measure.
  - Path B (partial_success): rejected_data_points is already in the
    response — the collector emits this as an exact counter.

The fix from the earlier review still applies, and Replay B is the
proof it was needed: emit refused_points as its own monotonic counter.
For path A, increment refused_points by the requested batch size at
refusal. For path B, increment by the value parsed from
partial_success.rejected_data_points. The expression then collapses to
attempted_points − received_points − refused_points, with a derived
zero-check panel.

0:00–4:30 — Floor mobility, no grip load
- 60s: wrist circles both directions, then wrist flexor stretch (arm out, palm up, pull back with other hand) and extensor stretch (arm out, palm down, pull back) — 30s each side
- 60s: forearm self-massage with opposite thumb or a tennis ball along the flexor and extensor bellies, sweeping from elbow toward wrist
- 60s: finger extensor stretch (palm down on the floor, gentle backward pressure) + prayer stretch both directions
- 60s: slow shoulder CARs, 5 each direction
- 30s: wall slides or prone Y-T-W if a mat is around

Goal: tissue warm, full painless ROM, no loading yet.

4:30–9:30 — Easy traversing
- Pick the lowest-angle terrain available (slab or low vertical)
- 5 minutes moving horizontally with open-hand grip on jugs / large holds
- Mix positions: undercling, side-pull, open-hand on big edges, gaston — just explore
- Stay RPE ≤ 4/10, no hard gripping, no max-effort moves
- Purpose: graded tendon loading through varied positions, blood flow into the forearms

A few material things to flag before this sketch is ready to compare against the 20k-permit version on the table:

  1)  Structural shift from semaphore to bounded reservations. The 20k-permit model has one invariant (cap = permits_held, tryAcquire is the only admission gate). This sketch replaces that with two length-bounded counters (global_pending, tenant_pending) plus a multi-step reserve/release/enqueue sequence. The cap invariant has to be restated explicitly: is it now a length invariant (sum of reserved slots <= 2,048, each tenant <= 64) or does permits_held still exist in parallel? If permits_held is gone, the accepted_point and restart checks need a different definition, and "defer 1:1 with admit" needs to be re-mapped onto these counters.

  2)  Order vs. the established sequence. The April-18 invariant is tryAcquire BEFORE accepted_work++ BEFORE enqueue. The sketch does reserve tenant -> reserve global -> enqueue -> mark batch accepted. If "mark batch accepted" is the accepted_work++ step, the order is now enqueue before accepted_work++, which is the opposite of what the race-fix preserved. A request can sit in the queue while accepted_work hasn't been bumped yet, and any parallel admission path that reads accepted_work won't see it. Need to confirm what "mark batch accepted" refers to (HTTP 202 to client, accepted_work counter, accepted_point metric?) and ensure accepted_work++ still fires before enqueue, or that its definition has been intentionally changed.

  3)  Per-tenant cap raised 8 -> 64, and cross-tenant ordering is unspecified. The fairness canary worked at 8 waiting slots per tenant and showed low-volume tenants picking up the next usable ring slot when capacity was idle. With 64, a noisy tenant holds 8x more slots, and the "borrow unused queue capacity" rule (explicitly undefined in the prior draft) is now load-bearing. Also: the sketch doesn't say whether global_pending drains FIFO across tenants, LRU-on-tenant, or weighted round-robin. The earlier invariant was "tenant round-robin is acceptable only if per-tenant FIFO is preserved inside the tenant slot" — that needs to be stated here, not assumed.

  4)  Global cap 2,048 vs. 20k permits. 10x tighter. What's the calibration? 20k was sized to absorb burst + the 1:1 defer/backlog relationship; 2,048 will return 429 under bursts that the prior model would have absorbed. If 2,048 is layered on top of the active-4-per-pod / waiting-N-per-tenant limits (i.e., a third cap), the relationship between global_pending, permits_held, and the active ring needs to be explicit, or the cap invariant becomes ambiguous.

  5)  "Release each held reservation exactly once" — what's the enforcement mechanism? The guarantee is stated but not proven. The cancel-mid-reservation race is the worst case: cancel fires after the tenant reservation but before the global reservation. The sketch handles "global reservation fails -> release tenant," which is the rejection path. It doesn't say what the cancel path does between the two reservations. Options: a per-request released flag with CAS; per-tenant locks (kills throughput); try/finally around the full sequence with cancel observed only at well-defined points. Pick one and write it down — "intended to" isn't enough for a race-fix review.

  6)  Enqueue-failure response to the client. Both reservations succeed, enqueue throws, both are released. Has the client been told anything yet? If a 202 was already sent, the client believes work is queued while the server is about to reject it. The "mark batch accepted only after enqueue" step covers this if "mark accepted" is the response send, but the response code on enqueue failure must be 5xx or 429-with-Retry-After, never 2xx.

  7)  Worker-side release. Cancellation and enqueue-failure are covered. Decompression failure after dequeue is not. The release-on-completion rule from the race-fix needs to apply on worker exit (success, exception, timeout), or the cap silently shrinks as reservations leak.

Before I can compare this against the 20k-permit model line-by-line, I'd want answers to:
   a) Does permits_held still exist, or is it fully replaced by global_pending / tenant_pending?
   b) What is "mark batch accepted" — accepted_work++, HTTP 202, or both?
   c) What synchronization primitive enforces the exactly-once release (CAS flag, lock, try/finally)?
   d) What is the cross-tenant drain order (FIFO / round-robin / weighted)?
   e) What releases the reservation when the worker fails or times out?

Required regressions before load evidence can be accepted for the above-forecast replay. Assumes the candidate preserves the September 5 baseline: 8-waiting cap, 4-active/pod, 2-active/tenant, pre-acceptance accounting, accepted-point integrity, Retry-After on queue-cap 429, empty-tenant removal, restart reconciliation, /healthz generation distinctions, and the Wes race-fix (tryAcquire BEFORE accepted_work++ BEFORE enqueue, release-on-completion, cap=permits_held).

CONCURRENCY (6)
1. Ring-insertion atomic with enqueue: 100 simultaneous requests across N tenants on a single pod. Tenant appears in active ring iff first request passed admission. Failure mode = phantom ring entry from tryAcquire success / enqueue failure.
2. tryAcquire vs ring-insert race: with the Wes fix held, 2x permits-held arrivals for one tenant in the same tick. Exactly 2 enter ring; remainder get 429 with Retry-After; no transient third slot.
3. Eight-waiting cap under burst: 16 concurrent requests for one tenant. Exactly 8 enqueue, 8 receive 429 with Retry-After in [1,3]s. Run 10k iterations.
4. Decompression-slot acquisition race: noisy tenant at 8 waiting + decompression slot available; 100 concurrent requests from a low-volume tenant. Exactly one enters the decompression slot; rest queue or 429. No double-allocation.
5. Cross-pod admission under saturation: 4 pods, verify 2-active/tenant holds globally under concurrent ingest, not just per pod.
6. Bounded decompression holds: verify the bounded decompression limit is honored when admission and ring-insert interleave with cancel and complete.

CANCELLATION (6)
1. Cancel-before-ring: cancel after enqueue but before any ring entry exists for the tenant. Tenant must not appear in the ring.
2. Cancel-with-active: cancel a request holding a ring slot. Slot returns to available pool within bounded time; tenant stays in ring iff other queued requests remain.
3. Cancel-during-decompression: cancel the request holding a decompression slot. Slot returns to ring; no leak.
4. Cancel-empty-queue: cancel all requests for a tenant. Tenant removed from ring; does not block decompression for other tenants.
5. Cancel-vs-completion race: 10k runs of cancel and complete arriving in the same tick for the same request. Exactly one terminal outcome (cancel OR success), never both. The prior 7-of-1000 regression must hold at 0/10k.
6. Cancel-during-restart: in-flight cancellations during restart do not leave orphaned ring entries across the boundary.

SLOT-RELEASE (5)
1. Natural-completion release: ring slot returns to available pool on worker success.
2. Failure-path release: ring slot returns on worker error, not only on cancel.
3. Tenant-removal release: all ring slots held by a removed tenant are released.
4. Decompression-slot reclamation: decompression slots are reclaimable, not pinned by removed tenants.
5. No-leak / no double-release: 10k mixed-completion/cancellation cycles; ring size returns to baseline when all tenants empty; no phantom available capacity from double-release.

NOISY-TENANT FAIRNESS (5)
1. Single-noisy + many-low-volume: 1 noisy tenant at 8 waiting, 20 low-volume tenants fire requests. All low-volume tenants enter ring within bounded time (<100ms) while noisy is still queued.
2. Multi-noisy + low-volume: 4 noisy tenants at 8 waiting each, 20 low-volume tenants. Low-volume still gets ring slots via decompression; not starved behind 32 waiting.
3. Next-usable-slot guarantee: under load, the scheduler patch's claim holds — low-volume tenant does not wait for the 1-second rebuild when a decompression slot is available.
4. /healthz fairness signal: attempted/validated/active counters distinguish correctly; no false-positive 200 under noisy load.
5. Above-forecast saturation: replay at >100% forecast; low-volume p99 admission latency stays bounded while noisy tenants remain at 8-waiting.

ACCEPTANCE-ACCOUNTING (6)
1. Exactly-one-terminal per accepted request: never two terminal records.
2. Exactly-one-accounting per accepted request: cancel and worker-completion paths do not both increment accepted_total / accepted_work.
3. Pre-acceptance accounting preserved: no retroactive adjustment after the point of acceptance.
4. Drop accounting: queue-cap 429 requests do not enter accepted_work, do not produce terminal records, do increment drop counters.
5. Cancel is not double-counted as both drop and completion: terminal record is one or the other; counters reflect exactly one increment.
6. Restart reconciliation: total_accepted = total(success + failed + cancelled) + total_dropped across restart; no leaks, no double-counts. Analog of A1–A5 from the metrics-router owner (active generation advances exactly once per successful reload, /healthz 200 never false-positive, reload failure does not change active generation) applies.

Before-deductible services typically cost the full charge up to the deductible on an HDHP (preventive is exempt, but the stated visits are ordinary office visits, not preventive). I'll assume the visits are subject to deductible on the HDHP — that's the standard HDHP mechanic and the conservative reading.

PPO (deductible already irrelevant here — the deductible is $500 but you won't hit it with five visits):

- 4 primary × $25 = $100
- 1 specialist × $45 = $45
- Total visit cost: **$145**

HDHP (assume each visit is at billed amount until deductible is met; we don't know billed amounts, but a reasonable common assumption for a primary-care visit is ~$150–$250 and specialist ~$300–$450. I'll work this two ways):

Best-case for HDHP (low billed amounts: primary $150, specialist $300):

- 4 × $150 = $600 + 1 × $300 = $300 → $900 total billed, all applied to deductible since under $2,200
- You pay full $900, then 10% coinsurance after deductible — but deductible isn't met, so all $900 out of pocket.

Typical billed (primary $200, specialist $400):

- 4 × $200 = $800 + 1 × $400 = $400 → $1,200, all under $2,200 deductible
- All $1,200 out of pocket.

Higher billed (primary $250, specialist $450):

- 4 × $250 = $1,000 + 1 × $450 = $450 → $1,450, still under $2,200
- All $1,450 out of pocket.

So HDHP visit cost is roughly **$900–$1,450** depending on billed amounts — call it ~$1,200 as a working middle.

HDHP minus PPO visit cost: ~$1,200 − $145 = ~**$1,055 more out-of-pocket on visits**.

**Net HDHP cost vs PPO (year with 4 primary + 1 specialist, no procedures):**

Premium savings: +$1,456
Visit cost increase: −$1,055
Employer HSA contribution: +$900 (effectively dollars in your HSA pocket)

Net HDHP advantage: $1,456 − $1,055 + $900 = **+$1,301 in HDHP's favor** for this utilization profile.

Even at the worst-case visit billing ($1,450), HDHP still wins: $1,456 − $1,305 + $900 = $1,051 ahead.

**The crossover point — when does PPO catch up?**

PPO wins when (premium_diff + HSA − visit_savings) ≤ 0, i.e. when visit out-of-pocket on PPO exceeds HDHP by more than $1,456 + $900 = $2,356.

On the HDHP, that requires enough spending to meet the $2,200 deductible. PPO catches up only in a year with real medical spend beyond ordinary visits — exactly the case you flagged by saying "no planned procedure."

Side-by-side, using 26 paychecks and your expected use (4 office visits + 1 specialist, no planned procedure):

Annual premiums
- HDHP: 26 x $92 = $2,392
- PPO:  26 x $148 = $3,848
- Delta: PPO costs $1,456 more across the year

Employer HSA contribution
- HDHP: +$900 (employer-funded)
- PPO:  $0
- Delta: HDHP wins by $900

Routine visit costs (estimates; HDHP applies negotiated rates to the deductible until met)
- HDHP: 4 PCP + 1 specialist at typical in-network rates ($200 / $400), all applied to the $2,200 deductible -> ~$1,200 paid before any coinsurance
- PPO:  4 x $25 + 1 x $45 = $145 in fixed visit copays
- Delta: HDHP pays ~$1,055 more at the visit counter for the same visits

Net for stated use
HDHP advantage = $1,456 (premium savings) + $900 (HSA) - $1,055 (extra visit cost) ~= $1,301 in your pocket.

Cash-flow timing
- Every paycheck the HDHP leaves you $56 more take-home; across 26 paychecks that's the $1,456 above, available throughout the year instead of paid upfront as premium.
- HSA contribution timing depends on Sphere's schedule. Lump-sum at plan start is friendliest; if it's spread, the cash lands pro-rated across the year. Either way, it's your money to spend on qualified care.
- HDHP also lets you contribute your own pre-tax dollars into the HSA, which can cover the deductible and lower taxable income further. (Not counted in the $1,301.)
- PPO: more leaves each paycheck; less surprise at the visit because copays are fixed and small.

Downside exposure
- HDHP: $2,200 deductible before the 10% coinsurance. Each non-preventive visit is paid at full negotiated rate until the deductible is met. OOP max is typically ~$5,000-$6,500 individual for an HDHP, which is lower than most PPOs.
- PPO: $500 deductible, then 15% coinsurance. Lower front-end per-visit exposure, but OOP max usually runs ~$7,000+.
- For your stated use (no procedure, deductible comfortably coverable) neither max binds. If a major event hits mid-year, the HDHP's typically lower OOP max caps total exposure sooner, and any balance you've built in the HSA cushions it.

Recommendation
HDHP is the better fit for your expected year. The $1,456 premium savings plus the $900 employer HSA contribution comfortably outweigh the ~$1,055 extra you'd pay at the visit counter, and your stated ability to cover the deductible makes the front-loaded exposure manageable. The PPO only makes sense if you expect a high-cost event early in the year or strongly prefer predictable per-visit copays over building an HSA balance.

SHOPPING LIST (for 3; pantry staples in italics)

Produce
  - 1 whole chicken, 4–5 lb
  - 2 lb Yukon Gold potatoes (creamy) or russets (fluffy)
  - 1 lb fresh green beans
  - 12 oz fresh cranberries
  - 1 orange, 1 lemon (optional, for cavity)
  - 1 head garlic
  - 1 small bunch fresh thyme (or dried poultry seasoning)

Dairy
  - 1 lb butter (≈1 stick: chicken rub, mash, beans)
  - ½ pint heavy cream or whole milk

Pantry — confirm on hand
  - olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper
  - sugar (cranberry sauce)
  - chicken broth, low-sodium (~2 cups, or 1 bouillon cube + water)
  - cornstarch or AP flour (gravy)
  - Anya brings dessert — skip

────────────────────────────────────────────────

WEDNESDAY PREP (≈45 min, evening)

The point is to push every Thursday task you can off Thursday. Cranberry sauce is the biggest win — it actually improves overnight in the fridge.

  0:00  Pat chicken very dry with paper towels; season generously all over and inside the cavity with salt and pepper. Place uncovered on a plate or rack over a sheet pan in the fridge. Dry skin = crispier roast.   ~5 min

  0:05  Cranberry sauce: 12 oz cranberries + ¾ cup sugar + zest and juice of 1 orange + pinch salt + ½ cup water in a small saucepan. Simmer 8–10 min until berries burst and the sauce jells on a spoon. Cool, jar, refrigerate.  ~12 min, mostly hands-off

  0:17  Peel and cube potatoes into 1-inch chunks; submerge in cold water in a covered pot in the fridge.  ~8 min

  0:25  Trim green beans (snap ends, wash, spin dry). Store in a container with a paper towel in the fridge.  ~6 min

  0:31  Stage Thursday gear: roasting pan, instant-read thermometer, masher, colander, tongs. Set out 1 stick butter to soften. Pour 2 cups broth into a jar; refrigerate.  ~4 min

  0:35  Wipe counters, run the dishwasher if needed, set the table. Done by 0:45.

────────────────────────────────────────────────

THURSDAY (Anya arrives 4:00 PM, dinner 5:30 PM)

  2:30–3:30 PM   Kibo's substantial afternoon walk. Aim for 60 min, 6-ft leash, water. Land back by 3:30.

  3:25 PM  Preheat oven to 425°F, rack lower-middle.

  3:35 PM  Chicken: stuff cavity with halved lemon + thyme sprigs (optional). Rub all over with 2 Tbsp softened butter, salt, pepper. Roast on a rack in a shallow pan, breast-up.
            Target ~60–65 min → done ~4:35–4:40 PM.
            (No other burner needed yet.)

  4:00 PM  Anya arrives. Drink, catch up — chicken is hands-off.

  4:25 PM  Potatoes on: drain cold water, refill with fresh cold salted water, bring to boil, then simmer 15 min until fork-tender.  (Single burner in use.)

  4:40 PM  Probe chicken thigh (avoid bone). Pull at 160–165°F — carryover lands at 165°F. Transfer to a board, tent loosely with foil. Rest 15–20 min; this is your window.

  4:55 PM  Drain potatoes. Return to the hot pot off-heat. Add 4 Tbsp butter, ¼–⅓ cup warm cream/milk, salt. Mash, cover. (Off-burner, covered, holds fine.)

  5:05 PM  Green beans: large skillet, 1 Tbsp olive oil + 1 Tbsp butter, 1 smashed garlic clove, all the beans, big pinch salt. Sauté 6–8 min until bright and just tender. Pull garlic.  (One burner, ~8 min.)

  5:13 PM  Gravy: pour all but ~2 Tbsp drippings from the roasting pan; set pan on a burner over medium heat. Whisk in 1 Tbsp flour, cook 1 min, whisk in 1½ cups warm broth, simmer 3–4 min until glossy. Salt/pepper.  (One burner, ~5 min.)

  5:15 PM  Carve chicken (rested ~25 min — plenty). Slice breast, separate thighs/drumsticks, arrange on a warm platter.

  5:25 PM  Plate: warm bowl for mashed potatoes, dish for beans, platter for chicken, small bowl for cranberry sauce (pull from fridge at 5:10 so it loses its chill), gravy boat. Carry to table.

  5:30 PM  Sit down.

  ~6:45 PM  Anya's dessert + coffee/tea.

  7:30 PM  Kibo's evening walk.

  ~8:00 PM  Wind-down. Laptop closed. Thursday rule still holds — Anya out the door by 8 keeps the evening intact.

────────────────────────────────────────────────

CHECKPOINTS & FAILSAFES

  - Single burner in active use at any moment (potatoes → beans → gravy, staggered). Four-burner limit is not binding; oven + 1 burner does the day.
  - If chicken runs 5 min long: pull potatoes to lowest possible heat (covered); start green beans anyway — they hold 5 min no problem.
  - If chicken runs 10 min long: tent it loosely, crank oven to 450°F for the last stretch, serve green beans and potatoes as they finish and let people start on sides.
  - Mashed potatoes stiffen on hold: re-whisk with a splash of warm milk right before carrying to table.
  - Don't carve before 15 min rest — juices will run and the breast goes dry. 25 min is fine, 30 min is the ceiling.

Net: Wednesday is one focused 45-minute session (most of it hands-off); Thursday active cooking is ~50 minutes between 3:35 and 5:25 PM, with Anya arriving into a calm, chicken-scented kitchen rather than a working one.

The December 31 rule

For both the IRS and New York, your filing status is locked in by your status on the last day of the year. Because you were married on December 31, 2025, you are treated as married for the entire 2025 tax year. You cannot file Single or Head of Household, regardless of when in November the wedding happened. That leaves exactly two choices: Married Filing Jointly (MFJ) or Married Filing Separately (MFS). The same two choices apply on the New York return, with the same Dec 31 lock-in.

Why MFJ is the default

For most married couples, MFJ produces a lower combined tax. The MFJ brackets are roughly twice the Single brackets up through the higher brackets, the MFJ standard deduction is double the MFS standard deduction, and a long list of credits and deductions are denied, sharply limited, or phased out at much lower incomes at MFS. If neither of you has unusual circumstances, MFJ is almost certainly the right call.

Compact MFJ vs MFS comparison

Item                        MFJ                              MFS
Standard deduction (fed)    $30,000                          $15,000 each
Bracket structure           Wider brackets, combined income  Two parallel Single schedules
EITC                        Allowed if you qualify           Denied
Education credits           Allowed                          Limited/denied
Student loan interest       Allowed (phase-out ~$155-175k)   Denied
Roth IRA contribution       Phase-out ~$236-246k MFJ         Phase-out $0-25k each
Traditional IRA deduction   Phase-out ~$126-146k MFJ         Phase-out $0-10k each
  (active participant)
Child Tax Credit            Up to $2,000 per child           $1,000 each (split)
Medical 7.5% AGI floor      Combined AGI                     Each spouse's own AGI
Capital loss limit          $3,000 combined                  $3,000 each
SALT cap                    $10,000 combined                 $5,000 each
Itemize choice              Free (either, both, or neither)  Forced parity (NY: same)
Refund offset risk          Either spouse's debt offsets it  Clean spouse's refund protected
Tax liability               Joint and several                Each only on their own return

When MFS is actually worth modeling

  - One of you has unusually high itemized deductions (medical over 7.5% of AGI, mortgage interest on a large loan, large charitable gifts) that get drowned by the other's income at MFJ
  - One of you is on an income-driven student loan repayment plan (IBR/PAYE/SAVE); MFS bases the payment on one income
  - One of you has tax debts, back support, defaulted federal student loans, or other liabilities that could seize a joint refund; MFS isolates the clean spouse
  - One of you has questionable items (hobby-loss Schedule C, complex K-1s, basis problems) you don't want to put on a joint return
  - A large medical expense is concentrated in one spouse

If none of those apply, MFJ is the answer and MFS is not worth the lost credits.

New York specifics

  - NY is not a community property state for income tax, so at MFS each of you reports only the income you personally earned — the Sphere W-2 stays with you, the hospital W-2 stays with Devika
  - NY forces both spouses to take the same itemize-or-standard choice; if one itemizes, the other must itemize too
  - NY largely conforms to the federal MFS denials (EITC, student loan interest, etc.); NY has its own EITC and Empire State Child Credit, both unavailable at MFS
  - NY 2025 standard deduction is roughly $16,050 MFJ vs about $8,000 each MFS (confirm in-software — these get adjusted annually)

Quick frame: this is explanation, not a recommendation to file. Three pieces, in order.

What usually moves the number between joint and separate

The split comes from a handful of mechanical things, not anything exotic.

  - Standard deduction. MFJ gets one combined standard deduction ($30,000 for 2025). MFS gives each spouse their own $15,000, so each return has a lower floor before income is taxed. On its own this almost always favors joint for a two-earner couple.

  - Bracket width. MFJ brackets are wider than two MFS brackets stacked together, so the same combined income lands in lower marginal rates when filed jointly. For two solid earners this is usually where the biggest savings come from.

  - Credits and phase-outs. Lots of credits (education, saver's, child-related, EV, residential energy) phase out at much lower incomes for MFS, and a few (student loan interest deduction, Roth IRA contributions at higher incomes) are unavailable entirely on MFS. Even when MFS looks slightly better on tax owed, losing credits can flip it.

  - Itemized deductions. If one of you carries most of the medical, mortgage interest, or charitable deductions, MFS can let that person's lower AGI push those over the 7.5% or 2% floors more easily. But both spouses have to itemize, and the standard-deduction comparison above still has to be paid.

  - Net Investment Income Tax and Additional Medicare Tax. These surtaxes kick in at much lower income on MFS, so investment income or wages past the MFS thresholds get hit harder.

  - Capital loss limit. MFS lets each spouse use up to $3,000 of net loss against ordinary income — a $6,000 total ceiling instead of $3,000. Rarely the deciding factor, but real.

  - NY side. New York largely follows the federal choice. MFS in NY is just two separate NY returns; the community-property rules that apply to MFS in some other states don't apply here.

How meaningful the comparison is while the interest statement is missing

A typical 1099-INT from a HYSA or checking account is small — a few hundred to maybe a couple thousand over a year. The federal tax on it at your marginal rate is usually tens of dollars, maybe low hundreds. NY tax on top is small in proportion.

So the missing interest almost certainly does not flip a clear-cut joint-vs-separate outcome. What it does:

  - Make the current numbers not-quite-final. Treat them as directionally right, exact number pending.
  - Be a tell that the document set isn't complete. If 1099-INT is missing, double-check whether 1099-DIV, 1099-B, the South Slope 1098 mortgage interest, HSA statements, and any K-1s are all in hand. A missing $400 of interest is small; a missing $4,000 of dividends or a K-1 you forgot is not.
  - Be worth flagging if the two scenarios are genuinely close — within a few hundred dollars of each other. In that case, get the interest statement before deciding.

  - Marital status as of December 31, 2025. That is the lock. If you were legally married by 12/31/2025, MFJ or MFS are the only choices — Single and Head of Household are off the table.

The 1099-INT is one form reporting one number: $364.27 of taxable interest from a jointly held savings account. So there is exactly one underlying dollar amount to account for — the only question is how to place it on each of the three drafts without letting the same dollar appear twice in any single filing.

In the joint (MFJ) draft

Enter the full $364.27 once on Form 1040, line 2b — the "taxable interest" line on the front page. Because the account is in both your names, the entire interest amount belongs on the joint return. There is nothing to split here. That is the "enter once" answer.

In the two separate (MFS) drafts

Because the account is jointly owned, IRS Publication 555 says each spouse reports their own share — a 50/50 split is the default when nothing else has been agreed. So you put half on each return:

- Alex's MFS draft: $182.14 on Schedule 1, line 4b (taxable interest)
- Devika's MFS draft: $182.14 on Schedule 1, line 4b (taxable interest)

The two halves add back to $364.27 — the same number that lives on the MFJ draft. That is not double counting; it is the same $364.27 carved in half for the MFS view. Double counting would be putting $364.27 on each MFS return (which would inflate interest to $728.27 across the two MFS drafts), or treating all three drafts as live returns at once — which is why only one of them ever gets filed.

What to verify before you lean on the updated comparison

- The account is actually titled jointly in both names, not as a convenience, custodial, or "and/or" account. The 1099 lists Alex's TIN as the recipient, but the IRS allocation rule follows ownership, not whose TIN is on the form.
- There is not a second 1099-INT for the same account issued to Devika with her TIN. If there is, that becomes a nominee 1099 — the spouse who physically received it reports the full amount on their own return and then reallocates the owner's share, rather than each return picking up a fresh $364.27.
- Box 4 is $0, so no backup withholding was taken; nothing extra to reconcile there.
- The blank state box is normal here — it just means the payer did not withhold state tax, which is common for federally chartered banks paying NY residents; the income is still NY-taxable.
- The payer name and EIN on the form match the actual bank, so you are not keying in a stray 1099.

No-double-counting checklist

- MFJ draft: one entry of $364.27 on Form 1040 line 2b.
- Alex's MFS draft: $182.14 on Schedule 1 line 4b.
- Devika's MFS draft: $182.14 on Schedule 1 line 4b.
- Confirm $182.14 + $182.14 = $364.27 — the halves must reconcile to the full 1099 amount.
- Do not import the same 1099-INT as a full $364.27 into both MFS returns.
- Only one of these drafts becomes the actual filed return; the others are comparison views.
- If your tax software has a scenario or what-if mode, use it so the same 1099 entry is not auto-duplicated across all three views.
