10-MINUTE OUTLINE — How the Cross-Service Intake Rule Works in Practice

OPEN (~30 sec)
- Recurring pattern: cross-boundary proposals needed the right reviewers in the right seats, but the naming was inconsistent.
- Today: walk the April 17 Lantern incident-load shared-registration migration as one completed example.
- Thesis: naming reviewers created clarity, not a new gate.

THE RULE (~2 min)
- Three roles, separately named in each cross-boundary proposal:
  1. Mapped implementation and release owner — same owner as before; ordinary release authority.
  2. Rollback owner — separately named.
  3. Exception owner — only present when a specific boundary is triggered: invariant, provenance, failure-mode, ownership, or escalation.
- The exception owner reviews one thing: that one boundary.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO (~90 sec)
- It is not a centralized approval gate. No Staff IC signs off as a default approver.
- It does not move implementation or release readiness off the mapped owner.
- It does not move day-to-day operational ownership.
- The exception owner is a boundary reviewer, not a release approver.

LANTERN — WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED (~4 min)
- April 17 incident-load shared-registration migration:
  - Product Engineering owned implementation and release. Unchanged.
  - Iris owned customer interpretation. Unchanged.
  - I reviewed only the shared-registration safety and failure-mode boundary — the triggered exception.
- What my review covered:
  - The shared-registration safety gate.
  - The 240-lookup LPS-001 rerun: 16 denied requests made no adapter call; 12 stale or missing inputs rendered explicit unknown; no safety or authorization violation.
- What my review did NOT cover:
  - Whether the code was ready to ship — that was the mapped owner's call.
  - Whether telemetry was healthy — not my lane.
  - Customer-facing interpretation — Iris.
  - Whether rollback was correctly staged — the rollback owner.
- Outcome: customer access unchanged. Owner map unchanged.

CLOSE (~2 min)
- Take-away: when a cross-boundary proposal lands, ask which boundary is actually triggered, and name only the reviewer for that boundary.
- If no boundary is triggered: mapped owner follows the ordinary release process. No exception review, no separate sign-off.
- Mapped owner keeps the release. Exception owner reviews the boundary. That's the whole rule.

## What the rule requires, given this fact pattern

The May 14 decision binds the join to interval coverage of the source event's timestamp. It does not authorize ordering-based selection, and it does not authorize disambiguation of overlapping intervals by storage position. The decision says nothing about overlapping intervals because Iris and you didn't face one — but the structure of the rule is what tells you what to do:

- The rule permits a rename join **only** on the basis of a published alias record with a covering effective interval.
- There is no mention of "if multiple cover, prefer X." There is no tie-breaker by ordering, recency, storage position, or canonical-id preference.
- The rule explicitly forbids heuristic inference from anything other than the published alias record's covering interval.
- The fallback for "alias is missing OR timestamp falls outside the interval" is to keep signals separate and render ownership as explicit unknown.

So when two aliases both cover, the rule as written is **not satisfied by either one alone** — the candidate has two records, both covering, no defined tie-breaker, and the deployed rule does not authorize picking one.

The conservative and decision-consistent read is: **do not join; keep signals separate; render ownership as explicit unknown.** That is the same fallback the rule mandates for absent and out-of-interval aliases. The doc text Iris and you settled on was deliberately written that way — the "absent or out-of-interval" cases share a fallback because the rule's contract with the UI is "the only reason to join is a single covering alias; otherwise, stay separate and say so."

## Why the candidate's behavior is a fail, not just a gap

The candidate is not a partial implementation of the May 14 rule. Its observable behavior is the opposite of the rule's contract:

- The candidate says: when two records cover, the chosen canonical service is determined by storage order.
- The rule says: a rename join is permitted only on the basis of a covering alias, with no inference from anything else.
- Storage order is, structurally, an inference from a non-rule signal. It is operator-chosen (or insertion-chosen, or shard-chosen, or replica-chosen). The candidate's selection changes when that operator flips a knob. That is exactly the "heuristic inference from non-rule signals" the rule forbids.
- The candidate is also non-deterministic in a way that matters operationally: two runs against the same data can produce two different canonical owners. That's not a coverage-based rule.

A candidate that "renders ownership for that canonical service; reversing storage order changes the selected service" is, by construction, **not a coverage-based join**. It is an order-dependent lookup. That's a different rule and not approved.

Reasoning, grounded in what we've already established across the Lantern fixtures:

  Provenance comes from the source, not from transport. Authority freshness is measured from the source timestamp the record carries when it leaves its source (owner-map pipeline, deploy pipeline, incident-load source, etc.). The 24-hour owner-map limit, the stale-permitted-source handling, and the "missing_provenance → explicit unknown" rule all assume the source timestamp is the only timestamp that determines freshness. Rehearsal-generation time is transport timing — it tells you when an artifact was rendered in your test harness, not when the underlying authority was observed at its source.

  Substituting it would break the rehearsal's purpose in three concrete ways:

  1. Old records appear fresh. A fixture whose underlying source timestamp is 30 hours old would render as 0 hours old because rehearsal-generation is "now." The freshness gate would never trip, and the "explicit unknown for stale permitted source" path becomes unreachable in rehearsal.
  2. Timestamp-less records get an implicit timestamp. That contradicts "if any required provenance field is missing, the external result is 'unknown' with a 'missing_provenance' reason" and re-introduces the failure mode we already locked down — fallback to non-source timing.
  3. The fail-closed correction stops being testable.   - For stale-authority tests, the fixture's source timestamp is set to >24h ago and the rehearsal verifies explicit unknown. For missing-provenance tests, the fixture omits the source timestamp field entirely and the rehearsal verifies explicit unknown with missing_provenance. For fresh-authority tests, the source timestamp is recent and within the freshness window.
  - Rehearsal-generation time is recorded separately as observation/access time on the rehearsal artifact, labeled as such. It is never written into the authority record and never compared against the freshness window.

Authority-identity mismatch in the Lantern context is the gap between two things:

1. The **authoritative record at its source** — the owner map for published service identity, Cardinality Guardrails for pipeline limits and cost. Each has its own `source_timestamp` baked into the record itself, and Iris's 2026-05-28 alias strings make that timestamp load-bearing: an owner-map alias is valid only "effective at this source event timestamp," and absent that coverage the answer is "Ownership unknown."
2. The **authority reference** that travels through the contract — a pointer, encoded as `(authority_type, authority_record_id, source_timestamp)`. Not values. Not a copy.

The mismatch arises when those two don't line up. Concretely:
- The triple doesn't resolve to one real authoritative record (record missing, retired, or wrong authority_type for what's being asked).
- The `source_timestamp` carried in the reference isn't the record's own source_timestamp — it's a fetch, generation, or attempt time being smuggled in as provenance. That's the substitution failure mode the 2026-07-30 clarification calls out: fetch/gen/attempt times are separate metadata, not the record's own timestamp, and a record that has no source_timestamp of its own must fail closed as unavailable.
- The reference says one `authority_type` (e.g., `owner_map` for service identity) but the consumer reads values from another (e.g., Cardinality Guardrails limit/cost). This is the no-copied-values boundary expressed as an identity question — Lantern can't act as if it's holding a Cardinality Guardrails record when it isn't.
- Cross-tenant or stale-resolution paths where the reference resolves at all but to a record that no longer covers the timestamp in question. That's the missing-or-stale regression requirement covering both candidates.

A coherent authority reference is one where `authority_type`, `authority_record_id`, and `source_timestamp` identify the same authoritative record at its true source, the record's own timestamp matches what's in the reference, and nothing in the contract substitutes a non-source timestamp for provenance.

What the passing drift check failed to prove

The drift check is a comparison: generated output vs recorded output. A pass means byte-equality between those two sides. It does not establish any of the following:

  - Provenance. A pass on iOS/Android only proves they match the recorded baseline. It says nothing about which canonical-package version produced either side of that comparison.   - Completeness. Drift-check runs over what was submitted. A pass on iOS/Android tells you nothing about whether web was enumerated as expected, whether another platform was enumerated and omitted, or whether the expected set was fully represented.
  - Authority binding. The dedup key (team, release-candidate, canonical-package-version) is recorded in artifact metadata, not derived from drift output. A passing drift check does not bind the RC to canonical-package version 3.14.2; it only confirms the compared artifacts are identical.
  - Signal on the failed platform. Two clean passes give no information about why web failed — only that web's generated output is not byte-equal to its recorded counterpart.

In short: a drift pass is a "no-difference detected" verdict, not a "this RC is bound to canonical-package version X and all expected outputs are accounted for" verdict. The latter requires the source owner (or artifact metadata) to assert it.

Timing aimed at eating ~6:30 PM so Kibo's loop fits after. Start ~5:50.

Quantities (2 people, light leftovers possible):
- Couscous: 3/4 cup dry + 3/4 cup boiling water + pinch salt + 1 Tbsp olive oil
- Eggplant: about 2/3 of the large one, cubed 3/4"
- Chickpeas: full can, drained
- Tomatoes: ~1 cup halved (most of the pint)
- Yogurt sauce: ~1/3 cup yogurt + juice of 1/2 lemon + 1 small grated garlic clove + pinch salt + olive oil drizzle
- Garnish: ~1/3 block feta crumbled, small handful parsley chopped, remaining lemon in wedges
- Pan: 2-3 Tbsp olive oil, 2 garlic cloves minced, salt, pepper, and either cumin, smoked paprika, or Aleppo/sumac

Order of operations:
- 5:50 — Kettle on. Cube eggplant, halve tomatoes, mince garlic, chop parsley, drain chickpeas.
- 5:52 — Couscous: boil 3/4 cup water, pour over couscous in a bowl with salt + 1 Tbsp oil, cover tight with a plate.
- 5:53 — Large skillet, medium-high, 2-3 Tbsp oil. Eggplant in, salt, leave it alone 3-4 min to brown.
- 5:57 — Stir eggplant, add HALF the garlic. Cook 3-4 min more.
- 6:01 — Push eggplant aside, add chickpeas + tomatoes + remaining garlic + spice of choice to the pan. Cook 4-5 min, tomatoes should blister and slump.
- 6:02 — Sauce: 1/3 cup yogurt + half a lemon's juice + grated garlic clove + pinch salt + olive oil, stir, into the fridge.
- 6:06 — Couscous done, fluff with fork, keep covered.
- 6:08 — Check eggplant tenderness. If a knife slides in easily, you're plating. If not, another 2 min on low.
- 6:10 — Plate: couscous base, eggplant-chickpea-tomato on top, big dollop of cold yogurt sauce, feta crumbles, parsley, lemon wedge.
- 6:15 — Eat.
- 6:35 — Out the door with Kibo.

Cleanup: one skillet, one bowl, cutting board, knife. Soak the skillet while you eat; the yogurt sauce bowl goes straight in the dishwasher. Fits your usual one-pan rule.

If you start closer to 6:00, drop the eggplant cubes to 1/2" so they cook in 8 min instead of 12 — you'll still plate by ~6:30.

**Expected-use scenario (no other care):**

| | PPO | HDHP |
|---|---|---|
| Premium | $3,848 | $2,392 |
| HSA contribution | — | −$900 |
| Office visits (4 PCP + 1 specialist) | 4×$25 + 1×$45 = $145 | $0 (under $2,200 ded) |
| Other care | $0 | $0 |

HDHP saves about **$2,501/yr** at your expected use.

**Sensitivity — when does HDHP lose?**

For HDHP to cost more than PPO, you'd need enough *non-preventive* care beyond office visits to eat the $2,501 premium gap. Office visits are absorbed by the HDHP deductible with no HDHP advantage over PPO copays ($145 of PPO copays already offsets $145 of HDHP deductible spending), so the relevant question is: what total allowed amount X (beyond preventive + office visits) makes PPO ≤ HDHP?

PPO: $3,848 + $145 + min(X, $500) + 0.15·max(0, X−$500)
HDHP: $2,392 − $900 + min(X+office, $2,200) + 0.10·max(0, X+office − $2,200)

Setting them equal for X > $500 and ignoring office (already counted): no positive solution exists — HDHP wins across the entire range.

That's because PPO's $3,848 − $2,392 + $900 = $2,356 premium gap is more than PPO's $500 deductible advantage ($500 − 10%×($2,200−$500) = $320), and coinsurance favors HDHP by 5 points.

**Recommendation:** Based on your stated expected use and no planned procedure, **the HDHP with the $900 HSA contribution is substantially cheaper**. The margin is wide enough that even one moderate unforeseen episode (e.g. an ER visit + follow-up, minor procedure) still leaves HDHP ahead. HDHP only loses if you have a major event AND you can predict it ahead of open enrollment — which contradicts the "no planned procedure" framing.

Two problems, two different systems — the comparison matters more than the grade.

V5 compression + heel-hook transition:
  - Sustained tension = continuous load on forearms, core, scapulae
  - Heel-hook transition = discrete motor skill (hip mobility + hamstring + shifting tension source from arms to legs)
  - The transition itself is probably the single highest-stress move on the problem
  - Limiters: pump ceiling and quality of the transition
  - Stop signal: pump >7/10, hips sagging, heel slipping off, breath holding

V6 vertical + small edges + footwork:
  - Discrete, defined sequence — each move is rehearsable
  - Small edges = finger/tendon load accumulates subtly even when pump is low
  - Footwork = precise and repeatable from the ground
  - Pulling power isn't the limiter — position and foot sequence are
  - Limiters: finger tendon tolerance, foot precision, mental fade from perfectionism
  - Stop signal: sloppy feet, crimping harder than needed, finger tenderness, micro-pump you stop noticing

The shared trap: each problem punishes a different failure mode. V5 punishes going too long on a single burn (the pump floor hides). V6 punishes grinding (the finger tendons stay quiet until the next morning).

Four-session plan, ~75-90 min total each, longer warmup retained, total project time per session capped at 30-40 min:

Session 1 — Read, rehearse, learn the moves
  Warmup (15-20 min):
    - Traversing, easy V0-V2, open-hand grips, easy footwork problems
    - Get blood into forearms and feet before any project work
  V5 (15-20 min):
    - Walk it off, name holds and resting positions out loud
    - Try the heel-hook transition in isolation from a stick or low start — that move is the project, learn it first
    - Drill compression body positions on easy terrain: hip-in, scapulae engaged, breath held through the line
    - 1-2 single-move or 2-move links at sub-max effort
    - Stop at first sign of pump, hip drop, or sloppy heel
  V6 (15-20 min):
    - Walk it off, identify holds and resting hands
    - Downclimb the line foot-only twice to memorize the foot sequence
    - Rehearse each move statically: stick the hold, place feet deliberately, breathe, lower
    - 1-2 single-move or 2-move links with deliberate feet
    - Stop at first sloppy foot placement, crimp creep, or finger tenderness
  Cooldown (5-10 min):
    - Easy traversing, walk home
    - Same-day stop: pump >7/10, any sharp pain, mental fade
    - Next-morning check: finger tenderness, ankle awareness, heel-hook knee/hip niggle

Session 2 — Drill discrete skills into short links
  Warmup (15-20 min): same longer warmup, plus 1-2 easy moves on each problem's wall type
  V5 (20-25 min):
    - 4-6 isolated rehearsals of the heel-hook transition and adjacent compression positions
    - One 3-4 move link from the start, focused on resting between moves
    - Rest 5+ min between attempts (pump recovery, especially after compression links)
    - Stop when heel slips, hips drop, or pump reaches 7/10
  V6 (15-20 min):
    - Foot-only downclimb x 2 — confirm foot sequence is memorized
    - 4-6 static move rehearsals (stick each, deliberate feet, 2-3 sec pause)
    - One 3-4 move link, breathing at every resting hold
    - Rest 3-5 min between attempts (tendon recovery, not pump)
    - Stop when feet get imprecise, crimping intensifies, fingers feel hot or tender
  Cooldown (5-10 min): same

Session 3 — Link progression, approach the send window
  Warmup (15-20 min): same, plus 1-2 moves at project grade or one grade easier to dial grip
  V5 (20-25 min):
    - 2-3 longer links (4-6 moves) with emphasis on finding and using resting positions
    - One full attempt from the ground if previous links felt clean
    - If the first full attempt felt strong, allow a second
    - Hard cap: 2 full attempts on V5 this session
  V6 (15-20 min):
    - 1-2 longer links (4-6 moves) emphasizing footwork continuity and breath at rests
    - One full attempt if links were clean
    - Hard cap: 2 full attempts on V6 this session
  Both: stop after the second full attempt on either problem regardless of outcome. Form decay on the third attempt is how you wreck a tendon or blow the heel-hook transition.

Session 4 — Send window
  Warmup (15-20 min): same; arrive slightly warmer and more dialed in than usual
  Decide which problem gets the day:
    - If one feels a session or two away, give it the bulk
    - If both feel close, alternate: V5 attempt → rest → V6 attempt → rest, repeat
  Per-problem send attempts:
    - Cap at 2-3 full attempts per problem
    - Rest fully between attempts (5+ min for V5, 4+ min for V6)
    - Stop on the first attempt where form slips, even if you think you can push through
  Cooldown (5-10 min): same
  Four possible endings:
    - Both sent: walk away. Don't grind repeats — you have nothing to prove and more sessions are coming.
    - One sent: that problem is done. Give the other 1-2 send attempts only, then stop.
    - Neither sent but close: stop while you still trust the moves. Session 5 starts clean.
    - Neither sent and form is shot: stop and reassess — either problem may need more single-move drilling before another send session.

Cross-session stop rules (apply to all four):
  - Pump or grip quality >7/10: stop project work, cool down
  - Sharp or pinching pain anywhere: stop, ice only if new ache, contact clinician if it persists
  - Heel-hook quality degrading (heel slipping, hip dropping, knee tracking off): stop V5 immediately
  - Foot precision degrading (slapping, missing, hesitation): stop V6 immediately
  - Crimp intensity creeping up on small edges: stop V6, the tendons are talking
  - Mental fade (going through the motions, breath holding, "just one more"): stop. That's how you learn nothing and injure something.
  - Total project time per session: 30-40 min hard cap, no exceptions
  - Next-morning check: finger tenderness, heel-hook knee/hip niggle, ankle awareness, persistent fatigue — note it and back off next session

The progression logic in one line: each session should teach you something you didn't know the previous session. If you finish and can't name what you learned, you went too hard or didn't rehearse enough. The four sessions are read → drill → link → send, in that order, and skipping ahead is how problems get "almost sent" forever.

Plan choice (PPO vs HDHP) — locked for the plan year

HSA payroll amount — adjustable any time
- A per-paycheck pre-tax deduction. Most employer portals let you change it per-paycheck or monthly.
- You can set $0 on Oct 23 and raise it in March. Set it higher now and lower it later. Both work.

The HSA amount is the lever you keep tuning all year. The plan is the lever that's binding.

Based on tonight's findings, here's a revised plan for sessions 3 and 4. The structure is the same on both nights; session 4 just biases toward send attempts under freshness rather than further drilling.

SESSION SPACING
  Sessions 3 and 4 should be at least 6-7 days apart, ideally a week. Tonight (Oct 21) plus the 11-day gap from session 1 worked well — your CNS and skin recovered, and you came in with a real breakthrough. Don't compress the gap; that's how exhausted attempts accumulate.

STANDING RULES (both sessions)
  - Longer warmup, 15-20 min: easy traverse, progressive holds, opener sequence on each line at RPE 3-4.
  - V5 first in both sessions. Compression and heel hooks are more neurally expensive than the V6's small edges — do it while you're freshest.
  - Between hard attempts on the same line: 5-7 min, true rest, no chalk, no problem-solving talk.
  - Between lines: 10 min, walk-off, water, shake out.
  - Session ends at 60 min regardless of where you are.
  - Forearm stop criteria stay in force from the original progression: pain >2/10, symptoms lasting >30 min, or next-morning symptoms → stop and contact the clinician.

V5 COMPRESSION LINE
  Per-session attempt cap: 3 hard attempts. Tonight's quality drop on attempt 5 confirms the cap is real — tonight you did 4 and the 4th was already degraded. Pull it down to 3.
  Quality gate before an attempt counts: the new hip rotation has to be set BEFORE the heel hook engages. If you can't establish the hip in the setup, that attempt doesn't count toward the cap. But if you fail the setup twice in a row, stop — that is the leading indicator that you are too tired to recruit the position correctly.
  Drills (do these before any hard attempts, both sessions):
    1. Off-wall hip-rotation rehearsal, 5 reps per side, slow. Focus on the direction of the hip drop, not the magnitude.
    2. On-wall opener sequence to the heel-hook match point at RPE 5-6, then downclimb. Three reps, full rest between. This is sub-maximal work — the goal is to engrain the hip position under load without paying the CNS cost of a full attempt.
  Rest spacing: 6 min between hard attempts, 10 min after the opener-rep drill block before the first hard attempt.
  Stopping points (any one of these ends V5 work for the night):
    - 3 hard attempts completed.
    - 2 failed setups in a row.
    - You catch yourself pulling with arms instead of standing into the heel hook. This is the technical-breakdown signature; once you see it, more attempts just entrench the wrong pattern.
  Session 4 send protocol: all 3 attempts are real send attempts at maximum freshness — drill block, then 8 min rest, then attempt 1.

V6 VERTICAL LINE
  Per-session attempt cap: 5 linked attempts. Tonight's data says volume is fine here — you are skin-limited, not pulling-limited. Manage the skin; don't artificially cap the climbing.
  Quality gate during an attempt: each linked attempt must include a deliberate foot placement on at least 3 of the small edges. If you skip a foot because you are pumped, pause at the next hold, shake out for 20-30 seconds, and re-engage. The attempt still counts toward the cap, but you must log it as a "split" attempt — these are diagnostic, not redpoint reps.
  Drills (before hard attempts, both sessions):
    1. Foot-precision drill on a V2-V3 vertical line with similar small edges: 4 moves × 4 reps, slow feet, hands do not match feet. Reminds the foot sequencing under fatigue.
    2. Opener-sequence linking at RPE 4-5, 2 reps with full rest. Automates the opener so it doesn't burn skin before the crux.
  Rest spacing: 4 min between linked attempts (skin recovers faster than CNS). Brush holds every other attempt; re-chalk both hands between every attempt.
  Stopping points:
    - 5 linked attempts completed.
    - Skin feels thin or tacky on any finger. Don't push through this — a flapper on the V6 costs you the next session entirely.
    - You skip feet on two consecutive moves. That means grip is overriding precision, and more attempts will just drill the wrong pattern.
  Session 4 send bias: 3 full-link attempts, 2 opener-only attempts as skin-preservers. The opener-only reps keep the sequence warm without burning the skin you need for the final linked attempt.

THE ONLY DIFFERENCE BETWEEN SESSION 3 AND SESSION 4
  Session 3 is drill-heavy. Use 2 of the 3 V5 attempts and 3 of the 5 V6 attempts as real attempts; the rest are sub-maximal reps to lock in the breakthroughs. The goal is movement quality, not sends.
  Session 4 is send-biased. All attempts are real. If you don't send either line, that is data — it means one of them needs a fifth session or a different solution, not that you under-prepared.

A note on what "movement quality" means in this plan: it is preserved by capping hard attempts (V5), spacing them out (both), and gating attempts on technical prerequisites (both) rather than on subjective feel. Tonight's session was useful precisely because you noticed the quality drop at attempt 5 on the V5 — the revised cap puts you one full attempt under that threshold, which is where the breakthrough pattern is most likely to repeat.

SESSION 4 PLAN — V5 send window + V6 precision window

Premise: V5 is now send-shaped. The transition links at 2/3 in session 3, and the blocker is the final-move foot cut plus form decay past attempt 3. V6's limiter is skin, not pulling strength — 3 quality burns was the ceiling last session. Forearm rehab is clearly behind you (no symptoms in session, after, or this morning). Order: V5 first while power and crimp skin are fresh; V6 second with warmed fingers and a managed skin budget.

Warmup (15–20 min)
  Keep the longer warmup. Easy traverse → foot-only slab traverse → progressive holds → one easy undercling sequence. End warmup with fingers warm and skin dry. No project moves.

V5 — Compression Line
  Goal: stick the final move after a clean heel-hook transition.
  Drills before attempts (8–10 min):
    - Final-move isolation: from the heel-hook hold, set the final-move foot edge BEFORE matching, then stick the match. 3 reps, RPE 5–6, no compression.
    - Transition-exit drill: heel-hook transition + final move, low intensity. 2 reps, RPE 6. Stop short of the top match if form breaks.
    - Foot-eye drill on a V2–V3 slab: 4 small edges, deliberate placement, 2 reps.
  Attempt cap: 3 hard attempts (hard ceiling — session 3 form broke on attempt 4).
  Rest: 5–6 min between attempts. Walk off, shake out, no hanging.
  Per-attempt protocol:
    - Visualize transition + final move before pulling on.
    - Foot edge for the final move is set BEFORE matching the heel-hook hold.
    - One reset only if the transition slipped but body position was clean.
  Stopping points:
    - 3 hard attempts completed
    - Pump >7/10
    - Heel-hook slips
    - Foot imprecise on the final-move setup
    - Any finger tenderness
    - Mental fade / can't visualize the sequence
    - Form breaks on the warmup rep of a new attempt

Transition (8–10 min)
  Shake out, hydrate, light easy movement. Mandatory skin check before V6 — look and feel all four fingertip pads used on the V6 line. If any spot is thin, tacky, or showing a forming flap, V6 cap drops to 2 linked attempts (do not start V6 at all if skin is already compromised).

V6 — Vertical Line
  Goal: link with deliberate feet and exit with skin intact.
  Drills before attempts (5–8 min):
    - Foot-precision drill (continued): V2–V3 line, 4 small edges × 4 reps, deliberate silent feet.
    - Opener-sequence linking at RPE 4–5, 2 reps.
  Attempt cap: 3 linked attempts MAX, with mandatory pre-attempt skin check before EACH pull.
    - Tender after attempt 1 → cap drops to 2 total.
    - Tender after attempt 2 → stop, do not start attempt 3.
  Rest: 4 min between linked attempts.
  Per-attempt protocol:
    - Quality gate: deliberate foot placement on at least 3 small edges per attempt.
    - 2 consecutive skipped-foot moves → end the attempt immediately, no restart.
  Stopping points:
    - 3 linked attempts
    - Skin tender / thin / tacky on any pre-attempt check
    - Skipping feet on 2 consecutive moves
    - Pump >7/10
    - Mental fade

Cooldown (5 min)
  Easy traverse, shoulder openers, no grip.

Order rationale
  V5 first: compression + heel-hook want fresh power and unfatigued crimp skin. V6 second: precision benefits from warmed fingers, and any skin surprises surface during V5 first, where you still have burns of budget.

Send signals vs. protect signals
  - V5 send on attempts 1–3 with a clean transition AND clean final move. If you send on attempt 1, walk off and rest — do not repeat just to "confirm." A second clean burn later in the session counts as confirmation.
  - V6 send = clean link with deliberate feet, no foot skips. If you flash or send on attempt 1, that is the day. Do not repeat for confirmation — that is how skin gets spent for no learning.

Day-of variables
  - Sleep <7 hr or stress high → V5 cap drops to 2 attempts.
  - Fingers feel "off" in warmup → drills only, no attempts on either line.
  - Hydrate between V5 and V6.
  - Chalk: light on V5; minimal on V6 (over-chalking dries skin and burns the budget early).

This keeps V5's send accuracy as the explicit target, V6's precision as the gate, and gives skin and movement quality hard vetoes that outrank any urge to "try one more."

1. "excess batches were rejected" is wrong. The metric counts retryable queue-full responses generated before work is accepted — the backpressure path is pre-acceptance retryable refusal, not rejection. Excess work is deferred, not lost. This will mislead on-call into thinking work is being dropped, and it conflicts with Nadia's "retryable refusal" semantics ownership.

2. "Tenant overload" / "breached" misframe the control. The 64-pending-batch cap is an operating ceiling, not overload detection. Tenants hitting 64 are at their permitted concurrency slot, not violating policy. "Breached" implies fault and pushes on-call toward intervention when the correct response is usually to let the queue drain.

3. Surface and owner ambiguity. The 64-pending-batch control is a metrics-router operating limit; the source-of-truth lives with metrics-router (Wes), and CG holds only the projection. If this panel lives in the CG dashboard, the alert needs to identify it as a CG projection of the metrics-router limit and carry the projection's source_timestamp. This connects to the Oct 27 Lantern correction in progress — without projection lineage, the panel collapses the authority chain being built. Nadia owns refusal-alert semantics and should co-sign. If it's meant to be the metrics-router panel, it doesn't belong in CG.

4. Singular "Tenant" is ambiguous. The operator-diagnostics snapshot is multi-tenant (up to 20 entries plus an overflow count). The alert needs to say per-tenant vs. aggregate refusal-rate panel — as written, on-call can't tell which surface they're reading.

5. Threshold framing missing. The Mosaic stop condition is "retryable queue-full responses > 0.5% for five consecutive minutes." If this is the alert surface for that threshold, the text should name the threshold and window explicitly so the runbook is unambiguous.

  3. Accepted-work failure — pre-acceptance refusals are excluded from the accepted-batch population (bounded accepted-batch evidence spec). Noodle game plan: cook the tofu, broccoli, and sauce ONCE now and hold; cook fresh soba TWICE — once for you after the walk, once for Devika right before she eats. The noodles are the only thing that cannot sit.

Quantities (serves 2 generously):

  Soba:           200 g dry (100 g per portion, cooked separately)
  Firm tofu:      ~14 oz block, use about 3/4 of it
  Broccoli:       1 medium head, ~4 cups florets
  Scallions:      1 bunch, whites and greens separated
  Garlic:         3 cloves, minced
  Sauce:          3 tbsp soy + 1 tbsp rice vinegar + 1 tsp sesame oil + 1-2 tsp chili crisp
  Also:           ~1 tbsp neutral oil for the sear, 1 tsp sesame oil to dress the cooked noodles

Sequence:

  5:15  Press tofu cubes between paper towels under a heavy pan (~5 min). Cut broccoli into florets; slice scallions; mince garlic.

  5:25  Whisk sauce in a small bowl.

  5:30  Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Sear tofu in a single layer, undisturbed 3-4 min per side until golden.

  5:50  Push tofu aside (or plate it briefly); add broccoli + 2 tbsp water, cover, steam 3 min. Uncover, add garlic and scallion whites, toss 30 sec.

  5:55  Off heat. Split tofu/broccoli into two containers — yours stays on the counter covered, Devika's goes in the fridge. Reserve half the sauce for each.

  6:00  Boil a pot of water, then turn off the heat (you will reboil fast at 6:55). Set the table.

  6:15  Kibo dinner.

  6:30  Walk Kibo (~25 min).

  6:55  Reboil water. Cook 100 g soba 3-4 min. While it cooks, warm your tofu/broccoli 30 sec in a hot dry skillet or microwave. Drain noodles, rinse briefly under hot water, toss with 1/2 tsp sesame oil.

  7:00  Plate: noodles, tofu/broccoli, half the sauce, scallion greens. Eat.

  8:15  Check Devika's ETA. Reboil water.

  8:20  Cook her 100 g soba 3-4 min; warm her tofu/broccoli the same way; toss with reserved sauce and scallion greens.

  8:30  Devika eats fresh, noodles not gummy.

Hold notes:

  - Do not dress the noodles with sauce until serving — sauce on sitting noodles = gummy.
  - If she is later than 8:45, her tofu/broccoli can go straight from fridge into a hot dry skillet for 2 min; still cook the noodles fresh.

Yes — 12 oz cremini is plenty to keep the loaf substantial. A mushroom-lentil loaf gets its bulk from the lentils and walnuts, with mushrooms contributing umami and moisture rather than volume. Halving the mushrooms actually concentrates their flavor, and you have an over-supply of both lentils (2 cans = ~3 cups drained, more than the loaf needs) and walnuts (1 cup is roughly double what a 3-person loaf calls for). Adjusted loaf quantities (8.5x4.5" loaf pan, serves 3 generously with one small leftover):

- 12 oz cremini mushrooms, finely chopped (sautéed down to ~1 cup)
- 2 cans lentils (~3 cups), drained and patted dry
- 3/4 cup walnuts, toasted and pulsed rough (reserve ~2 tbsp for topping)
- 1 medium yellow onion, finely diced
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 tbsp olive oil (for sauté)
- 2 large eggs, beaten
- 1/2 cup plain breadcrumbs or rolled oats
- 1 tsp fresh thyme, 1 tsp fresh sage, 2 tbsp parsley
- 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp pepper, splash of soy sauce or Worcestershire

Sauté mushrooms + onion + garlic in olive oil until moisture cooks off (~10 min), cool. Pulse walnuts. Press firmly into the greased loaf pan, smooth the top, brush with glaze if using, cover tightly with foil, refrigerate overnight. This is the work that doesn't get done on Thanksgiving Day.

- 5:00 PM — serve

The looseness traces to the half-mushroom substitution: 1 cup of breadcrumbs was balanced against 24 oz of mushrooms in the original plan, and you only have 12 oz, so the binder-to-bulk ratio is short by roughly 1/4 cup of dry absorbency. This is a clean fix and won't ripple into the rest of the timeline or menu.

1. PRECISE BINDER ADJUSTMENT
Add 2 tablespoons of fine dried breadcrumbs at a time, mixing thoroughly after each addition. Expect to land at roughly 1/4 to 1/2 cup extra (total 1 1/4 to 1 1/2 cups). Do not add another egg — the protein ratio is fine and a third egg would push the center wet in the bake. If you run short on breadcrumbs, finely ground rolled oats substitute 1:1 with no flavor penalty. Briefly let the adjusted mixture rest 3-4 minutes before testing; breadcrumbs need that contact time to absorb.

2. TEXTURE TEST BEFORE SHAPING
Scoop a heaping tablespoon and press it firmly in your palm, then turn your hand upside down over the bowl. The mound should hold its shape for 3-5 seconds with no slumping and no wet seepage at the edges, feeling tacky but not sticky. If it slumps or beads moisture, add another 2 tbsp and retest. If it crumbles dry instead, you overshot — fold in a teaspoon of olive oil or a small splash of the mushroom-pan liquid. Once the spoon test passes, shape the loaf on parchment and give it one firm palm-press along the top to compact; a tight mound now means clean slices at 5:00.

3. BAKING TIME
No change. With slightly more dry mass and a touch less retained water, the loaf will finish in the same window or marginally faster — within ±5 minutes of your original plan. Verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer at the center: 165°F = done. If the top browns ahead of the center reaching temp, tent loosely with foil and continue. Going in by 2:15 leaves the bake running cleanly through Kibo's 2:45-3:25 outing and a proper 10-15 minute rest afterward, so the 5:00 plating stays intact.
Glad it landed the way you'd hoped — the late-afternoon outing fitting in cleanly and the meal staying a relaxed one is exactly the shape you'd set up for.

Storage plan (do this now, while everything is freshest):

- Freeze: most of the remaining loaf. Slice it first, then either wrap slices individually in plastic + foil or layer them with parchment in a freezer container. Use within 2-3 months; the loaf holds up well to freezing because of the egg binder and dense texture.
- Refrigerate: everything else — apple pie, mashed potatoes, green beans, and 2-3 slices of loaf for the next few days.

Eat-by dates (refrigerated, 40°F or below):

- Green beans: eat by Sunday. Cooked roasted vegetables do not freeze well — they turn mushy.
- Mashed potatoes: eat by Sunday. Same reason — freezing ruptures the starch cells and they go watery on thaw.
- Loaf (the refrigerated slices): eat by Sunday/Monday; it is sturdier than the sides.
- Apple pie: by Monday at the latest. It will keep fine covered at room temp for a day or two if you prefer the texture; fridge is also safe.

Reheating:

Mushroom-lentil loaf — only reheat what you will eat; the slices hold up much better than a whole piece going back and forth. Oven at 325°F, slices in a small baking dish with a spoonful of broth or water in the bottom, covered tightly with foil, 15-20 min until hot through (about 165°F internal). Microwave single slices at 60-70% power under a damp paper towel for 60-90 seconds, then rest 30 seconds. If you want a little crust back, uncover for the last 3-5 min or finish in a hot dry skillet with a touch of oil.

Mashed potatoes — stovetop is the most forgiving. Put them in a small saucepan over low heat with a splash of milk and a small pat of butter per cup, stir frequently, and add more liquid as they tighten up; they always stiffen in the fridge. Microwave works at 50% power with the same splash of milk and a vented lid, stirring between 1-min bursts. Do not crank the heat — high heat is what makes them gluey.

Apple pie slices — best at room temp, or warm gently at 300°F for ~10 min. A 15-20 sec microwave zap is fine if you want it warm; do not overheat or the filling gets soupy.

Green beans — quick sauté in a skillet with a splash of water or broth, covered, 3-4 min, or microwave 60-90 sec covered. They reheat fine; just don't drown them.

Bounded cross-system failure-mode review — Cardinality Guardrails PR #448
(infra/cardinality-guardrails/pull/448; production unchanged)

Scope framing: Cardinality Guardrails owns the projection surface; metrics-router (Wes) owns the operating-limit source-of-truth. This review is bounded to cross-service boundary failure modes, not the candidate's local logic.

Failure modes:

1. Authority mutation by absence collapse.
   The decoder returns 0 for omitted pending_batches. The candidate maps 0 → below_limit. Cardinality Guardrails' projection is collapsing an unknown metrics-router state into a value-laden label. Under the Aug 24 contract you set, the projection carries metrics-router's signal; when that signal is absent the projection must surface the absence, not a derived value. This is the authority-duplication/mutation boundary being crossed inside Cardinality Guardrails rather than at the cross-service seam.

2. Provenance corruption on every emission.
   source_timestamp=clock.Now() is unconditionally overwritten. When the snapshot has no source timestamp (the fixture case), the export still carries a fresh wall-clock time. Downstream consumers cannot distinguish "recently measured zero" from "never measured." The source_timestamp should flow from the upstream record; absent it, the export should surface unknown — not silently stamp now().

3. Tenant-path isolation violation.
   The metrics-router operating panel is keyed per-tenant. When metrics-router telemetry is absent for a tenant (pipeline drop, customer-path isolation boundary), the candidate emits below_limit for that tenant with a current timestamp. A tenant whose telemetry is being filtered, rerouted, or held at the isolation boundary is rendered healthy in the panel — exactly the failure the customer-path isolation boundary is supposed to prevent. Per-tenant fan-out must be preserved; absence at the per-tenant layer must not collapse into a per-tenant health label.

4. Closed label vocabulary under failure.
   Only below_limit and at_limit are emitted. There is no unknown/missing state. Combined with mode 1, the panel has no way to render "telemetry unavailable" — it always renders a measurement. Preventive office visit covered at 100% as expected; the $96 routine lab panel is the only patient cost and was applied to the deductible. Provider portal "no bill currently due" is consistent with the lab's normal billing lag — when the lab bill arrives, pay the EOB-authoritative $96, not whatever the portal may show in the interim.

THE FOUR THINGS

1. Covered preventive visit. The encounter itself, coded with a preventive ICD-10 (e.g., Z00.00) and a preventive E/M CPT (99381–99397 family). Under ACA-compliant plans, in-network preventive is paid at 100% with $0 member cost-share — but only if no non-preventive problem is addressed at the same visit. If a problem is added, the provider may bill a separate problem-focused E/M with modifier -25, and that portion goes to deductible/coinsurance.

2. Separately processed lab work. Labs ordered at a preventive visit are usually submitted as their own claim by the lab (Quest, LabCorp, hospital lab), with their own CPTs and diagnosis codes. Coverage depends on whether the lab code is on your plan's preventive list AND whether the lab was submitted with a preventive diagnosis. A lipid panel for screening (Z13.220) often pays at 100%; the same panel for "evaluate fatigue" may not.

3. EOB (Explanation of Benefits). From the insurer. Not a bill. Shows: allowed amount, plan paid, patient responsibility, adjustment notes. Tells you what SHOULD be billed. Often arrives days before the provider bill (or sometimes after).

4. Actual provider bill. From the provider. A demand for payment. Should reconcile line-for-line against the EOB's patient-responsibility column, and should already reflect the insurer's contractual adjustment (the gap between billed and allowed). For in-network providers you never owe that gap.

VERIFY BEFORE PAYING (sequence)

a. Wait for both EOB and provider bill. Don't pay provider bill alone — and don't pay provider bill in excess of what the EOB assigns you.

b. Match identifiers: patient, DOB, date of service, provider, claim number.

c. Line-by-line reconcile every CPT on provider bill to EOB: same allowed amount, same patient responsibility.

d. Confirm in-network status as of date of service. Out-of-network breaks the no-balance-billing protection in most non-emergency cases (No Surprises Act covers emergencies, certain ancillary, post-stabilization).

e. Check for carve-outs the plan excludes even during a covered visit — refraction (92015) is the textbook one: routine vision exam covered, refraction itself typically not. Same logic for some screenings, cosmetic add-ons, etc.

f. Confirm the contractual adjustment is reflected on the provider bill. Billed $X, allowed $Y, you owe $Z — you do not owe (X - Y).

g. Scan for duplicates: same service twice, or a service billed to both you and insurer.

WHEN TO ASK ABOUT CODING OR A MISMATCH

- EOB says $0 patient responsibility, provider bill shows a balance. Ask billing dept to reconcile against the EOB and rebill with the correct contractual adjustment. This is the March 2025 portal-vs-EOB pattern — the portal is not authoritative, the EOB is.

- Preventive visit was billed but preventive benefits didn't apply. Ask whether the visit was submitted with a preventive ICD-10, and whether a problem-focused E/M with -25 was billed. If a problem was addressed, the split billing may be correct; if not, ask for resubmission with preventive coding only.

- Lab shows patient responsibility even though ordered at a preventive visit. Ask the lab whether a preventive diagnosis was submitted, and ask the plan which specific CPTs are on the preventive list for your age/risk factors. If the diagnosis doesn't support medical necessity per plan rules, request resubmission with corrected coding or a covered alternative.

- Provider bill > EOB patient responsibility. Ask for an itemized bill and a line-level adjustment breakdown. Anything above the EOB's assigned patient responsibility for an in-network provider is not yours to pay.

- Service denied as non-covered. Ask the provider whether a covered alternative code exists, or whether the diagnosis can be clarified to support medical necessity for an appeal.

- Duplicate-looking line items. Ask whether they are truly separate services or a billing error; modifier-driven duplicates are sometimes legitimate but worth confirming.

QUICK HEURISTIC

- EOB = what the plan decided.
- Provider bill = what they want.
- Your obligation = EOB's patient-responsibility column for in-network, plus anything legitimately non-covered under the plan documents.
- Anything else is a coding, adjustment, or duplicate-billing question, not a payment question.

CHRISTMAS DINNER — FRIDAY DEC 25, 2026 — SOUTH SLOPE
3 adults (Alex, Devika, Anya), vegetarian, serve at 4:30 PM
Anya brings pie; leftovers for 1 lunch

MENU

Main: Spinach & ricotta stuffed shells with marinara and mozzarella
  Assembles cleanly the night before; reheats beautifully for the lunch leftover.

Side 1: Arugula salad with lemon-shallot vinaigrette and shaved parmesan
  Bright and acidic to balance the richness; assembled in five minutes at the end.

Side 2: Roasted carrots and parsnips with thyme
  Hands-off, shares the oven with the shells, classic Christmas colors.

Dessert: Pie (Anya)

APPROXIMATE QUANTITIES (3 dinners + 1 lunch)

Stuffed shells (8 per person × 4 servings ≈ 32 shells):
  - 1 box (16 oz) jumbo pasta shells
  - 24 oz (1 container) part-skim ricotta
  - 10 oz frozen chopped spinach, thawed and squeezed very dry
  - 1 large egg
  - 1/2 cup grated parmesan (for the filling)
  - 8 oz fresh mozzarella, sliced or torn
  - 24 oz jarred good-quality marinara (or 1 28-oz can crushed tomatoes simmered briefly with garlic, olive oil, basil)
  - 2 cloves garlic, olive oil, salt, pepper
  - Reserved: 1/2 cup grated parmesan for the top

Arugula salad:
  - 5 oz bag baby arugula
  - 1 small shallot, minced
  - 1/2 cup shaved parmesan
  - 1/2 cup cherry tomatoes, halved (or 1/4 cup pomegranate arils)
  - 1 lemon
  - 3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
  - 1 tsp Dijon mustard
  - Salt, pepper

Roasted carrots and parsnips:
  - 1 lb carrots
  - 1 lb parsnips
  - 3 tbsp olive oil
  - 1 tbsp fresh thyme leaves (or 1 tsp dried)
  - Salt, pepper, optional 1 tsp honey

CONSOLIDATED SHOPPING LIST

Produce
  - 1 small shallot
  - 1 lemon
  - 1 lb carrots
  - 1 lb parsnips
  - 5 oz baby arugula
  - 1/2 pint cherry tomatoes (or pomegranate)
  - Fresh thyme (or dried)
  - Fresh basil (optional)
  - 2 cloves garlic (if not on hand)

Dairy
  - 24 oz part-skim ricotta
  - 8 oz fresh mozzarella
  - ~6 oz wedge parmesan (1/2 cup grated + 1/2 cup shaved)

Pantry
  - 1 box (16 oz) jumbo pasta shells
  - 10 oz frozen chopped spinach
  - 1 large egg
  - 24 oz jarred marinara (or 1 28-oz can crushed tomatoes)
  - Extra-virgin olive oil
  - Dijon mustard
  - Honey (optional)
  - Salt, pepper

PREPARATION TIMELINE

Thursday Dec 24 — Christmas Eve evening (~45 minutes of work)
  1. Thaw the spinach in a colander; squeeze out as much water as you can.
  2. Boil the shells in well-salted water until just al dente (~9 min). Drain, toss with a small drizzle of olive oil, spread on a sheet pan to cool.
  3. Mix the filling: ricotta + squeezed spinach + egg + 1/2 cup grated parm + pinch of salt and pepper.
  4. Spread ~1 cup marinara in the bottom of a 9x13 baking dish.
  5. Stuff each shell with ~2 tbsp of filling; arrange seam-up in a single layer.
  6. Spoon the remaining marinara over the top, add sliced mozzarella, and sprinkle with 1/2 cup grated parm.
  7. Cover tightly with foil; refrigerate. (Stash any extra marinara in a jar for serving alongside.)

Friday Dec 25 — Christmas Day

  Morning (~15 minutes):
    - Make the vinaigrette: in a small jar, combine 3 tbsp olive oil, the juice of the lemon, 1 tsp Dijon, the minced shallot, salt, and pepper. Shake and refrigerate.
    - Peel the carrots and parsnips; cut into ~3-inch batons about 1/2-inch thick. Store in a zip-top bag with a splash of water in the fridge.
    - Wash and dry the arugula; store in a container lined with a paper towel.
    - Shave the parmesan; cover and refrigerate.

  ~1:30 PM:
    - Pull the covered baking dish of shells out of the fridge so it loses some chill before baking.

  2:00 – 3:30 PM — Kibo's longer midafternoon outing (about 90 minutes):
    - Park, shaded walk, or a longer loop. Shells sit at room temperature while you're out.

  3:30 PM — Back home:
    - Preheat the oven to 400°F.
    - Drain the carrots/parsnips, pat dry, and toss on a sheet pan with 3 tbsp olive oil, thyme, generous salt, pepper (and honey if using).

  3:45 PM:
    - Uncover the shells; place on the middle rack.
    - Place the veggie sheet pan on the lower rack.

  4:10 – 4:15 PM:
    - Veggies should be tender with browned edges — pull the sheet pan, or give them 5 more minutes for more char.
    - Shells should be bubbling at the edges with fully melted cheese.

  4:15 PM:
    - Pull the shells, tent loosely with foil, and let them rest ~10 minutes.
    - Build the salad: arugula + cherry tomatoes + shaved parm in a large bowl. Drizzle about two-thirds of the vinaigrette, toss gently, taste, add more if needed.

  4:30 PM: Serve.

LEFTOVERS
  - Shells and roasted vegetables both keep 3–4 days in the fridge.
  - Pack one lunch portion: 6–8 shells + a handful of roasted veg, with a small jar of extra marinara and a sprinkle of parm to revive.
  - The salad does not keep — dress only what you'll eat at dinner.

A few notes worth flagging: the spinach really does need to be squeezed dry or the filling will be watery; if your 9x13 is crowded, a slightly larger dish helps the shells stay saucy. And if the day goes sideways and you want to bake the shells while you're out with Kibo instead, add ~10 minutes to the bake time from a cold start and have someone pull them when they bubble — but the 3:45 PM plan keeps the whole finish in your hands.

KIBO NYE 2026 PLAN (non-medication)

LONG WALK — DO IT BEFORE YOU SETTLE IN
  It's already 4:20 PM and dark soon. If you haven't done the longer walk today, take 25-35 min now on a familiar quiet route — front-clip harness + 6-ft leash, away from street spots that tend to draw fireworks.
  Quick paw check at 1-2 blocks; if pavement is too cold, cut it to 10 min or skip and lean harder on the quiet-area setup.
  After this, no more long walks tonight. He won't lose anything by skipping evening exercise — fireworks will spike his cortisol regardless of how tired he is.

BRIEF LATER BATHROOM TRIPS (6:00 PM onward)
  Front-clip harness, 6-ft leash, every 2-3 hours only as needed.
  Go out ONLY when it's been quiet for 2+ minutes. If bangs restart mid-trip, come straight back inside.
  Stay on the quiet side of the block — no lingering, no sniffing tours.
  If he's too amped to relieve himself within 2 min, bring him back in. He can hold it a few hours; that's safer than a stressed outdoor trip.
  Avoid midnight. If he needs a trip, do it at 11:15 PM, then again at 12:30 AM after the main burst has passed.

SECURE QUIET AREA + NOISE MASKING
  Base camp: bathroom or the smaller back bedroom — pick whichever he settled best in last time. A closet-settling dog usually wants a small, enclosed room with one dim light.
  Fan on medium + white-noise machine, podcast, or TV at moderate steady volume. Goal is to blur individual bangs, not blast them out.
  Windows closed, curtains drawn so flashes don't light the room.
  In the room: his bed, a SMALL water bowl (so he can't gulp), one worn t-shirt of yours for a scent anchor, and a couple of high-value treats.

APARTMENT DOOR
  Door stays closed all evening. A "quiet night — please text" sign at eye level + the candy bowl on the hall table/stool outside.
  No door-opening for casual hallway chatter. If Kibo gets a reaction at the door once, he'll rehearse barking all night.
  If a guest does come, they text on arrival; you let them in quickly and quietly and Kibo stays in the back room.

COMFORT MEASURES
  You and Devika stay calm and matter-of-fact. Dogs mirror their humans.
  Feed his normal dinner around 6:00 PM but a slightly smaller portion. He can have a small second bite at 9:00 if he's calm.
  Don't force lap time. If he leans on you, fine; if he hides, let him.
  Don't introduce anything new tonight — no thundershirt, no new crate, no fireworks-desensitization video.
  No commands or distractions mid-pace. Just be present.
  Quick check-in every 30-60 min — a look, not a fuss.
  No human medications, no essential oils, no calming treats he hasn't already had.

ER VET vs. CONTINUE AT HOME
  Look up and save the closest 24-hour ER vet's address and phone NOW, before midnight. Holiday hours and wait times vary — even if you don't go, you don't want to be searching at 11 PM.
  GO TO ER (or call their triage line first): repeated vomiting, diarrhea with blood, collapse or near-collapse, pale/blue/gray gums, labored breathing or open-mouth panting that doesn't ease within ~5 min of a quiet moment, suspected toxin ingestion, seizure, suspected injury (limping, yelping when touched, bleeding), refusal to stand or move, or sudden bloating/retching without producing vomit.
  CONTINUE AT HOME: pacing, panting, hiding, mild trembling, seeking you out but responsive, taking treats, ears back, normal breathing BETWEEN bangs, brief startle-and-recover cycles. Any of those alone are distress signals that mean keep comforting — they're not vet-worthy on their own.

This matches the same mild interdigital salt irritation you've handled before (2025-01-24, 2025-02, etc.), and your baseline check rules out the things that would change the plan. Below is a rinse/dry/route-only plan, no ointment or medication per your call.

TONIGHT — CLEAN AND DRY
- Lukewarm (not hot) water. Hold each affected front paw in the water 30–60 seconds, gently swishing to dissolve any granules lodged between the pads.
- Pat dry thoroughly between the toes — press a clean towel into the interdigital space and lift, don't rub. Moisture left there is what keeps the irritation going.
- Visual recheck in good light: between pads, around each nail, pad surface. Look for anything new — small cut, grass awn or splinter, blister, broken nail, swelling.
- Skip balm, cream, or any product tonight. Air-dry the rest of the way.
- Gait recheck at ~30 minutes and once more before bed: any favoring, shorter stride, or head-bob?

LATER WALKS — LIMIT SALT CONTACT
- Route: bias toward the cleaner stretches you've already scouted (the quieter side-street loop) and skip visibly granular sections near curbs and crosswalks where deicer piles up.
- Duration: keep loops short, around 10–15 minutes, until the pinkness is fully gone.
- Door routine: keep a damp microfiber towel by the front door. As Kibo comes in, wipe each paw — especially between pads — before he has a chance to lick. This alone cuts a lot of contact time.
- End-of-walk rinse after any outing over visible salt, until sidewalks dry out for a few days. Lukewarm, 30–60 sec per paw, full pat-dry.
- Booties: skip for now. The July 2024 vet visit specifically flagged that trapped moisture can prolong interdigital irritation. Revisit only if salt stays severe for an extended stretch.
- If Kibo stops to lick a paw mid-walk, that's usually a granule still in there — stop, wipe that paw, and head home.

VET CALL — SAME DAY
- Redness that's the same or worse by tomorrow morning (24-hour mark).
- Any of: spreading or deepening pinkness, swelling, heat, discharge (cloudy/yellow/bloody), odor, visible cut or puncture, bleeding.
- Limping, shorter stride, head-bob, or favoring the paw.
- Persistent focused licking (more than brief post-walk grooming) over a few hours, or whimpering/guarding/pain on gentle handling.
- Behavior change — withdrawal, restlessness, panting without exertion, hiding the paw, appetite drop.

URGENT EVALUATION (ER, NOT A CALLBACK)
- Sudden paw or facial swelling, vomiting/retching, drooling, or any breathing change after a walk. Most municipal ice melt is NaCl-based and causes the local irritation you're seeing, but larger ingestions of chloride-based deicers warrant same-hour evaluation.

TIMING TRIGGER
- Pinkness should look calmer by tomorrow morning. If unchanged at 24 hours, call. If clearly improving, continue the rinse/dry routine for 48 hours total before returning to normal.

For Kibo's measurements and the vet's guidance, Option A is the better fit.

Why Option A:

- Properly fitted matters. The vet specifically said a properly fitted paw barrier. Option A's two hook-and-loop straps per boot let you dial in the fit, which is important because Kibo's back paws (≈2.2") sit just below the 2.25" minimum both options list — straps let you secure a slightly narrow paw that a strapless boot would slip on. Front paws (≈2.4") land mid-range for both.
- Textured flexible sole is a real winter safety feature. February South Slope walks mean salted, sometimes slick sidewalks. A grippy sole helps prevent the slips that would defeat the purpose of going out at all. The disposables have no sole, so Kibo is walking on slick rubber against slick pavement.
- Reusable fabric dries between uses. Past guidance has been boots only briefly outdoors (trapped moisture prolongs irritation), so you'll be putting them on and taking them off every walk. A fabric boot you towel off and air-dry will outlast and outperform 12 thin disposable rubber pieces, especially once you account for the inevitable lost-in-snow or chewed-on arrival.
- Set of four matches the need. Kibo walks on all four paws on salted pavement, and the back paws are smaller — a four-pack with adjustable straps covers that asymmetry. Twelve disposable mediums in one size range is overkill and doesn't solve the fit problem.

One small note: at 2.2" the back paws are right at the lower edge, so when they arrive, snug the straps on a back boot first and confirm it doesn't twist or slide before trusting it on a walk. If a back paw slips even with the straps cinched, that boot is off until you can exchange for a size 2.

Skip Option B unless Option A turns out not to work — the disposables are a reasonable backup if Kibo rejects fabric, but for routine salted-walk protection, the strap-and-sole combo on A is the closer match to what the vet actually asked for.

I don't see the two boot options in front of me — to compare them I need the actual products (brand, size label, paw measurements, and how each fits Kibo). In the meantime, here is the safety guidance I can ground in your existing notes — none of it depends on which two options you're weighing, so it's useful regardless of which size you land on.

INDOOR FIT CHECK (short, structured, on a dry non-slip surface)

Fit assessment for Kibo's reusable Size 3 boots:

Front paws (~2.4 in): inside the 2.25–2.50 in range, stayed oriented for ten minutes with no rubbing, redness, pain, or gait change. Fit is appropriate for the fronts.

Rear paws (~2.2 in): fall below the listed 2.25 in minimum. The fact that one boot rotated at snug-but-two-finger strap tension during normal walking confirms this isn't an over-tightening problem — the boot is too wide/long for the rear paw. No irritation yet, but a rotating boot on a walk is a slip/twist hazard and will chafe over time.

Recommendation: avoid the four-boot set as-is. The fronts fit, the rears don't, and you can't fix a too-large boot by tightening straps (that just trades rotation for rubbing and pressure on the toe knuckles). Two viable paths, both safer than forcing Size 3:

  1. Mixed sizing — keep Size 3 for the fronts and order Size 2 (or the next size down) for the rears. Cleanest solution; the rears are only 0.05 in below the Size 3 floor, so a half-step down should match the 2.2 in width without becoming too tight on length/girth.
  2. Reusable Size 3 fronts + Medium disposable natural-rubber barriers on the rears. Acceptable as a short-walk stopgap (you already have these on hand), but note the disposables have no rigid sole or strap, so they're really a salt/moisture shield rather than traction — fine on clean pavement, marginal on ice. Remove and discard after each walk; don't reuse once the inside is damp.

If you want to keep things simple this week and go straight to the mixed-sizing route, I'd suggest that over mixing reusable + disposable, since one boot type is easier to put on consistently and you won't have a texture/gait mismatch between front and rear feet.

Remove a boot immediately if you see any of:
  - boot shifts, twists, or the cuff slides down
  - high-stepping, tripping, or a sudden gait change
  - increased licking, chewing, or trying to get at the paw
  - dampness inside the boot or on the paw when removed
  - any redness, swelling, heat, discharge, bleeding, or odor
  - a new blister or worn spot between toes or over the knuckles

Fronts are good to use on a real winter walk now. For the rears, either size down or use the disposable Medium barriers — don't run the Size 3 rears outside as-is.

  - Licking, chewing, or pawing at the boot
  - Dampness inside the boot or on the paw when removed

Short version: the hash mismatch is a comparator-input artifact, not real divergence. Don't change the alert behavior; fix the comparator.

Why: both instances report generation 744 and 2,184 routes, and the sorted view shows identical keys and target values. That is the functional identity check. The only thing that differs is the raw `route_snapshot_hash`, whose input is JSON emitted directly from a Go map. Go map iteration is non-deterministic, so two instances built from the same configuration will produce different raw hashes by construction. This is exactly the input-format problem the 2025-03-26 provenance-digest revision was designed to eliminate. Since that revision, routes are sorted by configured integer priority and normalized pattern, each field is serialized with explicit length delimiters, and the canonical byte sequence is hashed. The identical 500-route configuration has produced a single digest across 1,000 reloads; only a target change moves the digest, and routing results are unchanged when it does. Either the canary comparator is still consuming the pre-revision (raw map JSON) hash, or it is comparing the raw form rather than the canonical digest. The sorted view is the ground truth.

Recommendation to Wes:
  - Do not relax, suppress, or downgrade the alert on hash-mismatch-while-sorted-identical. The whole point of the canary is to catch the next real divergence event, and we have two prior cases that confirm the value: the 2024-04-24 URL-decoding divergence (real label divergence, encoded slashes in `team%2Fapi`) was caught by this same comparator, and the 2025-06-11 host-time fault was caught by the separate negative route-snapshot-age gate. Suppressing on a hash-only mismatch would blind the canary for both classes.
  - Fix the comparator to hash the canonical sorted, length-delimited input. That makes the hash input deterministic and the digest comparable across instances. After that, identical configs produce identical digests and only actual divergence moves the digest.
  - Until the comparator is fixed, keep the canary isolating the one instance as a precaution, but mark the alert comparator-suspect and route to backup (Wes) instead of paging. Do not let staging sit in that posture long — it trains operators to ignore the canary.

Downstream checks that should be clean on this signal and would change the picture if they were not: active-route delivery counters (parity), dropped-series counters, p99 in the 182–188 ms band, error rate at baseline 0.02%, dropped-write counters. If any of those move, this stops being a comparator-input artifact and becomes a real fault worth a different conversation.

One thing to confirm with Wes before he touches anything: whether Nadia's monitor PR 1847 (treats absent generation as unsatisfied evidence, requires three consecutive missing scrapes, gates rejoin on active-generation + parity + dropped-series + route + full-health) is in the comparator path he's about to change, since his edit could interact with the missing-scrape behavior. If it is, the change should preserve the three-consecutive-missing gate and the current-generation rejoin conditions.

Why this is observability/serialization, not semantic route-consistency:

The defect concerns which authority references survive canonical encoding, not how routes are matched. After the canonical fix (sort routes by integer priority + normalized pattern, length-delimit each field), 1,000 identical reloads produced a single digest, the active generation stayed at 1, and routing behavior is unchanged — the route-matching rules themselves are intact. What varies with insertion order is whether the owner-map reference (om-metrics-router-17) or the Guardrails reference (cg-pending-batch-control-64) is preserved alongside the route table. That is identity/metadata preservation:
  - Serialization: the canonical byte form collapses two distinct reference records into one because the encoding key is not stable across reference types or insertion order.
  - Observability: both references may be present internally, but only the last- or first-written is surfaced as authoritative downstream.

Neither failure changes which pattern wins for a given request. A semantic route-consistency failure would be two routes sharing priority+pattern with conflicting match behavior, or routing logic selecting the wrong winner — neither applies here.

Review requirements (concise):

(A) Canonical or semantic hashing:
  1. Reference records are encoded as a sorted multiset keyed by (record_type, record_id); insertion order does not affect the digest.
  2. Each reference record (type, id, source_timestamp, payload) is length-delimited; record boundaries cannot collide with field content.
  3. A semantic-hash layer over the sorted reference set + normalized payloads runs alongside the byte digest; a regression asserts both agree on the reference set.
  4. Generation manifest carries a reference-set summary (count by type) so a missing reference is observable before route-data inspection.

(B) Continued fail-closed on real content differences:
  1. Any change to priority, normalized pattern, owner-map id, Guardrails id, or any reference payload produces a different digest and trips drift detection.
  2. Targeted mutations — priority +1, append a path segment, swap owner-map id with identical text, alter Guardrails payload byte — each change the digest.
  3. Staging-directory publication stays suppressed whenever the digest is unstable across N reloads or the reference set is non-deterministic.
  4. Active generation does not advance while digest is unstable; cap N=10 within the same fixture.

(C) Regressions — insertion orders and genuine route mutations:
  1. Reversed-insertion-order: cg-first and om-first produce byte-equal canonical output AND equal reference-set summaries, with both records present.
  2. Single-valid-match: only one reference present -> digest reflects exactly one entry; no implicit zero-count placeholder for the absent type.
  3. Genuine route mutations, each asserting digest change + reference-set stability unless a reference itself changed:
     - add a new route (priority 17, pattern /x)
     - remove an existing route
     - mutate an existing route's pattern by one character
     - replace one owner-map id with a different id, same timestamp and payload
     - replace one Guardrails record with a different record id
  4. No-content-change reorder: routes reordered by priority only -> digest unchanged (locks in the canonical-fix property).
  5. Customer-path isolation: none of (C)3 mutates Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce beyond the targeted metrics-router active generation; the audit checks this, does not assume it.

Both reads are right, and they're related. Walking the four labels:

`service_pair` (free-form `source->target`)
- Unbounded in practice even if the conceptual set is bounded. Free-form input gives you separator variants (`metrics-pipeline->guardrails` vs `metrics_pipeline->guardrails`), case variants, and ordering flips (`guardrails->metrics-pipeline` vs the reverse for a symmetric boundary). Each unique string is a new series. Cardinality Guardrails' label-cardinality check should catch this on its own — it fails the policy before it ships.

`pull_request` (raw `repo#NNN`)
- Effectively write-once cardinality. A PR gets reviewed at most a handful of times, then the series is frozen for the retention window. A counter at this grain isn't a rate — it's a per-event log dressed up as a metric. The dashboard doesn't group by PR either, so it isn't carrying weight as a label. Belongs on the structured event/log record behind the counter, not in the label set.

`exception_reason` (reviewer-supplied text)
- Unbounded vocabulary even after normalization, and not used as a dashboard dimension. Worst of both: high cardinality, low analytical value in the label position. The bounded form is a small taxonomy — invariant, provenance, failure-mode, ownership-seam, escalation-boundary — which is also what the cross-service lane actually distinguishes between. Free text belongs on the event record.

`owner_email`
- The unnecessary employee-identifier surface. The mapped owner is already determined by `service_pair` via the owner map; the dashboard can join against it at query time. Putting the email in the label (a) parks a personnel identifier in metric storage where retention and access controls are typically looser than identity systems, (b) silently re-keys series when someone changes alias or leaves, and (c) isn't needed for grouping — the owner map is the source of truth for who owns a boundary, not the counter. If the dashboard wants the human name, join on the owner map; don't bake the identifier into the series.

Structural read
- Three of the four labels are write-once or unbounded-vocabulary, and the dashboard only slices by two of them. That's a counter being asked to store events. The bounded version: counter labeled by canonical `service_pair` (enum of known cross-service boundaries) and `exception_kind` (the taxonomy above), with PR and reason text on the structured event record that the counter is incremented from. Owner map stays the source of truth for ownership; the metric stays employee-identifier-free.

Scope note: I'm flagging the cardinality and identifier surfaces — that's within the cross-service lane. Whether to ship a metric in this shape, what taxonomy to adopt, and how the dashboard joins the owner map are decisions for you and the mapped telemetry owner; this read doesn't pre-empt them.

Cardinality and identifier risks

A metric label is part of an indexed time series. Every distinct (name, label-set) tuple the system has ever seen in the retention window is a live series in the index — it costs storage, it costs query time, and it shows up on dashboards whether anyone intended it to or not. Four failure modes that follow from that:

  1. Unbounded raw identifiers as label values turn the label into an open enumeration. A 24-hour staging fixture on the full 40-char build SHA hit ~2,940 distinct values; that is the shape of the failure, not an edge case. The same shape applies to tenant_id_hash, replay_source_id, raw limiter error strings, etc.

  2. Owner / source ambiguity on the dashboard. When the label is the raw ID, the panel stops telling you whether the series is live-path, validation-path, or replay-path. Cardinality Guardrails flags this as a Section-2 fail (no owner / no source / no declared cardinality shape) and a Section-6 fail (alert source not classified), because responders have historically read validation or replay evidence as a live rollback trigger.

  3. Retention and index cost. Unbounded series inflate the index linearly with the source population and slow the distinct-count queries the rest of the platform depends on.

  4. The fix is not "ban raw identifiers" — raw IDs are exactly what you need to debug. The fix is to put them where they belong (structured logs, trace spans) and keep the metric itself bounded.

Bounded metric design (Track A label / Track B raw)

Two-track separation, both kept in place:

  Track A — metric labels. Closed, owned, enumerated value set with small stable cardinality. Owner, source (live vs validation vs replay), expected cardinality shape, and alert-source classification are declared in the PR, per Cardinality Guardrails sections 2 and 6.

  Track B — raw identifiers. Out of metric labels. Live in structured log fields and trace span attributes, where they are queryable, joinable, and unbounded-safe.

Concrete shape, following the metrics-router#452 pattern (same shape that landed for refusal_reason on the limiter work):

  Metric:  <service>_<thing>_total  (counter)

  Labels (all closed enums, all declared in the PR):
    reason   ∈ { soft_limit, hard_limit, spike, recovered, other }   # canonical limiter shape
    source   ∈ { live, validation, replay }                          # Section-6 classification
    class    = bounded classification chosen for this PR             # e.g. tenant_class, build_class
    The "other" bucket is a sentinel only. Non-zero "other" means the enum needs a new value, and that addition is a deliberate PR — not an emergent label.

  What does NOT go on the metric:
    - raw tenant_id_hash, account_id, replay_source_id
    - full 40-char build SHA
    - raw limiter error / refusal message
    - any free-form path segment or user-controlled string

  What DOES go on the log record / trace span (Track B):
    - the raw identifier (tenant_id_hash, replay_source_id, build SHA, etc.)
    - owner details: who proposed it, who signed off, PR link, runbook entry id
    - the full refusal / error string
    - any context needed to root-cause from a metric bucket back to a specific instance

  Net effect: aggregate operational visibility is preserved — counts, rates, and breakdowns by the bounded enum stay meaningful — and the raw debugging identifier is one log-join away when someone actually needs it.

Where the proposal and owner details live

  PR / audit record:
    - Section-2 declarations (owner, source, cardinality shape, alert-source classification)
    - proposed enum values, with justification for each new dimension
    - link to the matching runbook entry
    - Section-4 distinct-count sample (cardinality shape named from the data, not from assertion)

  Runbook entry:
    - the closed enum, its owner, its declared cardinality budget
    - the procedure for adding a new value (which is a deliberate PR, not a code change buried somewhere)

  Log records / trace spans:
    - raw ID and owner / proposal context that the metric deliberately omits

  Dashboard / alert text:
    - source classification (live | validation | replay) so the panel cannot be misread as a live rollback trigger

Pre-merge verification (24-hour replay)

  Replay the last 24 hours of traffic through the proposed label set in staging and confirm distinct-count on every label stays inside the declared cardinality shape. Non-zero "other" is treated as a signal that the enum needs another value before the PR lands — not after.

Guardrails references

  Section 2 — owner + source + expected cardinality shape declared in the PR.
  Section 4 — distinct-count sample with cardinality shape named from the data.
  Section 6 — alert-source classification on any panel or alert text using the new dimension.
  Approved pattern — metrics-router#452 (refusal_reason enum is the reference shape).

Two things this design is NOT

  It is not a blanket ban on raw identifiers. Raw IDs are still allowed and still encouraged — in logs and trace context, which is where they belong.

  It is not a rule that says "no new dimensions ever." New bounded dimensions are welcome when a dashboard need justifies them; the rule is that the value set must be closed, owned, and small, and the justification must be in the PR.
