Warranty replacement is the clear call — $0 vs $85 vs $430, the cylinder is a pure wear item and the rest of the chair (seat, back, arms, casters, base) is sound, and 7-10 days is easy to bridge with the dining chair. Install is typically a 10-15 minute press-in swap after removing the base; if you don't already know the exact model, a photo of the label (usually under the seat) will identify the correct cylinder and confirm compatibility when you order.

One small practical note: when the new cylinder arrives, sit on the chair for a few minutes before returning to regular use to verify it holds height — that confirms the seal seated properly and you're not just reinstalling a marginally-better-but-still-failing part.

Quick comparison, then the recommendation.

Option A — Manufacturer warranty gas cylinder
- Cost: $0
- Turnaround: 7–10 business days for delivery
- Work: you install; about 10–15 minutes (pull the base, press the new cylinder in)
- Risk: a one- to two-week gap where the chair is unusable for height-adjustable work

Option B — Local chair-service cylinder swap
- Cost: ~$85
- Turnaround: next business day
- Work: drop-off or in-home, depending on the shop
- Risk: small; you're paying for speed and convenience

Option C — New comparable chair
- Cost: ~$430
- Turnaround: same day if in stock, longer if ordered
- Work: assemble (usually 15–25 minutes)
- Risk: you replace a chair whose seat, back, arms, casters, and base are all still sound

Practical recommendation: Option A.

The warranty cylinder is reasonable. A gas cylinder is a pure wear item — the internal seal slowly loses gas over years, which is exactly the "sinks a few inches over twenty minutes" symptom you're seeing. Manufacturers expect and cover it; receiving a replacement cylinder rather than a whole-chair swap is the normal and correct outcome. Nothing about a warranty cylinder suggests a downgrade in part quality versus what was originally in the chair. The $0 cost vs. $85 vs. $430 is decisive, and the rest of the chair is sound, so there's no reason to throw it out. The 7–10 day wait is also genuinely easy to absorb because you have a stable dining chair to bridge it.

Is the warranty cylinder reasonable: yes — it is the standard, expected resolution for exactly this failure mode.

How to use the chairs safely while you wait

1. Stop using the broken chair for desk work. The sinking is gradual, not catastrophic — it is not a collapse hazard — but it is ergonomically unreliable, and you will find yourself constantly readjusting.
2. Use the dining chair at your desk. It's stable, it's known, and it removes the temptation to "just sit for a minute" on the sinking chair.
3. Park the broken chair out of the path of habit. Push it against a wall, or to a different corner of the room, so you don't sit in it on autopilot.
4. Do not stand on it, kneel on it, or let anyone else use it as a step or perch. The cylinder losing pressure means it's no longer supporting design load predictably.
5. Keep it away from areas where Devika or a guest might grab it casually without thinking.
6. If the chair has a height-adjustment lever or knob, leave it at the lowest setting — that minimizes how far it can sink while you're waiting.
7. Once the new cylinder arrives: photograph the label (usually on a sticker under the seat) to confirm it's the correct class/size before you press it in; after the swap, sit on it for a few minutes and verify it holds height without drift.

You don't need to baby-monitor the chair; you just need to not depend on it for the next week or so.

15-MINUTE PRE-RIDE INSPECTION (post-layup)

TIRES — 3 min
  Press both tires with your thumbs at the top: should feel very firm. Spin each wheel and watch for true rotation; listen for hiss. Squeeze the tire against the rim on both sides — the bead should not shift. Eyeball sidewalls for cuts, cracks you can catch a fingernail in, or bulges.
  STOP if: hissing, soft sidewall, visible bulge, dry-rot crack your nail catches, cut reaching casing/threads, rim-strike sound, pressure drops in 5 min.

BRAKES — 2 min
  Squeeze each lever: firm, not spongy, not bottoming to the bar. Walk the bike forward and pull each brake — should lock the wheel without pull. Spin each wheel: light consistent rub is fine; rhythmic scrape or pulsing is not. Disc rotors should run true without visible wobble; pads should clear the rotor evenly.
  STOP if: lever spongy or bottoms, braking pulls to one side, pulse once per revolution, rotor visibly bent/cracked, pad rub louder than a whisper, wheel hard to spin by hand.

DRIVETRAIN — 3 min
  Look at the chain: clean, no rust pits, links flex freely. Pedal backward through every gear — shifts should be crisp, no delay or clunk. Lift the chain off a cog tooth with a finger: more than a millimeter of lift = worn. Check the smallest cog for hooked/shark-fin teeth. Spin the cranks with the rear wheel off the ground: no grinding, clicking per stroke, or rough spots.
  STOP if: any shift is sloppy, chain skips under load, clicking per pedal stroke, cassette cog visibly hooked, bottom bracket gritty or loose.

WHEEL RETENTION — 2 min
  Grab each tire at the top and rock laterally: no clunk, no play. Quick-release or thru-axle should close with firm resistance and leave a palm imprint; lever should point away from the drivetrain and away from the front fork. Lift the front of the bike and let it drop from a few cm: no thunk from the headset. Both wheels should spin freely for several seconds.
  STOP if: any lateral play at the axle, closure feels soft, drop test reveals a clunk, a wheel doesn't spin freely.

LIGHTS — 1 min
  Front (white) and rear (red) on. Confirm brightness, no flicker over bumps. Front beam should show the road 5–10 m ahead without dazzling you. If hub/dynamo powered, confirm the light comes on when you spin the wheel.
  STOP if: either light is dim, dies, flickers over bumps, or won't switch on.

LOADED TEST — 4 min
  Helmet on, water + phone, lights on. Ride 4–5 minutes in a traffic-free area, low speed. Brake gently front then rear — no pull, no pulse, no noise. Pedal through every gear under light load — no skip. Roll over one curb cut or speed bump — no rim strike, no harsh clunk. Sit on the bike at the end and eyeball tire compression — neither should look underinflated.
  STOP if: anything from the previous sections recurs, plus any new noise, vibration, pull, skip, or wobble.

FIRST 100 m AFTER THE TEST
  Scan for black ice, wet leaves, painted lines, gravel. Stay off sharp leans in the first turn. Build to normal speed over the next 5–10 minutes.

Rule of thumb for the whole sequence: if a finding is new since the last ride, or wasn't there when the bike went into storage, treat it as a stop. Old-known-and-stable (e.g., a faint consistent rub at the front rotor that you already recentered on 2024-10-20 and has not changed) is fine to ride through; anything new is not.

Premise: V6 has historically stopped at 3 quality attempts due to fingertip skin, not pulling strength. Feb 9 confirmed this ceiling. Spacing and interspersing easy climbing between hard burns is the lever that lets you get the most quality work without grinding into tender skin.

Structure (75 min total)

  0:00-0:15  Warmup (keep longer)
              - 5 min forearm prep (easy traversing, open-hand drills, no crimps)
              - 10 min easy climbing V0-V2, focus movement quality
              - No hard gripping before 0:30

  0:15-0:30  Build phase
              - V2-V4 moderate volume, varied hold types

This revision still blocks on the accounting contract. The terminal CAS correctly arbitrates which path returns the result to the caller — so caller-facing behavior is fixed — but the counter increments are decoupled from the CAS.

Mechanism: on the cancellation path, `cancelled_total` is incremented *before* the terminal CAS is attempted, with no rollback on CAS loss. In the interleaving you describe, cancellation increments cancelled_total, completion wins the CAS and increments success_total, and cancellation's increment is never reversed. Sum = 2 contributions for one accepted request. The completion path gets it right (CAS first, increment only if CAS wins); the cancellation path needs the same ordering.

Minimum fix, mirror the completion path:

  1. CAS terminal_state unset → cancelled
  2. If CAS won: cancelled_total += 1; return cancellation to caller
  3. If CAS lost: exit without touching the counter, do not return cancellation

Stronger fix: fold the counter into the atomic itself so one CAS writes the terminal result *and* selects which counter to increment. That makes the accounting and the terminal outcome inseparable and removes any future ordering hazard.

Either way, the cancel-vs-completion regression must assert the per-request invariant the contract requires:

  accepted_total == success_total + rejection_total + cancelled_total + refused_total

and per-request, exactly one terminal record. Under the current design that assertion still fails in the 7/1000 interleaving you cited.

Preserved by this design: single caller-visible result via CAS, separate queue/processing duration histograms. So the blocking issue is isolated to the counter ordering on the cancellation path.

**Blocking follow-up — ingest-edge cancellation revision (race assessment)**

The terminal-state improvement narrows the double-terminal window but does not close it under exactly-once accounting. Each path (cancel handler, worker-completion handler) still runs its own accounting side-effects — terminal-record emission and counter increment (`cancelled_total` / `succeeded_total` along with `accepted_work`) — and only afterwards observes the CAS result. The CAS picks one winner for *state*, but both handlers have already executed their *contribution*; the loser is dropped on the floor without rolling back its accounting. Concretely: `cancelled_total` can advance while the terminal record says `success` (or vice versa), `accepted_work` can move twice, and the acceptance ledger can be written by both paths.

The fix must couple terminal-state selection to accounting contribution, not just to terminal state:

1. The CAS (or equivalent single-writer primitive) that establishes the terminal outcome is the gate for accounting. If the CAS loses, the handler MUST skip both terminal-record emission and counter increments. If it wins, only that handler's accounting fires.
2. Whichever handler wins, its terminal record and its counter increment are co-atomic with the state selection — they commit together or not at all.
3. The invariant holds in both directions: cancel-arrives-during-completion and completion-arrives-during-cancel.

**Required regressions (deterministic, ≥10k runs each):**

- Cancel-vs-completion, both directions: exactly one terminal record per accepted request; record label matches the winning handler; counter increment count == 1; `accepted_work` advance == 1.
- Counter-label consistency: the winning counter (`cancelled_total` OR `succeeded_total`) increments exactly once; the losing counter does NOT increment; both cannot increment.
- Loser-path no-leak: no terminal record, no counter increment, no acceptance-ledger write, no in-flight set touch from the loser.
- Cancel-vs-dispatch: terminal record == `cancelled`, counter == `cancelled_total`, no worker-completion path ever ran accounting.

**Re-blocking (still open from prior review):**

1. Exactly one terminal outcome per accepted request.
2. Exactly one accounting contribution per accepted request, **aligned to the terminal outcome** — this is the gap the current revision does not close.
3. Race regression tests for cancel-vs-dispatch and cancel-vs-completion in both directions, with the counter/record invariants above.
4. Prior items still open: separate queue vs processing duration; deadline propagation from acceptance; five-second acceptance-to-terminal contract.

Here's a simple plan — one longer outing, three soft segments, with the abort signals built in. Total wall-clock 75–90 min including pauses.

Walk plan
- 0–10 min: warm-up loop near the hotel. Easy pace, leash check, paws down (a quick look at the same two front toes from the Feb baseline), first water offer in shade before you leave the block.
- 10–55 min: main out-and-back or easy loop. Steady but unhurried pace, ~30–35 min out, then turn. One shaded sit-and-water stop around the halfway point, ~5 min.
- 55–80 min: cool-down return. Slower pace, short sniff stops, second water offer in shade.
- 80–90 min: hotel reset. Towel paws (rinse if gritty), fresh water bowl, room cool and dim.

Turn-around cues — any one of these and you head back, no discussion
- Kibo lags, stops to lie down, or keeps glancing toward the hotel.
- Panting that doesn't ease within a minute in shade.
- Any paw issue: licking a foot, lifting a paw, shortening stride, or a hot spot on the same two front toes.
- Either of you wants to stop, or pavement feels warm to the back of your hand.
- A reactive dog, crowd, or traffic you didn't want to deal with today.

Water cadence
- Pre-walk (in shade), mid-walk (shaded sit), return (in shade). Collapsible bowl + one bottle is enough; you don't need to overthink refills.

Downtime after
- First 60–90 min back: water available, no outings, low lights.
- Afternoon: optional short relief loop only if he asks — otherwise skip and wait for the normal evening outing.

If at any point during the outing either of you says "tired" or "want to go home," that's the cue — same rule you've used before.

The pattern is clear enough to diagnose without seeing the wall: same edge, same moment, every attempt — that's a sequencing/loading problem on a single move, not a strength, skin, or fatigue issue. The fact that you stopped before fatigue and had no forearm symptoms confirms it.

ANALYSIS OF THE FOOT-AND-HIP SEQUENCE

The edge is doing its job; what's failing is what your hips do to the foot while the next hand is still in transit. Three root causes, in roughly descending order of frequency on this kind of move:

1.  Hip shift leads the hand, not follows it. When the hips drift toward the next hold before that hand is locked, your center of mass slides off the foot at the exact moment load on it spikes. The foot was placed, not loaded, so it has no friction reserve for the shear. Fix: commit the hand first (or at minimum simultaneously), then drive the hips through under the new hold.

2.  The foot is placed but not driven. A quiet touch on a small edge looks correct but carries no reserve. When the hips shift, the foot needs to be pressed into the edge with intent — actively loading the ball of the foot before the hip move starts. This is the same family as the quiet-foot work you've already been doing; here it's about drive, not placement.

3.  Foot position forces too much ankle torque. If the foot is too low or too far outside, the hip shift demands more torque than the foot can hold even when loaded. Sometimes the answer is a slightly higher or more inside replacement that lets the hips rotate around the foot instead of pulling off it.

To tell which one is yours, watch for one thing on the next attempt: at the moment of slip, is the next hand already on its hold, or still in transit? Still in transit → #1. Already on → #2 or #3.

BOUNDED PROGRESSION FOR NEXT SESSION

This keeps your existing framework (longer warmup, V6 quality gate, base stop criteria) and shifts emphasis from volume to sequencing learning, because more reps of a bad sequence reinforce it rather than retrain it.

Before hard attempts — drill block, ~10 minutes:
  - Off-wall rehearsal: right foot on a chair edge in the same orientation as the wall. Rehearse hip-shift + hand-reach 5 reps per side. Cue: hand reaches destination before hips move.
  - On the V6 line, opener sequence at RPE 4–5, two reps. Focus only on foot-load → hand-set → hip-shift ordering at the problem move; ignore everything else.

Hard attempts: 3 (down from the 5 cap)
  Rest between attempts: 5 minutes (up from 4). Sequencing learning needs a clearer motor system than link attempts.

Quality gate (sharpened for this session):
  Each hard attempt must include a deliberate loading pause on the right foot before the hip shift. If the foot is placed and immediately unweighted by the hip move, the attempt doesn't count — reset, and use the attempt only if you have one left.

Stop criteria (additions to the existing V6 set):
  - 3 hard attempts, OR
  - Foot slips on the same edge on two consecutive hard attempts (new, direct from tonight), OR
  - Any existing criterion: skin thin/tacky on any finger, skipping feet on two consecutive moves.

After the session: if the slip pattern persists on a majority of the three attempts, the move is more likely a foot-position problem (#3) than a timing problem, and worth getting Ren's eye on a specific replacement before another volume session.

This stays inside your established cap philosophy (bounded attempts, defined stop rules, no escalation of load), isolates the variable that's actually failing, and gives you a clean signal next session on whether the issue is sequencing or position.

The bounded finding is squarely in your lane (cross-service + failure boundary), and the contract violation is clear: the candidate sequence has a race window between "write authority record into the queryable index" and "commit the signed publication marker." During that window, 3 of 500 concurrent reads observed `publication_state=pending`, and the staff-only Lantern card rendered those records as ownership instead of explicit unknown. Per the dual-authority contract, anything short of a fully-committed publication renders explicit unknown -- `pending` is the same surface as stale or missing, not ownership.

Three bounded mitigations, smallest-to-largest:

  1. Render-side guard in Lantern: treat `publication_state != committed` as
     equivalent to missing/stale. Smallest patch, but leaves the race in the
     data layer.
  2. Atomic write at the publisher: combine the authority record + publication
     marker into a single transaction, or use a two-phase commit so reads
     don't see the index entry until the marker has committed. Eliminates
     the race entirely.
  3. Reorder the sequence: commit the publication marker first as a
     precondition, then write the authority record. Changes publish
     semantics; not worth it given 1 and 2 exist.

Recommendation: option 2 as the real fix, option 1 as a stopgap that ships first. The fix belongs with the owner-map publisher owner (PE), not Lantern -- this is an upstream source-record bug, not a Lantern rendering bug. The bounded review output is the contract violation + recommended mitigation; PE picks the implementation path.

Revised design = option 3 (reorder) plus staging pending records outside the published index. Within the ownership/provenance boundary the direction is sound — pending = explicit unknown is what the boundary requires. But the two missing tests are boundary blockers, not nice-to-haves.

1. Concurrent-read regression. The original bug surfaced exactly this way (500 concurrent staging reads, 3 saw publication_state=pending). Without the same or a stronger regression test (property-based with timing variance, not just unit tests), the revised design is unverified against the failure mode it claims to fix. The staff-only Lantern card lookup must use the same published-index path, or the test must explicitly prove that path cannot surface a pending record. Required for boundary acceptance.

2. Crash injection between marker commit and index promotion. This is a NEW failure window the original sequence did not have. The three-window crash discipline from rollup-service#317 (before commit, after commit before ack, before readiness publication) maps directly here: (a) before marker commit, (b) after marker commit but before promotion, (c) after promotion. Window (b) is the new one this design introduces — without an explicit test, two questions are unanswered:
   - On recovery, what promotes the stranded pending record? (Startup reconciliation scanning for committed-but-not-promoted, or other?) Without this, the record is durably stranded — fail-closed in the query sense but a durable inconsistency.
   - Is the signed marker durable indefinitely, or does it expire/revert? Stranded records accumulate unless there is a TTL or an explicit recovery path that handles an expired-but-committed marker.

Plus one related point: promotion idempotency on retry must be tested — duplicate retries must not duplicate the published record, and must not expose a partial mid-promotion state to a concurrent read.

Assessment of Wes's matcher-cache candidate (2027-05-27)

KEYING - CORRECT
  Candidate keys matchers by complete semantic route identity (route key, target, priority, fallback_policy, disabled, traffic_class). That closes the earlier "key by expression text" risk: two generations with identical expression strings but different per-generation missing-label defaults or normalizers will not collide. Insertion-order variants still hash equally. False↔true disabled, every traffic_class transition, and target/priority/fallback-only mutations each change identity and fail closed. No correctness gap in the key itself.

LEAK - NOT CORRECT
  Route deletion removes the route from the active table but not from the cache. In the 6h staging churn the cache grew ~7x (40K → 286K) while the active set stayed flat near 40K. RSS climbed 1.9 → 4.8 GiB. Restart restored baseline. The cache is effectively unbounded under churn. Whatever bound was assumed for it, that bound does not hold in the candidate as-is.

CONTAINMENT
  Production unchanged. Failure is in-process and isolated to staging. The cache can only be reset by process restart - config reload does not evict. Not self-healing in any reasonable deployment cadence.

WHAT IS NEEDED BEFORE A CANARY
  1. Cleanup specification. When does a cache entry go away? Three workable shapes - (a) event-driven on route removal, (b) generation-swap eviction of entries not present in the new active set, (c) bounded LRU with explicit cap. Wes picks; all three can be correct, but the choice has to be stated.
  2. Concurrency. In-flight matchers must not be freed mid-call. Reuse the explicit concurrency statement Wes already gave for the cleanup change.
  3. Failed-reload behavior. Entries added during a failed reload attempt must be evicted with the failed generation, not retained. The candidate currently says nothing about this.
  4. Boundedness evidence. Rerun the same 6h churn replay (or longer) with cleanup in place. Cache entries must track the active set within a small constant factor; RSS must stay flat; p99 must not regress.
  5. Generation-swap evidence. At least one swap where the new generation is largely disjoint from the prior. Confirm prior-generation entries that no longer apply are evicted, not just orphaned.

CANARY GATE
  Do not roll the candidate forward as-is. Even on the canary, a 6h-equivalent churn pattern would push RSS to ~5 GiB - near the canary's existing memory ceiling per the 2024-04-30 decoded-label incident. Two unrelated memory-bound issues on the same canary makes attribution and rollback messy.

SEPARATE FROM PRIOR
  This is retention (entries not freed), not allocation rate. Distinct from the 2025-02-13 snapshot-serialization question (1.8 → 2.6 GiB in 25 min). Don't conflate when reading later memory profiles.

[BLOCKING] Cache retention must be bounded to route or generation retirement, with an executed long-churn replacement regression.

Persisting compiled matchers keyed by deterministic route identity creates a retention obligation. Without bounded eviction tied to retirement, the cache either grows without limit or risks identity reuse against stale data after the underlying route or generation is retired.

Required:
1. Eviction must be tied to retirement of the route (route removed from active config) or retirement of the generation (generation no longer active). TTL or LRU alone is not sufficient; eviction must occur when the route or generation is retired.
2. If a stale entry cannot be evicted safely, the system must fail closed rather than silently retain or reuse it.
3. An executed regression demonstrating correct behavior under sustained long-churn replacement — many generations rotated over an extended period — showing the cache remains bounded in size, retired entries are not reused, and no identity collision occurs with stale data.

Here's the explanation and the bounded response.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

PROVENANCE DEFECT — WHAT IT IS

The two-phase publication design has a quiet invariant that isn't actually enforced by the storage layer: the signed publication marker is what carries provenance, but the marker is only authoritative while it lives. If the storage system compacts or rewrites the marker, and the marker is the only thing carrying source_record_id + the authoritative transition timestamp + the publisher's signature, then the published ownership is no longer provable from the on-disk artifact — it's provable only from the absence of compaction. That is the defect. It surfaces as a question the read model cannot answer: "this row says published, but what is the source it was published from, and when, and who signed the transition?" If the answer has to come from memory, a backup, or an inference ("we rebuilt from the canonical package"), the design is provenance-by-trust, not provenance-by-evidence.

Compaction is the obvious amplifier. A 7-day envelope retention rule, or a write-amortization compaction that re-encodes the marker block, can drop the signed transition evidence while leaving the published-state bit set. The read path will keep returning ownership; the audit path will have nothing to verify. That is exactly the failure mode Cyrus's shard-keeper audit-compaction proposal sketched, and it generalizes.

The defect is not that the marker is missing today. The defect is that the design has not specified what happens to it under compaction, and has not specified how a fresh process rebuilds provenance from durable state alone.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

WHY THIS MUST BE GATED BEFORE THE DESIGN PROCEEDS

The two-phase design's whole point is that the published read model is provable from a signed artifact. If the artifact can be silently rewritten by a routine storage maintenance job, then concurrent-read + crash-injection evidence from PR 431 only prove the in-memory/short-window behavior. They do not prove that "published" remains a claim backed by durable signed evidence over the artifact's lifetime. Executable rebuild and crash behavior are how that claim is proven or refuted.

So the gate is not "show me the marker schema." The gate is three concrete things:

1. Authoritative transition timestamp + signed transition evidence must survive compaction by construction — encoded in a way that any rewriter either preserves byte-equivalent or fails closed, with the marker block identifiable as such, not buried in opaque row state.

2. Executable rebuild: from the on-disk state plus the canonical inputs, a fresh process can reproduce the same (published_record, marker, signature) triple deterministically, with byte-equality between pre- and post-rebuild outputs. A drift check is the test, not the proof — the proof is that the rebuild ran end-to-end against the actual durable layout.

3. Crash behavior across the marker-to-promotion window, plus across compaction windows that intersect a pending record, plus across a rebuild that runs against a partially compacted marker — every one of those crashes must terminate with no published state whose backing evidence has been silently invalidated.

Until those three are demonstrated as executed evidence (not asserted, not designed-for), the design has not earned the word "provenance." PR 431's evidence stays valid for what it proved — the in-process, in-window behavior — but it does not cross the compaction boundary the user is now naming.

Analysis of the crash defect

The defect is in the swap sequence, not in the provenance model. The signed transition envelopes and their original source_timestamp values remain immutable and correct; the problem is how the rebuilt derived index is promoted.

What Cyrus's run showed (2027-06-05, 2,000 crash injections, 37 bad restarts): the replacement sequence removes the current derived index BEFORE the rebuilt file is durably promoted. A crash that lands in that window leaves no live index at the canonical path, and on restart the loader selected a partially-written temporary file and exposed it as the current index, omitting one or more retained transitions from historical lookup. Two coupled bugs:

  1. The swap is not atomic. unlink(old) runs before rename(new, old) is durable. Anything between those two steps — process crash, power loss, ENOSPC on the rename — leaves the canonical name pointing at nothing, or at whatever happens to be sitting there.
  2. The restart loader has no completeness gate. It accepts a parseable file as authoritative even when that file is a partial rebuild (truncated, missing trailing entries, stale temp from a prior failed attempt). That is how a partial index becomes visible.

Either bug alone is sufficient; together they guarantee that the next crash during compaction silently serves a torn historical view. The 37/2000 rate is the natural frequency of crashes landing in the unlink→promote gap; the rate would not drop with more retries, only with a correct swap.

What "correct" means here is small and well-understood: build to a sibling temp path, fsync the temp, atomically rename it over the canonical name (POSIX rename(2) is atomic on a single filesystem), and only then — never before — make the old file unobservable. The loader must validate the promoted file (checksum, entry-count vs the retained-log floor, structural parse of the trailing block) before exposing it; if validation fails or no valid file exists at the canonical name, it must fall back to the previous good index if one is recoverable, otherwise emit an explicit failed_reload signal. A partial temp must never be treated as live.

Yuki's exception — `failure_mode` — BLOCKING.

Defect. The candidate sequence is append terminal result → return success → sync terminal ledger. The durable terminal ledger commits AFTER the caller-visible success. A crash in the second gap (between return-success and ledger-sync) leaves the caller-acknowledged success unrecorded on durable state — that is exactly the 9 acknowledged requests missing after restart. On restart, no terminal result is durable, so the retry's "absent prior terminal → re-execute" rule fires and the same accepted request runs twice. This is a double-execution, not a missing audit row.

Required fix.
  1. Reorder: sync terminal ledger BEFORE return success. The caller's success is gated on the durable ledger commit.
  2. CAS-couple terminal result and accounting: one compare-and-swap selects the terminal enum returned to the caller; the same winning path is the only path that emits the terminal record and increments its counter. The loser emits nothing.
  3. Same shape as the prior ingest-edge correction: acceptance-ledger row before enqueue returns, terminal record coupled to the winning CAS, accounting side-effects only on the winner.

Required regressions (each ≥10,000 deterministic runs, on top of the 2,000 already executed):
  - Crash between append-terminal-result and sync-terminal-ledger: no acknowledged request missing after restart; retry returns the durable terminal result, not a re-execution.
  - Crash between sync-terminal-ledger and return-success: same outcome.
  - Retry when prior terminal result is absent: must NOT re-execute; durable ledger must already hold the terminal result. Counter increments exactly once.
  - Counter-label consistency: terminal record label matches counter (success/success_total, cancelled/cancelled_total, etc.). No off-label increments.
  - Loser-path no-leak: any path that loses the CAS emits no terminal record and no counter increment.

0:00–0:03  Exterior glance (unit off)
  - Look out the window at the outdoor sleeve: drain slot clear of debris, paint flakes, insect nest, or seed husks; no staining on the sleeve or wall.
  - Confirm the unit is silent.

0:03–0:07  Filter
  - Unplug from the receptacle.
  - Open the front panel per the manufacturer's path (lift/pull — no tools).
  - Remove the filter; vacuum it. Only rinse with lukewarm water if visibly soiled, and let it air-dry fully before reinstalling. If you rinsed, stop here and resume tomorrow with the cooling test.

0:07–0:10  Cord, receptacle, mounting
  - Cord: insulation intact end-to-end, no cracking, exposed wire, or deformation; plug prongs straight and clean; no discoloration.
  - Receptacle: faceplate flush, no soot or discoloration; plug fits snugly with no wiggle.
  - Chassis: confirm the familiar quarter-inch outward tilt is unchanged — that tilt is the as-designed drain orientation, not a defect. No new looseness, mounting tabs seated, panel closes firmly without forcing.

0:10–0:13  Reassemble and power
  - Dry filter back in; close panel.
  - Plug in; leave the unit OFF.

0:13–0:20  Cooling test
  - Fan High, mode Cool, thermostat a few degrees below room temperature.
  - Run ~5 minutes. Sweep the interior lower edge, sill, wall, and floor for any moisture.
  - At the exterior, confirm condensate is dripping from the drain slot.
  - Listen for a steady hum — no rattle, squeal, or grinding.

Stop using it and contact South Slope management if you see any of:
  - Any moisture, beading, or drip on the interior edge, sill, wall, or floor
  - Smoke, burning smell, or scorch marks at the plug or receptacle
  - Breaker or GFCI trip, or plug/receptacle warm or hot to the touch
  - Cord damage — cracks, exposed conductor, melting, deformation
  - Receptacle loose, cracked, discolored, or arcing on plug-in
  - Unusual noise (grinding, squealing, persistent rattle) or vibration beyond the normal hum
  - Ice on the coil or supply air, or no cool air during the test
  - Foul or moldy odor from the unit
  - Chassis shifted, new looseness, panel won't seat, or tilt changed from the prior quarter-inch
  - No exterior drip during cooling

After the test: if everything is dry and quiet, return the unit to Off until you actually need it. Optional follow-up next week — a longer cooling run and a photo of the interior pan area as a baseline.

Keep the 30-minute slot but plan to stop at 20–25 min. At 76°F with a 70°F dew point, evaporative cooling is roughly half what you'd get at a 55°F dew point — "easy" still loads thermoregulation. Path is dry, you're not primary, no restriction: go, but don't chase the full 30 if effort drifts up.

Pacing
- Run by feel, not pace. Target RPE ~3/10: nose-breathing, full sentences possible.
- Expect 20–40 sec/mile slower than your cool-weather easy pace.
- First 5 min walking or shuffle-jogging; don't start at goal pace.
- Cut to walk intervals if HR climbs >10% above your normal easy HR or breathing shifts mouth-only.

Hydration
- 6–8 oz plain water in the 15 min before start.
- Sip 2–4 oz at the 15-min mark; same again if you go past 25.
- Under 45 min, eating normally today → water is enough; skip electrolyte mix.

Pre-cool
- Light, light-colored, wicking shirt only — no cotton.
- Cold water on wrists and back of neck before stepping off.

Hard stop signals (walk immediately, then end the run)
- Dizziness, nausea, chills, or goosebumps in heat
- Sweating suddenly stopping or surging
- HR not dropping within 2 min of walking
- Cramping, stumbling, vision graying, confusion, slurred thoughts

Bail rules
- Plan A: stop at 20 min if RPE has crept above 4.
- Plan B: stop at 15 min at the first warning sign above.
- Don't extend past 30 even if it feels easy — finish clean and be back in South Slope before the workday starts.

If you want one rule instead of three: cap at 25 min and call it done. That's the cleanest cut for 70°F dew point without burning the protected weekend.

Bottom line: keep the asynchronous intake, decline the standing weekly meeting, define explicit triggers for the small set of cases that actually need a cross-system conversation. The 17-request corrected sample is itself evidence the async model is doing the routing correctly, and a fixed cadence would re-introduce the queue shape the April 7 2025 rule was designed to prevent.

What the 14/17 result actually shows

  Three things, in order of importance for this decision:

  1. The intake filter is catching misroutes. 3/17 (about 18%) bounced before consuming reviewer time. That is the gate working, not a gap that needs a meeting to close.
  2. The 14 that proceeded all carried the three required fields: named mapped owner, one listed exception class, concrete failed or at-risk condition. The bounded-review design is functioning as designed.
  3. Zero of the 14 asked you to approve routine implementation or release after entering your lane. The lane is staying narrow because the form is shaped right, not because you are policing it in conversation.

  A standing meeting does not add signal to any of these. It adds cadence.

Standing weekly meeting - what it would actually do

  On the dimensions that matter for your concern:

  - Gate risk: HIGH. Once a Tuesday slot exists, owners route ambiguous work there to "be safe" rather than back to the mapped owner. The 3/17 returns happened because there was nowhere to park ordinary work except the return path. A meeting is somewhere to park it.
  - Mapped-owner authority: ERODES. A standing reviewer slot reads as a second pair of eyes on ordinary release decisions, even if the agenda says otherwise. The April 7 2025 design is "exception -> that owner, that boundary only." A weekly meeting dissolves the "that boundary" framing.
  - Exception-handling speed: NO IMPROVEMENT in the median case. The 14 bounded exceptions are bounded precisely because they do not need a multi-party discussion. They need you to confirm the exception class is honored and the rollback owner is named. Async can do that in hours; a weekly slot can only do it on Tuesday.
  - Cadence pressure: REAL. Empty weeks get filled. Filled weeks drift toward status updates. Status updates become minutes; minutes become policy.
  - Staff IC scope fit: WORSE. Cross-service authority without people-management is the scope. A standing meeting where you are the named reviewer of cross-cutting items reads as a governance committee to anyone reading the calendar, regardless of what gets said in the room.
  - Thursday wind-down: BREAKS. A standing 15:00 Tuesday is fine. A standing meeting that drifts to "we'll just grab 30 minutes to talk through this one" by 18:30 Thursday does not.

  Net: a standing meeting would either be empty, fill with the wrong work, or both. None of those outcomes handles real exceptions better than the current model.

Ad hoc, boundary-triggered review - what it preserves

  - Gate risk: LOW. No standing slot, no place to park ordinary work. The return path stays the only path for it.
  - Mapped-owner authority: INTACT. Review fires only when a request names a cross-service exception that the intake form cannot resolve on its own. The mapped owner is still the implementation and release owner.
  - Exception-handling speed: ASYNC-FAST for bounded requests (most of the 14). SCHEDULED-FAST for the few that need a real cross-system conversation - you commit to a window, not a cadence.
  - Cadence pressure: NONE. No slot to fill.
  - Staff IC scope fit: GOOD. You show up only when a concrete named boundary is on the table, which is exactly what the role was scoped for.
  - Thursday wind-down: HOLDS. Ad hoc reviews get scheduled; they do not pre-empt protected time.

Recommended Q3 operating model

  1. Keep the May 12 corrected intake as the front door. Same three required fields: named mapped owner, one listed exception class, concrete failed or at-risk condition.
  2. Define the ad hoc trigger explicitly. A review is scheduled only when an intake item meets at least one of:
       - Cross-service parity or provenance boundary where two mapped owners disagree on the data contract.
       - A rollback path that crosses service ownership and needs a second named owner on the exception itself, not just the rollback.
       - A repeated exception class (same class, 2 or more requests in a rolling 4 weeks) where the pattern itself becomes the named boundary.
     The 14/17 sample suggests most bounded requests will not hit any of these and will resolve async.
  3. Set an explicit response SLA on async intake. First response within 1 business day; bounded exceptions confirmed or returned within 3 business days. This is what removes the perceived case for a standing meeting - visible speed without cadence.
  4. Add a monthly written aggregate (not a meeting) for Hema and Nadia to audit. One page: count returned before review, count bounded exceptions confirmed async, count that triggered ad hoc review, named-boundary patterns observed. This gives Hema the visibility she is asking for without giving you a standing seat.
  5. Re-evaluate at the end of Q3 using the same three required fields and the same return-rate metric. If the return rate drops below about 10% or the ad hoc trigger fires less than once a month, the model is over-provisioned. If it fires more than twice a month, the intake form needs tightening, not a meeting.

What to tell Hema

  The 17-request corrected sample shows the async model is doing the routing correctly: 3 returned before review, 14 proceeded as bounded exceptions, zero asked for routine implementation or release approval in-lane. A standing weekly meeting would add cadence without adding signal and would re-introduce the queue shape the April 7 2025 rule was designed to prevent. Instead: keep async intake, define explicit ad hoc triggers for the small set of cases that actually need a cross-system conversation, set visible response SLAs, and replace the meeting with a monthly written aggregate she can audit. The 30-minute invariant has to be enforced by the same mechanism that durably publishes the snapshot and index — not asserted by a separate marker that can disagree with disk state.   3. Binding: the retention marker must be published atomically with, or derived from, the durable snapshot+index state, so the marker can't claim retention the artifacts don't back.

Here's a draft outline for the packet. Two examples, three bullets each, no identifiers. Time stamps and details are illustrative — replace or adjust to match the cases Devika wants to use.

FACILITATOR PREPARATION PACKET — OUTLINE
Topic: Late entries and addendums that preserve the original record
Audience: attending-docs, documentation-update session
Due: July 30, 2027

Framing (1–2 lines for facilitators)
Late entries and addendums serve different purposes. A late entry records a clinical event that happened earlier than the time of documentation; an addendum preserves the original note and adds or corrects a detail without rewriting it. In both cases, the wording must make the timeline and the integrity of the original record explicit.

Example 1 — Late entry: reassessment time vs. documentation time
- What happened: A reassessment of a patient was performed at 16:55. The clinician was unable to enter the note immediately and documented the findings at 17:40, after finishing the next task.
- Safe wording: "Late entry entered at 17:40 for a reassessment performed at 16:55. This entry records the findings from the 16:55 reassessment and does not alter the note entered earlier in the day."
- What the wording must not imply: It must not imply that the reassessment occurred at 17:40, that the original earlier note was changed, or that the delay was clinically relevant. The reassessment time stays at 16:55; the entry time is the 17:40 documentation action only.

Example 2 — Addendum correcting a detail while preserving the original record
- What happened: A progress note was entered at 10:00 and recorded an administered dose that did not match what was actually given at 09:30. The original note was left in place; an addendum was added later the same day to record the correct dose and to state that the original had not been altered.
- Safe wording: "Addendum entered at 14:10: The dose recorded in the 10:00 progress note was transcribed in error. The dose administered at 09:30 was [X mg]. The original 10:00 note has not been altered."
- What the wording must not imply: It must not imply the correct dose was given at 14:10, that the original note was edited or replaced, or that the transcription error occurred at the time of administration. The administration time stays at 09:30; the original note is the historical record; the addendum is the only place where the correction appears.

Notes for facilitators
- Both examples keep the clinical event time and the documentation time as two separate, named values.
- Both examples state explicitly that the original record is unchanged.
- Replace bracketed values with whatever the chosen cases support; keep all identifiers out.

FOOD CALLS FIRST — these don't depend on the repair outcome. The fridge was above 40°F (danger zone) for 8+ hours, which already exceeds the 2-hour rule by a wide margin. Decide the food now.

FRIDGE (48°F, 8+ h above 40°F)
  - Milk — DISCARD. Dairy >40°F for >2 h is unsafe. Don't sniff-test; the bacteria that matter don't produce odor.
  - Eggs — DISCARD. Raw shell eggs above 40°F for >2 h per conservative guidance (8 h is past any leniency).
  - Cooked leftovers — DISCARD. Cooked starches and proteins carry the highest toxin-former risk (B. cereus on rice/grains, S. aureus on prepared foods). No sniff-test override.
  - Raw chicken — DISCARD. Poultry is the highest-risk category; no exceptions.

Bag the discards in a sealed bag and into a closed kitchen trash bin — keep Kibo away from it; raw chicken is dangerous to dogs too (salmonella, bones).

FREEZER (14°F, still solidly frozen)
  - All freezer items remain SAFE. 14°F is below the freezing point of food (salt/sugar content pulls freezing point to ~28–32°F); nothing has thawed. Quality is degrading faster than at 0°F, but no safety loss.
  - Don't open the freezer any more than necessary. Every opening wastes cold.
  - If a working freezer is reachable within an hour or two (friend, neighbor, family), transferring high-value frozen items into a cooler with ice packs preserves quality during the repair window. If not, leave the freezer closed and let it ride.

NO-DISASSEMBLY DIAGNOSTIC (~5 minutes, in this order)
  1. Verify your thermometer — put it in a glass of ice water, stir, read at 30 s. Should be 32°F ±1°F. If it reads high, your 48°F is overstated (good news — but recalibrate before trusting later checks).
  2. Dollar-bill seal test — close the door on a bill all the way around; pull. If it slides out easily, the seal has failed on that side.
  3. Listen at the freezer — open briefly, listen for the evaporator fan hum. No fan = cold air isn't circulating to the fridge, which fits a warm fridge with a still-cold freezer (a common failure mode).
  4. Feel for warm air at the back/bottom grille. Warm airflow = condenser doing work. Cold/silent grille = compressor running but not pumping.
  5. Check the air vent between freezer and fridge (small slot near the back/top of the fridge interior). Food stacked against it blocks cold transfer.
  6. Recheck both compartment temps at 1–2 h, 4 h, and 6 h. Targets: fridge ≤40°F, freezer ≤0°F. Anything trending up or flat by the 2 h mark is a real appliance failure, not a transient.

MONITORING + ESCALATION
  - If fridge is ≤40°F and falling by the 2 h check: let it run, recheck at 4 h and 6 h.
  - If still >40°F at 6 h with compressor running: full cooling failure. Don't restock; plan for a cooler.
  - Don't restock the fridge until it has held ≤40°F for at least 4 consecutive hours with normal door-opening, verified by your own thermometer (not the built-in display).

RELOCATION IF THE FRIDGE CAN'T BE FIXED TODAY
  - One styrofoam cooler + a bag of regular ice buys roughly 24 h for newly purchased perishables. Don't try to move the discards back — the exposure window is the issue, not the current temperature.

25-min pantry pasta e ceci for two

Quantities (sized to finish everything tonight):
  6 oz dry pasta (short shape: shells, ditalini, or broken spaghetti)
  1 can chickpeas, drained
  1 to 1.5 cups tomato sauce (a small jar is ~1.75 cups; use most of it tonight and discard the rest — opened sauce can't safely sit out overnight unrefrigerated)
  1 medium onion, diced

  4-6 slices bread

  0:00  Pot of salted water on to boil (4 qt, 1 tbsp salt). Skillet out for the sauce.
  0:02  Dice onion; drain chickpeas; open sauce.

  0:10  Water boiling: pasta in. Cook per package (most short shapes 9-11 min).
  0:12  Chickpeas into the onions. Splash of water (~1/4 cup). Add sauce. Season with salt, pepper, herbs, optional red pepper flakes. Simmer gently.

  0:18  Taste pasta; should be approaching al dente.
  0:20  Reserve ~1/4 cup pasta water. Drain pasta. Toss with the sauce in the skillet, or plate pasta and spoon sauce over; loosen with pasta water if it looks tight.
  0:22  Plate. Bread on the side. Drizzle of olive oil, grind of pepper.
  0:25  Eat.

Yes — a 6mm separation at the toe edge between the rand and toe-cap rubber is one of the classic resoling scenarios, and with the upper, rand, closure, and fit intact and no hole through the rubber, this is a plausible resole candidate rather than a write-off. Holding the shoe out of rotation until you decide is the right call.

WEIGHING RESOLE VS REPLACEMENT

Resoling (typically $45–$85 plus shipping, 2–4 week turnaround) usually wins when:
  - Uppers are structurally sound — no delamination between upper and midsole, no holes, no leather rot or fabric fraying
  - Rand is intact — toe-rand condition is the single biggest tell; if it isn't worn through or peeling back, the shoe has life
  - Closure works and shoe still fits your foot (climbing shoes pack out over time, so a resole can also restore some original downturn/edge if the upper hasn't collapsed)
  - It's the first or second resole — most shoes are designed for 2–3 resoles before rand and upper reach end of life

Replacement usually wins when:
  - Rand is shot in more than one spot or pulled back from the rubber
  - Closure is failing, upper is separating from midsole, or shoe has lost its shape
  - Shoe no longer fits because the upper has packed out and you can't size down — resoling won't fix a sloppy fit
  - It's already had two resoles and the rand/uppers are at end of life

For a single localized edge separation on an otherwise intact shoe, resole is usually the right call. It's roughly 30–50% the cost of a new pair, and a competent shop will re-bond the delaminated section as part of the work. The fact that the fit and upper still feel sound is the strongest signal in favor of resole.

WHAT A SHOP NEEDS FOR A USEFUL QUOTE

Minimum photos:
  1. Close-up of the separation itself, with a ruler or coin in frame for scale
  2. Top-down view of the whole shoe (both if sending both)
  3. Sole wear pattern — sole facing the camera on a flat surface
  4. Rand around the full perimeter, especially the toe rand
  5. Any other damage (closures, upper, heel)

Minimum written info:
  - Brand, model, size, and approximate age
  - Type of climbing and frequency
  - Whether it's been resoled before, and how many times
  - One-sentence description of what's wrong (e.g., "6mm separation at toe edge between rand and toe cap, no hole through rubber, no other damage")
  - Whether you want a standard resole or a full overhaul (rand replacement, etc.)

A shop that specializes in climbing shoes (not a generic cobbler) can usually quote from these without seeing the shoe in person. If you have a climbing-gear-specific resoler in your area, that's preferable — they keep the rubber stock, rand patterns, and adhesives matched to the construction. If you're mailing it, call or email first to confirm they handle your specific brand and model before shipping.

Two things to ask the shop at drop-off:

If inspection passes → resole at $72. If the shop flags hidden rand damage, delamination elsewhere, or the rand as marginal → new pair at $165, and retire the old upper or keep it as a beater. Either way, the decision is gated on what they find in-hand, not on the phone estimate.

Resole vs. replacement for climbing shoes/boots — using the criteria from your earlier sessions, with an explicit threshold for hidden rand damage.

OPTION A — RESOLE
  Cost: $45–$85 + shipping (round-trip to a climbing-shoe specialist).
  Turnaround: 2–4 weeks.
  What you get: fresh sole rubber; rand is normally retained unless it needs
    separate work. Most shoes are designed for 2–3 resoles in their life.
  Wins when: uppers structurally sound (no delamination, no holes), rand is
    intact (not worn through, not peeling), closure works, shoe still fits,
    and this is your 1st or 2nd resole.

OPTION B — REPLACEMENT
  Cost: roughly $150–$200+ for a comparable new pair (your earlier $118
    figure was the backpack, not shoes).
  Turnaround: ship/delivery, plus a break-in period before they feel right.
  What you get: a fresh rand and uppers, full structural life ahead, no
    hidden defects to discover later.
  Wins when: rand damaged in multiple spots or pulled back, closure failing
    or upper separating from midsole, shoe no longer fits, or the shoe has
    already had two resoles and the rand/uppers are at end of life.

RECOMMENDATION
  Resole — your 6 mm toe-edge rand/toe-cap separation is a classic, clean
  resole candidate (not a write-off), the uppers are still sound, and a
  $45–$85 repair against a $150–$200+ replacement is the practical call as
  long as the rand is otherwise intact. Use a climbing-shoe specialist
  (not a generic cobbler) and confirm they handle your brand and model
  before shipping; send the five photos you'd normally need (separation
  with scale, full top-down, sole wear pattern, full perimeter rand, any
  closure/heel damage) for a tight quote.

HIDDEN RAND DAMAGE — THE "STOP AND SWITCH TO REPLACEMENT" POINT
  A resole becomes uneconomical when the cobbler opens the shoe and finds
  any of the following underneath what you could see from outside:

  1. Rand-to-midsole bond failed along a continuous arc (not just the
     visible 6 mm spot) — the rand is no longer attached to the sole over
     a meaningful length, so a resole won't hold.
  2. Rand worn through to a hole at any point — new rubber can't bond to
     a void; the rand itself has to be replaced, and a rand swap roughly
     doubles the bill into replacement territory.
  3. Rand rubber crumbling, oxidized, or "spongy" under the surface — the
     substrate is gone, not just the tread.
  4. Rand-to-upper bond failing (peeling away from the leather/synthetic,
     not just from the midsole) — that's an upper-integrity problem a
     resole can't fix.
  5. Multiple hidden voids, bubbles, or adhesive-failure patches under
     the rand — the bond is unreliable across the shoe.

  Practical rule of thumb: if the cobbler's mid-repair finding forces a
  rand replacement on top of the resole, total cost lands around
  $120–$170+ and you're at or past half the price of new shoes without
  any of the rand's remaining life — that's the line. Stop, accept the
  inspection fee, and put the money toward a replacement pair.

  One pre-ship step that prevents surprise: ask the shop to quote the
  resole assuming the rand is sound, AND quote the additional cost if a
  rand replacement turns out to be needed. If the conditional quote
  pushes the total past roughly $130–$150, replacement is the cleaner
  answer up front and you save the round-trip shipping on a shoe you
  won't keep.

South Slope bathroom sink — bounded first-pass

Scope is tight: stopper + visible hair/soap only. No trap disassembly, no chemicals of any kind, no mixing.

Prep (one tray, small surface area):
- Towel folded under the basin
- Paper towels, small trash bag, rubber gloves
- Old toothbrush
- Zip-It strip, or a wire bent into a small hook (max 6-10 in reach)

Sequence:
1. Remove the stopper. Most South Slope bathroom stoppers pull out by hand; if yours has a pivot rod under the basin, reach behind the tailpiece and loosen the nut to release the rod before lifting the stopper out.
2. Wipe hair and soap scum off the stopper and out of the immediate drain opening with the toothbrush and paper towel. Bag the debris. This alone often fixes a two-minute drain.
3. Bounded reach only: feed the Zip-It straight down 6-10 in, pull back gently 2-3 times with a quarter-turn between passes. Do not push past light resistance. Do not fish past the visible opening into the trap.
4. Reseat the stopper. Run warm tap water 30-60 seconds to flush loosened material.
5. Controlled flow test: close the stopper, fill the basin about halfway, pull the stopper, and time how long the basin takes to empty. Compare against your ~2 min baseline.

Stop right away if any of these appear:
- Tool meets hard resistance (do not force it)
- Water rises in the basin instead of falling
- A new drip appears at the trap, supply, or wall
- Stopper will not reseat and water leaks past it
- No meaningful improvement after about 15 min of effort
- Any gurgling from the tub or toilet, sewage odor, or backup anywhere

No chemicals. Skip the baking-soda-and-vinegar experiment too — it does not clear hair, and if management or a plumber later needs to pull the trap, residual heat in the line is the last thing anyone wants. Do not mix anything in the drain.

Contact management (don't push further yourself) when:
- The ~2 min drain time does not improve noticeably after the mechanical pass
- The clog sits below where the Zip-It can reach without resistance
- Any stop condition above fires — especially a new drip, or any sign of backup elsewhere
- Or, even on full success, a short portal note is worth filing so the slow drain is on record before it becomes a full blockage

When you write them, state: you cleaned the stopper and visible hair/soap mechanically, no chemicals were used, and the drain now runs in X seconds (or "still ~2 min"). That keeps it easy to dispatch and keeps your "no chemicals" status on file.

INSPECTION — no ride, no hydraulic opening, externally visible only:

1. Pads. Remove the front wheel (does not open the hydraulics). View both pads straight down through the caliper window. If you see the backing plate, or pad material is roughly under 1.5 mm, pads are at or past wear-out. Markedly thinner on one side suggests a sticky piston.

2. Pad surface. Look for glazing (shiny, mirror-like) or any oily / wet film. Either points to contamination.

3. Rotor, edge-on. Sight down the rotor face from the side. Look for hairline cracks (especially near the edge or around the bolt holes), deep grooves, or blue / purple heat discoloration. A visible step where the swept area meets the unswept outer edge means the rotor is at or below minimum thickness — most rotors have a "Min. Th." value stamped on them.

4. Rotor face. Look for a uniform matte grey. Shiny patches, oil staining, or scoring need to be noted.

5. Lever body. With the bike upright, check the master-cylinder / reservoir area for any seep. Many Shimano levers have a small fluid window — the level should sit at the indicated mark. One gentle hand-squeeze of the lever is fine for observation only; do not pump or hold.

6. Hose. Trace the full visible run from lever to caliper. Look for kinks, abrasion, crushed sections, or dampness.

7. Banjo bolts. Check both ends (at the lever and at the caliper) for any seep, even a faint damp ring around the fitting.

8. Caliper mounting bolts. Confirm both bolts are present and seated; a light firm turn with the correct hex key to confirm tightness only — do not loosen the bolts that clamp the hose, and do not try to recenter the caliper by pushing pistons back.

9. Lever pivot. Hold the bar steady and push / pull the lever body sideways. Any looseness points to a mechanical pivot issue rather than hydraulics and changes the diagnosis.

Note anything you see in steps 1–9 — that becomes the "findings" line of the shop description.

Tenant-identity boundary — hard fail before batching or acceptance

The OTel collector must treat tenant identity as a hard precondition for any batch that could be exported, accepted, or attributed to a tenant context.

Definition of missing / malformed. tenant_id is absent, null, empty, a placeholder (e.g. "unknown", "default", "anonymous", "0", an empty string after trim), not parseable as the documented opaque identifier, or otherwise not bound to the calling authenticated context. Failure point. If tenant identity is missing or malformed, the collector must fail the affected path BEFORE either (a) co-batching with other spans, or (b) acceptance into any export pipeline or attributed tenant view. The failure must be observable (counter / log) so the missing-identity rate is visible.

Fallback rule. No synthetic, default, or shared tenant value may be substituted. The only exception is a separately authoritative tenant-binding contract: a signed, versioned, owner-attributed artifact that explicitly names the binding case, its scope, and the substitute value, and is referenced from this PR. Hi Anya,

On the measurement-boundary grouping — keep release_candidate in the upsert identity. The accepted key is (team, release_candidate, canonical_package_version); that's the one configuration where both behaviors hold at once: a retry against the same handoff updates one observation in place, and a distinct release candidate against the same team + package version stays its own row. Drop RC from the key and one of those breaks. If team + canonical_package_version collide across two different RCs in the same window, a two-field key collapses them — distinct handoffs stop being distinct, and the per-RC correction count becomes unrecoverable from the observation. Conversely, if you tried to compensate by widening anything else to disambiguate, you'd lose the stable handle the worker needs to upsert against, and the "retry updates one observation" behavior we closed on goes with it.

Net: the three-field identity is the only one that lets "retries update one observation" and "distinct handoffs stay distinct" both be true. With two fields you get one or the other, not both.

Why this shape works for the "relaxed, not errand-run" goal:
- It's one continuous walk with one destination and one return, just routed differently — no "while we're out, let's also…" stops.
- Parallel-avenue out-and-back adds maybe 5–8 minutes each way versus a straight reroute, which fits "deliberate outing" without becoming a hike.
- You keep the front-of-mind ritual intact: cortados, crossword at the back counter, leave when the puzzle's done or the cups are empty — no fixed return time.

If 8th feels uninspiring, the only meaningfully different alternative is swinging along the Prospect Park edge (Prospect Place west, then south along the park to 9th Street, back over to 7th). - Easy jog + dynamic mobility: leg swings, hip openers, ankle circles.
- Activation: calf raises (double → single-leg), A-skips, lateral shuffles, accelerations to ~80%.
- 2–3 progressive full-speed cuts — smooth, not cold max-effort decels. Smaller-sided means more change-of-direction per minute than usual, so rehearse it.

Substitution
- Expect short stints (~30 sec–2 min) with brief rotations; confirm the pattern with whoever is calling subs before kickoff.
- On every re-entry: 1–2 controlled touches before re-sprinting — don't go straight to top gear cold.

Hydration (Aug 1 in NYC = hot + humid even early)
- 12–16 oz water in the hour before; bring a bottle to the sideline, sip 4–8 oz between short games.
- Add electrolytes if you're sweating through kit on re-entry or session runs past 60 min.
- Headache, lightheadedness, or dark urine = you're behind — sub off and rehydrate, don't mask it.

Effort
- Format is repeated high-intensity bursts with partial rest, not steady-state. Lungs (not legs) tend to be the first limiter in this pattern — pace the first 2–3 rotations at ~80–85%, save top gear for mid-session.
- Stop or sub off immediately if you wheeze, feel a calf grab, or get lightheaded. Don't push through any of those.

Two invariants the new epoch-guard path has to prove, not just claim:

1. A reader that has acquired its epoch guard and observed the active generation pointer must continue to find that generation routable for the full critical section (Acquire → Load → Lookup → Match → Release). Reload, retire, and reclaim of the *replaced* generation cannot free any object that an epoch-pinned reader still references. Latency inside that critical section has to stay bounded by reader work, not writer work, or invariant 1 collapses under load.

2. Any reload path that does not reach successful Publish leaves `active_generation` and the routable gen set exactly as they were. No rejected candidate, no interrupted constructor, no partial worker-apply may cause a later reader's lookup to dereference a generation the active pointer never pointed at.

Interleavings I need to see addressed. Passing runs are fine; the proof has to live in the diff or its accompanying doc, not only in test names. Each one is a concrete way a valid in-flight lookup can lose its route:

A. Epoch-pin survives swap and drain. R: Acquire → Load returns gen G. W: Publish(G+1) → Retire(G) → quiesce-wait drains. R continues Lookup+Match against G for the full critical section. G stays reachable and intact, even if G+1 is later rejected and dropped. Cover the miss path: R's Lookup misses in G's cache and must populate from G's compiled matchers. The miss path must not fall through to a newer gen.

B. No use-after-free between Load and pin. R is between the primitive that loads the raw gen pointer and the primitive that pins its epoch. W's Retire+Reclaim runs in that window. The pin must be established *before* Load can observe a reclaimable pointer. Show the ordering guarantee explicitly. The previous revision's load-then-bump pattern fails this interleaving.

C. Rejected candidate never becomes routable. W's constructor inserts the candidate into the process-wide generation registry. Validation fails. W drops the candidate pointer. No reader — concurrent or subsequent — loads that pointer from the registry, either via the active slot or via a cache-key match that resolves to the candidate. The current failure path doesn't remove the registry entry, so interleaving C is not closed until either the registry insert moves past Validate or the failure path deletes the entry. Failed-reload generations being retained indefinitely in the registry is a related but separate defect.

D. Interrupted reload leaves active unchanged. W panics or is cancelled mid-construction, after some candidate fields are written but before Publish. The active pointer is never swapped. Readers continue to see the previous active gen. The constructor's defer/cleanup must not partially advance `active_generation` or leave a half-built gen in the registry that a later reader's key match could resolve to.

Specifics from the prior round, restated for the record:

- Cache key is `(Expr, MissingLabelMode, NormalizerVersion)` per the 2024-04-25 matcher-cache spec. A reader pinned to gen G must not miss a route that exists in G's compiled matchers because the key crossed generations.
- Registry insert currently happens before Validate. Until that moves past Validate (or the failure path deletes the entry), the candidate registry can leak failed generations indefinitely, independent of whether the candidate was ever published.

The offer's silence on the conversion question is itself the answer to act on. The safest reading is that conversion closes the existing product and therefore terminates (not satisfies) the 12-month commitment. Most issuers treat a product change as closing the original account and opening a new one under the same number, which is exactly the trigger retention terms are written to catch. The only thing that determines whether your $40 credit survives is what your specific issuer says for this specific account.

What I'd do before doing anything:

1. Don't accept the conversion yet. Conversions are usually one-way — there's no undo if the answer turns out to be "you forfeited the $40 credit and the 12-month clock."

2. Call the issuer and pin down two things, with a case number or rep name you can reference later:
   - "Does converting to the no-fee version count as keeping the existing account open through January 1, 2028, or does it close/terminate the retention agreement?"
   - "If I convert before the 12 months are up, is the $40 statement credit reversed, and over what billing cycle?"
   Verbal "yeah that should be fine" doesn't count — get it in chat, email confirmation, or a case number with notes.

3. The math we did earlier still holds and argues against rushing: keeping the existing card through Jan 2, 2028 nets $293 for the 12 months vs. $276 if you'd downgraded — a $17 swing driven entirely by the $50 transit credit. If your 2028 transit spend will be low enough that the $50 credit would go unused anyway, the calculation flips, but you don't need to decide that today.

4. Your Dec 27, 2027 reminder (event evt_1789580907331) is exactly the right window for this decision — after the 12-month commitment ends Jan 1, before the next $125 fee posts Jan 2. Converting today, Aug 14, is ~4.5 months early and pays you nothing the wait wouldn't pay you better, with the added risk of clawing back the $40 you already earned.

Bottom line: assume the conversion terminates the retention and puts the $40 credit at risk of reversal. Verify in writing with the issuer before you accept, and absent a clear answer that the commitment transfers to the new product, wait until after Jan 1, 2028 to do the downgrade.

Q3 structure confirmed: customer-session totals are reported separately from the operational sub-counts — 4 Harbor Health sessions share the stable release-follow-up identity, 3 Mosaic Commerce sessions share the stable incident-handoff identity. Categorization within the existing two-account read-only boundary, no authorization or safety implication.

EXPLANATION

Two metrics, two counting methods, on purpose.

Customer-session count is traffic. Every authorized session in the reconciled Lantern export — Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce, successful authorization outcome — is one row in the session total. No deduplication at the session layer. The same customer returning three times in a day is three sessions, because each one is an independent interaction with the view.

Operational-use count is occasion-of-decision-support. A release follow-up is not "the customer opened the view"; it is "the view was used to support a specific release." A release has a release identifier. An incident has an incident identifier. The question for the operational-use counter is not "how many sessions touched this" but "how many distinct releases (or incidents) did the view actually support." If four Harbor Health sessions all serve the same release follow-up — same release, same operational window — that is one release follow-up. If three Mosaic Commerce sessions all serve the same incident handoff — same incident, same handoff window — that is one incident handoff.

The split exists because the two metrics answer different questions and conflating them distorts both. Sessions measure surface interaction. Operational use measures whether the view is pulling its weight in real decisions. One release follow-up with eight sessions of digging is more meaningful than eight isolated lookups across unrelated contexts, and the counter has to reflect that.

Identity stability is what makes the dedup defensible. The identity (release tag, incident ID) has to be derivable from evidence outside the session — the release record or the incident record itself — not from session timestamps or session-derived features. Otherwise the dedup becomes a post-hoc grouping that an auditor cannot verify. That is also why the rule cannot ride on session timestamps alone, and why each increment has to be traceable back to a named external handle.


DRAFT — Lantern Evidence-Query Rule: Operational-Use Deduplication

1. Customer-session count is the raw count. Each session in the reconciled Lantern export that carries an authorized tenant identifier (Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce) and a successful authorization outcome contributes exactly one to the customer-session total. No deduplication is applied at this layer.

2. Operational-use count is deduplicated by stable identity. The Harbor Health release-follow-up total and the Mosaic Commerce incident-handoff total do not increment per session. They increment per stable identity, where a stable identity is the underlying release or incident the sessions serve, identified by a durable external handle (release tag, incident identifier, or equivalent).

3. Identity-stability requirement. A stable identity must be derivable from a record outside the session export — for example, a release record from Harbor Health's release pipeline or an incident record from Mosaic Commerce's incident pipeline. Session timestamps, sequence numbers, or other session-derived features do not, on their own, constitute an identity.

4. Window and boundary. Multiple sessions that fall within the same operational window for the same identity count as one. Sessions that fall outside that window, or that serve a different release or incident, count as separate identities even when the tenant is the same.

5. Worked example. Four Harbor Health sessions, all serving the same release follow-up (same release identifier, same follow-up window), contribute four to the customer-session total and one to the Harbor Health release-follow-up total. Three Mosaic Commerce sessions, all serving the same incident handoff (same incident identifier, same handoff window), contribute three to the customer-session total and one to the Mosaic Commerce incident-handoff total.

6. Audit traceability. Each increment of the operational-use total must be traceable to the stable identity that produced it and to the set of sessions that mapped to it. The mapping is retained in the operating-evidence record so reconciliation can verify both totals from the same underlying evidence.

Sunday prep, ~60-75 min start to finish. One cook, three meals, Mon-Thu. Everything fits inside the four-day window without freezing, but rice and a turkey portion can go in the freezer if you'd rather.

PREP SEQUENCE

0:00  Start rice. 1.5 cups dry, rinsed, 3 cups water, pinch salt, covered. Bring to boil, drop to low, 18 min, rest off heat 5 min. Don't peek.
0:05  While water heats: dice 2 bell peppers (half raw, half for sauté), 1 small onion, mince 2-3 garlic cloves.
0:10  Brown turkey. 1 tbsp oil, large pan, turkey in two batches so it sears not steams, ~10 min total. Season last 2 min: 2 tsp cumin, 1 tsp chili powder, 1 tsp smoked paprika, 1 tsp oregano, garlic, salt, pepper. Splash of water if dry. Pull off heat, reserve a small unseasoned portion if Kibo shares protein.
0:20  Sauté peppers + onion. 1 tbsp oil, medium-high, 6-8 min, salt, tender-crisp. Set aside.
0:28  Warm beans. Drain/rinse 1-2 cans, heat with cumin, garlic, salt, splash of water, 5 min. Mash a third for creamier texture.
0:33  Wash and dry spinach. Salad spinner or roll in clean towels. Bag with a dry paper towel.
0:38  Optional: hard-boil 6 eggs (10 min boil, ice bath 5 min). Snacks + meal-2 topping.
0:48  Portion into containers. Wipe counters. Done.

STORAGE PLAN

  Turkey (seasoned): 3-4 sealed portions, fridge 3-4 days. Freeze one if you want a buffer.
  Rice: one large container or 4 portions, fridge 4-6 days. Freeze what you won't reach by Wed.
  Sautéed peppers/onion: container, fridge 4 days.
  Raw peppers (for crunch): separate container or bag, fridge 5 days.
  Beans: 2-3 portions, fridge 4-5 days.
  Spinach: bag with paper towel, fridge 5-7 days.
  Tortillas: original bag or sealed container, room temp or fridge.
  Eggs: fresh in carton; hard-boiled in a separate container if made.

THREE MEALS (same components, three shapes; each 5-10 min to plate)

1.  Turkey tacos or wraps. Warm tortilla (skillet 30 sec or microwave 15). Layer turkey, sautéed peppers, raw peppers, spinach, beans on side or inside. Salsa, hot sauce, or yogurt if you have it. Assembly-only - fastest if you're paged or wiped out.

2.  Rice bowl. Reheat rice + turkey + beans together (microwave 90 sec, or stovetop with a splash of water). Top with raw peppers and spinach; heat wilts the greens. Optional: fried or jammy egg, or sliced hard-boiled egg. Most substantial - the real-dinner option.

3.  Stuffed peppers OR skillet burrito. Either: halve peppers, stuff with rice + turkey + beans + cheese if you have it, bake at 400°F 20-25 min. Or: one-pan skillet - reheat rice/turkey/beans, push to one side, scramble eggs into the other, fold together with raw peppers and spinach. Tortilla on the side to scoop or wrap.

INTERRUPTION FALLBACKS

  Cold plate: rice + turkey + beans + raw peppers + spinach is fine at room temp for 20-30 min. Eat components side by side.
  Devika solo: tacos and bowls are obvious from labeled containers.
  Short on any one component: eggs + tortilla + beans alone = emergency quesadilla or breakfast tacos.
  Skip dinner entirely: fruit, yogurt, eggs, toast covers a true gap.

KIBO
